etymology: Borrowed from English CD.

senses.note: Invariable: i CD. Pronounced 'ci-dì' using the Italian letter names.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English OK.

fact.text: The word came from a joke. Boston newspapers in 1839 used OK for 'oll korrect', a deliberate misspelling of 'all correct'. Now it is used in Italian and around the world.

senses.note: Borrowed from English and very common in speech. Native options: va bene, d'accordo.
Plural doesn't change: gli SMS. In everyday speech people often just say messaggio.
Short for torre in chess notation.
Invariable and feminine: la TV, le TV. Pronounced 'tivù' and sometimes written that way.

etymology: Borrowed from English Wi-Fi.

senses.note: Invariable masculine noun.

etymology: From Latin ac, alternative form of atque (“and, and also; as, then”).

senses.note: Used with cities: vado a Roma. Combines with the article: al, alla, ai, alle.
Used for times and places: a casa, alle otto.

etymology: From Latin ad. In a few phrases, a stems from Latin ā, ab.

senses.note: Merges with articles: al, allo, alla, ai… Used with cities: a Roma. Sometimes ad before a vowel.
For later the same day. Compare 'a presto' (see you soon) and 'a domani' (see you tomorrow).
Used for prices: 20 euro a persona. 'Per persona' is also correct.

etymology:
Literally, “at feet”.
Compare French à pied, Sicilian a pedi, Spanish a pie, Catalan a peu, Portuguese and Galician a pé.

senses.note: Andare a piedi = to walk (somewhere), to go on foot.
Also means 'at this stage' or 'in that case', e.g. 'A questo punto, andiamo.'

etymology: Literally, “at you for you”.

senses.note: Means one-on-one, often privately. 'Faccia a faccia' is a near-synonym.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French abandoner.

fact.text: From Old French abandoner, from the phrase a bandon, 'under someone's control', built on Frankish ban, 'command'. To abandon something was to hand it over to another's power.

senses.note: Also to give up: abbandonare gli studi = to drop out of school.

etymology: From a- + basso (“low”) + -are.

senses.note: Built on basso (low). Abbassare il volume = to turn down the volume.

etymology: Univerbation of a + bastanza (“sufficience”), from the verb bastare (“to suffice”). Cognate with Spanish bastante.

fact.text: Built from a + bastanza, from the verb bastare, 'to be enough'. It's the same verb as the everyday exclamation Basta! = Enough! / Stop!

senses.note: Also 'quite, fairly': abbastanza bene = pretty well. Invariable: abbastanza soldi.

etymology: Univerbation of a + bastanza (“sufficience”), from the verb bastare (“to suffice”). Cognate with Spanish bastante.

fact.text: Built from a + bastanza, from the verb bastare, 'to be enough'. It's the same verb as the everyday exclamation Basta! = Enough! / Stop!

senses.note: Also 'quite, fairly': abbastanza bene = fairly well. Goes before an adjective: abbastanza bravo.

etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from French habillement.

senses.note: Collective noun, as in negozio di abbigliamento (clothes shop). Single clothes are vestiti.

etymology: From abbonare + -mento.

senses.note: Also a travel pass or season ticket: abbonamento mensile = monthly pass.

fact.text: From Latin abundans (overflowing), related to the verb abundare meaning to overflow or abound, ultimately from ab- (from) + unda (wave).

etymology: From a- + braccio (“arm”) + -are, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *adbracchiāre, from Latin ad- + bracchium + -o. Compare Spanish abrazar.

fact.text: Built on braccio 'arm': literally to take someone into your arms. English embrace works the same way, coming via Old French from Latin bracchia 'arms'.

senses.note: Also 'to embrace' an idea or faith. Letters often end with Un abbraccio, 'a hug'.

etymology: Deverbal from abbracciare (“to embrace, hug”) + -o.

fact.text: Built on braccio (arm), from Latin bracchium: a hug is literally taking someone into your arms. English embrace comes from the same Latin root, by way of Old French.

senses.note: Verb: abbracciare. 'Un abbraccio' or 'Abbracci' is a warm sign-off in messages.

etymology: From Latin habilis.

fact.text: From Latin habilis (able to be held or managed), which shares the root with English 'habit'—someone with skill has the habit of doing things well.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin habilitātem.

fact.text: From Latin habilitates. English ability comes from the same Latin root habilitastem.

senses.note: Invariable noun in Italian (abilità), same form singular and plural.

etymology: From abit(are) + -ante.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: l'abitante (m/f).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin habitāre (frequentative of habeō).

fact.text: Comes from Latin habitare, the same source as English inhabit, habitat and inhabitant.

senses.note: Abito a Roma = I live in Rome. Vivere is 'to live' in the sense of being alive.

etymology: From Latin habitātiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin habitātiōnem, from habitāre (to dwell, inhabit). The same root as English habitat and habitual, all meaning to occupy or dwell in a place.

senses.note: Also: residence, house, habitation

etymology: Borrowed from Latin habitus (“habit, appearance”), a noun based on habeō (“have”).

fact.text: From Latin habitus 'condition, dress', the same source as English habit, which can also mean clothing, as in a monk's or nun's habit.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin habituāre.

senses.note: Mostly abituarsi a = to get used to; essere abituato a = to be used to.

etymology: From abituare + -si.

senses.note: Reflexive: followed by 'a' to express accustoming oneself.

etymology: From Late Latin habituātus, perfect passive participle of habituō (“to bring into a condition or habit”), derived from Latin habitus (“habit”). Doublet of habitué.

senses.note: essere abituato a + infinitive: era abituata a vivere = she was used to living.

etymology: Inherited from Latin habitūdinem. By surface analysis, abito + -itudine.

fact.text: From Latin habitudinem. Related to English 'habitual' and 'habitat'—all trace to the Latin habēre (to have, to be in a state).

senses.note: Also: practice, custom, routine.

etymology: From a- + cadere.

fact.text: Built from a- 'to' + cadere 'to fall': something that falls upon you. English 'accident' and 'incident' share the Latin root cadere.

senses.note: Takes essere and is mostly used in the 3rd person: è accaduto = it happened.

etymology: From a- + canto (“corner, side”).

fact.text: Built from a- + canto in its old sense of 'side, corner' (not 'song'), so it literally means 'at the side'.

senses.note: Takes a before a noun: accanto alla porta = next to the door. On its own it means nearby or next door.

etymology: From a- + carezza (“caress”, noun) + -are.

fact.text: Built on carezza (a caress), which comes from caro, 'dear'. English took 'caress' from French caresse, which borrowed it from this same Italian carezza.

senses.note: Also used figuratively: accarezzare un'idea = to toy with an idea.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin accelerāre (“to quicken, hasten, accelerate”), from ad (“to, towards, at”) + celerō (“to quicken”).

fact.text: From Latin accelerāre (ad- 'to' + celerō 'to quicken'). Cognate with English accelerate and celerity.

senses.note: Can be transitive (speed something up) or intransitive (go faster).

etymology: Inherited from Latin accendō, from ad- + candeō.

fact.text: From Latin accendere, ad- + candere 'to glow, shine'. The same root gave Latin candela, which became English candle.

senses.note: Also 'to light' (a fire, a cigarette). Irregular: acceso, accesi. Opposite: spegnere.
From accendere, 'to light'.

etymology: From Latin accentus.

fact.text: Latin accentus comes from ad- + canere 'to sing', a loan translation of Greek prosoidia. An accent was literally the 'song' added to speech.

senses.note: Covers a regional accent, word stress, and the written mark (è, é).

etymology: From Latin accessus.

fact.text: From Latin accessus (approach), the past participle of accēdō (to approach)—also the root of English access and accident.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin acceptāre.

senses.note: Regular -are verb: accetto, accetti, accetta... Past participle: accettato.

fact.text: It is the plural of accidente, which can also mean a sudden stroke or illness. The exclamation comes from curses like 'ti venga un accidente!' (may a stroke hit you!).

senses.note: A mild exclamation of annoyance or surprise, fine in most company.

etymology: Borrowed from Ligurian anciôa, from Vulgar Latin *apiuva, from Latin aphyē, from Ancient Greek ἀφύη (aphúē).

fact.text: From Ligurian anciôa, from Vulgar Latin *apiuva, from Greek aphúē. The word travelled through Mediterranean languages as the fish itself was traded widely.

senses.note: Small fish used in cooking

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *accolligere, derived from Classical Latin ad- + colligere (whence the Italian cogliere).

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin *accolligere: ad- + colligere (whence Italian cogliere, 'to gather'). Literally 'to gather to' or bring together.

senses.note: Transitive; also means to accommodate or receive. Irregular: accolgo, accolse, accolto.

etymology: From Latin accommodāre.

fact.text: You'll hear 'Si accomodi!' all the time. It's the polite way to say 'come in', 'have a seat' or 'make yourself comfortable'.

senses.note: Also 'to take a seat' or 'to come in'. Uses essere: mi sono accomodato.

etymology: From a- + compagno + -are.

fact.text: Built on compagno 'companion', from Late Latin companio, from com 'with' + panis 'bread'. A companion was someone you shared bread with, and English companion has the same origin.

senses.note: Also 'to take' someone somewhere: Ti accompagno a casa, 'I'll take you home'.

etymology: Univerbation of a + conto.

senses.note: Common phrases: versare un acconto (to pay a deposit), in acconto (on account).

etymology: Deverbal from accordare + -o.

fact.text: You'll hear D'accordo! ('Agreed!', 'OK!') constantly. The word comes from accordare, which is traditionally traced to Latin cor 'heart', as in hearts in harmony. It also means a musical chord.

senses.note: d'accordo = agreed/OK; essere d'accordo = to agree.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accorrigere, from Latin ad- + corrigō (“to correct”).

fact.text: From ad- + corrigere (to correct). Evolved from correcting/examining something into noticing it. Literally 'to turn toward.'

senses.note: reflexive; also means 'to realize'

etymology: Deverbal from accusare + -a.

fact.text: From Latin accusare (to call to account), which shares the root with English 'accuse' — both descend from ad- (to) + causa (cause, case).

etymology: From Latin accūsāre.

fact.text: From Latin accūsāre, the same root as English 'accuse', 'accuser', and 'accusation'.

senses.note: Also: blame, experience (pain), indicate, show, confess, acknowledge (receipt).

etymology: From Latin acētum (“vinegar”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin acetum, 'vinegar', which also gave English 'acetic', as in acetic acid, the compound that makes vinegar sour.

senses.note: Aceto balsamico = balsamic vinegar, a speciality of Modena.

etymology: From Latin acidus.

fact.text: From Latin acidus, from acere, 'to be sour'. The same root gave Latin acetum, 'vinegar', which is where English 'acetic' comes from.

senses.note: Also figurative: sour or sharp-tongued. As a noun, l'acido = acid.

etymology: Inherited from Latin aqua.

fact.text: Comes from Latin aqua, as in English 'aquarium' and 'aqueduct'. Italians say 'Acqua in bocca!' (water in the mouth) to mean 'Keep it secret!'.

senses.note: Acqua frizzante / naturale = sparkling / still water. Feminine: l'acqua.

etymology: Literally, “sparkling water”.
Literally, “natural water”.

senses.note: Waiters ask 'Naturale o frizzante?'. Sparkling = frizzante or gassata.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *acquīsītāre, from Latin acquīsītus, ultimately from Latin adquīrere.

fact.text: Ultimately from Latin adquirere (ad + quaerere 'to seek'), the same source as English 'acquire' and 'acquisition'.

senses.note: A bit more formal than 'comprare'. Gli acquisti = shopping, purchases.

etymology: From Latin ad.

senses.note: Form of 'a' used before a vowel, mainly before a-: ad Anna. With other vowels (ad un) it is optional.

etymology: From Latin adaptāre (“to fit, adjust, modify; to adapt, fit or adjust to”).

senses.note: Reflexive adattarsi = to adapt oneself, to fit: 'Non si adatta più' = it doesn't fit any more.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin adaptus, from ad- + aptus (“suitable”).

fact.text: From Medieval Latin adaptus (ad- + aptus: suitable, fit). The root aptus also gives English 'apt' and 'aptitude'. Adatto means literally 'made fit for' or 'adapted to'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin addictus and adapted to native detto.

fact.text: From Latin addictus (assigned, devoted). The same root gives English 'addict'—originally meaning assigned or bound to something.

senses.note: Often used for official roles (e.g., diplomatic attaché, airport employee).

etymology: From a Dio (“to God”), from Medieval Latin ad Deum (“to God”). Compare Aragonese, Asturian, Extremaduran, and Spanish adiós; Catalan adeu; Dutch ajuus; English, French, and Occitan adieu; German tschüss; Greek αντίο (antío); Galician and Portuguese adeus; Maltese addiju; Mirandese adius; Romanian adio; Serbo-Croatian ади̏о/adȉo; Slovene adȋjo.

fact.text: From a Dio ("to God"), reflecting the idea of commending someone to God's care. French adieu, Spanish adiós, and English adieu share the same Latin root ad Deum.

senses.note: Used for a final or long parting. For everyday goodbyes use ciao or arrivederci.

etymology: From a Dio (“to God”), from Medieval Latin ad Deum (“to God”). Compare Aragonese, Asturian, Extremaduran, and Spanish adiós; Catalan adeu; Dutch ajuus; English, French, and Occitan adieu; German tschüss; Greek αντίο (antío); Galician and Portuguese adeus; Maltese addiju; Mirandese adius; Romanian adio; Serbo-Croatian ади̏о/adȉo; Slovene adȋjo.

fact.text: From a Dio ("to God"), reflecting the idea of commending someone to God's care. French adieu, Spanish adiós, and English adieu share the same Latin root ad Deum.
Built on Latin dormire, 'to sleep', the same root as English 'dormitory' and 'dormant'.

senses.note: Reflexive, with essere: mi sono addormentato/a. Also used for a limb going numb.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *addessum. Documented since the late thirteenth century.

fact.text: Comes from Vulgar Latin *addessum, usually traced to ad ipsum (tempus), 'at this very (moment)'. The word has been recorded since the late 1200s.

senses.note: Means the same as ora. Per adesso = for now.

etymology: From Latin adolēscentem.

fact.text: From Latin adolescens, meaning 'growing up'. Related to English 'adolescent' and shares the same Latin root expressing the process of maturation.

etymology: From Latin adulēscentia.
From Late Latin adoperāre, from Latin ad + operāre.

senses.note: Regular verb; archaic intransitive sense 'to act' also exists.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin adōrāre. Cf. the older aorare.

fact.text: From Latin adōrāre, meaning to speak to or pray toward. The prefix ad- (to) + ōrāre (to pray) gives the literal sense of directing prayer toward someone or something worthy of reverence.

senses.note: transitive verb; to regard with deep respect and affection

etymology: From Latin adoptāre.

senses.note: Used both for children and for measures or methods: adottare misure = to take measures.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin adultus.

fact.text: Latin adultus comes from adolescere, 'to grow up', which also gave 'adolescent'. An adult is someone who has grown up, and an adolescent is someone still growing.

senses.note: Also a noun: un adulto, gli adulti. La vita adulta = adult life.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin adultus.

fact.text: Latin adultus comes from adolescere, 'to grow up', which also gave 'adolescent'. An adult is someone who has grown up, and an adolescent is someone still growing.

senses.note: Feminine: l'adulta. It is also an adjective meaning adult or grown-up.

etymology: From Latin āerius.

senses.note: Prendere l'aereo = to take the plane. In aereo = by plane.

etymology: From aero- + porto.
From a (“to”) + fare (“do”), probably based on the model of French affaire. Cognate with Sicilian affari.

fact.text: From a (to) + fare (to do), meaning 'something to do'. English 'affair' comes from French affaire, built the same way from à faire.

senses.note: Also: affair, matter, thing, business (plural).

etymology: From a- + fascino + -are.

fact.text: Fascino comes from Latin fascinum, meaning a spell or the evil eye, and also the phallic charm Romans wore to ward it off. To fascinate was originally to bewitch.

senses.note: Also used for people: to charm. Affascinante = fascinating, charming.

etymology: a- + fatto.

fact.text: Mostly used with negation. As a standalone reply, 'Affatto!' means 'Not at all!'—a common polite refusal or denial.

senses.note: Chiefly used with negation: 'non è affatto vero' (it's not true at all). Alone, means 'Not at all!'

etymology: From Latin affirmāre.

fact.text: From Latin affirmāre. English 'affirm' is cognate—both mean to declare something as true.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin affirmātiōnem (“affirmation, declaration”), derived from affirmō (“to affirm, assert”).

senses.note: Can also mean assertion, claim, or affirmation.

etymology: From affettare.

fact.text: Literally means 'sliced things', from affettare (to slice). It's used as a noun for the charcuterie platter or selection.

senses.note: Sliced charcuterie like salami; often used in plural.

etymology: From Latin affectus (noun).

senses.note: Con affetto = with love (a letter sign-off).

etymology: From Late Latin affectuōsus.

senses.note: Common letter sign-off: Un saluto affettuoso / Affettuosi saluti.

etymology:
Univerbation of a + fin(o) + che.
Compare similar constructions with French afin que, Spanish a fin de que and Portuguese a fim de que.

fact.text: Univerbation (combining) of a + fino + che. Similar structures exist in French (afin que), Spanish (a fin de que), and Portuguese (a fim de que), showing a Romance language pattern.

senses.note: Conjunction expressing purpose; requires subjunctive mood.

etymology: From Medieval Latin affictāre, itself from fictus.

fact.text: From Medieval Latin affictāre, derived from fictus (fixed, agreed upon), reflecting the fixed agreement between landlord and tenant.

senses.note: Can mean either renting out (as landlord) or renting (as tenant); context matters.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin affictum, deverbal from affictāre.

fact.text: From Medieval Latin affictum, from affictare, which goes back to Latin figere, 'to fix'. So rent was originally a fixed, agreed payment.

senses.note: In affitto = for rent. Affittare covers both 'to rent' and 'to let'.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *affrontāre, from Latin ad- + frons + -āre. By surface analysis, a- + fronte + -are.

fact.text: Built from fronte (forehead, front): to meet something head-on. From Vulgar Latin affrontāre (ad- + frons + -āre). Not to be confused with English 'affront,' which means to insult.
Agenda in Italian means diary or planner, not a meeting agenda. For a list of topics, Italians say ordine del giorno.

senses.note: Also means planner or daily schedule.

etymology: From Latin agentem.
Derived from Medieval Latin agentia.

senses.note: Agenzia di viaggi = travel agency. Also used for a bank's branch office.

etymology: From Late Latin adiectīvum [nōmen], translation of Ancient Greek ἐπίθετον [ὄνομα] (epítheton [ónoma]).

fact.text: Late Latin adiectivum translates Greek epitheton, roughly 'something added on'. An adjective is a word added to a noun. The Greek word also gave English 'epithet'.

etymology: From Latin adiungere (“add, join to”).

fact.text: From Latin adiungere, 'to join to', from iungere, 'to join'. It's related to English 'join', 'junction' and 'adjunct'.

senses.note: Irregular: aggiunsi (passato remoto), aggiunto (past participle).

etymology: From a- (“to”) + giusto (“just”, “right”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).

fact.text: Built from a- + giusto 'right', so it literally means 'to make right'. It looks like English 'adjust', but in everyday Italian it usually means to repair something.

senses.note: Everyday word for fixing things: aggiustare la bici. Riparare is a more formal synonym.

etymology: From Latin aggredior, from ad- (“towards”) + gradior (“to walk”).

Borrowed from Old Occitan aize, from Vulgar Latin *adjace(m), from Latin adjacēns, present participle of adjaceō (compare Medieval Latin in aiace). Cognate with Old French aise, eise, French aise and aisance; compare also Catalan eina. Doublet of adiacente.

fact.text: From Old Occitan aize, via Vulgar Latin. Cognate with Old French aise, and distantly related to English "easy" through Proto-Indo-European roots.

senses.note: Also: comfort or luxury; often in phrase 'con agio' (comfortably).

etymology: Borrowed from French agir, itself borrowed from Latin agere.
Inherited from Latin ālium.

senses.note: A clove of garlic = uno spicchio d'aglio. Plural: agli.

etymology: From Latin agnellus, diminutive of agnus. Cognates include Catalan anyell, French agneau and Romanian miel.

fact.text: From Latin agnellus (diminutive of agnus). Cognates appear across Romance: French agneau, Catalan anyell. All trace back to the same ancient Latin root for lamb.

etymology: From earlier aco, from Latin acus (“needle”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”). Compare Romanian ac.

fact.text: Comes from Latin acus (needle), the same word inside English acupuncture, which literally means needle-pricking.

senses.note: Plural aghi. Also a pine needle or a compass needle.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin agustus, from Latin augustus. Doublet of Augusto.

fact.text: Named after Emperor Augustus. The 15 August holiday, Ferragosto, comes from Latin Feriae Augusti, 'the festivals of Augustus'.

senses.note: Months are written in lower case in Italian: ad agosto = in August.

etymology: From Latin agricola (“farmer”).

fact.text: Latin agricola 'farmer' (ager 'field' + colere 'to farm') is the classic first Latin noun in textbooks: a masculine word that looks feminine.

senses.note: Feminine of agricolo: case agricole = farms. Farmer is agricoltore or contadino.

etymology: From Latin agricultūra.

fact.text: From Latin agricultūra, from ager (field) + cultūra (cultivation). English shares the same word path, making it a true cognate with a transparent root meaning 'field-working'.

etymology: From agri- + turismo.

fact.text: An Italian concept and term that became common in the late 20th century as rural tourism grew, now widely adopted internationally.

senses.note: Tourism that includes farm lodging or rural experiences.
Contraction of a + i, used before masculine plural nouns: ai pascoli, ai bambini.

etymology: Inherited from Latin adiūtāre. The archaic aggiutare represents the expected outcome in Italian. The modern form may reflect influence from central or southern Italo-Romance (cf. Sicilian ajutari), where in many places /-j-/ would be the regular outcome.

fact.text: From Latin adiutare, 'to help'. The same verb gave English 'aid' (through French) and 'adjutant', an officer who assists a commander.

senses.note: Takes a direct object: aiutare qualcuno a fare qualcosa. Aiuto! = Help!

etymology: From Late Latin adiūtus.

fact.text: From Latin adiutare 'to help' (via Late Latin adiutus). The same verb gave English aid, through Old French, and adjutant, an officer who assists a commander.

senses.note: A cry for help. As a noun, l'aiuto = help or assistance; the verb is aiutare.

etymology: From Late Latin adiūtus.

fact.text: From Latin adiutare 'to help' (via Late Latin adiutus). The same verb gave English aid, through Old French, and adjutant, an officer who assists a commander.

senses.note: Aiuto! = Help! Can also mean an assistant (aiuto regista = assistant director).
a + il. Used before masculine singular nouns: al mare, al cinema. Come al solito = as usual.
Price/weight measurement; 'a chilo' variant exists

etymology: From Latin āla.

fact.text: Latin ala also meant 'armpit'. Its diminutive, axilla, gives the medical word axilla, which English still uses for the armpit.

senses.note: Feminine: l'ala, le ali. In football it also means a winger.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *alba, from Latin albus (“white”). Compare French aube.

fact.text: From Latin alba, 'white', after the pale light of daybreak. The same root appears in English 'albino' and 'album'.

senses.note: all'alba = at dawn. Do not confuse with tramonto (sunset).

etymology: From Medieval Latin alberga, from Proto-West Germanic *harjabergu.

fact.text: From a Germanic compound meaning 'army shelter'. English 'harbour' comes from the same compound (Old English herebeorg), and so does French 'auberge' (inn).

senses.note: Hotel is also common in Italian. Plural alberghi.

etymology: From older alboro m (via dissimilation), from albore m (via masculinization of the ending), from Latin arborem f.

fact.text: From Latin arbor, with the first r changed to l. It shares a root with English arbor and arboretum.

senses.note: Also means a ship's mast and, in mechanics, a shaft.
Containing or relating to alcohol.
Usually used in the plural (gli alcolici).

etymology:
From Vulgar Latin *alicūnus, from Classical Latin aliquem (“someone, something”) + ūnum (“one”).
Cognate with French aucun, Spanish alguno, Galician algún, Portuguese algum.

fact.text: From Latin aliquis (someone) + unus (one). French aucun, from the same root, has gone all the way to meaning 'none', since it is used so often after a negative.

senses.note: Non c'è alcun problema = there's no problem at all. Plural alcuni/alcune = some, a few.

fact.text: From Latin aliquis (someone) + unus (one). French aucun, from the same root, has gone all the way to meaning 'none', since it is used so often after a negative.

senses.note: Plural alcuni/alcune = some, a few. In the singular it means 'any/no' in negatives: senza alcun dubbio.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin alphabētum, from Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos), from alpha and beta (the first two letters of the Greek alphabet), from Phoenician 𐤀 (ʾ /⁠aleph⁠/, “ox”) and 𐤁 (b /⁠beth⁠/, “house”), so called because they were pictograms of those objects.

fact.text: Named after the Greek letters alpha and beta, which come from Phoenician aleph (ox) and beth (house), letters that started out as pictures of those things.

senses.note: The Italian alphabet has 21 native letters. J, K, W, X and Y appear only in foreign words.

etymology: From Latin aliēnus.

fact.text: Same root as English alien: both from Latin aliēnus, meaning foreign or strange.

senses.note: Short for 'negozio di alimentari'; invariable: l'alimentari, gli alimentari.
Usually plural: gli alimentari, or 'generi alimentari'.

etymology: From alimentare + -zione.

senses.note: a + la. Alla fine = in the end; also 'in the style of': alla romana = Roman-style.

etymology: Univerbation of all' (“to the”) + arme (“weapons”, archaic plural of arma), literally “to the weapons, to arms”.

fact.text: From the Italian cry 'all'arme!' (to the weapons!), a call to arms that entered English via French as alarm. The univerbation of all' (to the) + arme (weapons) literally means to take up arms.

etymology: Borrowed from French allègre, from Latin alacer (“lively; happy, cheerful”). Compare the doublet alacre.

fact.text: You may know this from music: allegro marks a fast, lively tempo. The musical sense comes straight from the everyday meaning, 'cheerful'.

senses.note: Describes people, moods, music and colours.

etymology: From a- (“to, towards”) + lena (“energy, vigour”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).

fact.text: Formed from a- 'to' + lena, 'vigour, stamina'. Training literally means building up your energy. Lena is still used in phrases like lavorare di lena, 'to work hard'.

senses.note: allenarsi = to train or work out (mi alleno). allenatore = coach.

etymology: Borrowed from German Allergie, coinage crafted using Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work, activity”).

fact.text: From German Allergie, which combines Greek állos (other) and érgon (work/activity). The English word allergy shares the same root.

etymology: From allergia + -ico.

senses.note: Takes a: sono allergico alle noci = I'm allergic to nuts.

etymology: Inherited from Latin allevāre (“to lift up, alleviate”).

fact.text: From Latin allevare (to lift up, to lighten), the same source as English 'alleviate'. But careful: 'to alleviate' in Italian is alleviare, not allevare.

senses.note: Also to bring up children. Allevamento = animal farm or breeding.

etymology: From a- + loggia + -are.

fact.text: From a- + loggia (loggia being a covered gallery or arcade in Italian architecture). The word ultimately relates to how a loggia provides shelter—alloggiare means to provide that same shelter to a person.

senses.note: Can be transitive (accommodate guests) or intransitive with 'a' (lodge at a place)

etymology: Deverbal from alloggiare + -o.

fact.text: The related verb alloggiare goes back to the same Old French loge, meaning a hut or shelter, that gave English lodge and lodging.

senses.note: vitto e alloggio = room and board

etymology: From a- + lontano + -are.

senses.note: Reflexive verb; often with prepositions (da, per).

etymology:
Inherited from Latin ad illam hōram (“at that hour”).
Compare French alors, Occitan alara, Spanish alora, and Catalan aleshores.
By surface analysis, all' + ora.

fact.text: From Latin ad illam horam, 'at that hour'. It means 'then' in time, and also 'so' or 'well then' in conversation. French alors has the same origin.

senses.note: Also a very common conversation opener or filler: 'so…', 'well then…'

etymology:
Univerbation of al + meno, literally, “at the least”.
Compare Spanish al menos, Portuguese ao menos, French au moins, Catalan almenys.

senses.note: Same form for m/f: un alpinista, un'alpinista. Plurals: alpinisti (m), alpiniste (f).

etymology: From Latin Alpīnus.

fact.text: The Alpini, founded in 1872, are often called the oldest active mountain infantry in the world. They are known for their felt hat with a single black feather.

senses.note: As a noun, un alpino is a soldier in the Alpini, Italy's mountain troops.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin altitia, from Latin altus (“high”). Compare Portuguese and Spanish alteza, Catalan altesa. By surface analysis, alto (“high”) + -ezza.

fact.text: Also a royal title: Sua Altezza means 'Your Highness'. Like the English title, it is built on the word for 'high' (Latin altus).

senses.note: Also altitude; Sua Altezza = Your Highness.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin altitūdinem.

senses.note: In everyday speech, quota is common: ad alta quota (at high altitude).

etymology: From Latin altus (“high”), from Proto-Italic *altos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eltós, derived from the root *h₂el- (“to grow, nourish”). Cognate with English old and Welsh allt.

fact.text: This has nothing to do with Latin altus 'high'. It comes from the German military command halt, 'stop!', which is also where English halt comes from. It only looks like alto 'high' by coincidence.

senses.note: Means tall for people and high for things. The opposite is basso. Also means loud: a voce alta.

fact.text: Used as a standalone reply meaning 'same to you'—answer 'Altrettanto!' to 'Buon appetito!' or 'Buona giornata!'

senses.note: Often used as a polite reply: 'Grazie, altrettanto!' (Thanks, same to you!)

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin alterā mente. Documented since the thirteenth century.

fact.text: From Early Medieval Latin 'alterā mente' (with different mind). Documented since the 13th century. The compound structure literally means 'in another way/mind'.

senses.note: Or else; used to introduce an alternative consequence.

fact.text: From Latin alter (the other of two). English words alter, alternate, and alternative share this root, all stemming from the ancient concept of choosing between two options.

senses.note: d'altra parte = on the other hand. Un altro = another. Agrees: altra, altri, altre.

etymology: Inherited from Latin alterum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élteros.

fact.text: From Latin alter (the other of two). English words alter, alternate, and alternative share this root, all stemming from the ancient concept of choosing between two options.

senses.note: Used as determiner before nouns: un altro libro (another book)

etymology: Inherited from Latin alterum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élteros.

fact.text: From Latin alter (the other of two). English words alter, alternate, and alternative share this root, all stemming from the ancient concept of choosing between two options.

senses.note: un altro / un'altra = another; gli altri = the others. Often used before a noun: un altro biscotto.

etymology: From Latin aliter ubī. By surface analysis, univerbation of altro + ove.
From Vulgar Latin *altiāre, derived from Latin altus (“high”).

fact.text: From Latin altus, 'high', the same root as English altitude and alto.

senses.note: Reflexive alzarsi = to get up / stand up.
Also means to stand up. Mi alzo alle sette = I get up at seven.

etymology: Inherited from Latin amantem.

fact.text: When standing alone, amante usually means a lover in romantic/illicit sense. To say music lover, use amante della musica—'di' changes the meaning frame.

senses.note: Often implies an affair; use 'amante di' (music lover) when meaning enthusiast

etymology: Inherited from Latin amāre.

fact.text: Italians usually keep 'ti amo' for a romantic partner. Saying it to a friend or parent sounds odd. For them the phrase is 'ti voglio bene', literally 'I want good for you'.

senses.note: Ti amo is for romantic love. For family and friends, Italians say ti voglio bene.

etymology: From Latin amārus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₃mós (“bitter, raw”).

fact.text: Italian amaro is a herbal digestif traditionally served after dinner. Brands like Montenegro and Averna are iconic; each region has its own local varieties.

senses.note: Caffè amaro = coffee without sugar.

etymology: From Latin amārus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₃mós (“bitter, raw”).

fact.text: Italian amaro is a herbal digestif traditionally served after dinner. Brands like Montenegro and Averna are iconic; each region has its own local varieties.

senses.note: Often drunk after meals to aid digestion.

etymology: Old Italian, from Old Occitan ambaissada, from Gaulish ambaxtos.

fact.text: It goes back via Old Occitan to the Gaulish ambaxtos, meaning a servant or vassal. English 'embassy' and 'ambassador' come from the same Celtic source.

senses.note: Feminine. The ambassador is l'ambasciatore. In older or literary use it can also mean a message.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ambientem, present active participle of ambiō (“surround”).

fact.text: From Latin ambiens, 'going around, surrounding', from ambire. That verb also gave English ambient and ambition, which first meant going around asking for votes.

senses.note: Masculine: l'ambiente, gli ambienti. In property ads it means room: trilocale = 3 ambienti.

fact.text: From French ambulance, short for hôpital ambulant, a 'walking' field hospital that moved with an army. It comes from Latin ambulare 'to walk', like English amble.

senses.note: Feminine: l'ambulanza, le ambulanze. In Italy you call one on 118 (or the EU number 112).

etymology: From Latin ambulātōrius.

fact.text: From Latin ambulatorius, 'to do with walking'. Patients walk in and out again, which is why English medicine speaks of 'ambulatory care'.

senses.note: A doctor's surgery or an outpatient department. Not an ambulance (ambulanza).

etymology: From America + -ano.

fact.text: In an Italian bar, ordering 'un americano' gets you an espresso topped up with hot water, a nod to the longer, weaker coffee Americans are said to prefer.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian: la letteratura americana.

etymology: From Latin amīca (“friend”).

senses.note: 'La mia amica' usually just means a friend; for a girlfriend, Italians usually say 'la mia ragazza'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin amicitia.

senses.note: Fare amicizia (con) = to make friends (with).

etymology: From Latin amīcus. Compare Catalan amic, French ami, Portuguese amigo, Romanian amic, Sardinian amícu, Spanish amigo.

fact.text: From Latin amicus 'friend', related to amare 'to love'. English amicable shares the root, and enemy comes from Latin inimicus, literally 'not a friend'.

senses.note: Plural amici. A female friend is amica (plural amiche).

fact.text: Built on malato (ill), which comes from Latin male habitus, 'in poor condition'. Falling ill is literally becoming 'badly kept'.

senses.note: Reflexive and takes essere: mi sono ammalato/a = I got sick.

etymology: Probably from a- + mazza (“club, baton”) + -are, or alternatively possibly related to Latin mactāre, through a Vulgar Latin root *mactiāre, although this is less likely. Compare Sicilian ammazzari, Spanish mazar, Portuguese maçar, Occitan massar, Romansh mazzar, Venetan masar, Friulian maçâ, Istriot masà. See also archaic Italian mattare.

fact.text: Built on mazza (club or mace), so originally meant to strike someone down with a club. Mazza and English 'mace' share the same root.

etymology: Inherited from Latin admittere. By surface analysis, a- + mettere.

fact.text: From Latin admittere (ad- + mittere, to send). The root also gives English 'admit' and 'mission'—both share the idea of letting something in or go forward.

etymology: From Latin administrātor.

fact.text: From Latin administrātor. Shares its root with English 'administer' and 'administrator'—both from Latin ad- + ministrāre (to serve).

senses.note: May be feminine (amministratrice) or masculine; refers to manager or officer.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin admirāri.

fact.text: From Latin admīrāri (ad- + mīrārī 'to wonder at'). Related to Latin mīrus (wonderful). English 'admire' and Italian ammirare follow the same path.

senses.note: Transitive; to regard with wonder or appreciation.
Typical of rentals: appartamento ammobiliato = furnished flat. Related to mobile/mobili = furniture.

etymology: Inherited from Latin amōrem.

senses.note: Masculine. Amore mio = my love, a common term of endearment.

etymology: Inherited from Latin amplus.

fact.text: From Latin amplus, possibly connected to 'grab' or 'seize' (h₃emh₃-), making the etymological sense 'graspable'. The same Latin root appears in English 'ample'.

senses.note: Usually plural in Italian.

etymology: From ana- + alcolico.
From Medieval Latin analysis, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλυσις (análusis).

senses.note: The plural is unchanged (le analisi). Analisi del sangue = blood test.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin anatomia.

fact.text: From Ancient Greek ana- (up/apart) + témnō (to cut): 'cutting up'. The same Greek roots gave English 'anatomy', revealing the surgical origins of both terms.
Built from 'anche' (also) + 'io' (I). English speakers recognize the same structure: 'also I' → 'me too'. Common in everyday speech across all Italian regions.

senses.note: emphatic reply to someone else's statement; literally 'also I'

etymology: Assuming that anco represents the original form, likely a rebracketing of ancora as anc'ora. A borrowing from Old Occitan ancui (“on this day”) has also been suggested, but this would explain neither the stress position of anche, nor the lack of a final -ui (an acceptable ending in Italian; cf. lui).

senses.note: Goes right before the word it refers to: anche io = me too. Can also mean 'even'.
Goes before the word it refers to: anch'io = me too. Also means 'even': anche se = even if.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *hancōra, probably from Late Latin in hanc hōram (“until this hour”). Compare French encore, Occitan and Catalan encara.

fact.text: Where the stress falls changes the meaning: ancóra means still or again, while àncora, stressed on the first syllable, means a ship's anchor.

senses.note: Non ancora = not yet. Stressed on the second syllable: an-CÓ-ra.
Ancora una volta = once again. Ancora? can also mean 'more?'

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin andāre, of uncertain origin, with suppletion from vādō.

fact.text: Two verbs in one: vado, vai, va come from Latin vadere 'to go' (as in English invade and evade), while the origin of andare itself is still debated.

senses.note: Irregular: vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno. Takes essere in compound tenses.
Takes essere: è andato via. The imperative 'vai via!' means 'go away!'.

etymology:
From andarsi + -ne.
Compare French s'en aller, Catalan anar-se'n and to a lesser extent Spanish irse and andarse.

senses.note: Me ne vado = I'm leaving. Vattene! = Go away! Takes essere.

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of andare.

senses.note: Biglietto di sola andata = one-way ticket; andata e ritorno = return/round trip.
Un biglietto di andata e ritorno = a return ticket. Solo andata = one way.

etymology: Inherited from Latin ānellus, diminutive of ānus (“circle”). Compare Catalan anell, French anneau, Portuguese anel, Spanish anillo.

fact.text: From Latin anellus, a little ring, a diminutive built on anus 'circle'. Its sister form anulus gives English annular, as in an annular eclipse, when a ring of sun stays visible.

senses.note: Also a link in a chain. Anello di fidanzamento = engagement ring.

etymology: Inherited from Latin angelus, from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos).

fact.text: From Greek angelos, meaning simply 'messenger'. Angels were God's messengers, and the same root appears in evangelo (good news, literally 'good message').

etymology: Borrowed from Latin angulus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂engulos (“joint?”), from *h₂eng-, *ang- (“corner, hirn”).

senses.note: Also 'angle' in geometry. All'angolo = on the corner.

etymology: Derived from Ancient Greek ἀγγούριον (angoúrion) (plural ἀγγούρια (angoúria)). Probably originally meaning “cucumber”.

fact.text: From Ancient Greek angoúrion. Originally meant cucumber; the word travelled through medieval Italian to mean the larger melon we know today.

etymology: From Latin anima, from animus, from Proto-Italic *anamos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁mos, a nominal derivative of *h₂enh₁- (“breathe”). Doublet of alma.

fact.text: From Latin anima (breath, life force), root of English animate and animal—creatures literally defined as beings that breathe.

etymology: From Latin animālem, possibly borrowed.

fact.text: From Latin animal, built on anima, 'breath, soul'. An animal was literally 'a thing that breathes', a living creature.

senses.note: Masculine: l'animale, gli animali.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin anniversārius.

fact.text: From Latin anniversārius (yearly). English "anniversary" is borrowed directly from the same Latin root: annus (year) + versārius (turning).

senses.note: Masculine. Plural: anniversari. From Latin anniversārius (annual, yearly).

etymology: Inherited from Latin annus, from Proto-Italic *atnos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂et-no-, probably from *h₂et- (“to go”).

fact.text: Make sure to pronounce the double n. Said with a single n, ano means anus, so buon anno (happy new year) can turn into an embarrassing slip.

senses.note: L'anno scorso = last year; l'anno prossimo = next year. Avere 20 anni = to be 20.

fact.text: It shares a root with English 'annoy': both go back to Latin 'in odio', 'in hatred', via Late Latin inodiare. But in Italian it means getting bored, not getting irritated.

senses.note: Takes essere: mi sono annoiato. It does NOT mean 'to get annoyed' (that is irritarsi).

etymology: From annoiare.

fact.text: False friend: this means bored, not annoyed (that is infastidito or seccato). Both annoiare and English 'annoy' come from the Latin phrase in odio, 'in hatred'.

senses.note: Past participle of annoiare. Sono annoiato = I'm bored. Annoying = fastidioso.

etymology: From Latin adnuere, annuere.

fact.text: From Latin annuere, 'to nod toward'. The same root gave Latin numen, a god's nod or will, which is where English 'numinous' comes from.

senses.note: -isc- verb: annuisco, annuisci. Usually used on its own: annuì = he nodded.

etymology: From Latin annullāre.

fact.text: From Latin annullāre, meaning to nullify or make void—the same root as English 'annul'.

etymology: In the sense "act of announcing", deverbal from annunciare + -o. In the concrete senses, borrowed from Late Latin annūntium, from Latin ad- + nūntium (“notice, announcement”).

fact.text: It goes back to Latin nuntius, 'messenger, news', the same root as English 'announce' and 'nuncio', the Pope's ambassador.

senses.note: Also means an ad: 'annunci di lavoro' = job ads. Plural: gli annunci.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin anxia, derived from Classical Latin anxius (“anxious”).

senses.note: essere in ansia = to be worried; mettere ansia = to make someone anxious.

etymology: From Latin anxiōsus.

senses.note: Ansioso di + infinitive = eager to: ansioso di partire = eager to leave.

etymology: From Medieval Latin antenātus.

fact.text: From Medieval Latin antenatus, literally 'born before' (ante + natus), which is exactly what an ancestor is.

senses.note: Usually plural: i miei antenati = my ancestors.

etymology: Deverbal from anticipare + -o.

fact.text: Very common in the phrase 'in anticipo', meaning early: 'Sono arrivato in anticipo' (I arrived early). The opposite is 'in ritardo' (late).

senses.note: Also a deposit or down payment. In anticipo = early.

etymology: Inherited from Latin antīquus (“ancient”).

senses.note: Plurals antichi, antiche. Also means antique or old-fashioned.

etymology: From anti- (“prior to, before”) + pasto (“meal”).

fact.text: Nothing to do with pasta and not 'against' anything: anti- here means 'before' (like ante-), and pasto means 'meal', so it is the bit that comes before the meal.

senses.note: The course before the first course (primo). Beware: in US English, entrée means the main course.

etymology: From antipatia + -ico.

senses.note: The opposite of simpatico. Mi è antipatico = I don't like him.

etymology: Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *anteānus. Documented from the thirteenth century.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin anteanus, 'one who came before', built on Latin ante, 'before'. English 'ancient' comes from the same word through Old French ancien.

senses.note: Also a noun: un anziano, an elderly man; gli anziani, the elderly. More polite than vecchio.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin aperītīvus, from Late Latin apertīvus, from Latin aperiō, and partly from French apéritif.

fact.text: From Latin aperire, 'to open', which also gave Italian aprire: an aperitif opens the appetite. In Italy, aperitivo is also an early-evening ritual of drinks with snacks.

senses.note: Also the pre-dinner drinks-and-snacks ritual: andiamo a fare l'aperitivo.

etymology: Borrowed from Spanish apartamiento and adapted to appartare.

fact.text: Linked to appartare, 'to set apart': an apartment was a set of rooms set apart for one person. English got the word through French appartement, which comes from Italian.

senses.note: British English: flat. Often shortened to appartamento in ads as 'app.'

etymology: From Late Latin appertinēre, from Latin pertinēre; influenced by pars (“part”). Compare English appertain.

fact.text: Related to English 'appertain' (from Late Latin appertinēre). Both verbs mean to belong or pertain to.

senses.note: Intransitive; usually followed by 'a' (to belong to). Related: appertain.

etymology: From appassionare.

fact.text: It is also a music marking meaning 'with passion'. Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 23 is known as the 'Appassionata', a nickname given by a publisher after his death.

senses.note: Appassionato di = keen on, a fan of: appassionato di calcio = football enthusiast.

etymology:
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ad poenam.
By surface analysis, univerbation of a + pena (“pain, trouble”).
Compare French à peine, Spanish apenas, etc.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin *ad poenam, 'with pain/trouble', like French à peine and Spanish apenas. Doing something 'with difficulty' came to mean 'barely', and then 'just'.

senses.note: Goes before the past participle: siamo appena arrivati. Also means 'barely' or 'as soon as'.

etymology: From Latin appendere.

fact.text: From Latin appendere 'to hang on, weigh', the source of English append; an appendix is literally something hung onto the end.

senses.note: Past participle appeso. appendere le scarpe al chiodo = to retire (lit. hang up one's shoes).

etymology: From Latin appetītus.

fact.text: Italians say 'Buon appetito!' before a meal, and the usual reply is 'Grazie, altrettanto' (thanks, same to you).

senses.note: Buon appetito! = Enjoy your meal!

etymology: From Late Latin appretiāre, from Latin pretium.

fact.text: From Late Latin appretiāre, derived from Latin pretium (price). English 'appreciate' shares the same Latin root.

etymology: From a- + profitto + -are. Compare Portuguese aproveitar, Spanish aprovechar.

senses.note: approfittare di qualcosa = to make the most of something; approfittarsi di qualcuno = to exploit someone
Also a romantic date. Prendere un appuntamento = to make an appointment.

etymology: Deverbal from appuntare + -o.

fact.text: The same word is also a noun, 'un appunto', meaning a note. Students 'prendono appunti': they take notes in class.

senses.note: Mostly plural: prendere appunti = to take notes.

etymology: From Latin Aprīlis.

senses.note: Months are lowercase in Italian: 'ad aprile' = in April.

etymology: From Latin aperīre. Compare Sicilian ràpiri.

fact.text: Comes from Latin aperire, 'to open', which also gave English 'aperture', the opening in a camera lens. Italian 'aperitivo' has the same root: a drink that 'opens' the appetite.

senses.note: Irregular past participle: aperto (ho aperto la porta).

etymology: From Latin aquila.

fact.text: English 'aquiline' (eagle-like, as in a hooked nose) comes from the same Latin aquila. The word may come from aquilus, 'dark', making it the 'dark bird'.

senses.note: Always feminine, even for a male eagle: l'aquila, un'aquila.

etymology: Feminine form of arancio (“orange (tree)”), from Arabic نَارَنْج (nāranj), from Persian نارنگ (nârang), from Sanskrit नारङ्ग (nāraṅga).

fact.text: Shares its root with English 'orange': Arabic naranj, from Persian and Sanskrit. Both words lost the first n, which got absorbed into the article ('a norange' became 'an orange').

senses.note: The tree is 'l'arancio' (masculine). The colour is 'arancione'.

etymology: From arancia + -ata.

fact.text: From arancia (orange) plus the diminutive suffix -ata, literally meaning a drink made from oranges, similar to how limonata is made from lemons.

senses.note: The fruit is l'arancia. Some speakers keep the colour unchanged in the plural, but arancioni is standard.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ārea. Doublet of aia (“threshing floor”).

fact.text: Latin ārea first meant a level open space such as a threshing floor. Italian also inherited the word the everyday way, as aia ('threshing floor'), so the two words are twins.

senses.note: L'area circostante = the surrounding area. Also used for a field or sector (area commerciale).

etymology: From argento (“silver”) + -ina.

fact.text: From argento (silver), with feminine suffix -ina. The country's name reflects the Spanish conquistadors' initial hopes of finding silver; the fish argentina is also named for its silvery appearance.

senses.note: Proper noun; also refers to young eels or a type of fish.

etymology: From Latin argentum, from Proto-Italic *argentom. See also the obsolete variant form ariento, possibly from a Vulgar Latin *aregentum; cf. also Old Galician-Portuguese and Old Spanish arento, Spanish arienzo.

fact.text: It comes from Latin argentum, which gives silver its chemical symbol, Ag. Argentina, 'land of silver', was named after the precious metal early explorers hoped to find there.

senses.note: D'argento = made of silver. Silverware is l'argenteria.

etymology: Inherited from Latin argilla.

fact.text: It goes back to Greek árgillos, 'white clay, potter's earth'. This possibly comes from argós, 'white, shining', from the same root as Latin argentum, 'silver'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin argūmentum.

fact.text: Unlike English 'argument' (a quarrel), argomento means a topic, subject, or reason. A fight or quarrel is 'litigio' or 'discussione'.

senses.note: False friend: means topic or subject, not a quarrel (litigio).

etymology: Metathesis from Latin āera, Greek-type accusative of āēr, from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”). See also aere.

fact.text: English borrowed 'aria' (an opera solo) from this word, via its sense of 'tune'. Italian also uses it for someone's look: 'avere l'aria stanca' means to look tired.

senses.note: All'aria aperta = outdoors. Avere l'aria + adjective = to look (tired, happy...).

etymology: From Late Latin arma (“weapon”), from Latin arma (“defensive arms, weapons of war, war, defense, tools”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)rmos (“fitting”), from the root *h₂er- (“to join”).

fact.text: Feminine in singular (l'arma) but takes the regular feminine plural armi. Phrase 'alle armi!' means 'to arms!'

senses.note: Feminine singular (l'arma) but plural is le armi, not le arme.

etymology: From the older armario, borrowed from Latin armārium.

fact.text: From Latin armarium, a chest or cupboard for arma (tools, weapons). The same Latin word gave French 'armoire', which English borrowed.

senses.note: Also closet or cupboard. Armadio a muro = built-in wardrobe.

etymology: From Latin armāre.
Borrowed from Latin harmonia, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̔ρμονῐ́ᾱ (hărmonĭ́ā).

fact.text: Comes from Latin harmonia, borrowed from Ancient Greek harmonia (harmonia), literally meaning a joining or fitting together. The Greek root relates to joining and arrangement.

etymology: From a- + rabbia (“rabies; anger”) + -are.
From arrabbiare + -si.

fact.text: Built on rabbia (anger), from Latin rabies, 'madness, rage'. That is also the source of English rabies, so getting angry is literally 'becoming rabid'.

senses.note: Takes essere: mi sono arrabbiato. arrabbiarsi con qualcuno = to get angry with someone.

etymology: From arrabbiare, from rabbia.

fact.text: Comes from rabbia, which means both 'rage' and 'rabies'. Penne all'arrabbiata are 'angry' penne, named for their fiery chilli sauce.

senses.note: arrabbiato con qualcuno = angry with someone. For animals it means rabid.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arrestāre, from Latin ad- (“to”) + restō, restāre (“stop, remain behind, stay back”).

fact.text: From Latin ad- (to) + restare (to stop, remain). English arrest shares the same Latin root via Old French, making these true cognates.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin adrīpāre, perhaps influenced from Gallo-Italic or Old French in comparison to arripare. By surface analysis, a- + riva (“shore”) + -are.

fact.text: From Late Latin adripare, 'to come to the shore' (ad + ripa, 'bank, shore'). Arriving first meant landing a boat, and English arrive comes from the same source via French.

senses.note: Takes essere: sono arrivato/a. Also 'to reach': arrivare a Roma.

etymology:
Univerbation of a (“to”) + rivederci (“seeing ourselves again”). Compare French au revoir, Romanian la revedere, Catalan a reveure and Spanish hasta la vista.
Compare also parallel and more distant cognates Bulgarian довиждане (doviždane) and Russian до свида́ния (do svidánija) (both related to Proto-Slavic *viděti (+ Proto-Slavic *do)), Ukrainian до побачення (do pobačennja), Polish do zobaczenia, and Arabic إلى اللقاء.

fact.text: Literally 'until we see each other again' (a + rivedere + ci), the same idea as French au revoir and German auf Wiedersehen.

senses.note: Neutral or polite farewell; to one person you address formally, say ArrivederLa. Ciao is casual.
Masculine, takes l'. Also the finish line in a race. 'Arrivi' = arrivals at airports.

etymology: From arrostire + -o, ultimately of Germanic origin. See there for more.

fact.text: From the verb arrostire, ultimately of Germanic origin. This is why it resembles English roast so closely—both languages borrowed from the same medieval Germanic root for cooking.

senses.note: Invariable adjective.

etymology: From arrostire + -o, ultimately of Germanic origin. See there for more.

fact.text: From the verb arrostire, ultimately of Germanic origin. This is why it resembles English roast so closely—both languages borrowed from the same medieval Germanic root for cooking.

senses.note: Also used as an adjective: pollo arrosto = roast chicken.

etymology: From Latin artem (“art”, “skill”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂r̥tís, from the root *h₂er- (“to join, put together”).

fact.text: From Latin ars, artem, 'skill', from a root meaning 'to join or fit together'. Latin arma, 'weapons' (English arms), comes from the same root.

senses.note: Feminine: l'arte, le arti. 'Opera d'arte' = work of art.

etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin articulus, derived from artus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂r̥tús. Compare also the doublet artiglio.

fact.text: From Latin articulus, 'small joint', from artus, 'joint', the same root as English articulate. Its twin word artiglio, which came down a different path, means claw.

senses.note: Covers newspaper articles, grammatical articles (il, la), items for sale and clauses of a law.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin artificiālis.

fact.text: From Latin artificialis. Cognate with English 'artificial'—both derive from the same Latin root meaning 'made by art/craft' (artificium).

senses.note: Skilled handmade production; the work and skill of an artisan.

etymology: From arte + -ista.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: l'artista. Plural: gli artisti (m), le artiste (f).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ascēnsor, equivalent to ascendere + -tore.

senses.note: Masculine despite the -e ending: l'ascensore, gli ascensori. 'Lift' in British English.

etymology:
From Latin ascia (“axe”).
In spite of the similar pronunciation, unrelated to French hache, ultimately from Frankish *happjā (“axe, hatchet”).

fact.text: Sounds like French hache, the source of English 'hatchet', but the two aren't related. This word comes from Latin ascia, while hache comes from a Germanic (Frankish) word.

senses.note: Plural: le asce.

etymology: Verb-object compound, composed of asciuga (“to dry”) + mano (“hand”).

fact.text: A compound of asciuga, 'dries', and mano, 'hand'. Literally it is a 'hand-dryer'.

senses.note: Masculine even though mano is feminine: l'asciugamano, gli asciugamani.

etymology: From earlier *asciucare, from Latin exsūcāre, from ex- + sucus (“juice, moisture”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin exsucare, 'to take the juice out', from ex- 'out' + sucus 'juice, moisture'. The same sucus is behind English 'succulent'.

senses.note: Reflexive asciugarsi = to dry oneself; asciugacapelli = hairdryer.

etymology: From Latin exsūctus, past participle of exsūgō, from ex + sūgō. Compare Sicilian asciuttu, Spanish enjuto, Portuguese enxuto, Catalan eixut.

fact.text: From Latin exsuctus, 'sucked out', past participle of exsugere (ex + sugere, 'to suck'). Something dry has had the moisture sucked out of it.

senses.note: Means not wet (clothes, hands). Secco is more 'dried out'. Pasta asciutta = pasta not served in broth.

etymology: Inherited from Latin ascultāre, variant of auscultāre. Doublet of auscultare, a borrowing from Latin.

fact.text: From Latin ascultare, a variant of auscultare, 'to listen attentively'. The same root gives auscultation, when a doctor listens to your chest with a stethoscope.

senses.note: Takes a direct object, no preposition: ascolto la musica = I listen to music.
In broadcasting/media context: audience ratings or reception quality

etymology: From Latin asylum, from Ancient Greek ἄσυλον (ásulon).

fact.text: Same word as English 'asylum'. It comes from Greek asylon, 'not subject to seizure', a place where nobody could be dragged away. So a kindergarten is a little safe haven.

senses.note: asilo nido = daycare (0–3); asilo also means asylum: asilo politico = political asylum.

etymology: From Latin āsthma, from Ancient Greek ἆσθμα (âsthma, “laborous breathing”).

fact.text: From Greek ásthma (laborous breathing). The term has remained virtually unchanged from Greek through Latin and into modern languages.

etymology: Inherited from Latin exspectāre, aspectāre. By surface analysis, a- + spettare.

fact.text: From Latin exspectare, the source of English expect, but in Italian it means to wait for. 'To expect' is usually aspettarsi.

senses.note: No 'per' needed: aspetto il bus = I'm waiting for the bus.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin aspectus, perfect passive participle of aspiciō (“to behold, see”).

fact.text: Watch out for a lookalike: 'aspetto' is also 'I wait', from the verb aspettare. 'Aspetto il treno' means 'I'm waiting for the train', not anything about appearance.

senses.note: Also 'aspect, side' of an issue. Avere un bell'aspetto = to look good.

etymology: From Latin asperum (“rough”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂esp- (“to cut”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese áspero (“rough”), French âpre, Romanian aspru.

fact.text: It comes from Latin asper, 'rough', the same root as English 'asperity' and 'exasperate', which literally means to make someone feel rough.

senses.note: Also means sour (taste) or rugged (terrain): un sapore aspro, un terreno aspro.

etymology: From a- + saggio (“test, sample”) + -are. Compare Piedmontese assagé.

fact.text: Built on saggio, 'test, sample', from Latin exagium, 'a weighing'. The same Latin word gave English 'assay' and 'essay', which was first an attempt or trial.

senses.note: Means to try or sample food. 'To taste of' is sapere di.

etymology: From Arabic حَشَّاشِين (ḥaššāšīn, “hashish users”) or أَسَاسِيُّون (ʔasāsiyyūn, “fundamentalist”). Compare Piedmontese assassin, sassin.

fact.text: From Arabic ḥaššāšīn (hashish users) or ʔasāsiyyūn (fundamentalists), referring to a medieval Nizari Ismaili sect known for political killings. Crusaders brought the word to Europe.

etymology: Deverbal from assegnare + -o.

fact.text: Formed from assegnare, 'to assign'. Both come from Latin assignare, 'to mark out', built on signum, 'sign'. A check assigns money to someone, and you sign it too.

senses.note: Also means allowance: assegno di mantenimento = alimony. Assegno a vuoto = bounced check.

etymology: From Latin absentem.

fact.text: From Latin absentem, present participle of abesse ('to be away'). The same root as English 'absent'.

senses.note: Also figurative: absent-minded, detached.

etymology: From Latin absentia.

fact.text: From Latin absentia (from absum, to be away). English 'absence' is cognate. Both mean the state of being away or not present.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *assēcūrāre. By surface analysis, a- + sicuro + -are.

fact.text: Both 'assicurare' and English 'assure' derive from Latin assecurare. The word also covers 'insurance': assicurazione is the noun, an important cognate.

senses.note: Transitive. Also means 'to insure' (assicurare una casa) or 'to secure/tie up' in physical contexts.

etymology: From assicurare + -zione.
From associare + -zione.
From assoluto + -mente.

fact.text: Used alone as a reply, it can mean 'absolutely yes' or 'absolutely not' depending on the question. Many Italians, and usage guides, prefer adding sì or no to avoid confusion.

senses.note: Assolutamente sì = absolutely; assolutamente no = absolutely not.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *(as)similiāre, a verb based on Latin similis (“similar”). By surface analysis, a- + somigliare. Doublet of assimilare and assembrare.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin assimilare (to make similar), based on Latin similis (similar). Doublet of 'assimilare'.

senses.note: Intransitive verb (may take 'a' for the person/thing resembled).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin assūmere, from ad- + sūmō.

fact.text: False friend: assumere means 'to hire' or 'take on', not 'to assume' in the sense of 'suppose' (which is supporre or presumere).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin absurdus.

fact.text: From Latin absurdus, which first meant 'out of tune' and is linked to surdus, 'deaf'. Something absurd was originally jarring to the ear.

senses.note: Common exclamation: 'È assurdo!' = That's ridiculous!

etymology: From Latin abstractus.

senses.note: Adjective: astratto, astratta, astratti, astratte.

etymology: From astro- + -nauta.

fact.text: Combines astro- (star) and -nauta (sailor/navigator, from Greek nautés). It literally means 'star sailor'—a poetic term for those who navigate the cosmos.

senses.note: Can be masculine or feminine.

etymology: Replaced s- of staccare by a-.

fact.text: English 'attack' comes through French attaquer from Italian attaccare, from phrases like attaccare battaglia (to join battle). Its 'stick, fasten' sense is linked to the root behind English 'attach'.

senses.note: Attaccare il nemico = to attack the enemy. Also used for starting something: attaccare a lavorare.
Attaccare un francobollo = to stick on a stamp. Attaccarsi = to stick, cling.

etymology: From attaccare.

senses.note: Also a fit or bout (attacco di panico), and a connection or fitting, such as a plug or ski binding.

etymology: From atteggiare + -mento.
From Latin attendere.

fact.text: False friend: it means to wait for, not to attend. To attend a class is frequentare; to attend an event is partecipare a. Both words come from Latin attendere, 'to stretch toward'.

senses.note: More formal than aspettare. No 'per' needed: attendo una risposta. Common on signs: 'Attendere prego'.

etymology: From attento + -mente.

senses.note: Also 'closely, attentively': ascoltare attentamente = to listen closely.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin attentātus, perfect passive participle of attentō.

fact.text: From Latin attentātus, past participle of attentō ('to attempt'). The word retains the sense of a deliberate act, often violent or criminal.

senses.note: Often refers to a violent act or assault.

etymology: From Latin attentus.

senses.note: Attento! / Attenta! = Watch out! Careful! Attento a... = mind the...

etymology: Borrowed from Latin attentiōnem.

fact.text: Same root as English 'attention': Latin attendere, 'to stretch toward', from ad- + tendere. Paying attention is literally stretching your mind toward something.

senses.note: Fare attenzione a = to pay attention to, be careful with. Attenzione! = Watch out!

fact.text: Comes from attendere, which means to wait, not to attend. To attend a class is frequentare in Italian.

senses.note: Sala d'attesa = waiting room. In attesa di = waiting for.

etymology: Variant of atomo, from Latin atomus (“moment, instant”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin atomus and Greek atomos, meaning uncut or indivisible, which is also where English atom comes from. The idea is a slice of time too small to divide.

senses.note: Un attimo! = Just a moment! / One moment!

etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin āctivitātem.

fact.text: From Latin activitas (active state). The -ità suffix, common in Italian abstract nouns, comes from Latin -itas and regularly transforms Latin adjectives and nouns into Italian counterparts (e.g., città from civitas).

senses.note: Invariable noun; same form in singular and plural

etymology: From Latin āctīvus.

fact.text: From Latin āctīvus, the same root as English active. Both share the meaning of energetic or in motion.

etymology: From Latin actus.

fact.text: From Latin actus, the perfect passive participle of agere (make, do). Shares its Indo-European root with Sanskrit akta (driven) and English agent.

senses.note: A deed or action; often a formal document.

etymology: From Latin āctōrem (“doer”, “actor”).

senses.note: Female: l'attrice (actress). In law, l'attore is the plaintiff.

etymology: From attraverso + -are.

fact.text: Built on attraverso (across), which goes back to Latin transversus, the same source as English traverse and transverse.

senses.note: Transitive: attraversare la strada = to cross the street (no preposition needed).

etymology:
Univerbation of a + traverso (from Latin trānsversus).
Compare French à travers, Portuguese através and Spanish a través de.

fact.text: Univerbation of a + traverso (from Latin transversus). Cognate with French à travers, Portuguese através, and Spanish a través.

senses.note: Invariable singular noun.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin augurāre.

fact.text: From Latin augurāre (to divine). An augur was a Roman priest who predicted the future by observing bird flight.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin augurium. Related to Old Italian agurio, which was inherited.

fact.text: From Latin augurium, an omen read by Roman augurs, priests who watched the flight of birds. English augur and inaugurate come from the same root.

senses.note: Auguri! = best wishes, or happy birthday. Tanti auguri! is the standard birthday greeting.

etymology: From Latin aula, from Ancient Greek αὐλή (aulḗ, “courtyard”).

senses.note: Also a lecture hall, courtroom or parliament chamber.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin augmentāre (“to increase”), from Latin augmentum (“growth, increase”), from augeō (“increase”).

fact.text: From Late Latin augmentāre, related to Latin augeō (increase). The same root gave English 'augment'.

senses.note: Can be transitive (to raise/boost) or intransitive (to rise/spike).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin augmentum.

fact.text: From Latin augmentum (increase, growth). Related to English 'augment'. The root comes from augēre (to increase).

etymology: From Australia + -ano.
From Latin authenticus, from Ancient Greek αὐθεντικός (authentikós).

fact.text: From Latin authenticus, from Greek authentikós (genuine, principal). English authentic and Italian autentico are direct cognates sharing over two millennia of Romance and Latin history.

etymology: From auto + -ista.

fact.text: Autista means driver or chauffeur (from auto, automobile). Despite the English spelling 'autist', this word has nothing to do with autism; autistic is autistico in Italian.

senses.note: taxi driver or chauffeur

etymology: Clipping of automobile.

fact.text: Feminine (l'auto, le auto) even though it ends in -o, because it is short for l'automobile. It does not change in the plural.

senses.note: Invariable: l'auto, le auto. Macchina is the more common everyday word.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French autobus.

fact.text: Borrowed from French autobus, from auto + (omni)bus. Latin omnibus means 'for all', so the '-bus' in both bus and autobus is really just a Latin case ending.

senses.note: Invariable: l'autobus, gli autobus. Often shortened to il bus. A long-distance coach is il pullman.

etymology: From Ancient Greek αὐτονομία (autonomía).

fact.text: From Ancient Greek autonomía: auto- (self) + nómos (law). Literally 'self-law'—the right to be governed by one's own laws.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin auctōrem.

fact.text: From Latin auctor, from augere 'to increase'. An author was originally someone who makes something grow. English authority and augment share the root.

senses.note: Female: l'autrice. Can also mean the perpetrator of a crime (l'autore del furto).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin auctōritātem, derived from auctor.

fact.text: From Latin auctōritātem, the same root as English 'authority' and 'author'. Both mean the power to create or command something.

senses.note: Can mean official power, expertise, or an influential person/source

etymology: From auto- + strada.

fact.text: Italy opened the world's first motorway in 1924: the Milano-Laghi, a road from Milan to the lakes, planned by Piero Puricelli.

senses.note: Italian motorways are mostly toll roads (pedaggio).

etymology: From auto- + sufficiente.

Borrowed from Latin autumnus (“autumn, fall”), of uncertain etymology. First attested in 1306, replacing several inherited forms (cf. proto-Italian octummio, attested in a Latin document from 762, via Late Latin autumnius). The Latin etymon is directly continued by Romanian toamnă, Aromanian toamnã (unless these reflect the variant in a-), Italian autono (Northern Italy, 15th c.), Romansh utuon (Engadine), Spanish otoño (→ Logudorese Sardinian atónzu, Campidanese atógniu), Portuguese outono, and via Vulgar Latin *atumnus by Friulian atum (“october”), Romansh atun (Sursilvan), aton (Surmiran). Provençal autoun (“autumn harvest”) could be Latin-influenced; French automne is likely, and Catalan autumne certain to be a borrowing from Latin.

fact.text: From Latin autumnus, whose origin is a mystery. One theory says the Romans borrowed it from Etruscan, which had a word atune meaning autumn.

senses.note: US English: fall. 'In autumn' = in autunno / d'autunno.

etymology: From Late Latin ab ante.

fact.text: From Late Latin ab ante, 'from before'. Avanti! is what Italians call out when someone knocks at the door, meaning 'Come in!'

senses.note: Also 'ahead, onward'. Avanti! = Come in! / Go ahead! Andare avanti = to go on, to continue.

etymology: From Latin avārus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin avarus, greedy, which is also the source of English avarice and avaricious.

senses.note: Also a noun: un avaro means a miser. Molière's play The Miser is L'avaro in Italian.

etymology: Inherited from Latin habēre.

fact.text: The silent h in ho, hai, ha and hanno is a leftover of Latin habere, kept in spelling to tell them apart from o (or), ai (to the), a (to) and anno (year).

senses.note: Auxiliary for transitive verbs (ho mangiato). Present: ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno.

etymology: From avere (“to have”) + ragione (“reason”). Compare French avoir raison, Spanish tener razón, Portuguese ter razão, Catalan tenir raó.

senses.note: Literally 'to have reason'. Opposite: avere torto (to be wrong). Hai ragione! = You're right!

etymology: Borrowed from Latin adverbium.

senses.note: Plural: gli avverbi. Many are formed with -mente: lento → lentamente.

etymology: From Latin adversārius.

senses.note: Feminine: l'avversaria. Common in sport: la metà campo dell'avversario.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin advertere, with change of conjugation.

fact.text: Related to English 'avert' via Latin advertere (to turn toward). Both share the root ad- (to) + vertere (to turn), so avvertire literally means to turn someone's attention to something.

etymology: From a- + vicino + -are.

senses.note: Reflexive verb

etymology: Borrowed from Latin advocātus.

fact.text: From Latin advocatus, 'one called to (help)', from ad + vocare 'to call'. It is the same word as English 'advocate', but in Italian it is the everyday word for a lawyer.

senses.note: Female: l'avvocata (avvocatessa is dated). Also used as a title: l'avvocato Rossi.

etymology: From Latin vulturius, from vultur.

senses.note: Also figurative: a greedy, predatory person.

etymology: Borrowed from Old Spanish hazienda, from Latin facienda. Doublet of faccenda.

fact.text: Borrowed from Old Spanish hazienda (modern hacienda), from Latin facienda, 'things to be done'. Its native Italian doublet is faccenda, 'matter, chore'.

senses.note: Any business or firm, e.g. un'azienda agricola (a farm). Plural: le aziende.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin āctiōnem.

fact.text: In finance, azione also means a share of stock; azionista means shareholder. The word shares the Latin root with English action.

etymology: From Medieval Latin lazulum (through a variant lazurum and with rebracketing of the initial l- as the article l'), from Arabic لَازَوَرْد (lāzaward, “lapis lazuli”), from Persian لاجورد (lâjvard, “lapis lazuli”). Cognate with English azure, French azur, and Portuguese and Spanish azul.

fact.text: Comes from Persian lajvard, 'lapis lazuli', the source of English 'azure' too. The first l- disappeared because speakers took it for the article l'. That's why Italy's teams are called gli Azzurri.

senses.note: Italians treat azzurro (sky blue) and blu (dark blue) as separate colours. Gli Azzurri = Italian national teams.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *bábbọ, accusative-ablative form of *bábbọs, childish term of onomatopoeic origin.

fact.text: Even where people say 'papà', Father Christmas is called Babbo Natale all over Italy.

etymology: From older basciare, inherited from Latin bāsiāre (“to kiss”).

fact.text: From Latin basiare, from basium 'kiss'. The Roman poet Catullus made the word famous with his line 'da mi basia mille': give me a thousand kisses.

senses.note: Drops the i before e/i: bacerò, baci. Noun: il bacio (kiss).

etymology: Inherited from Latin bāsium (“kiss”). Cognate with Sicilian vasu.

fact.text: Baci Perugina are famous chocolates from Perugia. Each is wrapped with a small paper note carrying a love quote in several languages.

senses.note: Plural: baci. Ending a letter or message: baci / un bacio = love, kisses.

etymology: From Early Medieval Latin batāre.
Uncertain.

fact.text: Two fun idioms: 'ridere sotto i baffi' (to laugh under your mustache) means to snigger quietly, and 'leccarsi i baffi' means to lick your lips over good food.

senses.note: Usually plural: i baffi = a mustache. Also an animal's whisker.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French bagage.

fact.text: Borrowed from Old French bagage, which ultimately goes back to Old Norse baggi, 'bundle', the likely source of English 'bag' too.

senses.note: Countable in Italian: un bagaglio = a piece of luggage; i bagagli = luggage, bags.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *baneāre, from Late Latin balneāre, from Latin balneum. Compare French baigner, Sicilian vagnari, Spanish bañar.

senses.note: Transitive. 'To get wet' is the reflexive bagnarsi: mi sono bagnato = I got wet.

fact.text: A common saying is 'piove sul bagnato', literally 'it rains on what is already wet'. It means good or bad luck goes to those who already have plenty, like 'it never rains but it pours'.

senses.note: Past participle of bagnare (to wet). Bagnato fradicio = soaking wet.

etymology: Inherited from Latin baneum, variant of balneum.

fact.text: From Latin balneum, 'bath'. Fare il bagno can mean having a bath or swimming in the sea, and on the Italian coast i bagni are beach clubs where you rent umbrellas and sunbeds.

senses.note: Dov'è il bagno? = Where's the bathroom/toilet? Also bath: fare il bagno = to have a bath or a swim.

etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Germanic *balkô
Frankish *balkōbor.
Medieval Latin balcōbor.
Italian balcone
Borrowed from Medieval Latin balcōnem. Compare Old Italian balco (“scaffold”).

fact.text: It goes back to a Germanic word for 'beam', since early balconies were wooden platforms built on beams. English got balcony from Italian in the 1600s.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin ballāre.

fact.text: From Late Latin ballare, probably from Greek ballizein, 'to dance'. It shares this root with English 'ball' (a dance), 'ballet' and 'ballad'.

senses.note: Regular -are verb with avere: ho ballato.

fact.text: English borrowed ballerina directly from Italian. The word is feminine in both languages, from ballare (to dance).

etymology: From ballare (“to dance”).

fact.text: From Latin ballare, the same root as English 'ball'. The word travelled through dance traditions from ancient Rome through medieval times.

senses.note: can mean both the act of dancing and a formal ball
Masculine: bambino (little boy). Can also mean 'baby girl'.
