etymology: Onomatopoeic bambo for the first stammerings of children, plus -ino (diminutive suffix).

fact.text: English borrowed this word too: baseball legend Babe Ruth was nicknamed 'the Bambino'. It's built from 'bambo', imitating a baby's first babbling, plus the diminutive -ino.

senses.note: Masculine; also means 'little boy'. For a girl: la bambina. Plural: i bambini.

etymology: Onomatopoeic variant of bambino.

senses.note: Can also mean an attractive young woman, in colloquial speech.

etymology: Borrowed from French banal, derived from ban (“declaration, announcement”).

fact.text: From French banal, from ban (a feudal proclamation). Things 'banal' were facilities like the lord's mill that all tenants had to use. Shared by everyone came to mean commonplace.

senses.note: Used for ideas, problems or people: un errore banale = a silly mistake.

etymology: Borrowed from Lombardic bank (“bench”), from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg- (“to bend”). Cognates include Spanish banco and Portuguese banco. Doublet of banco and panca.

fact.text: Comes from a Germanic word for 'bench', because medieval moneychangers worked at benches. English bankrupt traces back to Italian banca rotta, 'broken bench'.

senses.note: Related words: il banco (counter, desk, school desk) and la panca (bench).

etymology: Borrowed from Lombardic bank, from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz. Doublet of banca and panca. Cognate with Sicilian vancu.

fact.text: Comes from the same Germanic root as bench and bank. Medieval Italian money-changers worked at a banco, and English bankrupt goes back to Italian banca rotta, 'broken bench'.

senses.note: A classroom desk. It also means a counter, a bench or a market stall.

fact.text: Originally the brand name of Italy's interbank cash network, it now names both the machine and the debit card: 'pago con il bancomat' means 'I'll pay by card'.

senses.note: Invariable plural: i bancomat. Also used for the debit card itself.
Used for US 'bill' (paper money) too. 'Biglietto' is also common: un biglietto da 50 euro.

etymology: From Old Occitan, of Germanic origin, from Frankish *bindā (“tie, join, link”). Compare French bande.

senses.note: A brass or marching band, as in a town band. It can also mean gang. A rock band is un gruppo.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English bar. Doublet of barra.

fact.text: An Italian bar is mostly a café. People stop in for an espresso at the counter, a cornetto or a sandwich, often standing up, from early morning on.

senses.note: The plural doesn't change: i bar. Serves coffee as well as drinks.

etymology: From Latin barba, from Proto-Italic *farðā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰeh₂ (“beard”).

fact.text: English 'barber' comes from the same Latin word barba, via French. A barber was originally the person who trimmed your beard.

senses.note: Che barba! = How boring! (colloquial). Farsi la barba = to shave.

From Late Latin barca, derived from Latin baris, from Ancient Greek βᾶρις (bâris), itself probably from Egyptian bꜣjr (“transport ship”).

fact.text: This word probably goes back to Ancient Egyptian bꜣjr, a transport ship, and came into Late Latin through Greek baris. English barque and barge are relatives.

senses.note: Usually means a small boat. A large ship is la nave. Plural: barche.

etymology: From bar + -ista (“-ist”).

fact.text: Barista is now an English word too, borrowed from Italian bar + -ista suffix, though it originally meant bartender before becoming associated with specialty coffee culture.

etymology:
The origin of this word is uncertain. Both a pre-Celtic origin (ancient Ligurian) and a Celtic origin have been argued for.
Numerous toponyms of the Western Alps find their etymology in this term and its variations: e.g., the comune of Balme, the Colle della Barma and the village of Barmasc (which also contains the ancient ligurian suffix -asc/ascu).

fact.text: Possibly pre-Celtic (Ligurian) or Celtic in origin, the word survives in Western Alpine place names such as the village of Balme and the Colle della Barma.

senses.note: A Western Alpine (Piedmont, Aosta Valley) word for a cave or overhanging rock.

etymology: From Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis).

fact.text: From Ancient Greek basis (step, foot, base), meaning something that you step on or stand on. Also used in chemistry for alkaline substances.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English baseball.

senses.note: invariable: same form in plural

etymology: From Latin basilicum, from Ancient Greek βασιλικόν (basilikón), nominalized neuter form of the adjective βασιλικός (basilikós, “royal, kingly”), derived from βασιλεύς (basileús, “master; king”).

fact.text: The name comes from Greek basileus (king), because the plant was considered regal. In Italian, it retained the royal adjective basilico (royal, princely).

senses.note: The herb Ocimum basilicum; essential in Italian cooking

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin bassus, possibly of Ancient Greek origin.

fact.text: English 'bass' in music grew out of 'base' (low), but its spelling was influenced by Italian basso. Opera still calls a bass singer a basso.

senses.note: For people's height. For length or duration use corto or breve.
Opposite of alto. in basso = down below.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin bassus, possibly of Ancient Greek origin.

fact.text: English 'bass' in music grew out of 'base' (low), but its spelling was influenced by Italian basso. Opera still calls a bass singer a basso.

senses.note: Covers the bass part, bass voice and bass guitar. As an adjective, basso means low or short.

fact.text: This is simply a form of the verb bastare, 'to be enough', so it literally means 'it's enough'. English speakers sometimes borrow it too, as in 'and that's it, basta!'

senses.note: Also used to end a list: 'and that's it'.

etymology: From Medieval Latin bastardus, perhaps from Frankish.

fact.text: From Medieval Latin bastardus, possibly from Frankish. Entered Romance languages from feudal/legal contexts to denote illegitimate children.

senses.note: Derogatory term; originally meant illegitimate child born outside marriage

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bastāre (“to be enough; to suffice”), possibly derived from a modification of Late Latin bastum (“stick, staff, rod, pole”), from Ancient Greek βαστάζω (bastázō, “to lift, carry, bear, support (weight)”). Compare Sicilian bastari, Spanish and Portuguese bastar, French baster.

senses.note: Takes essere. On its own, 'Basta!' means 'Enough!' or 'Stop!'

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin battālia, variant of battuālia, from Latin battuō.

fact.text: From Late Latin battālia, variant of battuālia, from Latin battuō (to beat). The word reflects the primal etymology of combat as striking.

etymology: Inherited from Latin battere, from earlier battuere.

fact.text: From Latin battuere 'to beat', which also gave English battle, battery, combat and debate, the last literally 'beating down' an opponent.

senses.note: Many uses: battere le mani = to clap; battere a macchina = to type.

etymology: From battere + -eria or borrowed from Old French baterie.

fact.text: From battere (to beat) + -eria, or from Old French baterie. Literally 'a hitting' or 'things that strike'—thus drums, batteries, and even military formations share the beating root.

senses.note: Feminine. Plural: batterie. Also means 'battery', 'heat', or 'percussion section' in music.

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of battere.

fact.text: Literally 'a beat' or 'a stroke', from battere. It also means a tennis serve, an actor's line and a musical bar, as well as a quick joke or quip.

senses.note: Fare una battuta = to crack a joke. A joke told as a story is a barzelletta.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin beātus.

fact.text: From Latin beātus (happy, blessed). Same root as English 'beatitude' and the musical term 'beatification'.

senses.note: Also: blessed, lucky.

etymology: From becco (“beak, bill”) + -are.

fact.text: In everyday speech it also means 'to catch' someone, or 'to catch' a cold or a fine. 'Mi hanno beccato' means 'They caught me.'

etymology: Inherited from Latin beccus, from Gaulish *bekkos, from Proto-Celtic *bekkos.

fact.text: From Latin beccus, borrowed from Gaulish. English 'beak' comes from the same source via French bec, making it a near-perfect cognate across Romance and English.

senses.note: of a bird; also used for anything pointed like a beak

etymology: Apocopic form of bene.

senses.note: A filler word to start a sentence. It's a shortened form of bene. Also spelled 'be''.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bellitia. By surface analysis, bello + -ezza.

senses.note: 'Che bellezza!' = How lovely! / How great!

etymology: Inherited from Latin bellus.

fact.text: From Latin bellus 'pretty', which also gave English 'belle' and 'embellish' by way of French.

senses.note: Before a noun it changes form like the article: bel ragazzo, bello zio, bell'uomo, bei/begli.

etymology:
Univerbation of ben(e) + che.
Compare French bien que.

fact.text: Always followed by the subjunctive mood in Italian. Univerbation of bene (well) and che (that), compare French bien que.

senses.note: Conjunction requiring subjunctive: benché sia stanco, esco (although I'm tired, I'm going out).

etymology: Inherited from Latin bene.

fact.text: It comes straight from Latin bene, 'well', which is also in English benefit, benefactor and benediction (literally 'speaking well').

senses.note: An adverb; the adjective is buono. Sto bene = I'm well. Molto bene = very well.

etymology: Inherited from Latin bene.

fact.text: It comes straight from Latin bene, 'well', which is also in English benefit, benefactor and benediction (literally 'speaking well').

senses.note: To show approval, say Bene!, not Buono! (buono means good to eat or good in character).

etymology: From Latin benedīcere. By surface analysis, bene- + dire.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bene venūtus, presumably a calque of a Frankish term, derived from Proto-Germanic *wiljakwemô (“a welcome guest or arrival”), from which many modern Germanic forms descend, such as English welcome. By surface analysis, ben (“well”, apocopic form of bene) + venuto (“come”, past participle of venire)

fact.text: Built from bene 'well' + venuto 'come', calquing a Frankish term from Proto-Germanic *wiljakwemo, the same root as English 'welcome'. Both languages independently inherited this phrase structure.

senses.note: Agrees with the person or people: benvenuta, benvenuti, benvenute. As a noun: dare il benvenuto.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bene venūtus, presumably a calque of a Frankish term, derived from Proto-Germanic *wiljakwemô (“a welcome guest or arrival”), from which many modern Germanic forms descend, such as English welcome. By surface analysis, ben (“well”, apocopic form of bene) + venuto (“come”, past participle of venire)

fact.text: Built from bene 'well' + venuto 'come', calquing a Frankish term from Proto-Germanic *wiljakwemo, the same root as English 'welcome'. Both languages independently inherited this phrase structure.

senses.note: Invariable singular form; used as a greeting without distinct plural.

etymology: Borrowed from German Benzin.

fact.text: Via German Benzin, named after benzoin resin. Benzoin comes from Arabic lubān jāwī, 'frankincense of Java'. Watch out: benzina means gasoline, not benzene.

senses.note: British English: petrol. To fill up: fare benzina. Diesel is il gasolio.

etymology: From a contraction of earlier bevere, from Latin bibere, from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *píph₃eti. Cognate with Albanian pi, literary Armenian ըմպել (əmpel), Hindi पीना (pīnā), and Irish ibh.

fact.text: Shortened from older bevere, from Latin bibere 'to drink'. The same root gives English 'imbibe' and 'beverage'.

senses.note: Irregular stem bev-: bevo, bevendo, bevuto (from older bevere).

etymology: From Old French bersail (“target for an arrow”), from berser (“to hunt with bow and arrow”), from Latin vervēx (“wether, kind of goat; blockhead, idiot”).

fact.text: From Old French bersail (target for arrows), from berser (to hunt with bow and arrow), ultimately from Latin vervēx (wether or blockhead).

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin bēstia, but some sources consider it inherited. Cognate to biscia, which is definitely inherited.

fact.text: 'Andare in bestia' means to fly into a rage, literally 'to go into beast'. 'Lavorare come una bestia' means to work like a dog.

senses.note: Can mean livestock or animals in general. Also used as an insult: brute, idiot.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *bibanda, from Latin bibenda, from bibendum.

fact.text: From Latin bibenda, 'things to be drunk'. Michelin's tyre mascot is named Bibendum after Horace's line 'nunc est bibendum', meaning 'now we must drink'.

senses.note: A general, slightly formal word, often seen on menus. An alcoholic drink is also un drink.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin blancus. Doublet of blanco, a borrowing from Spanish.

fact.text: Medieval Latin blancus was borrowed from a Germanic word meaning shining or pale. English blank comes from the same root through French blanc, as in a blank (white) page.

senses.note: Irregular plurals: bianchi, bianche. In bianco e nero = in black and white (note the reversed order).

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin bibita, from Latin bibere.

fact.text: Comes from Latin bibere 'to drink', the same root behind English 'imbibe' and, via Old French, 'beverage'.

senses.note: Usually a cold, non-alcoholic drink. For drinks in general, use bevanda.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin bibliothēca, from Ancient Greek βιβλιοθήκη (bibliothḗkē, “library”). By surface analysis, biblio- + -teca.

fact.text: False friend warning: a libreria is a bookshop (or bookcase), not a library. If you want to borrow books, go to the biblioteca, from Greek bibliotheke, 'book store'.

senses.note: Can also mean a bookcase.

etymology: From Late Latin bīcārium (cf. also Old French bichier, pichier, compare modern French pichet, English beaker, pitcher, German Becher, Dutch beker), itself possibly from bacarium, or from Ancient Greek βῖκος (bîkos).

fact.text: From Late Latin bicarium, which may come from Greek bikos (jar). The same Latin word is behind English beaker and German Becher.

senses.note: un bicchiere d'acqua = a glass of water. The material glass is il vetro.

etymology: From bicicletta, by shortening.

senses.note: Short for bicicletta. The plural doesn't change: le bici.

etymology: Borrowed from French bicyclette. By surface analysis, biciclo + -etta.

senses.note: Often shortened to 'la bici' (plural: le bici). To go by bike: andare in bici.

etymology: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from big shot.

fact.text: Italian pseudo-anglicism: 'big' is never pluralized in standard use. 'I tre big del cinema' (The three stars of cinema).

senses.note: Invariable noun; pseudo-anglicism from 'big shot'.

etymology: From biglietto + -eria.

senses.note: Also a box office (theatre, stadium).

etymology: From French billet, from Old French billette, derived from Latin bulla (“document”).

fact.text: Comes via French billet from Latin bulla, a sealed document. English bill and bulletin come from the same source.

senses.note: Also a banknote (biglietto da 10 euro) or a short note/card (biglietto d'auguri).

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bilancia, from Latin bilanx (“balance with two scalepans”), from bi- (see Latin bis) and lanx.

fact.text: From Latin bilanx, 'having two pans' (bi- + lanx, a dish). English balance comes from the same source, picturing an old two-pan scale.

senses.note: Also the zodiac sign Libra. A financial balance sheet is il bilancio.

fact.text: Italian flat ads count rooms, not bedrooms: monolocale (one room), bilocale (two), trilocale (three). Bathrooms aren't counted, so a bilocale is usually a one-bedroom flat.

senses.note: Common in property ads. Usually a living room plus a bedroom; kitchen and bathroom aren't counted.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin binārius.

fact.text: From Latin binarius, 'consisting of two', after the two rails of a track. As an adjective the same word means 'binary', as in codice binario.

senses.note: Il treno parte dal binario 5 = the train leaves from platform 5.

etymology: Medieval Latin blondus, of Germanic origin: probably from Frankish *blund (“a mixed color between golden and light-brown”), from Proto-Germanic *blundaz (“mixed, blinding”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlendʰ-. Compare French blond.

fact.text: As a noun, 'una bionda' can mean a blonde woman or a pale lager. In an Italian bar you can ask for una birra bionda (lager) or una rossa (amber beer).

senses.note: Agrees in gender and number: capelli biondi, una ragazza bionda.

etymology: Borrowed from German Bier.

fact.text: Italian borrowed this word from German Bier, which shares its Germanic origin with English beer. Native Latin had no word for beer.

senses.note: Birra alla spina = draught beer.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin biscoctus. Synchronicallty bis- (“twice”) + cotto (“baked, cooked”). Doublet of biscuit.

fact.text: From Latin bis coctus, 'twice cooked', because it was baked twice so it would keep longer. English 'biscuit' has the same origin and came in through French.

senses.note: In football slang, a biscotto is a draw two teams fix between them to knock out a third team.

etymology: From bisogno + -are.

senses.note: Impersonal: bisogna partire = we must leave. Used almost only in the 3rd person (bisogna, bisognava).

etymology:
Etymology tree
Frankish *bisunnijabor.
Vulgar Latin *bisonium
Italian bisogno
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bisonium, borrowed from Frankish *bisunnija.

fact.text: A Germanic word in disguise: it came into Vulgar Latin from Frankish, the language of the Franks who ruled much of Western Europe after Rome fell.

senses.note: Avere bisogno di = to need. 'Fare i propri bisogni' is a euphemism for relieving oneself.
Mostly used in 'avere bisogno di' (to need): Ho bisogno di aiuto.

etymology: Borrowed from English beefsteak.

fact.text: Borrowed from English beefsteak and respelled the Italian way. Florence's famous bistecca alla fiorentina is a huge T-bone steak, traditionally served rare.

senses.note: Al sangue = rare, ben cotta = well done.

etymology: Borrowed from French bloquer.

fact.text: From French bloquer, traced back through Dutch blok to Proto-Germanic *blukka. The same root gives English 'block'—a cognate pair across Germanic and Romance languages.

senses.note: Transitive verb; diverse meanings from physical blocking to sports tactics

etymology: Borrowed from French bleu (“blue”) from Middle French bleu, from Old French blou, bleve (“pallid, wan, discoloured/discolored, blue”), from Frankish *blāu, from Proto-Germanic *blēwaz (“blue, yellowish-gray”). Doublet of biavo.

fact.text: Italian borrowed this from French bleu, which came from a Germanic word, so it shares its root with English blue. The native Latin colour words were replaced.

senses.note: Invariable: una macchina blu, le scarpe blu. Azzurro is a lighter blue.

etymology: From Latin bucca.

fact.text: From Latin bucca, which meant 'cheek' (a puffed-out cheek). It replaced the classical word os. English 'buccal', meaning related to the cheek or mouth, comes from the same root.

senses.note: Also an opening, e.g. of a river or a tunnel. In bocca al lupo! = Good luck!
The game of bowls; plural form of boccia

etymology: From boccia + -are.

fact.text: From boccia, the ball used in bocce. The verb first meant knocking an opponent's ball out of the way, and from there it came to mean rejecting or failing someone.

senses.note: Essere bocciato = to fail an exam or be held back a year. Also: to reject or vote down a proposal.
Very common in speech and texting. Often comes with a shrug.

etymology: From Latin bulla.

fact.text: Latin bulla meant a bubble or knob, and later the round seal on a document. That is why a pope's decree is called a 'bull' in English.

senses.note: Also a blister, a papal bull, or a delivery note (bolla di accompagnamento).
Also figurative: una patata bollente = a hot potato (a tricky problem).

etymology: From bolla + -etta.

senses.note: Receipt or statement of charges

etymology: From bolletta + -ino.

fact.text: From bolletta (a form or receipt) with the diminutive suffix -ino, literally meaning a small note or document.

etymology: From Latin bullīre (“to bubble, boil”), from bulla (“bubble”).

fact.text: From Latin bullire 'to bubble', from bulla 'bubble'. English 'boil' comes from it via French, and 'ebullient', bubbling over with enthusiasm, has the same root.

senses.note: Intransitive or transitive: l'acqua bolle = the water is boiling; bollire la pasta.

etymology: From Latin bombus (“a boom”).

fact.text: Via Latin bombus from Greek bómbos, a word imitating a deep booming or buzzing sound. So 'bomb' began as an imitation of the noise itself.

senses.note: Colloquially, something great: è una bomba! It's also a cream-filled doughnut.

etymology: Deverbal from bonificare + -o.

senses.note: Italian banking term for electronic transfer between accounts.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bordum (“plank, board”), from Frankish *bord, from Proto-Germanic *burdą (“board; table”).

fact.text: It comes from a Germanic word for 'plank', related to English 'board'. Ship sides were planks, which explains both meanings: a bordo means 'on board'.

senses.note: Also border or rim. A bordo = on board (a ship, plane or train).

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin bursa.

fact.text: Also means stock exchange, named after the Van der Beurse inn in Bruges where merchants met. English purse and bursar share its root, Latin bursa.

senses.note: Often means handbag. Also: la Borsa = stock exchange; borsa di studio = scholarship.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin boscus, borrowed from Frankish *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz.

fact.text: A Germanic word that came into Latin via Frankish *busk. It is related to English 'bush', and through French bosquet 'little wood' to 'bouquet'.

senses.note: Plural boschi. Usually smaller than a foresta.

etymology: From Latin botanicus.

fact.text: From Latin botanicus, which comes from Greek botanē (plant, herb). The term entered European languages during the Renaissance when scientific study of plants became fashionable.

etymology: Borrowed from French bouteille.

fact.text: Borrowed from French bouteille, from Late Latin butticula, a 'little cask'. English bottle comes from the same Old French word.

senses.note: Plural of bovino (a bovine); i bovini = cattle, the bovine family.

etymology: Inherited from Latin brachium, bracchium, from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn).

fact.text: The plural is irregular: one arm is il braccio, but a person's two arms are le braccia, which is feminine. The arms of a crane or a river use the regular plural, i bracci.

senses.note: Masculine singular (il braccio). Body arms in the plural are feminine: le braccia.

etymology: Uncertain, from Old French braon (“slice of meat”) or Old Spanish brahon, from Frankish *brādon, from Proto-Germanic *brēdô. Compare English brawn.

fact.text: Possibly from Frankish *brādon via Old French 'braon' (slice). English 'brawn' (muscle/meat) shares the same Germanic root.
In Italian, 'brasile' originally meant brazilwood (a red dye source), and the country was named after the abundant tree. English 'Brazil' and Italian 'Brasile' share this origin, not the reverse.

etymology:
Uncertain. Probably from Vulgar Latin *bravus, from a fusion of Latin prāvus and barbarus. Less likely from Provençal brau (“show-off”), from Gaulish *bragos (compare Middle Irish breagha (modern breá) 'fine', Breton braga 'to strut'). Or perhaps borrowed from a descendant of Proto-Germanic *hrawaz (“raw, uncooked”). Or possibly from a root *bravus, from bravium. Borrowed into French and English as brave.
Pierre Carpentier, in an 18th-century edition of du Cange's 17th-century dictionary of medieval and modern Latin, argued Latin branus originated in a misreading of Italian and Spanish bravo. However, George Nicholson argues the opposite in a 1950 Festschrift article, namely bravo being a misreading of Latin branus, which would have the origin du Cange had originally argued for, from Old French brahaigne (“barren”) (see barren). Compare English gravy, possibly a misreading of French grané (“stew”).

fact.text: English brave came from this word via French, but in Italian bravo usually means good or skilled: un bravo medico is a good doctor. Brave is coraggioso. Its deeper origin is uncertain.

senses.note: Means skilled or well-behaved: bravo a scuola. Bravo! = well done (brava to a woman).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin brevis (“short”).

fact.text: From Latin brevis, the source of English brief and abbreviate. Surprisingly, it shares a distant root with English merry, which may first have meant 'making time seem short'.

senses.note: Usually means short in time or length of text. In breve = in short. For physical length, use corto.
Same form for masculine and feminine. As a noun, un brillante is a cut diamond.

From brocco (“shoot, sprout”) + -olo (which is also the origin of brocade), from Latin broccus (“projecting, pointed”), of Gaulish origin, related to Irish brog (“awl”). Cognate with Sicilian vròcculu.

fact.text: From Latin broccus ('projecting, pointed'), of Gaulish origin related to Irish brog ('awl'). The word literally means 'small shoots'.

etymology:
From a Vulgar Latin *brusiāre, itself of uncertain origin; possibly from a form *prustiāre < *per-ust(u)lāre, from Latin per + ustulāre (compare perurere), or alternatively from a corruption of *combustulāre, from a change of prefix of ambustulāre, influenced by combustus; see ambūrēre. However, an Italian word brustolare (cf. abbrustolire), from a related root *brustulāre, from ustulāre, also exists. The initial br- may also be of Germanic origin.
Compare French brûler (Old French brusler), Dalmatian brusur, Occitan bruslar, buizar, Romansh brischar, Venetan bruxar.

fact.text: A cousin of French brûler, so it is related to the 'brûlée' in crème brûlée, which is literally 'burnt cream'.

senses.note: Uses avere when it takes an object (ho bruciato la carta) and essere when it doesn't (la casa è bruciata). Mi brucia = it stings.
Mi sono bruciato la mano = I burned my hand. Takes essere.

etymology:
From Medieval Latin brūnus "brown, brunet" (whence also Spanish bruno, French brun, Dalmatian broin), from Frankish *brūn, from Proto-Germanic *brūnaz (“brown”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“shining, brown”).
Akin to Old Dutch brūn "brown" (Dutch bruin "brown"), Old High German brūn "brown" (German braun "brown"), Old English brūn "brown". More at brown.

fact.text: From Frankish brūn (brown), ancestor of English 'brown'. Both Germanic languages inherited the word from Proto-Germanic *brūnaz.

etymology: From brusca(re) (“to toast”) + -etta (noun-forming diminutive suffix).

fact.text: From bruscare (to toast) plus the diminutive suffix -etta. The word literally refers to something toasted or burned slightly.

senses.note: Toasted bread topped with tomatoes and garlic

etymology: Derived from Latin brūtus. Doublet of bruto.

fact.text: From Latin brutus, 'heavy, dull, stupid', the root of English 'brute' and 'brutal'. In Italian it shifted to mean ugly or bad, as in brutto tempo, 'bad weather'.

senses.note: Also 'bad, nasty': brutto tempo (bad weather), una brutta notizia (bad news).

etymology: From the verb bucare, from buca, or from either Old Frankish *būk (“cavity, stomach”) or Gothic *𐌱𐌿𐌺𐍃 (*būks), both from Proto-Germanic *būkaz (“belly, torso”). Compare Occitan/Catalan buc ("torso; cow's chest"). More at bouk.

senses.note: Plural buchi. fare un buco nell'acqua = to fail, literally to make a hole in water.
Same form for men and women; plural buddisti (m) / buddiste (f). Also an adjective: monaco buddista.

etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan bauzia, from Old Frankish *bausī (“deceit”) (possibly through a Vulgar Latin *bauscia (compare also Friulian bausie, Dalmatian bosca, Old French boisie), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bausuz (“puffed up, arrogant, bad”). Cognate with Dutch boos, German böse, English boast.

fact.text: From Old Frankish *bausī (deceit) via Old Occitan. The word shares a Germanic root with English 'boast' and German 'böse' (evil). A second meaning, candlestick, comes from Bugia (Béjaïa) in Algeria, a major wax exporter—the same origin as French 'bougie' (candle).

senses.note: Common noun, feminine. Plural: bugie.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *burius (“red, dark”), either from Latin burrus (“reddish-brown”) or, less likely, from Latin furvus (“dark, dusky”).

senses.note: al buio = in the dark; buio pesto = pitch dark. It is also an adjective: dark.

etymology: Literally, “good appetite”.

fact.text: Buon appetito is a universal Italian greeting before meals, literally 'good appetite', used far more commonly than English 'bon appétit'.

senses.note: Said to someone who is about to eat.

fact.text: Many Italians wish luck with 'in bocca al lupo', meaning 'into the wolf's mouth', especially before exams. The usual reply is 'crepi!', meaning 'may it die', not 'thank you'.

senses.note: Before exams or big events, Italians usually say 'in bocca al lupo!' instead.

etymology: Univerbation of buona (“good”) + notte (“night, nighttime”).

fact.text: Besides wishing someone good night, '...e buonanotte!' tacked onto a sentence means 'and that's that!', as in 'Paghi e buonanotte' (you pay and that's the end of it).

senses.note: Also written buona notte. Used when going to bed or leaving late at night.

etymology: Univerbation of buona (“good”) + notte (“night, nighttime”).

fact.text: Besides wishing someone good night, '...e buonanotte!' tacked onto a sentence means 'and that's that!', as in 'Paghi e buonanotte' (you pay and that's the end of it).

senses.note: Often said on its own as a greeting: Buonanotte! As a noun: dare la buonanotte.

etymology: Compare French bonsoir, Romanian bună seara.

fact.text: Italians often switch to buonasera earlier than English speakers say 'good evening'—sometimes as early as 2 or 3 p.m., depending on season.

senses.note: Also spelled buona sera. Used both when arriving and when leaving.

fact.text: Italians often switch to buonasera earlier than English speakers say 'good evening'—sometimes as early as 2 or 3 p.m., depending on season.

senses.note: Said from late afternoon onwards; used earlier than English 'good evening'

etymology: Univerbation of buono (“good”) + giorno (“day”).

senses.note: A polite hello used until about early afternoon; after that, say buonasera.
Used until about early afternoon, then buonasera. Also a polite 'hello' to strangers.

etymology: Inherited from Latin bonus. Doublet of bonus, a later borrowing.

fact.text: Inherited from Latin bonus 'good'. English later borrowed that same Latin word as bonus, which is literally 'a good thing' on top of what you expected.

senses.note: Shortens to buon before most masculine nouns: buon giorno. For 'good at something', use bravo.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French burre, from Latin būtȳrum, from Ancient Greek βούτυρον (boúturon). Doublet of butirro.

fact.text: Not a donkey (that's Spanish burro)! It came via Old French from Greek boúturon, usually explained as 'cow cheese', which is also the source of English butter.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French boiste, whence French boîte (“box”). Derived from Medieval Latin buxida, inflected form derived from Latin buxētum (“boxwood plantation”), from Latin buxus (“boxwood”).

fact.text: Goes back to Latin 'buxus' (boxwood), via Old French 'boiste', now 'boîte' (box). English 'box' also comes from 'buxus'.

senses.note: Also a (plastic or paper) shopping bag: 'una busta della spesa'.

etymology: From Old French bouter (“to strike”), of Germanic origin. Compare Neapolitan vottare and Sicilian vottare.

fact.text: Came in through Old French bouter 'to strike', from a Frankish word meaning 'to beat'. The same Old French verb gave English 'butt', as in head-butt.

senses.note: buttare via = to throw away; buttare la pasta = to put the pasta in the boiling water.

etymology: Borrowed from French cabine.

senses.note: Also booth or cubicle: cabina telefonica = phone box; at the beach = changing hut.

etymology: Deverbal from cacciare + -a, from Late Latin captiāre. Related to English chase, catch.

fact.text: From Latin captiāre (to seize). English 'chase' and 'catch' share this same root through French, making all three words distant cousins.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *captiāre, from Latin captus. Doublet of cazzare.
From Latin cadāver.

fact.text: Comes straight from Latin cadaver, like English 'cadaver'. It is often linked to cadere 'to fall', but that link is not certain.

senses.note: Stress falls on the second syllable: ca-DÀ-ve-re.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cadēre, from Latin cadĕre.

fact.text: From Latin cadere 'to fall', the root behind English cadence, decadent, accident and case, all originally about things that fall or happen.

senses.note: Takes essere: sono caduto/a. Irregular future cadrò and past caddi.

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of cadere (“to fall”).

senses.note: The act of falling, or a sudden drop.

etymology: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قهوه (kahve), from Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa).

fact.text: In Italy, ordering un caffè gets you an espresso by default. The word came through Ottoman Turkish kahve from Arabic qahwa.

senses.note: Also means café or bar. Same form in the plural: i caffè.

etymology: Non-Tuscan variant of calamaio, ultimately from Latin calamus.

fact.text: From Latin calamus (reed), ultimately from Ancient Greek kálamos. The word originally meant reed or writing instrument before referring to squid.

etymology: From Latin calx (“heel”).

fact.text: The sense 'kick' comes from Latin calx, 'heel'. The same Italian word also means calcium, which comes from a different Latin word calx, meaning 'lime'.

senses.note: Giocare a calcio = to play soccer. Un calcio = a kick (plural calci).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin calculāre.

fact.text: From Latin calculus, 'small pebble': Romans counted by moving pebbles on a counting board (abacus).

etymology: Inherited from Latin cal(i)dus. Doublet of calido, which was borrowed.

fact.text: It means hot, not cold! On Italian taps, C stands for caldo (hot) and F for freddo (cold).

senses.note: Also means warm. 'Fa caldo' = it's hot (weather).
As a noun: il caldo. 'Ho caldo' = I'm hot.

etymology:
Origin uncertain. Possibly from Late Latin cauma, from Ancient Greek καῦμα (kaûma, “heat, heat of the sun”). Compare Late Latin caumāre (“to rest during the heat (of the day), to siesta”), Sursilvan Romansh cauma (“resting place for livestock, especially during the noon heat”). If the Italian (and Ibero-Romance) word calma originally referred to the heat of the sun, especially around noon (and later to quiet during this time of the day), it may have been influenced by words like Latin calor (“heat”) and cal(i)dus (“hot”), accounting for cal- instead of the expected cau-.
Compare also Proto-Germanic *kalmaz (“frozenness, cold”).

fact.text: Probably from Greek kauma, 'heat of the sun', via Late Latin cauma: the hush of the hot midday, when everyone rests. Italian calma then passed into French, and English calm came from there.

senses.note: Common phrases: Calma! (Calm down! / Easy!) and con calma (take your time, no rush).

fact.text: English calm came through French from Italian calma, from Late Latin cauma and Greek kauma, meaning burning heat: the stillness of the midday heat, when everything rests.

senses.note: Reflexive, takes essere: mi sono calmato/a. Calmati! = Calm down!

etymology: From calmare (“to calm”) + -o.

senses.note: Stai calmo! = Stay calm! Also used of the sea: mare calmo.

etymology: From Latin calōrem.

fact.text: It comes from Latin calor ('heat'), which also gave English 'calorie': a unit for measuring heat.

senses.note: For hot weather, say fa caldo, not calore. It can also mean warmth (of welcome).

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin calcea, from Latin calceus (“shoe”).

fact.text: On the night before Epiphany (6 January), Italian children hang a stocking for La Befana, a kindly witch who fills it with sweets, or with coal if they've been naughty.

senses.note: Also a sock, but 'calzino' is the usual word for sock. 'Fare la calza' = to knit.

etymology: From cambiare + -mento.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin cambiāre, from change in conjugation of cambīre. Doublet of cangiare. Cognate with Neapolitan cagnà.

fact.text: English 'change' comes from the same Late Latin cambiare, by way of Old French changier. The Latin word is thought to come from Celtic (Gaulish).

senses.note: Also 'to exchange' (e.g. money). Used intransitively it takes essere: è cambiato = he has changed.

etymology: Deverbal from cambiare + -o. From verb cambiare inherited from Vulgar Latin cambiāre (“to change, exchange”) from Late Latin cambiō, or from corresponding noun Latin cambium (“change”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂emp- (“to bend, curve”). Compare Spanish cambio and Portuguese câmbio.

fact.text: Related to English 'change' and 'exchange' — all descended from Latin cambiāre meaning to barter or swap, ultimately from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to bend or curve.

etymology: From Latin camera, from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára). Doublet of zambra.

fact.text: Means room, not camera. English 'camera' is short for camera obscura, Latin for 'dark room'.

senses.note: camera da letto = bedroom. A general room is usually stanza. La Camera = Chamber of Deputies.
Can also mean maid or chambermaid in some contexts

etymology: From camera (“room”) + -iere. Compare Spanish camarero, Late Latin camerārius (“chamberlain”).

fact.text: Built from camera, 'room', so it first meant a servant who looked after someone's rooms. Late Latin camerarius, 'chamberlain', comes from the same root.

senses.note: Feminine: la cameriera (waitress, also maid).

etymology: From Late Latin camisia, from Transalpine Gaulish, of Germanic origin, from Proto-West Germanic *hamiþi.

fact.text: From Late Latin camisia. It is related to French chemise, which English borrowed for a loose undergarment or dress.

senses.note: A button-up shirt. A T-shirt is una maglietta.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French camion.

senses.note: The plural doesn't change: il camion, i camion. British English: lorry.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cammīnāre. By surface analysis, cammino + -are. Compare French cheminer, Spanish caminar and Portuguese caminhar.

senses.note: Walking as movement. For a leisurely stroll, use passeggiare.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cammīnāre. By surface analysis, cammino + -are. Compare French cheminer, Spanish caminar and Portuguese caminhar.

senses.note: Takes avere: ho camminato. For 'to go on foot', use andare a piedi.

etymology: From Late Latin campānia (whence also Spanish campaña, Portuguese and Occitan campanha, French champagne), from campāneus, based on Latin campus (“level field”). Doublet of champagne, borrowed from French.

fact.text: Shares its root with English campaign and champagne, from Latin campus 'field'. Champagne is a region named for its open plains; a campaign was time armies spent in the field.

senses.note: In campagna = in the country. Also means a campaign (electoral, advertising).

etymology: From campana + -ello.

fact.text: Campanello is the diminutive of campana (bell), from Latin campana, showing how Italian shrinks words with -ello to indicate smaller versions.

senses.note: The English loan il camping is also used for a campsite.
Andare in campeggio = to go camping.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English camper.

fact.text: Borrowed from English, but in Italian it only means the vehicle, a motorhome. A person who goes camping is a campeggiatore.

senses.note: Plural doesn't change: i camper. Means the vehicle, never a person who camps.

etymology: From Medieval Latin or Late Latin campiōnem, campiōnem (“champion, fighter”), from Frankish *kampijō (or a Lombardic equivalent) from Proto-Germanic *kampijô, based on Latin campus (“level ground”).

fact.text: It also means 'sample' (un campione di sangue = a blood sample). The word goes back to Latin campus 'field', through a Germanic word for a fighter in the field.

senses.note: Sei un campione! = You're a star! Also: sample (campione di sangue).

etymology: From Latin campus (“wild field”). Compare English camp.

fact.text: From Latin campus, which also gave English camp, campus and champion (someone who fights in the field). In Venice, most town squares are called campo, not piazza.

senses.note: Also a sports pitch or court: campo da calcio, campo da tennis.
campo base, campo profughi. A camping site is a campeggio.

etymology: From Canada + -ese.
Inherited from Latin canālem.

fact.text: English has two words from Latin canalis: channel came through Old French, and canal was borrowed later. Italian covers both meanings with this one word.

senses.note: Also a TV channel and a canal, as in Venice's Canal Grande (Canale Grande).

etymology: From Latin cancellāre. Sense “to cancel” influenced by English cancel.

fact.text: From Latin cancellare, 'to cross out with lattice-like lines', from cancelli 'grating'. English 'chancel' and 'chancellor' come from the same root.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cancrum. Compare the doublet granchio (“crab”), inherited through a Vulgar Latin diminutive form.

fact.text: From Latin cancrum meaning 'crab'. Ancient physicians compared tumours and their swollen veins to a crab's legs. The Italian il cancro also names the zodiac sign Cancer.

senses.note: Medical disease; also the zodiac sign

etymology: From the Latin canis, canem (“dog”). Cognate with Sicilian cani.

fact.text: From Latin canis 'dog', which also gives English canine. The Canary Islands were named after it too: the Romans called them Canariae Insulae, 'islands of dogs'.

senses.note: Masculine: il cane, i cani. A female dog is la cagna.

etymology: From French kangourou, from Guugu Yimidhirr gangurru.

fact.text: Comes from gangurru in Guugu Yimidhirr, an Aboriginal language. Captain Cook's crew wrote it down in 1770. The story that it meant 'I don't understand' is a myth.
Comes from cantare 'to sing', from Latin cantare. The same Latin verb gave English 'chant' and 'cantor', and via Italian, 'cantata'.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: il cantante (man), la cantante (woman). Plural: i/le cantanti.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cantāre, frequentative of canō. Cognate with French chanter, Occitan and Spanish cantar.

fact.text: From Latin cantare, which also gave French chanter and so English 'chant'. The same root is in 'cantata', 'cantor' and 'incantation'.

senses.note: Slang: also 'to squeal, spill the beans' (to the police).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cantherius.

fact.text: Latin cantherius meant a gelding, a castrated horse. It later came to mean a rafter or prop, a supporting frame like the ones used to build ships.

senses.note: Also a shipyard: cantiere navale.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *canthus (“corner”), from Gaulish *cantos, denoting the location for liquor storage, from Proto-Celtic *cantos (“corner”), from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂ndʰ-. Perhaps cognate with Ancient Greek κανθός (kanthós, “corner of the eye”), but this is unconvincing.

fact.text: English canteen comes from this word, through French cantine. It started as a wine cellar or sutler's shop, then became a mess hall and a water flask.

senses.note: Can also mean a winery or wine shop. Cantina sociale = wine cooperative.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cantiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin cantio, from canere 'to sing', which also gives English chant, cantor and canto. In English, canzone names a type of Italian lyric poem.

senses.note: Cantare una canzone = to sing a song.

etymology: From Latin capācem (“capacious; capable, able”).

senses.note: Essere capace di + infinitive = to be able to. Also means roomy or capacious.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin capācitātem.

fact.text: From Latin capax (able to hold). English 'capacity', 'capable' share the same Latin root capere (to take, hold).

senses.note: Invariable noun (no plural). Means both ability/skill and volume/space.

etymology: From Latin capillus.

fact.text: Don't mix it up with cappello (hat): one p is a hair, two p's is a hat. The plural capelli means a head of hair.

senses.note: One strand; a head of hair is plural: i capelli. Body or animal hair is pelo.

etymology:
Etymology tree
substratebor.?
Proto-Indo-European *kap-
Proto-Indo-European *-yéti
Proto-Indo-European *kapyéti
Proto-Italic *kapjō
Archaic Latin kapiō

Inherited from Latin capiō (“to take in, understand”), from Proto-Italic *kapiō, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂pyéti, from the root *kap- (“to seize, grab”). Compare Galician, Spanish, and Portuguese caber (“to fit”), Catalan capir (“to understand”), and German kapieren (“to understand”).

fact.text: From Latin capere 'to take, seize', so understanding is 'grasping' an idea. English capture and capable come from the same root.

senses.note: An -isc- verb: capisco, capisci, capisce. Capito? = Got it?

etymology: Noun use of the above adjective.
Inherited from Late Latin capitaneus, from Latin caput.

fact.text: From caput (head), literally 'the leader'. The title absorbed Byzantine military ranks from the Catepanate of Italy, which also influenced its form.

senses.note: Feminine form capitana exists; comes from caput (head)

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *capitāre, from Latin caput. Compare Romanian căpăta.

fact.text: Comes from Vulgar Latin capitāre, derived from Latin caput (head). The connection between 'head' and 'happen' may reflect how chance events 'come to a head' or arrive unexpectedly.

senses.note: Often used for unexpected or chance events

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput, from Proto-Italic *kaput, from Proto-Indo-European *káput. Doublet of chef.

fact.text: From Latin caput, 'head'. It is a doublet of French chef (literally 'head, chief'), and it is also related to English 'chief' and 'capital'.

senses.note: Also 'head' or 'leader'. Ehi, capo! = hey, buddy! A capo = new paragraph.

etymology: From capo d'anno (literally “head of [the] year”).

fact.text: From capo d'anno, literally 'head of the year', the same image as Hebrew Rosh Hashanah. Capo comes from Latin caput 'head', as in English capital.

senses.note: Usually capitalized; 'a Capodanno' often means the New Year's Eve celebration too.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin cappellus, diminutive from Late Latin cappa.

fact.text: Watch the double p: cappello is a hat, but capello (one p) is a single hair. Mixing them up is a classic learner slip, and Italians find it funny.

senses.note: Don't confuse with capello (a hair). Hat has two p's.

etymology: From cappa.

fact.text: In games and sport, fare cappotto means winning without letting the opponent score at all, a clean sweep or whitewash.

senses.note: A long overcoat. A lighter jacket is a giacca or giubbotto.

etymology: From cappuccio (“hood, cowl”) + -ino. The coffee gets its name from the color of the beverage, which is reminiscent of the color of monks' habits.

fact.text: Named after the Capuchin friars, whose name comes from cappuccio, 'hood'. The coffee's colour reminded people of the brown habits the friars wore.

senses.note: English uses the same word. In Italy it is mostly a breakfast drink, rarely ordered after a meal.

etymology: From carabina + -iere.

fact.text: The Carabinieri is Italy's national gendarmerie force, dating to 1814. Distinct from Polizia di Stato; carabinieri wear distinctive military-style uniforms.

senses.note: member of Carabinieri (Italian gendarmerie)

etymology: From Latin charactērem (““characteristic”, “mark””), from Ancient Greek χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr).

fact.text: From Ancient Greek kharaktḗr, originally meaning a tool for engraving or stamping. The metaphorical leap from 'engraved mark' to 'distinctive feature' to 'personality trait' happened in Greek itself.

senses.note: The letter or symbol itself, as opposed to personality.
A person's distinctive psychological traits and temperament.

etymology: From Latin carcerem, from Proto-Italic *karkros, from Proto-Indo-European *kr-kr- (“circular”), reduplication of *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”), in the sense of “enclosure”. Cognate to Old Catalan càrcer/carçre, Spanish cárcel and Portuguese cárcere.

fact.text: From Latin carcer, from Proto-Indo-European *kr-kr- (circular, enclosure). Related to English 'incarcerate', 'circus', and 'ring'—all trace to the idea of enclosing or turning.

senses.note: Also: jail, imprisonment. Plural 'carceri' is feminine.

etymology: From Late Latin carricāre (“to load, to charge”).

senses.note: office or rank

etymology: From Late Latin carricāre, from Latin carrus. Cognate with Sicilian carricari.

fact.text: From Late Latin carricare 'to load a cart', from carrus 'wagon'. English 'charge' and 'cargo' come from the same root, and 'car' and 'carry' are relatives too.

senses.note: Also: to charge (a phone), to upload (a file). Spelling: carico, carichi.

etymology: From the short past participle of caricare (“to load”) in Tuscan; compare the Standard Italian participle caricato.

senses.note: Also means cargo or shipment; charge of a battery.

etymology: From caro + -ino.

senses.note: Also 'nice' or 'kind': è stato carino da parte tua = that was nice of you.

etymology: Inherited from Latin carnem (“flesh”, “meat”), from Proto-Italic *karō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut off”).

fact.text: From Latin caro, carnis 'flesh', the root of English carnivore, carnal and incarnate. Carnevale is often traced to 'carne levare', removing meat before Lent.

senses.note: Also 'flesh'. Plural carni for kinds of meat: carni bianche, carni rosse.

etymology:
From Latin carnem levāre (“to take away/remove meat”), calque of Ancient Greek ἀπόκρεως (apókreōs). Compare Old Italian carnasciale (“carnival”) from carnem laxāre, Romanian cârneleagă from carnem ligat, Sicilian carnaluvari and carruali, Spanish carnestolendas (“three days preceding the beginning of Lent”) from carnis tollendus.
Other theories suggest it comes from Latin carneālis (“meaty”) or carnuālis (“feast”).

fact.text: Probably from Latin carnem levare, 'to take away meat', since the party comes just before the meatless days of Lent. English 'carnival' was borrowed from this Italian word.

senses.note: Also means the pre-Lent season itself. Famous ones are held in Venice and Viareggio.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cārus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin carus, meaning both beloved and costly, just like English 'dear'. Latin caritas (dearness, love), which comes from it, gave English 'charity'.

senses.note: Also used to open letters: Caro Marco, Cara Anna.
Opposite: economico. Costa caro = it's expensive.

etymology: From Latin carōta, from Ancient Greek κᾰρωτόν (kărōtón).

Borrowed from Old Occitan carreira or its variants (compare modern Occitan carrièra, also French carrière), from Late Latin carrāria, from Latin carrus. Compare the inherited doublet carraia, now archaic.

fact.text: From Old Occitan carreira via Late Latin carrāria, originally from Latin carrus (cart). The sense evolved from a cart's path to a race course to a life course.

etymology: Inherited from Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, “papyrus, paper”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin charta, from Greek khartes, meaning 'papyrus sheet'. English chart, charter and card all come from the same root.

senses.note: Un foglio di carta = a sheet of paper.
Giocare a carte = to play cards.
Also means engine oil sump in a car. Invariable (no separate plural).

etymology: From cartola (“little paper”) + -lina.

senses.note: Mandare una cartolina = to send a postcard.

etymology: From carta (“paper”) + -one (“augmentative suffix”).

fact.text: English 'cartoon' comes from this word. It first meant a full-size drawing on heavy paper that artists used to plan frescoes and tapestries. The word itself is carta (paper) plus the 'big' suffix -one.

senses.note: Also a carton or box (un cartone di latte). Cartoni animati = cartoons.

etymology: Inherited from Latin casa (“house”).

fact.text: English casino comes from Italian casino, meaning 'little house', a diminutive of casa. It first meant a small country house or a social club.

senses.note: a casa = at home / home, with no article: Vado a casa = I'm going home.

etymology: From casale + -ingo; compare Piedmontese casalengh.

senses.note: The feminine casalinga (housewife) is far more common. As an adjective it means homemade.

etymology: From casa + -ino; cognate with Piedmontese casin.

fact.text: False friend: a gambling house is casinò, stressed on the last syllable. Without the accent it means a mess or a racket. Literally 'little house', it also came to mean a brothel.

senses.note: Fare casino = to make a mess or a racket. Un casino di = loads of.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cāsus.

fact.text: It never means a case you carry things in (that's valigia, astuccio or custodia). It also means chance: per caso = by chance, a caso = at random.

senses.note: In caso contrario = otherwise; in ogni caso = in any case; per caso = by chance.

etymology: Inherited from Latin capsa. Doublet of capsa.

fact.text: English cash comes from this word: Middle French casse (money box) was borrowed from Italian cassa, from Latin capsa (box). English case (a box) also comes from capsa.

senses.note: Also the checkout or till in a shop: pagare alla cassa. The person is il cassiere / la cassiera.

etymology: From cassa + -etta (diminutive suffix).

senses.note: Formed from cassetto (drawer) + -iera.

fact.text: Comes from castagna 'chestnut' (Latin castanea), so it literally means chestnut-coloured, which is why it is used for hair and eyes.

senses.note: Used almost only for hair and eyes (capelli castani). For other brown things use marrone.

etymology: Inherited from Latin castellum, diminutive of castrum.

fact.text: From Latin castellum, a diminutive of castrum ('fort'). The word traveled through Romance languages with similar forms—Spanish 'castillo', French 'château'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin captīvus (“captive” → “caught by the devil” → “bad”). Compare the semantic development of French chétif (“puny, scrawny”) and Galician cativo.

fact.text: From Latin captivus, 'prisoner', which came to mean 'held captive by the devil', and so 'bad'. English caitiff, an old word for a villain, has the same origin.

senses.note: For people: mean or naughty (un bambino cattivo). Also bad news or smells: cattive notizie, cattivo odore.

etymology: Inherited from Latin captīvus (“captive” → “caught by the devil” → “bad”). Compare the semantic development of French chétif (“puny, scrawny”) and Galician cativo.

fact.text: From Latin captivus, 'prisoner', which came to mean 'held captive by the devil', and so 'bad'. English caitiff, an old word for a villain, has the same origin.

etymology: From cattura + -are.

fact.text: From the noun cattura (capture), related to Latin captura—the same root as English 'capture'. The -are suffix makes it a regular -are verb.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin causa. Doublet of the inherited cosa. Cognates include English and French cause, Portuguese and Spanish causa.

fact.text: Latin causa also turned into the everyday word cosa, 'thing' (French chose too). So causa and cosa are twin words: one borrowed from Latin, one inherited.

senses.note: a causa di = because of. Also a lawsuit: fare causa a qualcuno = to sue someone.

etymology: From causa + -are.

From Late Latin caballus (“horse”), from Latin caballus (“pack horse”), of disputed origin. Compare Portuguese cavalo, Asturian caballu,
Galician cabalo, Dalmatian caval, Catalan cavall, French cheval, Spanish caballo, Romanian cal,
Corsican cavallu, Sardinian cabaddu, Sicilian cavaḍḍu.

fact.text: From Latin caballus, a colloquial word for a workhorse that replaced the classical equus. English cavalry and chivalry come from the same root.

senses.note: Also means the knight in chess and horsepower (cavalli).
Reflexive pronominal verb: cavarsela. Also: get out of trouble, make the best of something.

etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan cavilla (compare modern cavilha), from Vulgar Latin *cāvic(u)la, from Classical Latin clāvicula, diminutive of clāvis (“key”). Compare the doublets cavicchia (inherited from Latin), clavicola (borrowed from Latin).

fact.text: Goes back to Latin clavicula, 'little key', the same word behind English 'clavicle' (collarbone). Italian also has clavicola for the collarbone itself.

senses.note: Feminine: la caviglia, le caviglie. Slogarsi la caviglia = sprain your ankle.

fact.text: The word literally means cabbage but is also used as a family-friendly exclamation (like 'what the heck!'), standing in for the vulgar cazzo. Its vegetable sense anchors the euphemism.

senses.note: Literally 'cabbage'. Also 'Che cavolo...?' (What the heck...?).

etymology: Derived from Late Latin caulus, from Latin caulis,, through a southern Italian language. Possibly borrowed from Neapolitan cavolo or Sicilian cavulu. Doublet of caule.

fact.text: The word literally means cabbage but is also used as a family-friendly exclamation (like 'what the heck!'), standing in for the vulgar cazzo. Its vegetable sense anchors the euphemism.

etymology: From cazzo + -ata.

fact.text: Made from cazzo (a vulgar word for penis) plus the suffix -ata. Italians say it all the time in casual speech, but it is still vulgar. Stick to sciocchezza in polite company.

senses.note: Dire cazzate = to talk crap. Can also mean a stupid mistake, or something very easy.

etymology:
Of uncertain origin.
The most plausible etymon is Latin captiāre, interjection of the Latin verb captiō (“catching, capture”) as "to chase out", in the sense of to insert, to forcefully put in. Thus, the noun captum as accusative singular of captus (“having been taken in, captured”).
Antonio Lupis concludes that the term cazzo does not derive from cazza ("ladle") because cazzo is an original term from the Umbrian-Tuscan area since 1300CE.
Another possible etymon is Old Italian cazza (“ladle”), from Late Latin cattiam, in turn from Ancient Greek κυάθιον (kuáthion), diminutive form of κύαθος (kúathos, “ladle for wine”); cf. also cazzuola. Another is Byzantine Greek ἀκάτιον (akátion, “mainmast”). See also caspita.

fact.text: Nobody is sure where it comes from. Italians often swap it for milder stand-ins like cavolo (literally 'cabbage') or caspita, much as English speakers say 'heck' or 'darn'.

senses.note: Che cazzo...? = What the fuck...? Very common as a swear word but strongly vulgar.
Form of ci before lo, la, li, le, ne: ce n'è = there is one/some; ce lo dà = he gives it to us.

etymology: From Latin celebrāre.

fact.text: From Latin celebrāre, related to English celebrate—the connection is direct and the words have shared Roman roots for over two millennia.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin celebritātem.

fact.text: From Latin celebritas (crowding, throng), related to celeber (frequent, crowded). English 'celebrity' shares the same root and meaning: someone frequently in the crowd's attention.

senses.note: Invariable noun.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin caelebs (“unmarried”).

fact.text: From Latin caelebs, meaning unmarried or single. The same root produces English celibate.

etymology: From Latin cella, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelnā.

fact.text: Latin cella meant a small room or storeroom, such as the inner chamber of a temple. Latin cellarium, a storeroom, comes from the same word and gave English cellar.

senses.note: Prison, monastery or honeycomb cell. A phone is il cellulare, and a biological cell is usually la cellula.

etymology: From cellula (“cell”) + -are.

fact.text: The word also means a police van for transporting prisoners, named for its small cells. A cell phone is named for the 'cells' of a mobile network.

senses.note: Often shortened to 'il cell'. Telefonino is also common.

etymology: From Latin caementum, uncertain if inherited or borrowed. Cognate to the doublet and variant cimento.

fact.text: Latin caementum first meant rough chips of quarried stone (from caedere, 'to cut'). Later the name passed to the material that binds stones together.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cēna, from Proto-Italic *kertsnā, from Proto-Indo-European *kért-s-nh₂ (“portion”), from *ker-, *sker-. Compare Spanish cena, Portuguese ceia and Romanian cină.

fact.text: Leonardo's Last Supper is L'Ultima Cena in Italian, also called Il Cenacolo. That name comes from Latin cenaculum, 'dining room', which gives English 'cenacle'.

senses.note: The evening meal. Lunch is pranzo; cenare = to have dinner.

etymology: From Latin cēnāre (“to dine”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin cenare, from cena, 'dinner'. Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper is known in Italian as L'Ultima Cena.

senses.note: From cena (dinner). Ceniamo alle otto = we eat dinner at eight.

etymology: From cento (“hundred”) + -esimo (“-th”).

fact.text: Centesimo comes from cento (hundred) + -esimo (ordinal suffix), literally 'hundredth', as it is 1/100 of a euro or earlier currency unit.

etymology: From centi- + metro, modelled on French centimètre.

senses.note: Abbreviated cm. Stress falls on -TI-: cen-TI-me-tro.

fact.text: Irregular plural: un centinaio but due centinaia, which is feminine. It usually means 'about a hundred', like 'a hundred or so'.

etymology: From Latin centum, from Proto-Italic *kəntom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm.
From cento + cinquanta.
From cento + diciannove.
From cento + diciassette.
From cento + diciotto.

fact.text: Italian university degrees are graded out of 110. The top result is 110 e lode (110 with honours), and Italians often say 'centodieci e lode' to mean 'perfect'.

etymology: From cento + dodici.
From cento + due.
From cento (“hundred”) + mila (“thousand”).

fact.text: Mille (a thousand) has a special plural, mila, used for every higher thousand: duemila, centomila. It goes back to Latin mille, whose plural was milia.

etymology: From cento + novanta.
From cento + quaranta.
From cento + quattordici.
From cento + quindici.
From cento + sedici.
From cento + sessanta.
From cento + settanta.
From cento + tredici.
From cento + trenta.
From cento (“hundred”) + tre (“three”).
From cento + ottanta.
From cento + undici.
From cento (“hundred”) + uno (“one”).
From cento + venti.
Borrowed from Latin centrum, from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron, “sharp point”). The nonstandard pronunciation with -é- might be due to influence of entrare.

fact.text: Comes via Latin centrum from Greek kentron, 'sharp point' or 'goad': the fixed point of a drawing compass around which a circle is traced.

senses.note: 'In centro' means downtown, in the city centre.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin circāre, from Latin circa, circus.

fact.text: From Late Latin circare, 'to go around', from circus, 'circle'. Through Old French cerchier, the same verb became English 'search'.

senses.note: No preposition: cerco le chiavi = I'm looking for the keys. Cercare di + infinitive = to try to.

etymology: From Latin circulus, which is derived from circus. Cognate to the borrowed doublet circolo.

fact.text: Its doublet circolo, borrowed straight from Latin circulus, also exists. Circolo usually means a club or association, while this word is the everyday geometric circle.

senses.note: Also a hoop or wheel rim. Fare cerchio = to gather in a circle.

etymology: From Latin Cereālis (“relating to Ceres”), from Cerēs (“goddess of agriculture”).

fact.text: Named after Ceres, the Roman goddess of agriculture and grain. English 'cereal' comes from the same Latin word, Cerealis.

senses.note: Breakfast cereal is usually plural: i cereali.

etymology:
From Latin cērōtum (“wax plaster”), ultimately from Ancient Greek κηρός (kērós, “beeswax”).
Cognate with Piedmontese siròt.

fact.text: Goes back through Latin ceratum, a wax plaster, to Greek keros, 'beeswax'. Early plasters were cloth coated with wax.

senses.note: Also used for medicated patches: cerotto alla nicotina = nicotine patch.

etymology: From certo + -mente.

senses.note: A common polite 'of course!' reply. Similar to certo and sicuramente.

etymology: Inherited from Latin certus.

fact.text: Latin certus began as the past participle of cernere, 'to sift, decide', so something certain was originally something 'decided'. English discern comes from the same root.

senses.note: Before a noun = 'a certain' (una certa altezza); after it = sure (una cosa certa). Certo! = Of course!

etymology: Inherited from Latin certus.

fact.text: Latin certus began as the past participle of cernere, 'to sift, decide', so something certain was originally something 'decided'. English discern comes from the same root.

senses.note: Before a noun it's an adjective: un certo punto = a certain point. Certo! alone = Of course!

etymology: From Latin cerebellum, derived from cerebrum, from Proto-Italic *kerazrom, from a Proto-Indo-European form *ḱerh₂-s-rom, from the root *ḱerh₂- (“head”). The alternative plural cervella derives from the Latin plural form cerebella. Doublet of the borrowing cerebello; cf. the derived cerebellare.

fact.text: It comes from Latin cerebellum, 'little brain', a diminutive of cerebrum. In English anatomy, cerebellum is still the name of the small rear part of the brain.

senses.note: Plural cervelli; le cervella is used for brains as food and in idioms.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *citriŏlum. Doublet of citrullo.
Borrowed from French champagne, from Champagne, from Late Latin campania. Doublet of campagna.

fact.text: Named after the French region Champagne, from Late Latin campania meaning 'open country'. The same root (campania) gives the Italian region Campania.

senses.note: invariable (no plural)

etymology: Borrowed from French chance. Doublet of cadenza.
From Latin quod, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷod.

fact.text: Comes from Latin quod, which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *kʷod. That same ancestor gave Old English hwæt, so it is a distant cousin of English 'what'.

senses.note: Links clauses: 'I know that…'. Unlike English, it is almost never left out.

etymology: From Latin quid (but also usurping some roles of Latin quod), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid, compare *kʷís.

fact.text: Comes from Latin quod, which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *kʷod. That same ancestor gave Old English hwæt, so it is a distant cousin of English 'what'.

senses.note: Introduces clauses: penso che… = I think that… Never dropped as English 'that' can be.
Relative pronoun for people and things: l'amico che ho visto. Also 'what?' in questions.
Used for chaos or noise. 'Che casino!' is a very informal alternative.
Idiomatic expression; anche 'che hai?' more informally
It can also be the formal 'What are you doing?' (Lei). 'Cosa fa?' and 'Che fa?' are also common.

Che + noun! is used for exclamations, with no article.
Che + noun! is used for exclamations: che bello!, che meraviglia!
'Cosa succede?' and 'Che c'è?' are also common.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English check-in.

senses.note: Invariable: i check-in. Fare il check-in = to check in.

etymology: From Latin quis, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís, *kʷos.

fact.text: Comes from Latin qui 'who'. Its Proto-Indo-European root *kʷi- also gave the Germanic hw- words, so it is a distant cousin of English who and what.

senses.note: Takes a singular verb. Chi è? = Who is it? Also 'whoever': di chi paga = about whoever pays.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin chī, from Ancient Greek χεῖ (kheî).

senses.note: Never changes form. 'Di chi è?' = 'Whose is it?'

etymology: Onomatopoeic. Some link it to Old French claquer (“clap, clack, clatter”), which is ultimately from Proto-Germanic *klakōną (“to clap, chirp”). Cognate with Spanish cháchara and French tchatche.

fact.text: Chiacchiere, 'chatter', is also the name of crisp fried Carnival pastries dusted with sugar. They have many regional names, such as frappe, bugie and cenci.

senses.note: Can also mean to gossip. Noun: le chiacchiere (chatter, idle talk).

etymology: From Latin clāmāre, from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to shout”). Doublet of clamare, a borrowing.

fact.text: From Latin clamare 'to shout, call out', the same root as English claim, clamour and exclaim. Latin cl- often became chi- in Italian (clavis → chiave, clarus → chiaro).

senses.note: Also 'to phone'. Chiamarsi = to be called: mi chiamo Anna = my name is Anna.
Reflexive; uses essere as auxiliary. Also means 'to be named.'
Fare una chiamata = to make a call. Can also mean a summons.
chiarire + lo: the object pronoun attaches to the infinitive, which drops its final -e.

etymology: Inherited from Latin clārus. Compare Albanian qartë.

fact.text: English borrowed 'chiaroscuro'—the painting technique of bold light and shadow contrasts—directly from Italian: chiaro (light) plus scuro (dark).

senses.note: Also obvious or plain: è chiaro? = is that clear?
With colours: azzurro chiaro = light blue.

etymology: Inherited from Latin clārus. Compare Albanian qartë.

fact.text: English borrowed 'chiaroscuro'—the painting technique of bold light and shadow contrasts—directly from Italian: chiaro (light) plus scuro (dark).

etymology: From Latin clāvem, from Proto-Italic *klāwis, of ultimately Proto-Indo-European origin.

fact.text: From Latin clavis 'key'. English clavicle (collarbone) comes from clavicula, 'little key', and a musical clef is also named after a key.

senses.note: chiudere a chiave = to lock. Also means a wrench, and a clef in music.

etymology: Inherited from Latin quaerere, with dissimilation of /r–r/ to /d–r/.

fact.text: From Latin quaerere, 'to seek, to ask', which is also the source of English query, quest, question, request and inquire.

senses.note: chiedere qualcosa a qualcuno = to ask someone for something. To ask a question: fare una domanda.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin ecclēsia, a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía, “assembly”).
The original geminated -cc-, though lost in the standard language, is still found in many regional Italian varieties.

fact.text: From Latin ecclesia, from Greek ekklesia 'assembly'. English ecclesiastical comes from the same word.

senses.note: andare in chiesa = to go to church (no article).

etymology: Clipping of chilogrammo.

fact.text: An unrelated identical word means chyle, a digestive fluid. That is why 'fare il chilo' means to have a rest after a big meal, not to put on a kilo.

senses.note: Short for chilogrammo. Un chilo di mele = a kilo of apples. Plural: chili.

etymology: From chilo- + grammo.

senses.note: In everyday speech usually shortened to chilo: un chilo di pane.

etymology: From chilo- + metro.

senses.note: Abbreviated km. Italian spells it with chi-, not k-.

etymology: From chimico (“chemical”).

senses.note: Can also mean 'female chemist' (la chimica); a male chemist is il chimico.

etymology: From a diminutive of Cina (“China”), referring to the fruit's origin.

fact.text: From a diminutive of Cina (China), referring to the fruit's Asian origin. The plant (Citrus myrtifolia) produces bitter oranges used to make the traditional Italian soft drink.

senses.note: Italian citrus plant and bitter soft drink

etymology: From Vulgar Latin quī sapit (“who knows”). Cognate with Spanish and Galician quizá, Portuguese quiçá. By surface analysis, univerbation of chi + sa, literally “who knows”.

fact.text: It's literally 'chi sa?' (who knows?) fused into one word. Spanish 'quizá' (maybe) comes from the same Latin 'qui sapit'.

senses.note: Often used alone or with a clause: chissà se verrà = I wonder if he'll come.

etymology: Borrowed from Arabic قِيثَارَة (qīṯāra), from Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára). Doublet of cetra, inherited from Latin.

fact.text: In Abruzzo a chitarra is also a wooden frame strung with wires. Sheets of fresh pasta are pressed through it to make spaghetti alla chitarra.

senses.note: To play the guitar: suonare la chitarra.

etymology: Inherited from Latin clūdere, variant of claudere.

fact.text: Comes from Latin claudere 'to shut', the same root behind English close, conclude, include and claustrophobia.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle chiuso, passato remoto chiusi. Takes avere. chiudere con qualcuno = to be done with someone.

etymology: From chi (“who”) + -unque (indefinite suffix). Formed similarly to, and possibly influenced by, Latin quicumque. Compare also French quiconque.

senses.note: Singular. Introducing a clause it takes the subjunctive: chiunque sia arrivato.

etymology: Uncertain. Rohlfs and Von Wartburg favoured Late Latin ecce hīc. Maiden casts doubt on this etymology, pointing out that Italian ci is an unstressed 'weak' form, while Latin hic otherwise survives in Italian only in stressed forms (reinforced by Latin ecce or eccum) such as ciò, qua, and qui. (It should also be noted that all of the latter trigger syntactic doubling in a following word, thanks to their original final /k/, while ci does not.) Maiden proposes instead an origin in Latin hince, variant of hinc (“hence, from here, from this person”), pointing out that in parts of southern Italy there exists a 1PL pronoun 'nci (cf. also 'nce). Treccani, on the other hand, proposes an origin in Latin hīce, a variant of hīc (“here”). In any case, the Italian term is certainly cognate with Neapolitan ce, Sicilian cci and Sassarese zi, all three of which share similar adverbial senses, with the latter two also having pronominal senses.

senses.note: C'è / ci sono = there is / there are. Ci vado domani = I'm going there tomorrow.
Also means 'to us' and 'ourselves': ci vedi? = do you see us? ci laviamo = we wash ourselves.

Literally 'we see each other'. Ci vediamo domani = see you tomorrow.
'A presto' is shorter and common at the end of messages. 'Ci vediamo presto' is the full form.

etymology:
Of unknown origin shared with Spanish zapato and French sabot and savate and Sicilian savatta. Possibly from Tatar чабата (çabata, “overshoes”), ultimately either from Ottoman Turkish چاپوت (çaput, çapıt, “patchwork, tatters”), from Ottoman Turkish چاپمق (çapmak, “to slap on”), or of Iranian origin, cognate with modern Persian چپت (čapat, “a kind of traditional leather shoe”).
The bread type and the meaning power strip are built upon analogy as something long and thin of comparable size to the shoe-wear.

fact.text: Origin unknown but shared with Spanish zapato and French sabot. Possibly from Tatar çabata (overshoes), or Persian čapat, a traditional leather shoe.

etymology: Borrowed from Venetan s-ciao, sciavo (“slave”) (in particular the expression s-ciao vostro (literally “(I am) your slave”), in essence meaning "I am at your service", or "your humble servant"), from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”) (whence also standard Italian schiavo); in the Venetan language originally pronounced /stʃaʊ/. Development and use is similar to the Southern German and Central European greeting of servus and Swedish tjena.

fact.text: From Venetian s-ciao (vostro), 'I am your slave', a polite way of saying 'at your service'. It goes back to Medieval Latin sclavus, 'slave', like the Central European greeting servus.

senses.note: Means both hello and goodbye, but only with friends. Formal: buongiorno / arrivederci.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *cisque-unus, from Latin quisque ūnus, and influenced by cadauno. Cf. French chacun, Catalan cadascun.

fact.text: Related to French chacun and cognate with English 'each': both descend from Latin quisque unus ('each one') through Romance and Germanic paths respectively.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin cibus. Contrast Portuguese cevo and Spanish cebo (“bait”).

fact.text: Taken from Latin cibus, 'food'. The same Latin word survives in Spanish as cebo, but there it has narrowed to mean 'bait'.

senses.note: Usually uncountable, like English 'food'. Plural cibi = foods, dishes.

etymology: From Latin caecus, from Proto-Italic *kaikos (“blind”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ikos (“one-eyed”).

fact.text: From Latin caecus (blind). The anatomical term caecum—the pouch where the appendix connects—takes its name from the same root: it is the 'blind' gut, closed at one end.

senses.note: Also a noun: un cieco, a blind man. Vicolo cieco = dead end.

etymology: From Latin caecus, from Proto-Italic *kaikos (“blind”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ikos (“one-eyed”).

fact.text: From Latin caecus (blind). The anatomical term caecum—the pouch where the appendix connects—takes its name from the same root: it is the 'blind' gut, closed at one end.

etymology: From Latin caelum, from Proto-Italic *kailom, from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂i-lom (“whole”), from *keh₂i-.

fact.text: From Latin caelum, 'sky, heaven', the same root as English celestial.

senses.note: Also heaven: Santo cielo! (Good heavens!). Plural cieli.

etymology: From Latin cȳma, from Ancient Greek κῦμα (kûma).

fact.text: Comes from Latin cyma, a young cabbage sprout, from Greek kûma ('swelling, wave'). That is why turnip greens are called cime di rapa.

senses.note: in cima a = at the top of: in cima alla montagna.

etymology: From Late Latin coemeterium, Ancient Greek κοιμητήριον (koimētḗrion).

fact.text: From Greek koimeterion, 'sleeping chamber', from koimao, 'to put to sleep'. Early Christians thought of the dead as sleeping. English cemetery has the same origin.
Came through English chin-chin, from Chinese qing qing, a polite greeting that Western traders picked up in Chinese ports. In Italian it now also sounds like glasses clinking.

senses.note: Said while clinking glasses. Salute! is the other common toast.

fact.text: Thought to come from Chinese qing qing, a polite greeting, which sailors picked up in Chinese ports. The clinking sound of glasses helped it catch on.

senses.note: Said when clinking glasses. 'Salute!' is the common alternative.

etymology: Borrowed from French cinéma, from Ancient Greek κίνημα (kínēma, “movement”).

fact.text: It's short for French cinématographe, from Greek kinema, 'movement'. Moving pictures share that Greek root with the English words kinetic and kinematics.

senses.note: Invariable: i cinema. 'Andare al cinema' = to go to the movies.

etymology: From Cina + -ese.

fact.text: From Italian Cina (China) plus the suffix -ese, meaning relating to a place — used for many nationalities and languages (inglese, francese, giapponese).

etymology: Inherited from Latin cīnquāgintā.
From cinquanta (“fifty”) + cinque (“five”).
From cinquanta (“fifty”) + due (“two”).
From cinquanta (“fifty”) + nove (“nine”).
From cinquanta (“fifty”) + quattro (“four”).
From cinquanta (“fifty”) + sei (“six”).
From cinquanta (“fifty”) + sette (“seven”).
From cinquanta (“fifty”) + tre (“three”).

fact.text: Tre on its own has no accent, but at the end of a compound number it takes one: ventitré, cinquantatré, centotré.

etymology: From cinquanta (“fifty”) + otto (“eight”).

fact.text: Tens drop their final vowel before otto and uno, so it is cinquantotto rather than cinquantaotto, and likewise cinquantuno.

etymology: From cinquanta (“fifty”) + uno (“one”).
Inherited from Latin cīnque.
