fact.text: From Latin quinque, which became cinque in spoken Latin. English relatives include quintet, plus cinquefoil and the Cinque Ports, which came in through French cinq.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cīnque.

fact.text: From Latin quinque, which became cinque in spoken Latin. English relatives include quintet, plus cinquefoil and the Cinque Ports, which came in through French cinq.

etymology: From cinque (“five”) + cento (“hundred”).

fact.text: Il Cinquecento is the 1500s, meaning the 16th century of the High Renaissance. Una Cinquecento is also the classic small Fiat 500 car.

etymology: From cinque + mila.

fact.text: One thousand is mille, but from two thousand on Italian uses the plural form -mila (duemila, cinquemila), inherited from Latin mille and its plural milia.

etymology: From Spanish chocolate, from Classical Nahuatl chocolātl.

fact.text: Came into Italian through Spanish chocolate, which was borrowed from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, after the Spanish conquest of Mexico.

senses.note: Hot chocolate is usually la cioccolata (calda).

fact.text: Literally 'that is': it is ciò ('that') + è ('is') joined into one word, just like the English phrase it translates.

senses.note: Also a very common filler in speech, like 'I mean…' or 'like…'.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cēpulla, diminutive of Latin cēpa.

fact.text: It comes from Late Latin cepulla, 'little onion', which comes from Latin cepa. The same word cepa went into Old French as cive, which gave English the word 'chives'.

senses.note: Feminine: la cipolla, le cipolle.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin circā.

fact.text: In English, circa (c.) is mostly used with dates. In Italian it is an everyday word for 'about' with any number: costa circa venti euro.

senses.note: Comes before numbers: circa dieci minuti. Formally, also means 'concerning': circa la questione.
l'area circostante = the surrounding area. As a noun, i circostanti = the bystanders.

etymology: Derived from Latin citāre (“to summon”), from cieō (“move, stir”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱey-.

fact.text: Related to English 'cite'; both descend from Latin citāre meaning to summon or set in motion.

senses.note: Also means to sue or to summon in legal contexts.

etymology: From cittadino + -anza.

fact.text: From cittadino (citizen) plus the suffix -anza, which forms nouns from adjectives (like English -ance/-ency).

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cīvitātem (“city”). Doublet of city.

fact.text: From Latin civitas 'citizenship, city', which became Old Italian cittade and then città. English 'city' comes from the same word, and 'civic' and 'civil' share its root.

senses.note: Same form in the plural: le città. in città = in town / downtown.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English city. Doublet of città.

fact.text: City is an unadapted English borrowing in Italian, while città (from Latin civitas) is the native word for 'city'. Both now coexist—city refers specifically to financial districts.

senses.note: Borrowed from English; used in Italian for the City of London or similar finance hubs.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin ecce hoc, from ecce (“behold, voilà”) + hoc (“this”). Compare Sicilian zoccu, Catalan açò, French ce.

fact.text: From Latin ecce hoc, 'behold this', which was gradually worn down to ciò. It refers only to things, ideas or statements, never to people.

senses.note: Ciò che = what (that which). Slightly formal; in speech quello che is more common.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin classis.

fact.text: Latin 'classis' may come from a root meaning 'to call out', the root behind 'clamor'. Romans used it for citizens called up for military service, and later for social ranks.

senses.note: School class, classroom, social class or style: 'avere classe' = to have class.

etymology: From Latin classicus (“relating to the classes of Roman citizenry, especially the highest”), from classis.

fact.text: Latin classicus first meant a Roman citizen of the highest property class. Later, a first-rate writer was called 'classic', and the meaning 'top quality' stuck.

senses.note: Also 'classical' (musica classica) and 'typical' (il classico errore = the typical mistake).
Regular -care verb: adds h before e/i (clicchi, cliccherò). Cliccare su un link.

etymology: From Latin clientem.

fact.text: From Latin cliens: in ancient Rome a client was a dependant who owed loyalty to a powerful patron in return for protection.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: il cliente / la cliente. Also means client, or a guest in a hotel.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin clīma, from Ancient Greek κλῐ́μᾰ (klĭ́mă, “region, zone”), from κλῐ́νω (klĭ́nō, “to slope, incline”).

fact.text: From Greek klima, meaning 'slope' or 'zone', from klinein 'to incline'. Ancient geographers split the world into zones by the slope of the sun's rays. English incline and recline share the root.

senses.note: Masculine despite the -a: il clima, i climi. It can also mean atmosphere or mood (un clima teso).

etymology: Borrowed from French clinique, ultimately from Ancient Greek κλινική (klinikḗ).

fact.text: Comes ultimately from Greek kline, 'bed'. Clinical medicine was the medicine practised at the patient's bedside.

senses.note: Often means a private hospital. La clinica can also be clinical medicine as a discipline.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English club.

senses.note: English loanword, stays the same in the plural: i club.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English coach.

senses.note: Invariable; borrowed directly from English.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English Coca-Cola. Genericized trademark.

senses.note: Trademark; often used generically for cola drinks in Italian.

etymology: From Portuguese coco. Doublet of cocco (“cochineal”) and coque.

fact.text: From Portuguese coco. The Portuguese word itself may derive from a Malay or Sanskrit root relating to the head, due to the coconut's appearance.

senses.note: Also: coconut palm tree, or colloquially, darling/pet.

etymology: From Latin cōda, monophthongized variant of cauda.

fact.text: From Latin cōda (tail). English inherited 'coda' (musical tail section) and 'queue' comes from the same root via French. Expressions like fare la coda (to queue) preserve the original sense.

senses.note: Also: a queue or line (fare la coda = to queue). Musical coda also comes from this word.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin cōdicem.

fact.text: From Latin codex (caudex), 'tree trunk, block of wood': early books were made from wooden tablets, so the word came to mean a book, then a code of laws.

etymology: From Latin colligere.

fact.text: From Latin colligere 'to gather together', the same root as English 'collect'. The phrase cogliere l'occasione ('seize the opportunity') uses the same verb.

senses.note: Irregular verb; past participle is colto.

etymology: From Late Latin cōleōnem, derived from Latin cōleus (“sack, scrotum”).

senses.note: Literally 'testicle'. rompere i coglioni = to annoy someone (vulgar).

etymology: Feminine of cognato.

senses.note: Feminine form; masculine is 'cognato'.

etymology: From Latin cognātus (“related by blood”), from cum (“with”) + nātus (“born”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin cognatus, 'related by blood' (cum 'with' + natus 'born'). English 'cognate', used for related words in different languages, comes from the same source.

senses.note: Feminine: la cognata (sister-in-law).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cognomen.

fact.text: Latin 'cognomen' was a Roman's extra name or nickname, like Caesar in Gaius Julius Caesar. Literally 'with-name'; the g crept in from association with 'cognoscere' (to know).

senses.note: 'Nome' is the first name; 'cognome' is the family name.

etymology: From coincidere + -enza (compare Latin coincidentia).

fact.text: At Italian stations and airports this word usually means a connection. Your train 'coincides' with the next one, so you can change.

senses.note: Also means a connecting train or flight: perdere la coincidenza = to miss the connection.

etymology: From Latin collātiōnem (“putting together, meeting”). Originally it was the name of the meal that monks ate after the evening meeting. Doublet of collazione.

fact.text: From Latin collatio. Monks ate a light meal after their evening meeting, which was called the collatio. English 'collation', meaning a light meal, has the same origin.

senses.note: fare colazione = to have breakfast.

etymology: From collaborare + -tore.

senses.note: Co-worker, colleague, or contributor to publications.

etymology: From collo.

fact.text: It comes from collo, 'neck', from Latin collum. That Latin word also gives English 'collar'.

senses.note: Also a book series from a publisher: una collana di gialli.

etymology: From Latin collēga.

senses.note: il/la collega; plurals: i colleghi (m), le colleghe (f).

etymology: From Latin colligāre.
Borrowed from Latin collēgium.

fact.text: Watch out: it looks like 'college', but it usually means a boarding school. For college in the sense of university, Italians say università.

senses.note: Also an electoral constituency or a professional body. A university college is usually università.

etymology: From collezione + -are.

senses.note: For stamps, coins etc. For gathering things in general use raccogliere.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin collēctiōnem.

senses.note: For things gathered as a hobby or a fashion line. A money collection is a colletta.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin collīna, from the feminine of Latin collīnus, from collis (“hill”) + -ina, from Proto-Indo-European *kl̥Hnís (“top, hill, rock”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin collis ('hill'), which is distantly related to English 'hill' itself. Both go back to an Indo-European root meaning 'high' or 'prominent'.

etymology:
From Latin collum, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷolsom, derived from the root *kʷel- (“to turn”).
Cognate with French cou, Galician and Portuguese colo, Sicilian coḍḍu, Spanish cuello.

fact.text: It can also mean a parcel or piece of luggage. Shipping labels and airline forms count packages as colli.

senses.note: Also the neck of a bottle. A rotta di collo = at breakneck speed.

etymology: From collocare + -mento.

senses.note: Can mean job placement, arrangement of objects, or financial placement (securities).

etymology: From co- + -loquio, from Latin colloquium.

fact.text: Italian has two words for English 'interview': a job interview or private meeting is un colloquio, while a journalist's interview is un'intervista.

senses.note: Colloquio di lavoro = job interview. A press interview is un'intervista.

etymology: From colonna + -ello (diminutive suffix).

fact.text: From Italian colonna (column) with the diminutive suffix -ello, meaning 'little column'—the officer leading a column of troops. English 'colonel' comes from this Italian word via French, but it's pronounced 'kernel' due to an older form, coronel.

senses.note: Military rank; commander of a regiment.

etymology: From Latin colōrāre.

fact.text: Watch out: coloro can mean 'I color', but it is also a common pronoun meaning 'those people', as in 'coloro che partono' (those who leave).

senses.note: Regular -are verb: colorare un disegno = to color in a drawing.

etymology: From Latin colōrem, from Old Latin colos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to hide, conceal”).

fact.text: Latin color comes from a root meaning 'to hide, conceal', probably because colour is the surface that covers a thing. English conceal comes from the same root.

senses.note: Masculine, even though it ends in -e: il colore, i colori. 'Di che colore è?' = What colour is it?

etymology: Inherited from Latin culpa, from Proto-Italic *kʷolpā (“wrong, mistake”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷolp-eh₂ (“bend, turn”), from *kʷelp-.

fact.text: It comes from Latin culpa (fault, guilt), which also gave English 'culpable' and the phrase 'mea culpa', literally 'my fault'.

senses.note: È colpa mia = it's my fault. Dare la colpa a qualcuno = to blame someone.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin culpābilis.
By surface analysis, colpa + -evole.
Doublet of colpabile, which is borrowed.

fact.text: From Latin culpābilis (blameable). The Italian word works both as adjective (guilty) and noun (the guilty party, culprit).

senses.note: Also adjective: guilty

etymology: From colpo + -ire.

fact.text: Comes from colpo 'blow', which goes back through Latin colaphus to Greek kolaphos 'punch'. French coup, as in coup d'état, has the same origin.

senses.note: An -isc- verb (colpisco). Also used figuratively: mi ha colpito = it struck or impressed me.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin colpus, from Latin colaphus from Ancient Greek κόλαφος (kólaphos). Doublet of golfo.

fact.text: From Latin colpus via Greek kolaphos 'punch'. The same root produced French coup, as in 'coup d'état' (literally 'blow of state'), which became an English word too.

etymology: From Latin cultellus (“small knife, dagger”), diminutive of culter (“knife”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin cultellus, 'little knife'. English 'cutlass' comes from Italian coltellaccio, 'big nasty knife', by way of French coutelas.

senses.note: Forchetta e coltello = knife and fork (Italian puts the fork first).

etymology: Contracted from Vulgar Latin *eccum illui, (genitive-)dative masculine singular of *eccum ille, under the influence of Latin cui (“to whom”). Compare French celui. and Romanian acelui.

senses.note: Mostly used as 'colui che'. Feminine colei, plural coloro. In everyday speech people say 'quello che'.

etymology: From comandare.

fact.text: Derived from comandare (to command), which comes from Vulgar Latin commandare, built from com- (together) and mandare (to entrust).

senses.note: Of a ship or aircraft.

fact.text: From Latin commendāre, to entrust or commit; the noun evolved from the idea of something entrusted as an order. Related to English 'commend' and 'command' through the same root.

senses.note: order given by someone in authority; also the headquarters of a military unit

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *combattere, from Latin cum + battuō.

fact.text: From Latin cum + battuere, 'to beat together'. Battuere also gave English 'battle', 'battery' and 'batter', and of course 'combat'.

senses.note: Combattere contro (against) / per (for). Also used figuratively: combattere la povertà.

etymology: From combattere + -mento.
Borrowed from Late Latin combīnāre.
Inherited from Late Latin quōmodo et.

fact.text: Nothing to do with English 'come' (that's venire). It comes from Latin quomodo, 'in what way', shortened in Late Latin and combined with et.

senses.note: Come stai? = How are you?
Bianco come la neve = white as snow.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin quōmodo et.

fact.text: Nothing to do with English 'come' (that's venire). It comes from Latin quomodo, 'in what way', shortened in Late Latin and combined with et.

senses.note: Come stai? = How are you?
Un amico come Bruno = a friend like Bruno.

fact.text: Nothing to do with English 'come' (that's venire). It comes from Latin quomodo, 'in what way', shortened in Late Latin and combined with et.

senses.note: Com'è? = What is it like? It also means 'like' or 'as': come te (like you).
'Come al solito' is a common synonym.
Impersonal 'si'. E.g., Come si dice 'apple' in italiano?
Uses impersonal 'si': literally 'how is … written?'

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin quōmodo et.

senses.note: Before 'è', 'come' becomes 'com'' (Com'è?).

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cominitiāre.

fact.text: Comes from Vulgar Latin *cominitiare (com- + initiare, 'to begin'). English 'commence' comes from the same root, via French commencer.

senses.note: Takes avere with an object (ho cominciato il libro), essere without one (il film è cominciato). Cominciare a + infinitive.

etymology: Derived from Latin cōmoedia.

fact.text: Dante called his poem just Commedia because it moves from misery to a happy ending and is written in everyday language. Boccaccio later added 'Divina'.

senses.note: Also 'an act, a sham': fare la commedia = to put on an act.

etymology: From Latin commentārī.

fact.text: From Latin commentārī (to devise, contrive). Related to English 'comment' and 'commentary'.

etymology: From Latin commentum.

fact.text: From Latin commentum, the root also gave English 'comment'. Both languages inherited the meaning from Latin.

etymology: From Latin commercium.

fact.text: From Latin commercium: con- ('together') + merx ('merchandise'). The same root as English 'commerce'.

senses.note: Commerce and business; also the merchants/traders collectively.

etymology: From Latin commissus.

senses.note: Feminine: la commessa.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin commissiōnem.

fact.text: In everyday speech, 'fare commissioni' ('to run commissions') means to do errands, not to earn commissions or sit on committees. This colloquial use dominates modern Italian.

senses.note: Phrase 'fare commissioni' means 'to run errands', the most common everyday use.

etymology: From French commode + -ino.

fact.text: From French commode (a chest of drawers) plus the diminutive -ino, so it is literally a 'little commode'. English commode comes from the same French word.

senses.note: Also translated as 'bedside table'.

etymology: From Latin commodus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin commodus, 'convenient, fitting'. English 'commodity' and 'accommodate' come from the same root.

senses.note: Stress on the first syllable: CÒ-mo-do. Also means convenient or handy.

etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

fact.text: From Late Latin companio, 'one who shares bread' (com 'with' + panis 'bread'). English companion and company come from the same idea.

senses.note: Partner in a relationship; also companion, classmate (compagna di classe) or comrade.

etymology: Derived from older compagna (assimilated to -ia), from Vulgar Latin *compānia. By surface analysis, compagna (“companion”) + -ia (abstract noun-forming suffix).

fact.text: From Latin com- (with) + panis (bread). Your company were literally the people you shared bread with. English 'companion' has the same origin.

senses.note: Means both companionship and a business. Compagnia aerea = airline.

etymology: From Late Latin compāniō (nominative form), a calque of Proto-West Germanic *gahlaibō. Doublet of compagnone, which came via the Latin accusative compāniōnem.

fact.text: From Late Latin companio, built from com- 'with' and panis 'bread': someone you share bread with. It copied a Germanic word built the same way, and it's also where English 'companion' comes from.

senses.note: Also partner or comrade. Compagno di classe = classmate. Feminine: compagna.

etymology: From Latin compīlāre.

fact.text: Its most common meaning is 'to fill in': compilare un modulo means filling out a form, not compiling one.

senses.note: Compilare un modulo = to fill out a form. Can also mean to compile or draw up a list.
Plural: i compiti (per casa). Singular il compito = a task, or a written test (compito in classe).

etymology: Deverbal from compitare (“to spell; to enunciate”) + -o.

fact.text: Watch the stress: còmpito means task or homework, while compìto is an adjective meaning polite or well-mannered.

senses.note: Stress on the first syllable: còmpito.
Usually plural: fare i compiti, 'to do homework'.

etymology: Partial calque of Spanish cumpleaños and adapted to fit Italian anno (“year”) and perhaps compiere.

fact.text: Partly copied from Spanish cumpleaños ('completes years') and reshaped to fit Italian anno (year), probably also influenced by compiere (to complete).

senses.note: Buon compleanno! = Happy birthday! Compiere gli anni = to have a birthday.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin complēmentum. Doublet of complimento.

fact.text: A doublet of complimento (compliment). Both go back to Latin complere, 'to fill up', and English has the same pair: complement and compliment.

senses.note: Common in grammar: complemento oggetto = direct object.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin complexus.

fact.text: From Latin complexus (woven together), from com- (together) + plectere (to weave). English 'complex' is cognate with identical root meaning.

etymology: From completo + -mente.
Borrowed from Latin completus.

fact.text: On a hotel, campsite or bus sign, this word means full, with no places left. It works like the English 'no vacancies'.

senses.note: Also 'full': a hotel or bus showing 'completo' has no places left. As a noun, un completo = a suit/outfit.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin completus.

fact.text: On a hotel, campsite or bus sign, this word means full, with no places left. It works like the English 'no vacancies'.

senses.note: Also a matching outfit or set. As an adjective it means complete, or full.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin complicāre.

senses.note: Reflexive complicarsi = to get complicated: la situazione si complica.

etymology: Borrowed from Spanish cumplimiento. Doublet of complemento.

fact.text: Complimenti! means 'congratulations!', and non fare complimenti means 'don't stand on ceremony, help yourself'. The word came into Italian from Spanish cumplimiento, 'doing what is proper'.

senses.note: Complimenti! = Congratulations!/Well done! Non fare complimenti = help yourself, don't be shy.

etymology: From comportarsi + -mento.

senses.note: Conduct, actions, ways of acting.

etymology: From Latin comportāre.

senses.note: Reflexive, takes essere: Si è comportato bene. Comportati bene! = Behave yourself!

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *comperāre, from Latin comparāre (“to prepare, procure, get, purchase, obtain”), from cum + parō. Compare Portuguese and Spanish comprar, Romanian cumpăra.

fact.text: Comes from Latin comparare 'to procure', built on parare 'to prepare', the root of English 'prepare'. English 'compare' only looks related: it comes from a different Latin verb, from par 'equal'.

senses.note: Regular -are verb: compro, compri, compra. 'Comprare casa' = to buy a house.

etymology: From Latin comprendere, variant of comprehendere.

fact.text: Related to English 'comprehensive' and 'comprehend' — all three derive from Latin comprendere (com- 'with' + prehendere 'to seize'), so 'to understand' originally meant 'to grasp' something mentally.

senses.note: Often means 'to grasp' mentally or intellectually; also 'to include, comprise'

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English computer.

fact.text: Like most foreign loanwords in Italian, it doesn't change in the plural: il computer, i computer.

senses.note: Invariable: il computer, i computer.

etymology: From Latin commūne, noun use of the neuter form of commūnis.

fact.text: It comes from Latin communis, 'shared, common', the same root as English common, community and commune. A comune is the town that its residents share.

senses.note: Also the town council or town hall: andare in comune. As an adjective, comune means 'common'.

etymology: From Latin commūnicāre.

senses.note: comunicare qualcosa a qualcuno = to inform someone of something. Spelling change: comunichi, comunichiamo.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin commūnicātiōnem (“sharing, communication”).

senses.note: Also a message or notice: una comunicazione importante.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin commūnitātem.

fact.text: From Latin commūnitātem. Both Italian 'comunità' and English 'community' descend from the same Latin root, maintaining identical meaning.

senses.note: Invariable noun; covers all senses of English 'community'.

etymology: From come (“how”) + -unque (indefinite suffix).

fact.text: Built from come 'how' + the indefinite suffix -unque, the same ending found in chiunque 'whoever' and dovunque 'wherever'. So its literal meaning is 'however'.

senses.note: Also 'however' as a conjunction: comunque vada = however it goes.

etymology: From come (“how”) + -unque (indefinite suffix).

fact.text: Built from come 'how' + the indefinite suffix -unque, the same ending found in chiunque 'whoever' and dovunque 'wherever'. So its literal meaning is 'however'.

senses.note: Also 'however, in any case'. With the subjunctive: comunque vada = however it goes.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cum (“with”), from Proto-Italic *kom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm (“next to, at, with, along”).

fact.text: From Latin cum 'with', which lives on in the English prefixes com- and con-. A companion is literally someone you share bread (Latin panis) with.

senses.note: Can merge with the article: col = con il, coi = con i.

etymology: Borrowed from French concentrer.

fact.text: From French concentrer (con- + centrer). Cognate with English 'concentrate'. Same root as Latin centrum.

senses.note: transitive; also reflexive concentrarsi

etymology: Deverbal from concertare + -o.

fact.text: English took 'concerto' straight from Italian, and 'concert' itself came via French from Italian concerto, from concertare, 'to bring into agreement'.

senses.note: Also the musical form 'concerto'. Andare a un concerto = to go to a concert.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin conclūdere.

fact.text: From Latin conclūdere, literally 'to close together' (con- + claudere). Related to English 'clause'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin conclūsiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin concludere (to close, conclude) + -tion suffix. The Latin root con- (together) + claudere (to shut) literally means to shut together or close off a discussion.

etymology: From concorrere + -enza.

senses.note: Commercial rivalry; also refers to competitors

etymology: From Latin concursus.

fact.text: In Italy most public-sector jobs, including teaching posts, are filled through a concorso, a competitive exam. Thousands of candidates may compete for a handful of places.

senses.note: Business competition is concorrenza. Concorso pubblico = a competitive exam for a public-sector job.

etymology: From Late Latin condamnāre, from Latin condemnāre (“I condemn, convict, sentence”), from con- + damnō (“to discredit, find fault, disapprove, reject; to sentence someone to a punishment, declare guilty, condemn, doom, convict”), from damnum (“damage, injury, loss”).

fact.text: From Latin condemnāre, built from con- (with, together) + damnō (to condemn). The root damnum (damage, loss) lives on in English 'damn' and 'damage'.

senses.note: often legal: to sentence or convict; also: to express disapproval of

etymology: From con- + dividere.

senses.note: Past participle: condiviso. Conjugates like dividere.

etymology: From condizione + -are.

senses.note: Lasciarsi condizionare = to let oneself be influenced. Aria condizionata = air conditioning.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin conditiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin conditiōnem, the accusative of conditiō. Shares the same root as English 'condition' — both languages borrowed from Latin.

etymology: From condolersi + -anza.

senses.note: Almost always plural: 'Condoglianze!' = My condolences.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin condominium (17th century).

fact.text: From Latin con- (together) + dominium (ownership), so it literally means 'joint ownership'. English condominium, and so condo, comes from the same Latin word.

senses.note: Also the residents as a group, or co-ownership: riunione di condominio = residents' meeting.

etymology: Inherited from Latin condūcere (“to lead, bring or draw together”), from con- + dūcō (“lead”). By surface analysis, syncopic form of (archaic) conducere.

fact.text: From Latin conducere, con- 'together' + ducere 'to lead', the source of English conduct. A conduttore is a conductor, of a train or of electricity.

senses.note: Irregular (from old conducere): conduco, condussi, condotto, future condurrò.

etymology: From Latin cōnfirmāre.

fact.text: From Latin cōnfirmāre, meaning to make firm or strengthen. Related to English confirm through the same root.

etymology: From Latin cōnfīnis.

fact.text: From Latin confinis, 'sharing a boundary' (con- 'with' + finis 'end, limit'). English 'confines' and 'to confine' come from the same root.

senses.note: Can be a national border or any boundary or limit, literal or figurative.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin cōnfrontāre.

fact.text: From Medieval Latin cōnfrontāre (con- + front-, to place side by side). Cognate with English 'confront'.

senses.note: transitive; can also mean collate or confront

etymology: Deverbal from confrontare + -o.

senses.note: Also: confrontation or collation. Common phrase: 'a confronto' (by comparison).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cōnfūsiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin cōnfundō (to pour together, mix up). English "confuse" comes from the same source, both literally meaning 'to mix or blend together'.

senses.note: Feminine. Plural: confusioni. Also means 'chaos', 'mess', 'bustle'.

etymology: From Latin cōnfūsus.

senses.note: Also 'muddled' or 'hazy' (un ricordo confuso). It agrees: confuso, confusa, confusi, confuse.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin congrātulātiōnem, from congrātulor.

senses.note: Almost always in the plural: Congratulazioni! = Congratulations!
Always plural. 'Complimenti!' is a common, more casual alternative.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin coniugāre.

fact.text: Borrowed from Latin coniugāre. English "conjugate" comes from the same root, making it a cognate word across the Romance languages.

senses.note: Transitive verb; also means to marry or combine.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin coniugem.

fact.text: From Latin coniugem. English "conjugal" (relating to marriage) comes from the same root, from Latin coniugālis. Both languages use the same Latin source for married concepts.

senses.note: Gender-neutral for either husband or wife.
Connettersi a internet / al Wi-Fi. Past participle: connesso (mi sono connesso).

etymology: From Latin cōnus, from Ancient Greek κῶνος (kônos).

fact.text: Shares the same Ancient Greek root (kônos) as English 'cone', making both words geometrical siblings separated by Latin.

etymology: From Late Latin cognōscentia, from Latin cognōscēns.

fact.text: It comes from Latin cognoscere, 'to get to know', which also gave English recognize, cognition and, through French, connoisseur. English cognoscenti, 'people in the know', was borrowed from Italian.

senses.note: Also 'acquaintance': fare la conoscenza di qualcuno = to meet someone. Plural conoscenze can mean contacts.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin conōscere, variant of Latin cognōscere.

fact.text: Comes from Latin cognoscere, the same verb behind English recognize, cognition and cognizant.

senses.note: For people and places; use sapere for facts. In the past tense, ho conosciuto means 'I met'.

etymology: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *conquisitāre, derived from Latin conquisitus, perfect passive participle of conquirō. Cf. also conquista. Compare Occitan, Catalan, Portuguese, and Spanish conquistar.

senses.note: Also 'to win over' someone, as in l'hai conquistato? = did you win him over?

etymology: Deverbal from consegnare + -a.
Borrowed from Latin cōnsignāre and adapted to native Italian segnare.

fact.text: From Latin consignare, 'to mark with a seal' (con- + signare, 'to mark'). It is the same source as English 'consign': you hand something over once it has been sealed.

senses.note: Consegnare i compiti = to hand in homework; la consegna = delivery.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cōnsequentia.

fact.text: From Latin cōnsequentia. Same root as English 'consequence', 'consequent', 'subsequent'—all from sequī (to follow).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cōnsīderāre.

fact.text: Latin considerare may come from sidus, 'star', so it might first have meant studying the stars closely. The link is often repeated but not certain.

senses.note: Also 'to regard as': lo considero un amico = I consider him a friend.

etymology: From Latin cōnsīderātiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin cōnsīderātiōnem. English "consideration" and Italian considerazione are cognates with identical meaning and etymology.

senses.note: Can mean thought, reflection, regard, or esteem.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cōnsiliārī. By surface analysis, consiglio + -are.

senses.note: Consigliare a qualcuno di fare qualcosa. Also 'to recommend': mi consigli un ristorante?

etymology: From Latin cōnsilium.

fact.text: Comes from Latin consilium, the source of English counsel. English council comes from a different Latin word, concilium, but Italian uses consiglio for both.

senses.note: Countable in Italian: un consiglio = a piece of advice; dei consigli = some advice. Also means council.

etymology: From Latin consulatus.

fact.text: Watch out: consolato is also the past participle of consolare 'to console', so ho consolato means 'I comforted', which has nothing to do with embassies.

senses.note: Il consolato italiano = the Italian consulate. A consul is il console.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cōnsonantem (“consonant”).

senses.note: Feminine: una consonante doppia = a double consonant (as in 'notte').

etymology: From Latin cōnsūmere.

senses.note: consumarsi = to wear away or burn down. In a bar, consumare = to have something to eat or drink.

etymology: From contare. Compare French comptant (“cash”).

fact.text: From contare, 'to count'. Cash is money you can count out on the spot, and French comptant (cash) works the same way.

senses.note: Usually plural: pagare in contanti = to pay in cash.

etymology: From Latin computāre. Compare the doublets computare and compitare.

fact.text: From Latin computare, which also gave English both 'count' and 'compute'. Italian kept computare too, as a separate learned word.

senses.note: Also 'to matter': conta solo questo = only this matters. Contare su = to count on.

etymology: From contatto + -are.

senses.note: Takes a direct object: ti contatto domani. Also mettersi in contatto con.

etymology: From Latin contactus.

fact.text: From Latin contactus (touching, contact). English 'contact' comes from the same Latin root. Both languages share this precise meaning.

etymology: From contemporaneo + -mente.
From Latin contemporāneus.

senses.note: Also means 'happening at the same time': contemporaneo a qualcosa = concurrent with something.

etymology: From Latin continēre.
From Latin contentus, perfect passive participle of contineō (“to contain”), whence Italian contenere.

fact.text: It looks like English 'content', but it is a much more everyday word, closer to 'glad' or 'pleased'. Italians use it all the time for simple happiness.

senses.note: Sono contento che + subjunctive: Sono contento che tu sia tornato.

etymology: Past participle of contenere. Compare French contenu, Portuguese conteúdo.

fact.text: Past participle of contenere (to contain), like English 'content' meaning what is contained within something.

etymology: From continuo + -mente.

senses.note: Adverb; formed from continuo + -mente.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin continuāre, from continuus.

senses.note: Use 'a' before an infinitive: continuare a parlare = to keep talking.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin continuus, derived from contineō (“to hold together”).

senses.note: Also 'continual' (repeated): continue interruzioni = constant interruptions.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *contu(s), *comptu(s), from Latin computus. Doublet of computo and compito.

fact.text: Comes from Latin computus 'calculation', the same family as English 'count', 'account' and 'compute'. Its Italian doublet compito means homework.

senses.note: Il conto, per favore! Also means a bank account; i conti = finances or accounts.

etymology: Deverbal from contornare.

fact.text: Its basic meaning is 'outline' or 'contour', like the English word. A side dish got this name because it surrounds the main dish on the menu.

senses.note: Usually vegetables, served with the secondo (main course).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin contrārius.

senses.note: Al contrario = on the contrary. Also an adjective: in caso contrario = otherwise.

etymology: From Latin contractus.

senses.note: firmare un contratto = to sign a contract. Also an adjective: contracted.
Also a grant or subsidy; contributi also = social security contributions.

etymology: Inherited from Old Italian contra, from Latin contrā.

fact.text: From Latin contrā (against). English "contrary" and "counter" share this root, all meaning 'against' or 'opposite'. The prefix contra- appears in words like contradict and contrast.

senses.note: Preposition or adverb. Also used in compounds: controllo (control), controparte (counterparty).

etymology: Inherited from Old Italian contra, from Latin contrā.

fact.text: From Latin contrā (against). English "contrary" and "counter" share this root, all meaning 'against' or 'opposite'. The prefix contra- appears in words like contradict and contrast.

etymology: Borrowed from French contrôler.

fact.text: From French contrôler, derived from Medieval Latin contrarotulum (a counter-roll used to verify accounts). The prefix contra- (against) + rotulum (roll) originally meant checking one record against another—hence modern 'control' and 'check'.

etymology: Borrowed from French contrôle.

fact.text: Like English 'control', it comes via French from Medieval Latin contrarotulum, a 'counter-roll': a duplicate register kept so accounts could be checked against the original.

senses.note: sotto controllo = under control. Also a check or inspection: il controllo dei biglietti.

etymology: Inherited from Latin convenīre, from cum + veniō.
From Latin conversātiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin convincere.

fact.text: From Latin convincere: con- (together) + vincere (to conquer). The same root gave English convince.

senses.note: Transitive verb; from Latin convincere (con- + vincere, 'to conquer').
Partner or partner in a committed relationship living together; works for any gender.

fact.text: Coop, one of Italy's biggest supermarket chains, is a network of consumer cooperatives. Many Italian wineries and dairies are also run as farmers' co-ops.

senses.note: Short for società cooperativa. Often shortened to coop.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *coperclum, from Latin cooperculum, from cooperiō.

fact.text: From cooperiō meaning 'to cover'—the same Latin root that gives English 'cover' and related words, showing how Latin coverings became Italian protection.

etymology: Substantivized feminine of the adjective coperto.

senses.note: Also a ship's deck (in coperta = on deck). Related to coprire, 'to cover'.

etymology: From Late Latin coopertūra, from Latin coopertus.

fact.text: Related to English 'covert' and 'cover'—all derive from Latin cooperire ('to cover completely').

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cōpia (“abundance”).

fact.text: Latin cōpia meant 'abundance', which gave English copious and cornucopia. In medieval Latin it came to mean 'reproduction', and that sense gave both Italian copia and English copy.

senses.note: Also a copy of a book or newspaper. 'In duplice copia' means in duplicate.

etymology: From coppa + -etta (diminutive suffix).

fact.text: From coppa (cup, bowl) + -etta (diminutive suffix), creating a term for a smaller cup—a common pattern in Italian for size-related words.

senses.note: A small bowl or cup, typically for ice cream or dessert.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cōpla, from Latin cōpula. Doublet of copula, which was borrowed. Compare Sicilian cucchia.

fact.text: From Latin copula, 'bond, link'. English 'couple' comes from the same word via Old French, and grammar's 'copula' is a later learned borrowing of it.

senses.note: in coppia = in pairs, as a couple.
For everyday objects use 'un paio' (un paio di scarpe); coppia is for two as a unit.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cooperīre. For the past historic stem copers- compare perdere: pers-, morire: mors-, etc.
Borrowed from Old Occitan coratge, Old French corage.

fact.text: Like English courage, it came through Old French (and Old Occitan) from Latin cor, meaning heart. Saying 'Coraggio!' to someone is a lot like telling them to take heart.

senses.note: Exclamation of encouragement. As a noun, il coraggio = courage.

etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan coratge, Old French corage.

fact.text: Like English courage, it came through Old French (and Old Occitan) from Latin cor, meaning heart. Saying 'Coraggio!' to someone is a lot like telling them to take heart.

senses.note: Coraggio! on its own means 'come on!' or 'cheer up!'

etymology: From coraggio + -oso.
Inherited from Latin chorda (“cord”), from Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ, “string of gut, the string of a lyre”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek khorde, a string of gut used on a lyre, through Latin chorda. English got both 'cord' and 'chord' from the same word.

senses.note: Also a string of an instrument or racket. Dare corda a qualcuno = to encourage someone.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cordiālis. Noun meaning via French.

fact.text: Comes from Latin cor, 'heart', the root that also gave Italian cuore. Something cordial is literally 'from the heart'.

senses.note: Cordiali saluti = Kind regards, a standard way to close a letter or email.

etymology: From cordiale + -mente.

fact.text: Built on cordiale, which goes back to Latin cor, heart, so to greet someone cordially is to greet them from the heart. Italian cuore and English cardiac come from the same root.

senses.note: Often used to close letters, as is the adjective form: Cordiali saluti (Kind regards).

etymology: From Latin chorea.

fact.text: Lowercase, corea is the medical term chorea, from Greek khoreia 'dance', the same root as choreography. It is named for its jerky, dance-like movements.

senses.note: Capitalised, feminine, no article in most uses: la Corea del Sud / del Nord.

etymology: From corno (“horn”, from Latin cornū) + -etto (diminutive suffix).

fact.text: In Italy, cornetto is the common breakfast pastry, usually eaten with an espresso. The word literally means 'little horn' from its shape.

etymology: Inherited from Latin corpus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱrep-. Doublet of the borrowing corpus.

fact.text: It shares an ancient root with Old English hrif, 'belly', which survives in English midriff. Latin corpus also gave English corpse, corps and corpus.

senses.note: Can also mean a corpse, or a corps (corpo di ballo = corps de ballet).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin corrigere but adapted to the inherited reggere.

fact.text: Order a 'caffè corretto' in Italy and you get an espresso 'corrected' with a shot of grappa, sambuca or brandy. This is the 'spike a drink' sense.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle corretto, passato remoto corressi. Also to mark exams.

etymology: Inherited from Latin currentem.

fact.text: From Latin currens, 'running', from currere 'to run', the same root as English current, courier and course. A current is literally something that runs.

senses.note: Also a noun: la corrente = current, draught, electricity. acqua corrente = running water.

etymology: Inherited from Latin currentem.

fact.text: From Latin currens, 'running', from currere 'to run', the same root as English current, courier and course. A current is literally something that runs.

senses.note: La corrente = electricity, power. C'è corrente = there's a draught.

etymology: Inherited from Latin currere, from Proto-Italic *korzō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥s-é-ti, zero-grade thematic present of *ḱers- (“to run”).

fact.text: From Latin currere, 'to run', the source of English current, course, courier and corridor. A corridor is literally a place you run along.

senses.note: Uses avere for the activity (ho corso) and essere with a destination (sono corso a casa).

etymology: From correre. Compare Spanish, Portuguese, and Catalan corredor. Compare also Vulgar Latin *curritōrius and *curritor, from currō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin correspondēre, from Latin cum + respondeō.
Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of correre (“to run”).

senses.note: Also means race. Di corsa = in a hurry; fare una corsa = to go for a run.

etymology: From Latin cursus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin cursus 'a running', from currere 'to run'. It's related to English course, current and cursor.

senses.note: corso d'inglese = English course. in corso = in progress.
Common in street names, e.g. Corso Vittorio Emanuele.

etymology: From Latin cōrtem, shortened version of Latin cohors (“court; enclosure”). Doublet of the borrowing coorte.

fact.text: From Latin cohors—also the root of English court, cohort, and courteous. All share the sense of an enclosed space.

etymology: From cortese + -ia.

fact.text: From cortese ('courtly, polite'). Related to English courtesy and court, all rooted in notions of refined behavior at a royal court.

etymology: From corte (“courtyard”) + -ile. Compare Sicilian curtigghiu.

fact.text: Built on corte, from Latin cohors (accusative cohortem) 'enclosed yard', which also gave English court and cohort.

senses.note: An enclosed yard, e.g. of a building or school; also a farmyard.

etymology: From Latin curtus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-.

fact.text: It comes from Latin curtus. It is distantly related to English 'short' and 'shirt' through a root meaning 'to cut': a shirt was originally a cut-short garment.

senses.note: Used for length or duration. For a person's height, use basso: un uomo basso.

etymology: Inherited from Latin causa. Doublet of the borrowing causa. The pronoun is a clipping of che cosa.

fact.text: Comes from Latin causa, 'cause, lawsuit', the source of English cause. Italian later borrowed causa again, so it has both words. French chose has the same origin.

senses.note: Feminine: la cosa, le cose. On its own, Cosa? means 'What?' (short for che cosa).

etymology: Inherited from Latin causa. Doublet of the borrowing causa. The pronoun is a clipping of che cosa.

fact.text: Comes from Latin causa, 'cause, lawsuit', the source of English cause. Italian later borrowed causa again, so it has both words. French chose has the same origin.

senses.note: Short for 'che cosa'. 'Che?' and 'che cosa?' mean the same thing. Cos'è? means 'What is it?'

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cōnscientia.
Masculine form of cosa.

senses.note: Used when you can't remember what something is called

etymology: Inherited from Latin costa. Cognate with French côte, Romanian coastă, and Spanish cuesta.

fact.text: From Latin costa. Cognate with French côte, Spanish cuesta, and English coast (which developed the sense of shoreline). All share the same ancient root.

etymology: From Latin cōnstāre. Doublet of constare, a borrowing.

fact.text: From Latin constare, 'to stand firm' or 'to be fixed', as a price is. English 'cost' came from the same Latin verb through Old French coster.

senses.note: Takes essere in compound tenses: Quanto è costato? = How much did it cost?

etymology: Deverbal from costare (“to cost”) + -o.

senses.note: A tutti i costi = at all costs.

etymology: From costola (“rib”) + -etta (diminutive suffix). Doublet of cotoletta.

senses.note: A thin slice of meat, usually fried. The list entry 'ribs' refers to the cut of meat used.

etymology: From costare + -oso.

senses.note: Caro is the more everyday word. Costoso comes from costare (to cost).

etymology: Inherited from Latin cōnstringere.

senses.note: irregular verb

etymology: From Latin cōnstruere, probably a borrowing.

senses.note: An -isc- verb: costruisco, costruisci, costruisce, but costruiamo, costruite.
Costruire + lo. The object pronoun attaches to the end of the infinitive, and the infinitive drops its final -e.
costruire + mi. Costruirmi una casa = to build myself a house.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cōnstrūctiōnem.

senses.note: Both the act of building and the building itself. In costruzione = under construction.

etymology:
PIE word
 *ḱóm
 PIE word
 *swé
Inherited from Latin consuētūdinem. Doublet of consuetudine, which was borrowed.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum sīc. By surface analysis, ecco + sì. Closely parallel to Dalmatian coisa, Friulian cussì, Istriot cussèi, Sardinian gósi (bosìe, deàsi, etc.), Venetan cusì. Compare also Catalan així, French ainsi, Portuguese assim, Spanish así, Romanian așa, Sicilian accussì.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin eccum sic, roughly 'look, thus'. It's built from the same pieces as modern ecco ('here is') and sì ('yes', from Latin sic, 'thus').

senses.note: così lontano = so far. così così = so-so. Non così! = Not like that!

etymology: Borrowed from Arabic قُطُن (quṭun); see cotton for more.

fact.text: Borrowed from Arabic qutn, the same word that gave English 'cotton'. Arab traders brought both the plant and the name to Europe.

senses.note: Also cotton wool. Di cotone = made of cotton.

etymology: Inherited from Latin coctus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin coctus, the past participle of coquere (to cook). The same root gives English 'cook' and 'cuisine', through different paths.

etymology: If not direcly inherited, then a latinization of older criare (a more securely native form), from Latin creāre.

senses.note: Keeps both e's in the future and conditional: creerò, creerei.

etymology: Derived from Late Latin creātūra, from Latin creō.

fact.text: Italians often use it tenderly for a newborn or small child. In Naples the dialect form criatura is the everyday word for a baby.

senses.note: Can also mean a baby or small child, said tenderly.

etymology: Inherited from Latin crēdere (“to believe”).

fact.text: From Latin credere, 'to believe, to trust'. English took 'credit', 'credible', 'creed' and 'credo' from it. 'Credo' literally means 'I believe'.

senses.note: Credere a = to believe someone/something; credere in = to believe in. Non credo che + subjunctive.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin crēditum.

fact.text: From Latin creditum, 'something entrusted', from credere, 'to believe'. Giving someone credit literally means believing they'll pay you back.

senses.note: Used for finance, trust and university credits alike.

etymology: Borrowed from French crème.

fact.text: It came via French crème from a Gaulish word that got mixed up with Latin chrisma, 'anointing oil'. Chrisma comes from the same Greek verb 'to anoint' that gave us 'Christ'.

senses.note: Dairy cream is usually 'panna'. Crema is a cosmetic cream, a creamy soup or a filling.
Pastry cream is 'crema pasticcera'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cremāre. First attested in the 19th century.

fact.text: Despite the look, it has nothing to do with crema (cream): it comes from Latin cremare, 'to burn', and was only borrowed into Italian in the 19th century.

senses.note: Regular -are verb, auxiliary avere.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin crepāre (“to rattle, creak, crack”).
The informal sense of 'die' is shared with both the French and Romanian cognates crever and crăpa.

fact.text: Italians wish luck with 'In bocca al lupo!' (into the wolf's mouth). The reply is 'Crepi!' (may it die!). Answering 'grazie' is traditionally thought to bring bad luck.

senses.note: Rude when used of people. crepare dal ridere = to die laughing. Takes essere.
Fixed reply to 'In bocca al lupo!': 'Crepi (il lupo)!', meaning 'may the wolf die!'

etymology: From Latin crēscere, from Proto-Italic *krēskō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱreh₁- (“to grow, become bigger”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin crescere, 'to grow', the source of English crescent (the growing moon), increase and the musical crescendo.

senses.note: Takes essere when intransitive: sono cresciuto = I grew up.
Transitive: crescere un figlio = to raise a child. Sono stato cresciuto = I was raised.

etymology: From Latin crista.

fact.text: A rooster raises its comb when it feels cocky, so alzare la cresta (raise the crest) means to get uppity, and abbassare la cresta means to be humbled.

senses.note: Also a mountain ridge, a rooster's comb or a Mohawk haircut. Abbassare la cresta = to be taken down a peg.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English cricket.

senses.note: Unadapted English loanword; invariable plural.

etymology: From Late Latin or Juridical Latin criminālis (“criminal”), from Latin crīmen (“verdict; crime”).

fact.text: From Late Latin criminalis, derived from crimen (crime, verdict). English 'criminal' shares the same Latin root.

senses.note: noun; can refer to person of either gender

etymology: Borrowed from Latin crīmine.

fact.text: From Latin crīmine, the root of English 'incriminate' and 'criminal'. The Latin word originally meant 'charge' or 'accusation' before extending to the deed itself.

etymology: From Latin crisis, from Ancient Greek κρίνειν (krínein, “to decide”).

fact.text: From Greek krinein 'to decide': a crisis is the deciding moment. 'Critic' and 'criterion' come from the same Greek root.

senses.note: Invariable: la crisi, le crisi.

etymology: From Latin Christus, from Ancient Greek Χριστός (Khristós), proper noun use of χριστός (khristós, “the anointed one”), a calque of Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (māšīaḥ, “anointed”) (see also messia).

fact.text: From Greek Khristós, 'the anointed one', a translation of Hebrew māšīaḥ. So 'Christ' and 'Messiah' originally mean exactly the same thing.

senses.note: Capitalize as a proper noun; used in religious contexts and phrases like 'Cristo mio' (my God/goodness)

etymology: From critica + -are.

fact.text: From Latin critica, itself derived from Greek kritikos (able to judge). English 'critic' shares the same root through the same path.

senses.note: Often implies disapproval; can mean to critique unfavorably
Fare una crociera = to go on a cruise. Velocità di crociera = cruising speed.

etymology: From Latin chronica.

fact.text: From Latin chronica. English "chronicle" and Italian cronaca are cognates derived from the Greek word for time (chronos).

senses.note: Also: newspaper column or account of events.

etymology: Inherited from Latin crusta, from Proto-Indo-European *krustós (“hardened”), from *krews- (“to form a crust, begin to freeze”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin crusta, the source of English crust. Related Italian food words are crostata (a jam tart) and crostini (small toasts).

senses.note: Also the crust of bread or the rind of cheese. Colloquially, a bad painting.

etymology: From crosta (“crust”) + -ata.
From Latin crūdus (compare French cru, Spanish crudo). Doublet of cru.

fact.text: From Latin crudus 'raw, bloody'. English 'crude' comes from the same word, which is why crude oil is oil in its raw, unrefined state.

senses.note: Prosciutto crudo (cured, uncooked ham) vs prosciutto cotto (cooked ham).

etymology:
Inherited from Latin cochleārium, derived from cochlear, from cochlea (“snail”), which perhaps was an instrument used to eat eggs and snails. It's also possible that it derives from the use to which it was put, the concave shape, or perhaps originally it was made with the shell of a snail.
Cognate with Sicilian cucchiara, French cuillère, Portuguese colher, Catalan cullera and Spanish cuchara.

fact.text: It comes from Latin cochlearium, from cochlea, 'snail'. The Roman spoon may have been a tool for eating snails and eggs, or was named for its shell-like shape.

senses.note: A teaspoon is 'cucchiaino'. The word can also mean a spoonful or tablespoon.

etymology: From Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna.

fact.text: From Late Latin cocina (earlier coquina), from coquere 'to cook'. English kitchen comes from the same Latin word, via Old English cycene.

senses.note: Also means cooking or cuisine: la cucina italiana = Italian cuisine.

etymology: From Late Latin cocīnāre, from Latin coquīnāre. The slang sense is a semantic loan from English cook.

fact.text: From Latin coquinare, from coquina 'kitchen'. The same Latin word was borrowed early into Old English and became English kitchen.

senses.note: Also a noun: la cucina = kitchen or cuisine.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French cosin, cousin, from Latin cōnsobrīnus. Doublet of consobrino.

fact.text: Borrowed from Old French cosin, which also gave English 'cousin'. It goes back to Latin consobrinus, built on the root of soror (sister). At first it meant the child of your mother's sister.

senses.note: The feminine is la cugina. The plural i cugini can also mean a mixed group of cousins.

etymology: From Latin cūlus (“anus”).

fact.text: Direct descent from Latin culus (anus). The word retains its anatomical origin through all Romance languages and English 'cul-de-sac'.

senses.note: Slang term; also means luck or (derogatory) gay man; bottom of an object in neutral sense

etymology: From Latin cultūra.

senses.note: Can also mean a person's learning: una persona di grande cultura = a very cultured person.

etymology: From Late Latin cocere, from Latin coquere.

fact.text: The past participle cotto is hidden in biscotto, 'twice cooked', a relative of the English word biscuit. Latin coquere is also the source of English cook.

senses.note: Irregular: cuocio, cuociono; past participle cotto. Takes avere when it has an object, essere when it doesn't.

etymology: Inherited from Latin coquus (“cook”).

fact.text: From Latin coquus (cook), which traces back to Proto-Indo-European *pekʷ- (to cook/ripen). The same root gives English 'cook'.

senses.note: Masculine form; feminine is cuoca.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *corem m, from Latin cor n.

fact.text: Latin cor is distantly related to English heart. It also gave English cordial and, through French coeur, courage.

senses.note: Also the hearts suit in cards. Di cuore = heartfelt, sincerely.

etymology: From Latin cūra, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeys- (“to heed”).

fact.text: Latin cura meant care or concern. It gave English both cure and curator, a person who takes care of a collection.

senses.note: Prendersi cura di = to take care of. Can also mean a medical treatment or cure.

etymology: From Latin cūrāre.
From curare + -si.

senses.note: Reflexive verb. Covers health, appearance, and concern/attention.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cūriōsus.

senses.note: Like English, it can mean nosy or strange: che curioso! = how odd!

fact.text: Latin for 'the course of life'. Curriculum comes from currere, 'to run', so it is related to English current, courier and course. Your CV is literally the race you have run so far.

senses.note: Often shortened to 'il curriculum' or 'il CV'. In Italian it usually stays the same in the plural: 'i curriculum'.

etymology: Derived from Latin curvus (“bent”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn; to bend”).

senses.note: Also stooped or hunched, of a person: camminare curvo.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French coissin or Old Occitan coisin, from Vulgar Latin *coxīnum, *cossīnum, from Latin coxa (“hip; thigh”).

fact.text: It goes back to Latin coxa, 'hip, thigh'. It started out as a seat pad for your hips. English 'cushion' comes from the same Old French word.

senses.note: Used for both a bed pillow and a sofa cushion.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin custōdia, a noun derived from custōs (“guardian”).

senses.note: care or safekeeping

etymology: From Latin dē (“from”) + ā/ab (“of, from”). In the meaning of “at, near, by”, da probably comes from Latin unde + ad.

senses.note: Also 'at/to someone's place' (da Mario), 'since' (da due anni) and 'by' (da solo = by oneself).

fact.text: Literally 'you give', from the verb dare. Add ma and it becomes 'Ma dai!', meaning 'No way!' or 'Get out of here!'.

senses.note: Encourages or urges someone. Ma dai! = No way! / You don't say!

etymology: Borrowed from Latin damnātiōnem. Equivalent of dannare + -zione.

fact.text: From Latin damnātiō (damnāre 'to condemn'). The root damnare also gave English 'damn' and 'condemn', so all three words share the same ancient origin.

etymology: Inherited from Latin damnum, from Proto-Italic *dapnom, from Proto-Indo-European *dh₂pnóm (“expense, investment”), derived from *deh₂p- (“to sacrifice”).

fact.text: From Latin damnum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂p- (to sacrifice, to lose). The semantic shift from 'expense' to 'damage' reflects what is lost through harm.

etymology:
Univerbation of da + per + tutto.
Compare French partout, Catalan pertot and Spanish por todas partes for similar constructions.

fact.text: A fusion of da + per + tutto, roughly 'from through all'. French partout is built the same way.

senses.note: Synonym: ovunque. Example: Ho cercato dappertutto (I looked everywhere).

etymology: Inherited from Latin dō, from Proto-Italic *didō, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti, from the root *deh₃- (“give”).

fact.text: English 'data' comes from the Latin form of this verb: datum means 'something given'. 'Donate' and 'donor' come from the same root, meaning 'give'.

senses.note: Irregular: do, dai, dà; past participle dato. 'Dai!' also means 'come on!'

etymology: From dare + -si.
From Late Latin data, from Latin datus.

fact.text: False friend: this means a calendar date, not data, which is i dati. It comes from Latin data 'given', from letters marked 'given at' a place on a certain day.

senses.note: Not a romantic date (appuntamento). Data di nascita = date of birth.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin datum.

fact.text: English 'data' is the plural of the Latin datum (neuter), and Italian 'dati' is the plural of 'dato.' Both languages preserve the Latin distinction between singular and plural.

senses.note: Plural dati; singular dato means a single datum or piece of information.

etymology: From older davante. Presumably di + avante.

fact.text: Built from di + avante (modern avanti, 'forward'), from Late Latin abante. English advance comes from the same Latin source, via French.

senses.note: Before a noun use davanti a: davanti alla casa (in front of the house).

etymology: From older davante. Presumably di + avante.

fact.text: Built from di + avante (modern avanti, 'forward'), from Late Latin abante. English advance comes from the same Latin source, via French.

senses.note: Invariable noun. Most often used in 'davanti a', meaning 'in front of'.

etymology:
Univerbation of da + vero.
The pronunciation with -vv- is due to the word's spelling being fossilized with the syntactic gemination of the traditional (Tuscan) pronunciation of da. The pronunciation with a single -v- reflects the regional and now standard pronunciation of da. Compare Spanish de veras, de a de veras (“for real”)

fact.text: A fusion of da + vero, literally 'from true', i.e. 'for real'. Spanish has a similar phrase, de veras, 'for real'.

senses.note: 'Davvero?' = 'Really?' On its own, 'Davvero!' means 'Honestly!'

etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēbitum, noun use of the neuter form of dēbitus, perfect passive participle of dēbeō (“to owe”).

fact.text: English 'debt' comes from the same Latin debitum. Its silent b was added by scholars to make the spelling look like the Latin, something Italian debito never needed.

senses.note: Essere in debito con qualcuno = to be indebted to someone.

etymology: From Latin debilis.

fact.text: As a noun it gives a handy idiom: avere un debole per qualcuno means to have a soft spot for someone. It comes from Latin debilis, the root of English debilitate.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural deboli.

etymology: From Latin dēcīdere, from dē + caedō.

fact.text: From Latin dē + caedere, 'to cut off': to decide is literally to cut away the other options. The same root is in 'incision' and 'concise'.

senses.note: decidere di + infinitive: ho deciso di partire. Past participle: deciso. decidersi = to make up one's mind.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēcīsiōnem.

senses.note: To make a decision = prendere una decisione (not 'fare').

fact.text: Related to 'decrescendo', the musical term English borrowed from Italian. Both come from decrescere, 'to decrease'. Decrescendo is the gerund and decrescente is the present participle.

senses.note: Present participle of decrescere (to decrease). Opposite: crescente.

etymology: di (preposition) + il (article)

senses.note: di + il, before masculine singular nouns. Also means 'some': del pane = some bread.

etymology: From Latin dēlicātus.

senses.note: Also frail, sensitive, mild (of flavours) or tactful, depending on context.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēlīctum, from dēlinquō (“to transgress, err”); probably a semi-learned borrowing.
From Late Latin dēliciōsus.

senses.note: Also means 'delightful' or 'lovely' for places, people and things: un paesino delizioso.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēlūdō.

fact.text: From Latin dēlūdere (to mock, deceive): same root as English 'delude', though Italian shifted toward 'disappoint' in meaning.

senses.note: Transitive: to let down or fail to meet expectations. Irregular: past participle deluso.

etymology: From Latin dēlūsiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin dēlūsiōnem: cognate with English 'delusion', though Italian delusione focuses on emotional letdown.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin democratia, from Ancient Greek δημοκρατίᾱ (dēmokratíā). By surface analysis, demo- + -crazia.

fact.text: From Ancient Greek dēmokratía (dēmo- 'people' + -kratía 'rule'). The same Greek roots appear in English 'democracy,' making both languages share this classical political term.

etymology: Inherited from Latin dēnārius, via a non-Tuscan dialect where Latin /rj/ yields /r/.

fact.text: From Latin denarius, the Roman silver coin. The same coin explains the 'd' for pennies in Britain's old pounds-shillings-pence system.

senses.note: In everyday speech Italians usually say i soldi.

etymology: From Latin dentem. Doublet of zanna.

fact.text: Pasta cooked al dente, 'to the tooth', is cooked so it is still slightly firm when you bite it. English has borrowed the phrase straight from Italian.

senses.note: Plural: i denti. Also used for the teeth of a comb, cog or fork.

etymology: From Latin dentifricium.

fact.text: Literally 'tooth-rub', from Latin dens (tooth) + fricare (to rub). English has the same word in the formal 'dentifrice'.

etymology: From dente + -ista.

senses.note: One form for both genders: il/la dentista. Plurals: dentisti (m), dentiste (f).

etymology: From Late Latin dē intrō.

senses.note: Also means indoors. dentro a/di + noun = inside something. Informally, essere dentro = to be in prison.

etymology: Deverbal from denunciare + -a.

senses.note: Also: official denouncement or registration (births/deaths).
Transitive. Means to report someone to authorities, or more broadly, to expose or denounce.

etymology: Derived from English deodorant, or French déodorant. By surface analysis, deodorare + -ante.
From Latin dēprimō.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle depresso, passato remoto depressi. Deprimersi = to get depressed.

etymology: From Latin dēscrībere (“to describe”).

senses.note: Irregular like scrivere: descrissi, descritto.

etymology: Derived from Latin dēscrīptiōnim. By surface analysis, descrivere + -zione.

fact.text: Descrizione derives from Latin dēscrīptiōnem (descrivere + -zione), sharing the same root as English 'describe'.

etymology: From the older form diserto, from Latin dēsertum, substantivized neuter form of dēsertus, perfect passive participle of dēserō (“to forsake, abandon”).

fact.text: From Latin dēsertum, literally 'abandoned place' (from dēserō, 'to forsake'). The English word has the same origin.

etymology: From an alteration of the older disiderare, from Latin dēsīderāre (“to long for, desire, feel the want of, miss, regret”). Doublet of desirare, taken from Old Occitan.

fact.text: From Latin desiderare (to long for, miss). An alteration of the older disiderare. English 'desire' and 'desiderate' are cognates from the same Latin root.

etymology: From an alteration, based on its Latin root, of the older disidero, desidero, from Latin dēsīderium.

fact.text: Latin desiderare is often explained as de- + sidus ('star'), as if longing for something from the stars. This origin is possible but not proven.

senses.note: Also 'wish': esprimi un desiderio = make a wish.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin destinātārius and French destinataire.
From Latin dēstinātiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin destinatio (a purpose or intent). English 'destination' shares the same Latin root.

etymology: Deverbal from destinare + -o.

fact.text: From Latin destinare 'to make firm, intend', giving the deverbal noun destino. The sense evolved from 'what is intended' to 'fate ordained by destiny', reflecting philosophical views of determinism.

etymology: From Latin dextra or dextera. Compare French dextre, Portuguese destra.

fact.text: From Latin dextra, 'right hand'. English 'dexterous' comes from the same root: being skilful was linked to the right hand.

senses.note: a destra = on/to the right. Also 'the political right'.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English detective.

fact.text: Borrowed directly from English in the late 19th century; Italian lacks a native word for this modern profession, so detective remains unchanged in both singular and plural.

senses.note: Invariable in both genders (un/una detective)

etymology: From Latin dētestārī.

fact.text: From Latin detestari (de- + testari: to curse, curse against). The root testari means to call to witness; detestare originally meant to call the gods to witness one's hatred, hence 'to curse thoroughly'.

etymology: From French détail.
From Latin dictātus, dictātum.

senses.note: A classic school exercise: fare un dettato.

etymology: From Latin dē (the name of the letter D).

senses.note: Combines with the article: del, della, dei, delle. Also 'from' in origin: sono di Roma.

etymology: From Latin dē. Cognate with English to. For etymology 1, preposition sense 11, compare French delà, deçà and deci delà.

senses.note: Merges with articles: del, dello, della, dei, degli, delle. Often d' before a vowel.
Used after a noun: corso di cucina (cooking class), libro di cucina (cookbook).
'La mattina' is also common, especially for habits.
With clock times use del pomeriggio: alle tre del pomeriggio means at 3 p.m.

etymology: Literally, “of evening”.

senses.note: Fixed prepositional phrase; 'la sera' is also common
The most common everyday way to say it: Di solito ceno alle otto.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dialectos.

fact.text: Many Italian 'dialects', like Neapolitan, Sicilian or Venetian, are really separate Romance languages that grew out of Latin alongside Tuscan. They are not variants of standard Italian.

etymology: From Latin dialogus, from Ancient Greek διάλογος (diálogos).

senses.note: The plural is dialoghi, with an h to keep the hard g sound.

etymology: From Late Latin diamantem, from Latin adamantem, from Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas, “invincible, untamed; hard substance”), from ἀ- (a-, “un-”) + δαμάζω (damázō, “to overpower, tame, conquer”), from Proto-Indo-European *demh₂-.

fact.text: It comes from Greek adámas, 'unconquerable', the source of English 'adamant'. A diamond is, in effect, the 'untameable' stone.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin diārium.

senses.note: Diario scolastico = the planner Italian students use to write down homework.

etymology: From Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin diabolus (possibly semi-learned), itself from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos).

fact.text: From Greek diábolos (slanderer, accuser), same root as English 'diabolic'. Medieval Latin diabolus brought it into Italian.

etymology: From Latin Decembrem.

fact.text: From Latin decem 'ten': December was the tenth month of the early Roman calendar, which began in March.

senses.note: Months are not capitalised in Italian: a dicembre = in December.

etymology: From Latin dēclārāre.

fact.text: From Latin dēclārāre, the same root as English 'declare': both mean to make clear or manifest.

senses.note: Transitive: to announce, proclaim, state, or assert.

etymology: From dichiarare + -zione, based on Latin dēclārātiōnem.
Inherited from Latin decem ac novem (“ten and nine”). Compare Venetan disinove.
From Latin decem ac septem (“ten and seven”). Compare Venetan dixisete.
Inherited from Latin decem.

fact.text: It comes from Latin decem, the root of 'decimal' and of December, which was the tenth month when the Roman year began in March.

senses.note: In Italian schools, dieci is the top mark: un dieci.

etymology: Inherited from Latin decem.

fact.text: It comes from Latin decem, the root of 'decimal' and of December, which was the tenth month when the Roman year began in March.

etymology: From Latin diaeta (“diet, regimen”), from Ancient Greek δίαιτα (díaita, “way of living”).

fact.text: Comes through Latin from Greek diaita, 'way of living'. It first meant a whole lifestyle and regimen, and only later came to mean what you eat.

senses.note: Essere a dieta means to be on a diet; mettersi a dieta means to go on a diet.

etymology: From an earlier Italian form drieto, from Late Latin dē retrō, from Latin dē + retrō. Compare French derrière and Sicilian darreri

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin de retro, 'from behind'. French derrière has the same origin, and English borrowed that word as a polite term for the backside.

senses.note: Also a preposition: dietro la casa, or dietro alla casa (behind the house).

etymology: From Latin dēfendere.

fact.text: From Latin dēfendere (de- 'from' + fendere 'to strike, ward off'). English 'defend' and 'fend' are cognates.

etymology: From Late Latin dēfēnsa, from the feminine of Latin dēfēnsus, perfect passive participle of dēfendō.

fact.text: Cognate with English 'defense'. Both come from Latin defendere. Italian spelling (difesa) preserves the older form; modern English dropped the final 'a' and evolved the spelling independently.

etymology: From Latin defectus.

fact.text: From Latin defectus (failure, lack). English 'defect' comes from the same Latin root. Both preserve the original sense of falling short.

senses.note: Can mean a physical flaw, a fault, or a lack/shortage of something.

etymology: From Latin differentem.

senses.note: Used with 'da': differente da = different from. Diverso is the more common synonym.

etymology: From Latin differentia.

senses.note: fare la differenza = to make a difference; a differenza di = unlike.

etymology: From Latin difficilis.

senses.note: The same form is used for masculine and feminine; plural difficili.
Difficile means hard as in difficult. Duro means hard as in physically hard or tough, and also harsh.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin difficultātem.

fact.text: From Latin difficultātem. English 'difficulty' is cognate. Both derive from difficilis (hard, not easy).

senses.note: invariable noun (same singular and plural form)

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dismenticāre.

fact.text: Built from dis- plus mente (mind), so it literally means to put out of mind.

senses.note: Also reflexive: dimenticarsi di qualcosa.

etymology: From Latin dīminuō.

fact.text: From Latin diminuere (dis- + minuere: to make smaller). The root minuere also gives English 'minus' and 'minute' (small), so diminuire means to 'make minus' or reduce.

senses.note: Can be transitive or intransitive.
Dimmi is informal (tu). Mi dica is formal (Lei).

etymology: From Latin dēmōnstrāre.

fact.text: From Latin dēmōnstrāre (de- + mōnstrāre 'to show, point out'). Related to Latin mōnstrum (portent, monster) and the root meaning 'to warn'.

senses.note: To show, display, or prove something; usually transitive.

etymology: From Latin deus, from earlier *dẹ̄vos, from Old Latin deivos, from Proto-Italic *deiwos, from Proto-Indo-European *deywós, derived from the root *dyew- (“sky, heaven”).

fact.text: From the Proto-Indo-European root *dyew- meaning 'sky, heaven'. The same root gave Zeus, Jupiter, Latin dies (day), and through the god Tiw, English Tuesday.

etymology: From dipendere (“to depend”) + -enza. Doublet of dependance.

senses.note: Often refers to substance dependency; also means reliance or subordination.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dēpendĕre, from Classical Latin dēpendēre. By surface analysis, di- + pendere.

fact.text: From Latin dependere, literally 'to hang down' (de + pendere, to hang). The same root gives English pendant, pendulum and suspend.

senses.note: Followed by da: dipende da te. Takes essere; past participle dipeso. Dipende! = It depends!

etymology: From Latin dēpingō. Compare English depict.

fact.text: Comes from Latin depingere, the source of English 'depict'. Its root pingere also gave English 'picture' and 'pigment'.

senses.note: Irregular: dipinsi, dipinto. Un dipinto = a painting. Also 'to depict, describe'.

etymology: From dipingere (“to paint”). Possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin *dēpinctus for Latin dēpictus.

fact.text: Literally 'painted': it is the past participle of dipingere, from Latin depingere. English 'depict' comes from the same Latin verb.

senses.note: The art or act of painting is 'la pittura'.

etymology: From Ancient Greek δίπλωμα (díplōma).

fact.text: Greek diploma meant a document folded in two, from diploos, double. Diplomats were originally people who carried such official papers.

senses.note: Masculine even though it ends in -a: il diploma, i diplomi. Usually refers to the high-school diploma.
Takes essere: mi sono diplomato. For a university degree, use laurearsi.

etymology: Inherited from Latin dīcere, from Proto-Italic *deikō, from Proto-Indo-European *déyḱeti (“to show, point out”).

fact.text: From Latin dicere, which also gave English dictate, diction, dictionary, verdict ('a true saying') and predict ('to say beforehand').

senses.note: Irregular: dico, dici, dice; past participle detto. 'Dimmi' = tell me.

etymology: From diretto + -mente.

senses.note: diretto + -mente. Also means personally or in person.

etymology: From Late Latin dīrēctōrem, from Latin directus.

fact.text: Covers a lot more than 'director': a newspaper's editor, a school's head, a prison governor, and an orchestra conductor (direttore d'orchestra).

senses.note: Feminine: la direttrice. Also means manager, editor of a newspaper, or school principal.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin dīrēctiōnem.

senses.note: Can also mean management or head office.
Can be masculine or feminine depending on the person.

etymology: From Latin dīrigere (“to steer, direct”), probably borrowed in this form.

fact.text: From Latin dīrigere (to steer, direct). Same root as English direct and director.

senses.note: Also means to run/manage, lead, or conduct (orchestra).

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *dērēctus or *dirictus, both assimilated forms from Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of diretto.

fact.text: It comes from Latin directus, 'straight', and is a doublet of diretto. A right was what is straight and proper, and French droit took the same path.

senses.note: Avere il diritto di + infinitive = to have the right to. As a subject it means law: studiare diritto.

etymology: From dis- + abile.
From dis- + Latin astrum (“star”); compare Piedmontese disastr.

fact.text: From Latin dis- (away) + astrum (star), literally meaning "bad star". The Romans believed unfavorable stars caused misfortune.

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of discendere (“to go down, descend”). Cognate with Piedmontese dissèisa. Displaced Latin dēscēnsus.

senses.note: In discesa = downhill. Discesa libera = downhill skiing.

etymology: From Late Latin discursus, from Latin discurrō.

fact.text: From Late Latin discursus, from discurrō (to run about, discourse). The root currō (to run) also appears in English course, current, and excursion.

senses.note: Also: address, discourse, talk, conversation, subject, matter

etymology: From disco + -teca.

fact.text: Formed like biblioteca (library): disco (record) + -teca (repository). It first meant a record collection, and later a place where records were played for dancing.

senses.note: The normal word for a dance club. Italian 'night' or 'night club' often suggests a strip club.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin discussiōnem.
