fact.text: Learned borrowing from Latin discussiōnem, from discutere (to shake apart, examine), giving English discussion and discus (a thrown disc).

etymology: From Latin discutiō.

fact.text: Latin discutere first meant 'to shatter' or 'to shake apart' (dis- + quatere, 'to shake'). Discussing a problem started out as breaking it into pieces.

senses.note: Also 'to argue'. Irregular forms: past participle discusso, passato remoto discussi.

etymology:
Etymology tree
Latin designō
Latin designāre
Italian disegnare
From Latin designāre. Doublet of designare.

fact.text: From Latin designare, the same source as English design. But in everyday Italian it simply means to draw, like drawing with a pencil.

senses.note: Il disegno = drawing; also used for designing: disegnare un abito.

etymology: From disgusto + -oso.
From dis- + occupato; cognate with Piedmontese disocupà.

senses.note: Also an adjective: essere disoccupato = to be unemployed. Feminine: la disoccupata.

etymology: From Medieval Latin or Late Latin dīspēnsa, feminine past participle of dīspendō, from Latin dis- + pendō.

fact.text: Italian students study from 'dispense', which are photocopied lecture notes, so the same word can mean a food cupboard or your exam reading.

senses.note: In universities, le dispense are course handouts or lecture notes.

etymology: Inherited from Latin dēsperāre.

fact.text: From Latin de- (away from) + sperare (to hope), so it literally means to 'un-hope'. The same root gives Italian speranza (hope) and English 'desperate'.

senses.note: Takes avere. Disperare di + infinitive = to give up hope of. Disperarsi = to be in despair.

etymology: From dis- + piacere.

fact.text: Mi dispiace literally means 'it displeases me'. Like piacere, the thing causing the feeling is the subject and the person feeling it is the indirect object.

senses.note: Mi dispiace = I'm sorry. Works like piacere: the cause is the subject. Takes essere.

etymology: From Latin dispōnere.
From Latin distantia.

fact.text: From Latin distantia (dis- 'apart' + stāre 'to stand'). English 'distance' is cognate. Both languages preserve the metaphor of standing apart.

etymology: From Latin distīnctus, perfect passive participle of distinguō.

senses.note: Also means distinct or separate. Distinti saluti = Yours sincerely (in letters).
In full: distributore automatico. Distributore di benzina = petrol/gas station.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *destrugere, from Classical Latin dēstruō, from dē- (“un-, de-”) + struō (“to build”).

senses.note: Transitive verb; irregular conjugation.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin disturbāre.

senses.note: Spero di non disturbarti = I hope I'm not bothering you. Scusi il disturbo = sorry to bother you.

etymology: Deverbal from disturbare + -o. Cognate with Piedmontese disturb. Compare also Medieval Latin disturbium, Spanish disturbio, Portuguese distúrbio.

senses.note: Bother, inconvenience, or disturbance.

etymology: From Latin digitus, from Proto-Indo-European *deyǵ- (“to show, point out, pronounce solemnly”).

fact.text: From Latin digitus, the source of English 'digit'. Numbers are called digits because people counted on their fingers, and the root probably meant 'to point out'.

senses.note: Irregular plural: le dita (feminine). 'I diti' is used only for fingers named one by one, e.g. i diti indici.

etymology: Variant of detta, feminine past participle of dire, referring to the name of the company.

fact.text: A variant of detta, 'said', the past participle of dire. It referred to the name a business was 'called' by, and came to mean the firm itself.

senses.note: Usually a small or medium firm. Other words for company: azienda, società.

etymology: Borrowed from Arabic دِيوَان (dīwān), from Persian دیوان (dêvân), ultimately from Sumerian 𒁾 (dub).

fact.text: From Persian and Arabic diwan, meaning a register or council room with cushioned benches along the walls. The same word gives English 'divan' and Italian dogana (customs).

senses.note: Masculine: il divano. 'Divano letto' = sofa bed.

etymology: From a verbal derivative of Latin dēventum, perfect passive participle of dēveniō (“arrive, come”), possibly through a Vulgar Latin form *dēventāre as a frequentative of this verb.

senses.note: Takes essere in compound tenses: sono diventato/a. Also to turn (red) or to go (crazy).

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dīversus.

fact.text: It usually means 'different', not 'diverse', and before a plural noun it means 'several'. Diverse persone means 'several people', not 'diverse people'.

senses.note: Before a plural noun it means 'several': diversi amici = several friends.

etymology: Cognate with Piedmontese divertent.

fact.text: Comes from divertire (to amuse), from Latin divertere, 'to turn aside'. English diverting (entertaining) has the same source: fun turns your mind away from your worries.

senses.note: Means fun/entertaining. For 'funny' meaning strange, use strano.

etymology: From divertire (“to amuse, to entertain”, from Latin dīvertere) + -mento (“-ment”); cognate with Piedmontese divertiment.

fact.text: Comes from Latin dīvertere, 'to turn aside'. Fun is what turns you away from your worries, which is also why English calls an amusement a diversion.

senses.note: Buon divertimento! = Have fun! Also a light musical piece (divertimento).

etymology: From earlier divertere, from Latin dīvertere (“to turn away”).

fact.text: From Latin divertere 'to turn aside', the source of English 'divert'. Having fun means turning your mind away from your cares, which is why English 'diversion' can also mean entertainment.

senses.note: Reflexive, takes essere: mi sono divertito. 'Divertiti!' = Have fun!

etymology: Borrowed from Latin dīvidere (“to divide, to separate”).

fact.text: Directly from Latin dīvidere, the same root as English 'divide': both mean to separate or split into parts.

senses.note: Transitive: to split, separate, or share. Irregular past participle: diviso.

etymology: Deverbal from divietare + -o, from vietare (“to forbid”). Compare Piedmontese diviet.
Borrowed from Latin dīvīsiōnem.
From divorzio + -are; cognate with Piedmontese divorsié.

senses.note: Takes avere: hanno divorziato. 'Divorziare da qualcuno' = to divorce someone.

etymology: From Latin dīvortium (“separation, divorce”).

fact.text: Divorce became legal in Italy only in 1970. A 1974 referendum to repeal the law failed, and almost 60% voted to keep it.

senses.note: Masculine. Chiedere il divorzio = to file for divorce.

etymology: Borrowed from Renaissance Latin dictiōnārium.

fact.text: Short for Denominazione di Origine Controllata, Italy's quality label for wines introduced in 1963. The stricter DOCG adds 'e Garantita' (and guaranteed).

senses.note: Also colloquial after a noun: un romano doc = a true-born Roman, the genuine article.

etymology: Probably a back-formation of doccione (“conduit, spout”), from Latin ductiōnem, from ducere, infinitive of dūcō (“lead, guide; draw, pull”), or alternatively from a Vulgar Latin root *ducea, ultimately from the same root. Compare Dozza, a borrowing from Emilian Dòza.

fact.text: French borrowed this Italian word as douche, meaning a shower or jet of water. English then took douche from French, where it got its narrower meaning.

senses.note: Fare la doccia = to take a shower. Plural: docce.

etymology: From documento + -ario. Compare Piedmontese documentari.
Borrowed from Latin documentum.

fact.text: From Latin documentum, built on docere 'to teach'. A document was first a lesson or proof. The same root gives English doctor, doctrine and docile.

senses.note: 'I documenti' often means your ID papers: 'Documenti, prego!'

etymology: From Latin duodecim.

From Sicilian Medieval Latin doana, dovana (attested from the end of the 12th century), from Andalusian Arabic *duwān, an alteration of the Arabic دِيوَان (dīwān, “administrative office”), borrowed from Persian دیوان (divân, “customs, divan”). Compare Piedmontese dogan-a.

fact.text: It goes back through Arabic diwan to Persian divan, meaning 'office' or 'register'. That's the same word as the English sofa 'divan', and it also gave French douane.

senses.note: Passare la dogana = to go through customs.

etymology: Inherited from Latin dulcem.

fact.text: In sheet music it tells players to play sweetly, and Fellini's 1960 film La Dolce Vita made 'the sweet life' famous around the world.

senses.note: Also gentle or mild: acqua dolce = fresh water.
As a noun: il dolce (m.), plural i dolci. Also means a cake or sweet.

etymology: Inherited from Latin dulcem.

fact.text: In sheet music it tells players to play sweetly, and Fellini's 1960 film La Dolce Vita made 'the sweet life' famous around the world.

senses.note: As an adjective, dolce means sweet. I dolci = desserts or sweets in general.

etymology: From dolce + -ezza.
From English dollar.

fact.text: Italian took this from English. English got it from Dutch daler, short for German Joachimsthaler, the name of a silver coin minted in Joachimsthal, Bohemia, in the 1500s.

etymology: Inherited from Latin dolor, from doleō + -or.

fact.text: From Latin dolor, the source of English 'dolorous' and of the Spanish name Dolores ('sorrows'), from the Virgin Mary's title, Our Lady of Sorrows.

senses.note: Can be physical or emotional (grief). 'Ho dolore qui' means it hurts here.

etymology: From domandare.

fact.text: Watch out: it looks like English demand, but usually it means a question. It only means demand in economics (domanda e offerta) or as a formal application.

senses.note: To ask a question = fare una domanda.

etymology: From Latin dēmandāre, whence also Italian demandare (a borrowed doublet).

fact.text: Looks like 'to demand', but it usually just means 'to ask' (una domanda = a question). To demand something forcefully is esigere or pretendere.

senses.note: Domandare qualcosa a qualcuno. Chiedere is the more common everyday synonym.
'Chiedere' + object; 'domandare' also takes 'se' for yes/no questions

etymology: From Late Latin dē māne (“early in the morning”), from dē + Latin māne, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂- (“to ripen, mature”).

fact.text: From Late Latin de mane, 'early in the morning'. 'Morning' shifted to 'next day', just as German Morgen means both 'morning' and 'tomorrow'.

senses.note: Domani mattina = tomorrow morning. Dopodomani = the day after tomorrow.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin [diēs] Dominica (literally “day of the Lord”).

fact.text: English names the day after the sun, but Italian comes from Late Latin dies Dominica, 'the Lord's day'. Spanish domingo and French dimanche come from the same Latin phrase.

senses.note: Days take a lowercase letter in Italian. 'La domenica' with the article means 'on Sundays'.

etymology: From Late Latin domna, shortened variant of Latin domina (“lady, mistress of an estate or household”), from dominus (“master”), from domus (“home”). Doublet of dama. Cognate with Sicilian donna.

fact.text: From Latin domina, 'mistress of the household', from dominus 'master' and domus 'home'. It shares a root with English 'dame', 'dominate' and 'madonna', meaning 'my lady'.

senses.note: Plural: donne. Can also mean 'lady' or the queen in cards and chess.

etymology: From Latin dōnum (“gift”).
From earlier dopoi, dipoi, inherited from Vulgar Latin dē post.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin de post, literally 'from after'. That is the same Latin post found in English postpone and postscript.

senses.note: Preposition (dopo cena = after dinner) or adverb (ci vediamo dopo = see you later).

etymology: From earlier dopoi, dipoi, inherited from Vulgar Latin dē post.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin de post, literally 'from after'. That is the same Latin post found in English postpone and postscript.

senses.note: As an adverb it means 'later' (a dopo! = see you later); as a preposition, 'after' (dopo l'estate).
Dopo also means 'after'. Più tardi is strictly 'later on'. A dopo! means 'See you later!'

etymology: From dopo- + domani.

fact.text: Simply dopo (after) + domani (tomorrow), joined into one word. English needs four words to say the same thing.

senses.note: Written as one word. The opposite is l'altro ieri (or ieri l'altro): the day before yesterday.

etymology: From Latin duplus, whence also duplo (a borrowed doublet).

fact.text: From Latin duplus, 'twofold'. Its Greek relative diploos, 'double', gave English 'diploma', which was originally a folded document.

senses.note: camera doppia = double room. As a noun, il doppio = twice as much.

etymology:

Inherited from Latin dormīre, from Proto-Italic *dormiō, from Proto-Indo-European *dr̥m-yé-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”) + *-yéti.

fact.text: Comes from Latin dormire, the root behind English dormitory (a room for sleeping), dormant (asleep, inactive) and dormouse.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin dossum, from Latin dorsum. Doublet of the borrowed dorso.
Inherited from Latin doctōrem.

fact.text: In Italy, any university graduate can be called dottore, not only physicians. It comes from Latin docere, 'to teach', so a doctor was originally a teacher.

senses.note: Female form: dottoressa. Before a name it becomes dottor: il dottor Rossi.

etymology: From Latin dē ubi (“from where, whence”), or from a strengthening of the older form ove with a prothetic d-. Compare Piedmontese doa, French d'où.

fact.text: Nothing to do with the bird. It comes from Latin de ubi, literally 'from where', which lost its 'from' meaning. Old Italian also had plain ove, from Latin ubi.

senses.note: dov'è = where is. Also used as a relative: il posto dove abito = the place where I live.

fact.text: Nothing to do with the bird. It comes from Latin de ubi, literally 'from where', which lost its 'from' meaning. Old Italian also had plain ove, from Latin ubi.

senses.note: Before è it shortens to dov': Dov'è? = Where is it?

etymology: From Latin dē ubi (“from where, whence”), or from a strengthening of the older form ove with a prothetic d-. Compare Piedmontese doa, French d'où.

senses.note: Before 'è', 'dove' becomes 'dov'' (Dov'è?).

etymology: Inherited from Latin dēbēre (“to owe”). Cognate with Sicilian duviri.

fact.text: From Latin debere, 'to owe', which also gave English debt and debit. Italian dovere means both 'to owe' and 'must', capturing the original sense of obligation.

etymology: Inherited from Latin dēbēre (“to owe”). Cognate with Sicilian duviri.

fact.text: From Latin debere, 'to owe', which also gave English debt and debit. Italian dovere means both 'to owe' and 'must', capturing the original sense of obligation.

senses.note: Conditional dovrei/dovresti = should. Also means 'to owe'. The noun il dovere means duty.

etymology:
From dove (“where”) + -unque (indefinite ending).
Compare Spanish dondequiera for a similar construction.

fact.text: From dove (where) + -unque (indefinite suffix meaning 'ever'). Spanish has a parallel: dondequiera (wherever).

senses.note: Also: wherever, anywhere.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English drink.

senses.note: Unadapted English loanword, invariable; refers to cocktails and alcoholic beverages.

etymology: Contraction/syncopation of diritto, from Vulgar Latin *dērēctus (or from Late Latin drictus; compare French droit, Catalan dret, Romanian drept, Sicilian drittu), from Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of diretto.

senses.note: Often an adverb: vai dritto = go straight on. A variant of diritto. Colloquially, un dritto = a sly one.

etymology: Contraction/syncopation of diritto, from Vulgar Latin *dērēctus (or from Late Latin drictus; compare French droit, Catalan dret, Romanian drept, Sicilian drittu), from Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of diretto.

senses.note: Vai sempre dritto = keep going straight on. Also used as an adjective (straight) and as diritto.

etymology: Attested from the 1560s; ultimately from Middle Dutch drôge (“dry”), perhaps through Middle French drogue (c. 1462); see etymology at drug.

fact.text: Its older sense was 'spice', so a drogheria is a grocer's shop, not a drugstore. The word probably comes from Dutch droge, 'dry', as in dried goods.

senses.note: Usually illegal drugs. A medicine is un farmaco or una medicina.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dubium.

fact.text: Latin dubius is usually linked to duo 'two': to doubt is to be torn between two options. English doubt comes from the same Latin family.

senses.note: senza dubbio = without a doubt; avere un dubbio = to have a doubt

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dubitāre.

fact.text: From Latin dubitāre, related to the concept of being in two minds—its root connects to 'two' (like Greek dissós and German Zweifel), reflecting the ancient idea that doubt meant being divided between options.

senses.note: Often used with 'di' (dubitare di qualcosa). Also means to suspect or fear.

etymology: Inherited from Latin duae ~ duas, feminine plural of duo, from Proto-Italic *duō, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁. Attempts at gender distinction are still found in Old Italian, but the different forms soon became interchangeable variants. The victory of due may be due to its being the phonetically intermediate form.

senses.note: It never changes form: due ragazzi, due ragazze.

etymology: Inherited from Latin duae ~ duas, feminine plural of duo, from Proto-Italic *duō, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁. Attempts at gender distinction are still found in Old Italian, but the different forms soon became interchangeable variants. The victory of due may be due to its being the phonetically intermediate form.
From due (“two”) + cento (“hundred”).

From Vulgar Latin *dunquam, a cross of Late Latin dunc and Latin unquam (“ever”), with the former itself being a cross of Latin tunc (“then”) with dum (“while”). The final /-e/ may reflect an older form */ˈdonkwas/, with adverbial /-s/, for which cf. Middle French doncques.

senses.note: Also a conversational filler, like 'well then...': Dunque, dove eravamo?

etymology: Inherited as a shortening of Latin domus ecclēsiae (“meeting-house, house of the assembly”, a calque of Ancient Greek οἶκος τῆς ἐκκλησίας (oîkos tês ekklēsías), designating a private house placed at the disposal of the Christian community) and later domus Dominī (“house of our Lord”) or Deī (“of God”); from Proto-Italic *domos, from Proto-Indo-European *dṓm, derived from the root *dem- (“to build”).

fact.text: From Latin domus 'house', as in the house of God. English 'dome' came from this word through French dôme, because many of these great churches had domes.

senses.note: A city's main church, e.g. il Duomo di Milano. The technical term is cattedrale.

fact.text: Originally the present participle of durare (to last), just like English during. Dante Alighieri's real first name was Durante, and Dante is a short form of it.

senses.note: Durante la cena = during dinner. No article contraction: durante il film.

etymology: Inherited from Latin dūrāre, from Proto-Indo-European *dewǝ- (“to run forward”).

fact.text: From Latin durare, the family of English duration, durable and endure. La durata means 'the duration'.

senses.note: Usually takes essere: il film è durato due ore.

etymology: From Latin dūrus, from Proto-Italic *dūros, from Proto-Indo-European *duh₂-ró-s (“long”), from *dweh₂- (“far, long”). Cognate with Ancient Greek δηρός (dērós, “long”), Sanskrit दूर (dūrá, “distant, far, long”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin durus, which goes back to a root meaning 'long', so hard things are the long-lasting ones. English 'durable' and 'endure' come from the same family.

senses.note: Means both physically hard and difficult: un lavoro duro = hard work.

etymology: From Latin et.

senses.note: Often becomes ed before a vowel, especially before e-: ed era.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English e-mail.

senses.note: Usually feminine: la e-mail / l'email. It doesn't change in the plural: le e-mail. Also 'posta elettronica'.

etymology: From Latin excellentem (“distinguished”, “excellent”), present active participle of excellō (“to elevate, raise up”).

fact.text: From Latin excellentem, from excellō meaning 'to elevate, raise up'—the same root gives us English 'excel' and 'excellence'.

etymology: Phonetic spelling of Latin et cētera (“and the rest” or “and so forth”).

senses.note: Commonly abbreviated as 'etc.' in both languages.

etymology: From Latin exceptus, the past participle of excipere.

senses.note: Tutti eccetto lui = everyone except him. Tranne is a common synonym.

etymology: From eccezione + -ale.

senses.note: Often just means 'amazing': È stato eccezionale! = It was fantastic!

etymology: Inherited from Latin eccum, from ecce + eum.

fact.text: From Latin eccum, short for ecce eum, 'behold him'. Ecce is the 'behold' of Ecce homo. That built-in pronoun is why Italian still attaches pronouns to it: eccolo, eccoli.

senses.note: Pronouns attach to it: eccolo = here he/it is, eccomi = here I am.

etymology: Inherited from Latin eccum, from ecce + eum.

fact.text: From Latin eccum, short for ecce eum, 'behold him'. Ecce is the 'behold' of Ecce homo. That built-in pronoun is why Italian still attaches pronouns to it: eccolo, eccoli.

senses.note: Pronouns attach to it: eccolo (here he/it is), eccoli (here they are), eccomi (here I am).
senses.prompt: Here it is! / There you go!

etymology: Inherited from Latin eccum, from ecce + eum.

fact.text: From Latin eccum, short for ecce eum, 'behold him'. Ecce is the 'behold' of Ecce homo. That built-in pronoun is why Italian still attaches pronouns to it: eccolo, eccoli.

senses.note: Points something out; takes a direct object, not a verb: ecco il treno. Pronouns attach: eccolo, eccomi.

etymology: From ecologia + -ico.

senses.note: Plural: ecologici (m), ecologiche (f). Often means 'green, eco-friendly': un villaggio ecologico.

etymology: Derived from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía).

fact.text: Comes from Greek oikonomia, 'household management', from oikos (house) + nomos (law). English economy has the same origin: running a country's money started as running a home.

senses.note: Also means 'economics' as a subject: studiare economia.

etymology: From Latin oeconomicus, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομικός (oikonomikós, “skilled with household management”).

fact.text: From Greek oikonomikos, 'good at running a household', from oikos 'house' and nomos 'rule'. Being economical first meant managing your home well, and now also means cheap.

senses.note: Also 'economic': crisi economica. Unlike cheap, it is not negative; for 'low quality' use scadente.

etymology: From Latin aedificium.

fact.text: From Latin aedificium, from aedes (dwelling, temple) plus facere (to make). English edifice and edify, which first meant 'to build up', come from the same source.

senses.note: A neutral, slightly formal word. Palazzo is the everyday word for an apartment block.

etymology: From Latin ēditōrem.

fact.text: Usually means publisher, not editor. Someone who edits texts is normally a redattore or curatore, and a newspaper editor is a direttore.

senses.note: Feminine: editrice. Casa editrice = publishing house.

fact.text: Watch out: educato usually means 'polite, well-mannered', not 'educated'. A highly educated person is istruito or colto. Maleducato means rude.

senses.note: educare + lo (him). Educare means to raise or bring up a child, especially their manners, as well as to educate.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ēducātiōnem.

fact.text: Partial false friend: avere educazione means having good manners, and una persona educata is polite, not necessarily well schooled. For academic education Italians usually say istruzione.

senses.note: Often means good manners: 'che maleducazione!' = how rude! For schooling, istruzione is more common.

etymology: From Latin effectus.

fact.text: Both Italian effetto and English effect come from Latin effectus (accomplished, done). The same Latin root produced both words through different Romance and Germanic pathways.

etymology: From ego- + -ista.

senses.note: The masculine and feminine singular are the same (egoista). It is also a noun: un/un'egoista = a selfish person.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ēgregius.

fact.text: From Latin egregius, from e grege 'out of the flock', i.e. standing out. English 'egregious' once meant that too, but now means shockingly bad. The Italian stays positive.

senses.note: Common in formal letters: Egregio Signore = Dear Sir. Also means excellent: un lavoro egregio.
A filler for hesitation or resignation ('well…'), and also used to ask 'huh?'
Used to get someone's attention or as a casual greeting.

etymology: From Latin ēlegantem.

fact.text: Latin elegans is usually linked to eligere, 'to choose' (as in 'elect'). An elegant person was originally a choosy, discerning one.

senses.note: Also 'dressed up': Come sei elegante stasera! Same form for masculine and feminine.
Le elementari = primary school (la scuola elementare). It also means simple or basic.
Same form for both genders: l'elettricista. Plurals: gli elettricisti, le elettriciste.

fact.text: From Greek elektron 'amber'. Rubbed amber attracts light objects through static, which gave scientists the word for the force.

senses.note: Feminine and doesn't change in the plural (stressed final -à).

etymology: From elettronico (“electronic”), on the model of English electronics.

senses.note: Singular in Italian: l'elettronica è... (the field or industry).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ēlectiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin eligere, 'to pick out', the same verb behind English elect and elite. So an election is literally a picking out.

senses.note: Often plural for a vote: le elezioni politiche = general election.

etymology: Borrowed from French hélicoptère.

fact.text: Coined in French in 1861 from Greek helix (spiral) and pteron (wing), so it splits as helico-pter, 'spiral wing', and not heli-copter.

senses.note: Masculine: l'elicottero, gli elicotteri.

etymology: From Latin ēlīmināre.

fact.text: Latin eliminare comes from e- 'out' + limen 'threshold', so it first meant to turn someone out of the house. English eliminate and subliminal share limen.

senses.note: Also means to get rid of or remove something, as in the context: eliminare il tavolo.
Borrowed directly from English; can be masculine or feminine in Italian

etymology: From emergere + -enza; cf. Medieval Latin ēmergentia, from Latin ēmergentem.

senses.note: In caso di emergenza = in case of emergency. Pronto soccorso = A&E / ER.

etymology: From French émotion.

senses.note: Also means excitement or a thrill: Che emozione! = How exciting!

etymology: Borrowed from Latin energia, from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια (enérgeia).
From Latin ēnormem.

fact.text: From Latin ēnormem, the source of English 'enormous': literally means 'out of the norm'.

senses.note: Also: huge, immense, great.
Feminine: entrambe. Before a noun it needs the article: entrambi i fratelli.

etymology: From earlier intrare, from Latin intrāre (“to enter”).

senses.note: Takes essere: sono entrato/a. Use 'entrare in' + place: entrare in casa.

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of entrare (“to go in, to enter”). Already found in Medieval Latin intrāta.

senses.note: Ingresso is a common synonym. In the plural, le entrate means income or revenue.

etymology: Inherited from Latin intrō.

senses.note: Temporal: e.g., entro domani (by tomorrow).

etymology:
From Ancient Greek ἐπεισόδιον (epeisódion) "parenthetic addition, episode", neuter of ἐπεισόδιος (epeisódios) "following upon the entrance".
Cognate with Piedmontese episòdi.

fact.text: It comes from Greek epeisodion, meaning roughly 'coming in after the entrance'. In Greek tragedy, an episode was the scene with actors that came between two songs by the chorus.
From Latin epocha, derived from Greek epoche meaning a point in time when something stops or holds. English 'epoch' shares the same root.

etymology: Borrowed from French équipage.
From Latin herba, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow, become green”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin herba, the source of English 'herb' and 'herbal'. Like English 'grass', it is also slang for marijuana.

senses.note: Also means herb (erbe aromatiche) and, in slang, marijuana.

etymology: From Latin hērēditāre.

senses.note: Related nouns: l'erede (heir), l'eredità (inheritance).

etymology: From Latin heroem (“hero”).

fact.text: From Latin hērō. English hero comes from the same source via Old French. Both languages borrowed the word from ancient Greek hērōs.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin errōrem. Sense 2 is built from the original Latin sense of errō (“to wander”). By surface analysis, errare + -ore.

fact.text: Latin errare first meant 'to wander', so an error was literally a straying from the path. The same idea survives in English 'knight-errant' and 'erratic'.

senses.note: fare / commettere un errore = to make a mistake; per errore = by mistake.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin exāmen. Doublet of sciame, which was inherited.

fact.text: Latin exāmen meant both 'swarm' and 'tongue of a scale', hence weighing up or testing. The swarm meaning survives in Italian sciame, its doublet.

senses.note: Dare/sostenere un esame = to take an exam. Passare un esame = to pass it.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin exāmināre.

fact.text: Latin examen meant the pointer on a pair of scales, so to examine was originally to weigh something carefully. English examine comes from the same root.

etymology: From Latin exactus.

senses.note: On its own, Esatto! means 'Exactly!' or 'That's right!'

etymology: From Latin ēsca.

fact.text: Direct descent from Latin ēsca ('food'). The word has narrowed in meaning over time from general food to bait for catching, then extended to figurative allure.

senses.note: Modern use; earliest sense '(animal) food' is obsolete.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin exclūdere. Compare the inherited doublet schiudere.

fact.text: From Latin exclūdere (ex- 'out' + claudere 'to shut'). The past participle escluso gave English 'exclusive'. The inherited doublet schiudere evolved differently.

senses.note: Usually transitive; can mean to rule out possibilities or shut someone out.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin excursiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin excursio (a running out). Shares root with English 'excursion' and 'excursus'. The word originally meant running or moving outward on a journey.

senses.note: A short trip or journey, often for leisure or hiking.

etymology: From earlier esemplo, essemplo, probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin exemplum, derived from Latin eximō (“to take out, take away”). Compare the inherited doublet scempio.

fact.text: Latin exemplum also produced an inherited Italian twin: scempio, meaning 'havoc, massacre'. It originally referred to a punishment meant to serve as an example.

senses.note: per esempio = for example (abbreviated ad es. or p. es.).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin exercitus.

fact.text: From Latin exercitus, from exercere 'to train, exercise'. An army was literally a 'trained' body of men. English exercise comes from the same verb.

senses.note: Stress on the first e: ESercito. Can also mean a big crowd (un esercito di turisti).

etymology: From Latin exercitium.

senses.note: Used for physical exercise and textbook exercises. Plural: esercizi.

etymology: From Latin exsistere.

senses.note: Takes essere in compound tenses: è esistito.

etymology: From Latin experientia.

senses.note: Spelled with s, not x. Fare esperienza = to gain experience. In science teaching it can mean an experiment.

etymology: From Latin expertus.

fact.text: Latin explodere (ex + plaudere, 'to clap') meant to drive an actor off the stage by clapping and hissing. The sense of a loud burst came much later.

senses.note: Irregular: esplosi, esploso. Uses essere for 'blow up' (la bomba è esplosa) and avere for 'fire shots'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin explōsiōnem, derived from to eject” ← “to drive out by clapping.
Borrowed from Latin expressiōnem (“a pressing out”).

senses.note: Can mean: look on a face, feeling, phrase, or a general utterance.

etymology: Past participle of esprimere; borrowed from Latin expressus.

fact.text: Literally 'pressed out': past participle of esprimere, from Latin expressus. English express shares the root, which is why people often misspell it 'expresso'.

senses.note: In Italy you usually just order 'un caffè' and get one of these.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin exprimere. Compare the inherited doublet spremere.

fact.text: Its past participle is espresso, meaning 'expressed' or 'pressed out'. Its everyday doublet spremere still means 'to squeeze', as in spremuta, freshly squeezed juice.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle espresso, passato remoto espressi.

etymology: From essere + -ci.

fact.text: Combines essere (to be) + ci (there/here), creating the impersonal 'there is' structure. Similar to French 'y a' and Spanish 'hay', all Romance languages shifted from Latin's impersonal forms to prepositional compounds.

senses.note: Impersonal verb; subject typically follows: c'è un problema (there is a problem).

etymology: Inherited from Latin sum, esse. The infinitive form is attested already from Early Medieval Latin essere. The past participle stato, shared with the verb stare, is from Latin stātus.

fact.text: Its past participle, stato, is shared with the verb stare and comes from Latin status 'stood'. So sono stato, 'I have been', literally comes from 'stood'.

senses.note: Irregular: sono, sei, è, siamo, siete, sono. As a noun, l'essere = being, creature (pl. esseri).

etymology: Inherited from Latin sum, esse. The infinitive form is attested already from Early Medieval Latin essere. The past participle stato, shared with the verb stare, is from Latin stātus.

fact.text: Its past participle, stato, is shared with the verb stare and comes from Latin status 'stood'. So sono stato, 'I have been', literally comes from 'stood'.

senses.note: Highly irregular (sono, sei, è, siamo…). Also the auxiliary for many intransitive and all reflexive verbs.
Plural: gli esseri umani. Essere is also the verb 'to be', used here as a noun meaning 'being'.

fact.text: Essere has no past participle of its own. It borrows stato from stare (Latin status), so 'I have been' and 'I have stayed' look identical in Italian.

senses.note: Siamo stati = we were / we have been. Stato is the past participle of both essere and stare.

etymology: Inherited from Latin ipsum.

fact.text: From Latin ipsum, 'itself'. The Esso petrol brand has nothing to do with it: that name comes from S.O., the initials of Standard Oil.

senses.note: Mostly written. In speech the subject is usually dropped. Feminine: essa.

etymology: Borrowed from French est, from Old English ēast.

senses.note: Takes the elided article: l'est.

etymology: Latinizing modification of state, inherited from Latin aestātem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ- (“burn; fire”).

fact.text: Watch out: this means summer, not an estate or property (that would be tenuta or proprietà). It comes from Latin aestas, from an Indo-European root meaning 'to burn'.

senses.note: Feminine: l'estate. d'estate = in summer.

etymology: From Latin externus.

senses.note: As a noun: all'esterno = outside.

etymology: From Latin externus.

senses.note: 'All'esterno' means outside. Also an adjective meaning external.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin exterus, from exter (“of another country”).

fact.text: From Latin exterus, 'outside, of another country'. Its comparative exterior gave English 'exterior'.

senses.note: Usually all'estero: vivere all'estero = to live abroad. Also an adjective meaning 'foreign'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin aestīvus.

fact.text: It comes from Latin aestivus, from aestas (summer). The rare English word 'aestivation' (summer dormancy, the hot-weather version of hibernation) shares this root.

senses.note: Example: una giornata estiva (a summer day). The noun 'summer' is estate.
Opposite: introverso.

fact.text: At Italian deli counters, cold cuts and cheese are ordered by the etto, not by the gram or kilo: due etti di mortadella. The prefix comes from Greek hekaton, 'hundred'.

senses.note: Used when buying food: un etto di prosciutto. Mezz'etto = 50 g. Short for ettogrammo.

etymology: Inherited from Latin aetātem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin aetas, built on aevum ('lifetime, age'). The same root gave Latin aeternus, the source of English eternal.

senses.note: Invariable: le età. To ask someone's age, Italians usually say: Quanti anni hai?

fact.text: From Greek eu- (well) and kalyptos (covered), referring to the tree's distinctive flower buds that are capped like a lid before blooming.

etymology: From Ancient Greek εὐφορία (euphoría), from εὔφορος (eúphoros) "bearing well".

fact.text: From Ancient Greek euphoría, meaning a sense of well-being. Eu- means 'well' and -phoría comes from phérō, 'to bear'—literally 'bearing well'.

etymology: Borrowed from English euro, from eurocurrency.

fact.text: The name 'euro' is credited to Belgian teacher and Esperantist Germain Pirlot and was officially adopted in 1995. Italians keep it unchanged in the plural: cento euro.

senses.note: Invariable in standard Italian: un euro, venti euro.

fact.text: From Greek 'Europa', a mythological princess abducted by Zeus. The continent was named after this figure from classical mythology.

senses.note: Proper noun; continent name

etymology: From Latin Eurōpaeus.
From Latin ēvidentem.

fact.text: From Latin ēvidentem. Cognate with English evident and evidence, all sharing the Latin root for 'seeing' (vidēre).

etymology: From Latin ēvidentia.

fact.text: Directly from Latin ēvidentia, the same root as English evidence. Both share the notion of being clear or obvious.

etymology: From Latin ēvītāre (“to avoid”), from ē- + vītō.

fact.text: From Latin ēvītāre (to shun), from ē- (out) + vītō—literally to turn away from.

etymology: From evolvere + -si.

senses.note: Reflexive: mi evolvo, si è evoluto. Takes essere.

etymology: From Latin fabrica (“workshop”), from faber (“forger, smith”). Compare French fabrique, German Fabrik. Doublet of forgia.

fact.text: Comes from Latin fabrica, the workshop of a faber (smith). English 'fabric' and 'fabricate' share the root, but in Italian it means factory. Fabric is tessuto.

senses.note: Not 'fabric', which is tessuto or stoffa. Plural: fabbriche.

etymology: From Latin facienda, neuter plural of faciendus (“that which is to be done”). Doublet of azienda. Cognate with Sicilian facenna.

fact.text: From Latin facienda (things to be done), the neuter plural of faciendus—literally what must be faced or handled.

etymology: From Late Latin facia, from Latin faciēs (“face”).

fact.text: Faccia tosta (literally 'hard face') means cheek or nerve: Che faccia tosta! = What a nerve!

senses.note: Everyday word; il viso is softer and more neutral. Faccia a faccia = face to face.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin facilis (“easy”), from faciō (“to do, make”).

fact.text: It is a false friend. In Italian it simply means easy, while English 'facile' means shallow or glib. Both come from Latin facilis, from facere (to do).

senses.note: È facile che… = it's likely that…

etymology: From Latin facultātem, probably a borrowing.

senses.note: Invariable plural: le facoltà. Teaching staff is 'il corpo docente', not facoltà.

etymology: From fallo + -are or falla + -are, from Vulgar Latin *falla, or from Late Latin fallāre, from Latin fallere.
From Vulgar Latin *fallīre, from Latin fallere.

fact.text: It goes back to Latin fallere, 'to deceive', the same root behind English false, fallacy and fallible. English fail comes from that root too, via Old French faillir.

senses.note: Ha fallito = he failed / missed; è fallito = it went bankrupt. Fallito also means 'a failure' (person).

etymology: Deverbal from fallare (“to make a mistake”) + -o. Compare Spanish fallo.

fact.text: From Latin fallere (to deceive, fail). The Italian noun fallo developed from the verb fallare (to make a mistake), paralleling Spanish fallo—both Romance languages preserving this ancient root meaning.

senses.note: Common word in sports (foul) and general usage.

etymology: From Latin falsus, from fallere.

senses.note: Also fake or forged: soldi falsi (counterfeit money).

etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek φανός (phanós).

fact.text: Comes from Ancient Greek phanós, 'torch, lantern', from a root meaning 'to shine'. English 'phenomenon' and 'phantom' come from the same Greek family.

senses.note: Stressed on the last syllable. Plural doesn't change: i falò.

etymology: Inherited from Latin famem (“hunger”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *dʰH- (“to disappear”). Compare Galician fame, French faim, Portuguese fome and Romanian foame, Sicilian fami.

fact.text: From Latin fames, 'hunger', which also gave English 'famine' via Old French. Italians 'have hunger' (ho fame) instead of 'being hungry'.

senses.note: Avere fame = to be hungry (literally 'to have hunger'). Morire di fame = to starve.

etymology: Inherited from Latin familia (“servants, domestic staff, household”).

fact.text: Latin familia first meant a household's servants and slaves, from famulus (servant). Only later did it mean relatives by blood.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin familiāritātem.

senses.note: Avere familiarità con = to be familiar with. The plural is the same as the singular: le familiarità.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fāmōsus.

senses.note: Can also mean 'notorious' in a negative sense.

etymology: Borrowed from English fan.

fact.text: Borrowed from English, where this fan is short for fanatic, from Latin fanaticus 'inspired by a temple' (fanum). It's unrelated to the fan that cools you.

senses.note: Invariable: il/la fan, i/le fan. Tifoso is the usual word for a sports fan.

fact.text: From Latin 'in anum' (in/into the anus), contracted into a single Italian term. A classic example of Latin anatomical insults surviving in modern Romance languages.

senses.note: Vulgar slang; literally anatomically explicit insult. Use with extreme caution.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin phantasma, or Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma).

fact.text: Related to English 'fantasy' and 'phantom': all derive from Ancient Greek phantasma, meaning an appearance or apparition.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin phantasticus (“imaginary”), from Ancient Greek φανταστικός (phantastikós).

senses.note: Very common as praise: Fantastico! = Great! Also means imaginary, from fantasy.

fact.text: Literally 'to do it for oneself' — a colloquial verb combining fare (to do) with the pronoun ce la (it to yourself). Essential for expressing capability and resilience in everyday Italian.

senses.note: Often with infinitive: ce la fai a finire? (can you manage to finish?)

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin fāre.

fact.text: Comes via Late Latin fare, a shortened form of Latin facere, which also gave English fact, factory and manufacture.

senses.note: Irregular: faccio, fai, fa, facciamo, fate, fanno; past participle fatto.

etymology: Inherited from Latin farīna (“flour, meal”), from far (“kind of grain”).

fact.text: From Latin far, an ancient grain (emmer wheat). English kept it too: farina is a fine cereal meal, and starchy foods are called farinaceous.

senses.note: farina integrale = wholemeal flour.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (pharmakeía, “the use of drugs”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek pharmakeia, 'the use of drugs', from pharmakon, a word that could mean both 'remedy' and 'poison'.

senses.note: Usually marked by a green cross. Pharmacist = farmacista.

etymology: From fare (“to do, make”) + -si (“oneself”).

fact.text: Literally 'to do/make oneself', the reflexive form acquired the meaning 'to become' — a pattern seen across Romance languages where reflexive constructions evolved to express change of state.

senses.note: Reflexive verb; very common in Italian

etymology: From Ancient Greek φάσις (phásis, “appearance”).

fact.text: From Ancient Greek phásis ('appearance'). English 'phase' is a direct borrowing of the same Greek word via Latin.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fastidium.

fact.text: Comes from Latin fastidium, 'disgust, disdain', the same source as English fastidious. In Italian it doesn't mean fussiness, it means annoyance.

senses.note: Dare fastidio a = to bother someone: ti dà fastidio? (does it bother you?)

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *fatīga, from Latin fatīgō (“to tire, weary”).

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin fatica, ultimately from Latin fatigare (to tire, weary). The English 'fatigue' is a direct borrowing from the French form of this root.

senses.note: Can also mean effort, work, labour, or difficulty. Often used in plural: fatiche (travails, ordeals).

etymology: From fattore (“farmer”).

fact.text: False friend alert: this word looks like 'factory' but means a farm. It comes from fattore, the farmer or estate manager. A factory is la fabbrica.

senses.note: Not a factory! Factory = fabbrica.

etymology: Inherited from Latin fābula. Compare the doublets fiaba and fola.

fact.text: Comes from Latin fabula, which is also where English 'fable' and 'fabulous' come from. Italian has a sister word from the same root: fiaba, 'fairy tale'.

senses.note: Also fairy tale. Da favola = fabulous, dreamlike (una vacanza da favola).

etymology: From Latin favor.

senses.note: Per favore = please. Fare un favore a qualcuno = to do someone a favor.

etymology: Borrowed from English fax.

fact.text: Borrowed from English, where fax is short for facsimile, from Latin fac simile, 'make (it) similar'. So the word returned to Italy's ancestral language in disguise.

senses.note: Invariable: i fax. Also the fax machine.

etymology: From Late Latin Febrārius, from Latin (mēnsis) Februārius. Compare Sicilian frivaru.

fact.text: Latin Februarius is named after the Februa, a Roman purification festival held in mid-February. That made it the month of cleansing before the old Roman year began in March.

senses.note: Months are lowercase in Italian: a febbraio = in February.

etymology: Inherited from Latin febrem, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰris, an extension of the root *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn, warm”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin febris, which goes back to an ancient root meaning 'to burn, to warm'. A fever is literally a burning.

senses.note: Avere la febbre = to have a temperature or fever.

etymology: From Latin fidem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ-.

fact.text: From Latin fidem, traced to Proto-Indo-European *bheydh- (to command, persuade, trust). Cognate with Germanic languages.

etymology: From earlier *fecato, from Late Latin fīcātum (“liver”), from Latin iecur fīcātum (“fig-stuffed liver, foie gras”).
Borrowed from Latin fēlīcem.

fact.text: From Latin felix, 'lucky, happy', which gave us the names Felix and Felicity and the English word 'felicitous'.

senses.note: Felice di + infinitive = happy to: sono felice di vederti.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fēlīcitātem. By surface analysis, felice + -ità.

fact.text: Latin felix first meant fruitful or fertile, and only later lucky and happy. It goes back to a root meaning 'to suckle', which also gave Latin femina, source of feminine.

senses.note: Invariable: le felicità. Felicità is also a famous 1982 hit by Al Bano and Romina Power.

etymology: Inherited from Latin fēmina.

senses.note: Used for animals and for girls (opposite: maschio). For 'woman' use 'donna'.

etymology: From Latin fēminīnus, with change of suffix by dissimilation. By surface analysis, femmina (“female”, noun) + -ile.

senses.note: Also women's (calcio femminile = women's football) and the grammatical gender.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fēria.

fact.text: Latin feriae meant 'days of rest, festival days'. Italy's 15 August holiday, Ferragosto, comes from Feriae Augusti, 'the holidays of Augustus'. English 'fair' goes back to the same Latin word.

senses.note: Almost always plural: le ferie. Andare in ferie = to go on holiday; essere in ferie = to be on holiday.
Relational adjective; from Latin feria

etymology: From Latin ferīre, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH-.

fact.text: Latin ferire meant 'to strike'. Old French s'entreferir, 'to strike each other', which comes from it, gave English the word 'interfere'.

senses.note: Present tense adds -isc-: ferisco, ferisci. Ferirsi = to get hurt, to hurt oneself.
From ferire, 'to wound'. Also used for emotional wounds.
Past participle of ferire. Also means 'wounded', or 'hurt' emotionally.

etymology: Inherited from Latin firmāre. Doublet of firmare.

fact.text: Comes from Latin firmare, 'to make firm', related to English firm and confirm. Stopping something is really fixing it in place.

senses.note: Fermare qualcuno = to stop someone; fermarsi = to stop oneself, come to a halt (ci fermiamo).

fact.text: Comes from fermo 'still', from Latin firmus 'firm, steady'. Stopping is making yourself firm in place, and English 'firm' shares the root.

senses.note: Can also mean to stay a while: fermarsi a cena = to stay for dinner.

etymology: From fermare (“to stop”).

fact.text: English musicians borrowed this word: in sheet music a fermata is the eye-shaped sign that tells you to hold a note, literally a 'stop'.

senses.note: 'Fermata dell'autobus' = bus stop. From fermare, 'to stop'.

etymology: From Latin firmus, from Proto-Italic *fermos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer-mo-s (“holding”), from the root *dʰer- (“to hold”).

fact.text: From Latin firmus, which also gave English firm. Its ancient root *dher- meant 'to hold' and also produced the Sanskrit word dharma.

senses.note: Stai fermo! = Keep still! The related verb fermare/fermarsi means to stop.

etymology: From Latin ferrum.

fact.text: Comes from Latin ferrum, which may have been borrowed, perhaps through Etruscan, from a Phoenician word like barzel, 'iron'. It is the source of the chemical symbol Fe.

senses.note: A clothes iron is ferro da stiro. Plural ferri also means knitting needles.

etymology: From Late Latin fēsta, from the plural of Latin fēstus (“festive”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin festa, from festus 'festive'. It's a cousin of English feast, festival and festive, and of Spanish fiesta.

senses.note: Also a holiday or feast day: 'domani è festa' = tomorrow is a holiday. 'Buone feste!' = Happy holidays!

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *festizāre. Derivable from festa + -eggiare.

senses.note: Used for events and people: festeggiare un compleanno, festeggiare qualcuno.

etymology: From Latin fēstīvus.

fact.text: From Latin fēstīvus, related to festa (feast, festival). Related to English 'festival' and 'festive'.

etymology: Uncertain; several possibilities exist. Probably ultimately from Latin findere, through an alteration of its past participle fissus into a form *fictus > *fectus, later becoming feminine. (Compare the change from fixus to fitto). An alternative may be a Vulgar Latin *offetta (“little piece”), diminutive of offa. Compare Galician and Portuguese fita, Dalmatian fiata, Sicilian feḍḍa, Sardinian fitta.

fact.text: Greek feta cheese gets its name from this Italian word: Greek borrowed 'feta' from Italian, since the cheese is cut and stored in slices.

senses.note: Una fetta di torta/pane = a slice of cake/bread. 'Fetta biscottata' = rusk.

etymology: From fettuccia + -ina (diminutive suffix).

fact.text: From fettuccia (ribbon) plus the diminutive suffix -ina. The word literally means 'little ribbons', referring to the pasta's thin, flat shape.

senses.note: Ribbon-shaped pasta; normally used in plural

etymology: From fiamma (“flame”) + -ifero (“-iferous, producing”).

fact.text: It literally means 'flame-bearer': fiamma (flame) + -ifero (bearing, producing), the same suffix as English '-iferous' in 'coniferous'.

senses.note: A sports match is una partita. 'Accendere un fiammifero' = to strike a match.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French flanc (“flank, side”).

fact.text: Fianco and English 'flank' share a common ancestor in Frankish *hlanku, making them true cognates. The Italian word kept the original sense while English developed it into both the anatomical term and the military maneuver.

senses.note: Also means 'side' of something; from Old French flanc

etymology: From Latin ficus.

fact.text: In the idiom 'non me ne importa un fico secco' (I don't care a dried fig), the fruit becomes a symbol of absolute indifference—meaning 'I couldn't care less'.

senses.note: the fresh fruit and the tree it grows on

fact.text: Watch out: if an Italian says 'guardo una fiction', they mean a TV drama series, often a homegrown RAI or Mediaset one, not a novel.

senses.note: Plural doesn't change: le fiction. Fiction as a literary genre is 'narrativa'.

etymology: From fidanz(are) + -ato. Compare French fiancé.

fact.text: Italians call any steady partner il fidanzato or la fidanzata, even with no wedding planned. It comes from fidanza (trust), related to fede (faith) and English fidelity.

senses.note: As a noun, il fidanzato / la fidanzata = boyfriend/girlfriend or fiancé(e).

etymology: From fidanz(are) + -ato. Compare French fiancé.

fact.text: Italians call any steady partner il fidanzato or la fidanzata, even with no wedding planned. It comes from fidanza (trust), related to fede (faith) and English fidelity.

senses.note: Feminine: la fidanzata. In everyday speech it often just means 'boyfriend'.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *fīdāre, from Latin fīdere.

fact.text: Comes from Latin fidere 'to trust', the same root as English confide, fidelity and confidence. The classic dog name Fido is usually traced to the same Latin root.

senses.note: Almost always reflexive: fidarsi di qualcuno (aux. essere). Plain fidare is rare.

etymology: From fidar(e) (“to entrust”) + -si (enclitic reflexive pronoun).

senses.note: Always reflexive (fidarsi di). Takes preposition 'di' with the object of trust.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fīdūcia.

fact.text: From Latin fiducia (trust, confidence), derived from fidus (faithful). The root also appears in English 'fidelity' and 'fiduciary'.

senses.note: Can also mean confidence, faith, or credit. Example: avere fiducia in qualcuno (to trust someone).

etymology: Inherited from Latin fīlia, from fīlius (“child, son”), from Old Latin fīlios, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁y-li-os (“sucker”), a derivation from the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck”). Cognate to French fille, Portuguese filha, Galician filla, Romanian fie, Spanish hija, Sicilian figghia, Sardinian filla, Romansh feglia.

fact.text: It goes back to Latin filia, from a root meaning 'to suck', so a child was a 'suckling'. Latin femina, the source of English 'feminine', comes from the same root.

senses.note: figlio = son; figli = children (or sons).

etymology: From Latin fīlius, from Old Latin fīlios, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁y-li-os (“sucker”), a derivation from the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck”). Cognate to French fils, Portuguese filho, Galician fillo, Romanian fiu, Spanish hijo, Sicilian figghiu, Corsican figliu, Sardinian fillu, Romansh fegl.

fact.text: Comes from Latin filius, which goes back to an Indo-European root meaning 'to suck'. A son was originally 'the suckling'.

senses.note: Plural figli can mean 'sons' or 'children'. figlio unico = only child.

etymology: From Latin fīliolus. By surface analysis, figlio (“son”) + -olo (diminutive suffix).

fact.text: From Latin fīliolus (little son), the same root as figlio. The -olo suffix is a diminutive, originally expressing affection or smallness, now mainly literary.

senses.note: Archaic or literary diminutive form of figlio.
Northern Italian slang, alternative to fico.

etymology: From Latin figūra, possibly borrowed.

fact.text: Directly related to English 'figure': both come from Latin figūra, meaning shape or form.

senses.note: Also: diagram, illustration, character, or face of a playing card.

etymology: Compare French se figurer.

fact.text: Compare French se figurer ('to imagine'). Both come from Latin figura and express the idea of forming a mental picture.

senses.note: Reflexive; also idiomatic: 'figurarsi!' (don't mention it!) or expressing disbelief.

etymology: Probably from filo, or from Latin fila, plural of filum. Compare French file, Portuguese fila.

fact.text: Probably from filo (thread) or Latin fila (threads). French file and Portuguese fila share the same origin.

senses.note: Can mean queue/line of people, a row of bricks/blocks, or a rank in formation.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English file.
Unadapted borrowing from English film.

senses.note: Invariable: il film, i film. Borrowed from English.

etymology: Inherited from Latin fīlum.

fact.text: From Latin filum 'thread', the source of English filament and, via French, file: papers were once kept strung on a thread or wire.

senses.note: Plural fili; figurative plural le fila (e.g. tirare le fila). Also wire: filo elettrico.

etymology: From Late Latin fīnālis, from Latin fīnis (“end; boundary, limit”), whence fine. By surface analysis, fine (“end; limit; goal”) + -ale.

senses.note: As a noun: il finale = the ending (of a film or book); la finale = the final (sports).

etymology: From finale + -mente.

fact.text: Careful: it means 'at last!' after a long wait, not 'finally' as in the last point of a list. For that, Italians say 'infine' or 'alla fine'.

senses.note: Shows relief after a wait. For 'lastly' in a list, use 'infine'.

etymology: Univerbation of fino (“fin(o)”) + che.

fact.text: Univerbation of fino (until, by the end of) + che (that). Created by joining two words into one, a common process in Romance language evolution.

senses.note: Temporal conjunction; can also mean 'as long as'.

etymology: From Latin fīnem.

fact.text: Gender changes the meaning: la fine is the end, but il fine is the goal, as in il fine giustifica i mezzi. As an adjective it means thin or refined, never 'okay'.

senses.note: alla fine = in the end, finally. Masculine il fine means aim or purpose.

etymology: From Latin fenestra.

fact.text: Comes from Latin fenestra, probably borrowed from Etruscan. The same Latin word gives English 'defenestration', the act of throwing someone out of a window.

etymology: Inherited from Latin fingere (“to fashion, make up”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to mold”).
Inherited from Latin fīnīre.

senses.note: An -isc- verb: finisco, finisci. È finita = it's over.

etymology: From some such adjectival form as Vulgar Latin *fīnus, from Latin fīnis (“a boundary, limit”), whence Italian fine. The prepositional usage is directly paralleled in Latin fīne, fīnī (“up to, as far as”).

fact.text: From Latin finis 'boundary, limit', the same root as English finish, final and finite. 'Until' and 'as far as' both mean going up to a limit.

senses.note: Usually fino a (+ time/place): fino a domani, fino alla valle. As an adjective fino means fine or thin.
Also 'as far as' for places: fino a Roma. Combines with articles: fino alle cinque.

etymology: From fino (“until”) + ora (“now”).

fact.text: Composed of fino (until) + ora (now), literally meaning until the hour or moment. Related to the English word "hour" through their shared Indo-European root.

etymology: From the feminine of finto.

senses.note: From the feminine of finto (feigned, pretended).

etymology: From Latin fictus, perfect passive participle of fingō, probably through a Vulgar Latin root *finctus, with a nasal infix. Compare French feint, Lombard fint and Piedmontese fint.

fact.text: From Latin fictus, the past participle of fingere (to dissemble, deceive). This root appears in English feign, fiction, and figure.

senses.note: Also: false, insincere, hypocritical, artificial

etymology: Inherited from Latin flōrem.

fact.text: Latin flos goes back to a root meaning 'to bloom', the same source as English 'blossom' and 'bloom'. English 'flour' was originally 'flower', meaning the finest part of the meal.

senses.note: A fior di... = on the surface of... In card games, fiori = clubs.

etymology:
Etymology tree
Latin firmoder.
Italian firmarebf.
Italian firma
Back-formation from firmare, from Latin firmāre, from firmus; cognates include English firm (adjective). Doublet of dharma.

fact.text: A signature 'makes firm' a document (Latin firmare). English borrowed the word as 'firm', at first meaning the name a business signed under, then the business itself.

senses.note: Mettere la firma = to sign. Raccolta firme = petition (collection of signatures).

etymology: From Latin firmāre, from firmus. Doublet of fermare.

fact.text: From Latin firmare 'to make firm', a twin of fermare 'to stop'. English firm (company) comes from Italian firma 'signature', the name a business signs under.

senses.note: la firma = signature. Don't confuse with fermare = to stop.

etymology: From Latin physicus (“physical”, “natural”), from Ancient Greek φυσικός (phusikós).

fact.text: As a noun, il fisico usually means your physique, as in 'ha un bel fisico' (he's in good shape). It can also mean a physicist, but never a physician (that's il medico).

senses.note: Also a noun: il fisico = physique or physicist; la fisica = physics.

etymology: Inherited from Latin flūmen.

fact.text: It comes from Latin flumen, from fluere 'to flow', the same source as English fluid and flume. Fiume was also the Italian name of Rijeka, a city in Croatia.

senses.note: Un fiume di parole = a flood of words.

etymology: From Occitan and Old Occitan flaut.

fact.text: From Occitan flaut. The word travelled from Occitan (southern France) into Italian, then into other European languages, spreading musical terminology across the continent.

senses.note: The primary meaning; also refers to a recorder.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin focācium (via its plural focācia), derived from Latin focus (“hearth”). Doublet of fugassa. Compare Sicilian fugazza.

fact.text: From Latin focus (hearth), because focaccia was originally cooked on the hearth. The same root gives English focus and fire-related words.

senses.note: Italian flatbread, typically seasoned with olive oil and salt.

etymology: From Late Latin folia, from the plural of Latin folium (“leaf”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolh₃yom (“leaf”), from *bʰleh₃- (“blossom, flower”).

fact.text: It comes from folia, the plural of Latin folium ('leaf'), later treated as a singular. The same Latin word gave English 'foliage', 'folio' and 'portfolio'.

senses.note: Idiom: mangiare la foglia = to catch on, to see through a trick.

etymology: From Latin folium.

fact.text: From Latin folium, 'leaf', like English 'folio' and 'foliage'. Watch the ending: il foglio is a sheet of paper, but la foglia is a leaf on a tree.

senses.note: Not a bed sheet (that is lenzuolo). Compare la foglia, 'leaf'.

etymology: Deverbal from follare + -a. Compare Sicilian fuḍḍa.

senses.note: Plural: le folle. Don't confuse it with the adjective folle, 'mad' or 'crazy'.

etymology: From Latin fundus (“deep”).

fact.text: From Latin fundus, 'bottom' or 'base'. That's also the source of English fund, fundamental and founder (as in sinking to the bottom).

senses.note: 'In fondo' means at the bottom/end or 'after all'. Can also mean fund or background.

etymology: From Late Latin fontāna, from Latin fontānus, from fōns. The meaning of fountain, as an artificial installation, may be partly derived from or influenced by the Old French equivalent.

fact.text: Tradition says that tossing a coin over your shoulder into Rome's Trevi Fountain means you will return to Rome. The coins are collected and given to charity.

senses.note: Also a public drinking fountain; la Fontana di Trevi in Rome.

etymology: Inherited from Latin fontem m, of Proto-Indo-European origin.

fact.text: From Latin fontem, meaning spring or fountain. English 'font' also derives from the same Latin root, though Italian fonte covers broader meanings from water sources to suppliers.

senses.note: A place where water naturally emerges from the ground.
A person or thing that supplies or provides something.
A basin or vessel for holding baptismal water in a church.

fact.text: In Italian, 'football' specifically means American football. Soccer is 'calcio'—a distinction important for sports discussions.

senses.note: Invariable English loanword; refers to American football, not soccer (calcio)

etymology: From forca (“gardening fork”) + -etta (diminutive suffix). Compare French fourchette. Sense four is calqued from French.

fact.text: Literally a 'little pitchfork': forca (pitchfork) plus the diminutive -etta. French fourchette was formed the same way.

senses.note: A fork in the road is un bivio, not una forchetta.

etymology: Derived from Early Medieval Latin foresta. Documented since the thirteenth century.

senses.note: For smaller woods, Italians usually say il bosco.

etymology: Inherited from Latin fōrma.

fact.text: Formaggio (cheese) comes from this word: cheese was pressed in a mould (Latin caseus formaticus). A whole cheese is still called una forma di formaggio.

senses.note: Essere in forma = to be in shape / fit.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French formage, from Medieval Latin fōrmāticum, from Latin fōrma (“mould/mold”). Compare modern French fromage.

fact.text: Comes from Medieval Latin formaticum, meaning cheese shaped in a mould (Latin forma). French reshuffled the letters to get fromage, but Italian kept the 'form'.

etymology: From Latin formāre.

senses.note: Reflexive formarsi = to take shape, or to be educated/trained.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fōrmātiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin fōrmātiōnem. The root fōrma (form) traces back through Proto-Indo-European to Ancient Greek morphḗ, the same source as English morphology.

senses.note: Also: formation, group, team lineup

etymology: From forno + -ello (“diminutive suffix”), or from Vulgar Latin *furnellus, from Latin furnus. Compare French fourneau, Sicilian furneddu, Catalan fornell, Romansh furnel, Sardinian furredhu, Occitan fornèl, Portuguese fornilho, Spanish hornillo.

fact.text: Literally a 'little oven': forno (oven) + the diminutive suffix -ello.

senses.note: Usually the hob or a single burner. Ai fornelli = at the stove, cooking.

etymology: From fornire + -tore.
From Latin furnus, from Proto-Italic *fornos, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰr̥-nós, from *gʷʰer- (“warm, hot”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin furnus (oven). The related Latin word fornax gave English 'furnace'. Both go back to a root meaning 'to be warm'.

senses.note: Al forno = baked (pasta al forno). Also means bakery.

etymology: Inherited from Latin forsit.

fact.text: From Latin forsit, from fors sit, 'let it be chance'. Fors (chance) is also behind fortuna, which gave English 'fortune'.

senses.note: Forse sì = maybe so. Forse often goes with the indicative: forse ha ragione.

etymology: From Latin fortem

fact.text: Musical forte ('loud') came to English from Italian. Forte meaning 'strong point' came via French fort and was later respelled. Both go back to Latin fortis, 'strong'.

senses.note: Also means 'loud' (parla forte = speak up). Colloquially, che forte! = how cool!

etymology: From Latin fortūna, from fors (“chance, luck”).

fact.text: In English a fortune is usually a lot of money, but Italian fortuna mostly means luck. Fortuna was also the Roman goddess of chance, from Latin fors, 'chance'.

senses.note: Che fortuna! = How lucky! Per fortuna = luckily.

etymology: From fortunato + -mente.
From Latin fortūnātus.

senses.note: Essere fortunato = to be lucky. Also a male given name: Fortunato.

etymology: From Late Latin fortia, a noun derived from the neuter plural of Latin fortis (“strong”).

fact.text: Italians shout it to cheer on teams, as in 'Forza Italia!'. It comes from Late Latin fortia, the neuter plural of fortis 'strong', as in fortia facta, 'brave deeds'.

senses.note: Forza! = Come on! / Go on! Used to cheer or encourage someone.
An encouraging set phrase, literally 'strength and courage!'

etymology: Clipping of fotografia.

fact.text: Short for fotografia (photography), common across Romance languages for this clipped modern term.

senses.note: Invariable: stesso form in singular and plural

etymology: From foto- + -grafia.

senses.note: Usually shortened to la foto (plural le foto). Fare una foto = to take a photo. Also means photography.

etymology: From Latin futuere (“to fuck”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to hit”).

senses.note: Fottiti! = Fuck off! For 'not to give a fuck', use fottersene: me ne fotto.
Strong swear word used before a noun: quel fottuto sogno. Milder: maledetto.

etymology: From Latin īnfrā, which stems from inferus.

fact.text: Fra and tra mean exactly the same thing. Italians pick whichever sounds better, avoiding repeated sounds: 'tra fratelli' but 'fra tre giorni'.

senses.note: Means the same as tra. With time it means 'in': fra due giorni = in two days.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fragilem.

fact.text: From Latin fragilem (breakable). Related to frangere (to break) and English 'fraction', 'fragment'—all from the same Indo-European root.

etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *dʰreh₂ǵ-der.?
Proto-Indo-European *sróh₂gsder.?
Proto-Italic *frāgom
Latin frāga
Proto-Indo-European *-lós
Proto-Indo-European *-elós
Proto-Italic *-elos
