Inherited from Vulgar Latin *frāgula.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin *frāgula, derived from Proto-Indo-European root d̸reh₂ǵ. Cognate with English fragrant; the berry was named for its sweet scent.

senses.note: Also means strawberry colour (invariable masculine noun in that sense).

etymology:
From Francia + -ese.
Borrowed from Old French franceis.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian. Also the noun for the language: parlo francese.

etymology: From franco- (“free from duty”) + bollo (“stamp”).

fact.text: Literally a 'free stamp': franco means 'free from duty' and bollo means 'stamp'. It was the mark showing that postage had already been paid.

senses.note: Buy them at the tabaccheria. Mettere un francobollo = to put a stamp on.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”).

fact.text: It looks like 'phrase', but in everyday Italian it usually means a full sentence. Both come from Greek phrasis, 'manner of expression'.

senses.note: A court sentence is 'condanna'. 'Phrase' as an expression is often 'espressione'.

etymology: From fratello + -astro.

senses.note: Means either stepbrother (from a parent's remarriage) or half-brother (same father or mother but not both parents).

etymology: From Latin frātellus, a diminutive of Latin frāter, from Proto-Italic *frātēr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr.

fact.text: Comes from a diminutive of Latin frāter, the source of 'fraternal' and, through French frère, 'friar'. English 'brother' comes from the same Indo-European root.

senses.note: Plural fratelli can mean siblings: Hai fratelli? = Do you have any brothers or sisters?

fact.text: Made of fra 'between' + tempo 'time', so nel frattempo literally means 'in the between-time'.

senses.note: Almost always appears in the phrase nel frattempo = in the meantime.

etymology: Inherited from Latin frīgidus (“cold”) (through a syncopated Vulgar Latin or Late Latin form frigdus, fricdus, attested in the Appendix Probi, or fridus, found in a Pompeian inscription), itself from frīgeō (“to be cold”), from frīgus (“cold, coldness”), from Proto-Indo-European *sríHgos. Doublet of frigido, a later borrowing.

fact.text: From Latin frigidus, source of English frigid and refrigerator. The Appendix Probi, a Roman list of mistakes, already warns 'frigida, not fricda': the vowel was being dropped.

senses.note: As a noun: ho freddo = I'm cold; fa freddo = it's cold (weather).

etymology: Inherited from Latin frīgidus (“cold”) (through a syncopated Vulgar Latin or Late Latin form frigdus, fricdus, attested in the Appendix Probi, or fridus, found in a Pompeian inscription), itself from frīgeō (“to be cold”), from frīgus (“cold, coldness”), from Proto-Indo-European *sríHgos. Doublet of frigido, a later borrowing.

fact.text: From Latin frigidus, source of English frigid and refrigerator. The Appendix Probi, a Roman list of mistakes, already warns 'frigida, not fricda': the vowel was being dropped.

senses.note: 'Ho freddo' = I'm cold. A cold (illness) is il raffreddore. Also an adjective: caffè freddo.

etymology: Borrowed from English freezer.

senses.note: Invariable plural: i freezer. Native synonym: il congelatore.

etymology: From earlier *frecàre, from Latin fricāre.
From fregarsi + -ne. Coined or popularized by Gabriele d'Annunzio as a translation of the English to not give a fuck.

fact.text: Coined or popularized by the early 20th-century Italian writer Gabriele d'Annunzio as a defiant expression of indifference, reflecting a distinctly Italian attitude toward authority and convention.

senses.note: Pronominal verb; literally 'to not care about it'. Popularized by Gabriele d'Annunzio.

etymology: From freno + -are, or possibly from Latin frēnāre.

fact.text: Derived from freno ('bridle'), ultimately from Latin frēnum. The verb meaning shifted from 'to bridle' to 'to brake,' reflecting how braking mechanisms work like a bridle on movement.

etymology: Inherited from Latin frēnum.

fact.text: Latin frenum meant 'bridle'. Its verb refrenare, 'to rein in', is the source of English 'refrain', as in holding yourself back.

senses.note: Tirare il freno a mano = to pull the handbrake. Figuratively a curb: tenere a freno = to keep in check.

etymology: From Latin frequentāre.

senses.note: Means attending regularly. Also to frequent a place or to hang out with people.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *friscum.

fact.text: English 'fresco' comes from Italian painting on fresh plaster, 'affresco' or 'a fresco'. The pigment soaks into the wet lime and becomes part of the wall as it dries.

senses.note: Pane fresco = fresh bread. Also wet paint: vernice fresca.
Fa fresco = it's cool (weather). Mild coolness, not cold (freddo).

etymology: Deverbal from frettare + -a.

senses.note: Avere fretta = to be in a hurry. In fretta = quickly. Usually singular.

etymology: Inherited from Latin frīgere, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-.

fact.text: Comes from the same Latin verb, frigere, as English 'fry', which reached English through French frire. Fritto misto and frittata come from the same root.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle fritto, passato remoto frissi. Vai a farti friggere! = Get lost!

etymology: Clipping of frigorifero.

senses.note: Masculine, invariable (no plural). Short form of frigorifero (refrigerator).

etymology: Word build upon the model of the French calorifère (“heater, radiator”), as an adaptation made using Latin frigor (“coldness”) + -fer (“-bearing, -carrying, -bringing”).

fact.text: A made-up learned word modelled on French calorifère (heater): Latin frigor (cold) + -fer (bearing), so it literally means 'cold-bearer'.

senses.note: Usually shortened to il frigo in everyday speech.

etymology: From Latin frīctus, from frīgō.

fact.text: From Latin frīctus (fried, past participle of frīgō). The root is related to English fry, both tracing back to the same ancient cooking method.

senses.note: Of wine, water, or a person's character.

etymology: Inherited from Latin frontem (“forehead”). For noun 1 sense 2 compare the Latin etymon and derivatives in Italian like sfrontato (“shameless”). Cognate with Sicilian frunti.

senses.note: Feminine la fronte = forehead. Masculine il fronte = a military or political front.

etymology: From frullare + -tore.
From Late Latin fructa, from Latin fructus.

fact.text: Italian splits fruit in two: la frutta is fruit you eat, il frutto is a single fruit or a result. So seafood is frutti di mare, literally 'fruits of the sea'.

senses.note: Collective, usually singular: mangio la frutta. A single fruit is un frutto.

etymology: From frutta + -vendolo.

senses.note: Fruiterer or vendor of fresh produce

etymology: From Latin fructus, itself from the verb fruor.

fact.text: From Latin fructus, related to fruor (to enjoy), which gave English 'fruit' and other words like 'fruitful' and 'fruition'.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *focīlis [petra], derived from Latin focus. Compare French fusil, Friulian fusîl, Piedmontese fusil.

fact.text: Cognate with English fusil. Both derive from Vulgar Latin focīlis (from focus, meaning fire or hearth), reflecting the gun's role as a fire-based weapon.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fuga. Compare the inherited doublet foga.

fact.text: From Latin fuga, shared root with English 'fugitive' and 'fugue'. All relate to the idea of running away or fleeing.

senses.note: Also: flight, leak, a fugue in music, or a breakaway in cycling.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *fugīre, from Latin fugere, from Proto-Italic *fugiō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg-. Cognate with Sicilian fùjiri.

fact.text: From fulmine, a lightning bolt. 'Fulminare qualcuno con lo sguardo' means to glare daggers at someone. A blown light bulb is also 'fulminata'.

senses.note: Past participle of fulminare (to strike with lightning, to electrocute).

etymology: From Latin fulmen.

fact.text: Italians call love at first sight 'un colpo di fulmine', a lightning strike. The Latin source fulmen also gave English 'fulminate'.

senses.note: Un fulmine = a bolt of lightning.

etymology: From Latin fūmāre.

fact.text: From Latin fumare, from fumus 'smoke'. English fumes and fumigate come from the same word.

senses.note: Vietato fumare = No smoking. Il fumo = smoke.

etymology: From fumo + -etto.

fact.text: It literally means 'little puff of smoke' (fumo + -etto). The name first described the speech balloons, which look like puffs of smoke, and later came to mean comics in general.

senses.note: Plural 'i fumetti' also means comics as a medium: leggere i fumetti = to read comics.

etymology: From Latin fūmus, from Proto-Italic *fūmos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós.

fact.text: From Latin fumus, 'smoke', the source of English 'fume' and 'fumigate'. 'Perfume' comes from it too, literally 'through smoke', since early perfumes were burned as incense.

senses.note: Also means 'smoking': 'Il fumo fa male.' The verb is fumare.

etymology: From Late Latin fūnerālis (“pertaining to a funeral”), from Latin funus.

senses.note: Formal/plural form: funerali. From Latin funeralis.

etymology: From Latin fungus.

fact.text: From Latin fungus. Possibly connected to Germanic 'swamp' through a non-Indo-European substrate language, linking fungi to wet environments where they thrive.

etymology: Borrowed from French fonctionner. Cognate with Piedmontese funsioné.

senses.note: Use it for things that work (non funziona = it's broken). For people working a job, use lavorare.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fūnctiōnem.

senses.note: Also a church service. In funzione = working or operating.

etymology: From Latin focus (“hearth”).

fact.text: From Latin focus, 'hearth'. English 'focus' is the same word: Kepler used it for the point where a lens or mirror gathers light, the burning point.

senses.note: Also a light for a cigarette: 'Grazie per il fuoco' = thanks for the light.

etymology: From Latin forīs.

fact.text: From Latin foris, 'outdoors', literally 'at the doors'. A related Latin word, foras, is behind English 'foreign', via Late Latin foranus, 'from outside'.

senses.note: Fuori di/da = out of. Fuori! = Get out! Opposite: dentro (inside).

etymology: Borrowed from French fourgon. Cognate with Piedmontese furgon.

fact.text: From French fourgon, ultimately from Latin furō (to steal)—originally a thief's wagon.

etymology: From Latin fūrtum, derived from fūr (“thief”).

fact.text: From Latin fūrtum, derived from fūr (thief). The root is related to English furtive, meaning done stealthily or secretly.

etymology: From Latin futūrus (future participle of esse).

fact.text: Latin futurus, the source of English 'future' too, meant 'about to be'. It was the future participle of esse, 'to be', so the future is literally 'what is going to be'.

senses.note: Also the future tense in grammar. In futuro = in the future.

etymology: Archaic variant of galea (“galley”) used in the nautical sense, from which the primary modern usage derives.

fact.text: Archaic variant of galea (galley). The slang 'prison' sense arose because galley slaves were imprisoned on ships—the word shifted from the ship to the punishment itself.

senses.note: Informal/slang for jail. Historically from the nautical 'galley' sense.

etymology: From Medieval Latin galeria (“gallery”), perhaps an alteration of galilea (“church porch”), probably from Latin Galilaea (“Galilee”), region of Israel. More at Galilee.

fact.text: From Medieval Latin galeria, possibly altered from galilea (church porch), which may derive from Galilaea (Galilee). The connection is disputed but intriguing.

senses.note: Can mean tunnel, arcade, or theatre balcony depending on context

etymology: Inherited from Latin gallus.

fact.text: Latin 'gallus' means both rooster and Gaul, leading to a pun: in Italian 'gallo' retained the rooster sense while the Gallic meaning faded.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin gamba. Cognate with Sicilian gamma ~ jamma.

fact.text: Late Latin gamba first meant a horse's hock, from Greek kampe (bend). Through Old French gambe it gave English gammon (ham), and through Italian gambata it gave gambol.

senses.note: Also leg of furniture. Idiom: in gamba = capable, smart.
Tuscan dialect, dated/informal. Archaic sense: extra-marital lover.

etymology: Uncertain. Possibly borrowed from Arabic غارة (ḡāra), whence also Spanish algara.

senses.note: fare a gara = to compete with each other; gara d'appalto = public tender.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French garage.

senses.note: Invariable: il garage, i garage. Pronounced the French way.

fact.text: A made-up word! The Flemish chemist Jan Baptist van Helmont coined 'gas' in the 1600s, basing it on the Greek word chaos.

senses.note: Invariable: il gas, i gas. Also 'gas' for cooking or heating: il fornello a gas.

etymology: From gastronomia + -ico.

senses.note: Plurals add an h: gastronomici, gastronomiche.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cattum.

fact.text: Late Latin cattus, its source, replaced the older word felis. Its origin is unknown, perhaps North Africa (compare Nubian kadis). English cat may share that same source.

senses.note: Gatta = female cat. Gattino = kitten.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English gay.

fact.text: Directly borrowed from English 'gay'. Italian adopted this modern English usage in the late 20th century; older Italian used terms like 'omosessuale' or 'finocchio' (the latter considered offensive).

senses.note: In Italian, typically refers to a man; use 'lesbica' for women.

etymology: From gelato (“ice cream”) + -eria (“-ery”).

fact.text: From gelato (ice cream) + -eria (-ery, a suffix denoting a shop or place). The -eria suffix is common in Italian for commercial establishments, like pizzeria and pasticceria.

senses.note: Italian gelato is thicker and denser than typical ice cream

etymology: From Latin gelātus, derived from gelū (“frost, chill”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”). By surface analysis, gelo (“frost, cold”) + -ato (past participle suffix). Literally, “frozen.” Akin to Russian моро́женое (moróženoje).

fact.text: Literally means 'frozen', from Latin gelare 'to freeze'. English jelly and congeal come from the same root.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin gelidus, derived from gelū, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *gel- (“cold”).

fact.text: From Latin gelu 'frost', the same root behind English gelid, gelatin, jelly and congeal: things that set or freeze solid.

senses.note: Can be literal (acqua gelida) or about manner (uno sguardo gelido, an icy look).

etymology: From Latin generālis.

senses.note: in generale = in general. As a noun, il generale = an army general.

etymology: From generale + -mente.
From Latin generātiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin generis.

fact.text: From Latin genus, generis. The same root gives English gender, genre, general and generate, all from an old Indo-European root meaning 'to produce, beget'.

senses.note: Also means 'kind, type' and 'genre'. 'In genere' means 'generally'.

etymology: From Latin generum, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵm̥ros, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵem-.

fact.text: It comes from Latin gener, from a root linked to marriage. Greek gamos, 'marriage', is usually traced to the same root, and English gets monogamy from gamos.

senses.note: Don't confuse it with genere (kind, genre, gender). Daughter-in-law = nuora.

etymology: From Latin generōsus.
Borrowed from Latin genius.

fact.text: From Latin genius (divine spirit, guardian deity), from the same Proto-Indo-European root as English 'kin' and 'generate'. Not related to jinn despite the similar sound.

senses.note: Also: spirit, genie; or the engineering corps

etymology: Borrowed from Latin genitōrem, from genitus, from participle of gignere.

fact.text: Watch out: Italian parenti means relatives, not parents. Your parents are i genitori, from Latin genitor, 'begetter'.

senses.note: Mostly used in the plural: i miei genitori = my parents.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin ienuārius, from Latin Iānuārius.

fact.text: Named after Janus, the two-faced Roman god of doorways and beginnings, who looks back at the old year and forward to the new. The word 'janitor', a doorkeeper, comes from the same name.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian and usually no article: a gennaio = in January.

etymology: Inherited from Latin gentem, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁tim. Doublet of genesi via Ancient Greek, and compare etymology 1.

fact.text: From Latin gens, gentis 'clan, family', which also gave English 'gentle', 'genteel' and 'gentile'. A gentleman was originally a man from a good family.

senses.note: Singular collective noun with a singular verb: la gente è. The plural 'genti' means peoples or nations.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin gentīlis.

fact.text: Latin gentilis meant 'of the same clan or family'. It also gave English gentle, genteel and gentile, but in Italian it simply means kind or polite.

senses.note: Same form for both genders. Gentile signora / Gentile signore = Dear Madam / Dear Sir in letters.

etymology: From Latin geōgraphia, from Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía).
Back-formation from gestione.

senses.note: Transitive verb; primary modern meaning related to administration/handling

etymology: Inherited from Latin gestus.

fact.text: From Latin gestus, the perfect participle of gerere (to carry, bear, wear). Originally meant a carrying or bearing, it evolved to mean bearing oneself through physical movement, hence 'gesture'—a visible bearing or comportment.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin iectāre, from Latin iactāre. Cognate with Sicilian jittari.
Calque of French glacier as ghiaccio + -aio.

fact.text: Modelled on French glacier: Italian built it from its own word ghiaccio (ice) plus the suffix -aio, so it literally means 'ice place'.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *glacium/a, from Latin glaciēs. Doublet of ghiaccia. Compare Sicilian chiatru.

fact.text: From Latin glacies 'ice', the root of English glacier and glacial. Latin gl- often became ghi- in Italian, as in glans becoming ghianda (acorn).

senses.note: Ascia da ghiaccio = ice axe. Freddo come il ghiaccio = ice-cold.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French jaque.

fact.text: From Old French jaque, which also gave English jacket. It is often linked to the name Jacques, once a nickname for a French peasant who wore this short padded coat.

senses.note: Giacca e cravatta = jacket and tie. A heavy winter coat is il cappotto.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French jalne (variant of jaune), from Latin galbinus. Crime fiction sense is in reference to the yellow covers of a series of mystery novels published by Mondadori from 1929.

fact.text: Un giallo is also a crime story. Starting in 1929, Mondadori published a series of mystery novels with yellow covers, and the colour became the name of the genre.

senses.note: Plurals: gialli/gialle. As a noun, un giallo = a crime novel or thriller.

fact.text: Via French and Portuguese from Malay Jepang, ultimately from Chinese 日本 (sun origin), the idea behind 'Land of the Rising Sun'. English Japan took the same route.

senses.note: Proper noun, masculine. The Italian name follows the same etymological path as English: via Portuguese and Malay from Chinese 日本 (origin of sun).

etymology: From Giappone (“Japan”) + -ese. The neologism is based on the story of Japanese holdouts.

fact.text: Italians use 'un giapponese' to describe someone stubbornly loyal to a lost cause, inspired by Japanese soldiers who kept fighting in the jungle for decades after WWII ended.

senses.note: Adjective meaning of/from Japan; colloquially, stubbornly loyal to a lost cause

etymology: Borrowed from French jardinage. By surface analysis, giardino + -aggio.

fact.text: Borrowed from French jardinage. French jardin goes back to a Germanic word for an enclosure, which is related to English 'garden' and 'yard'.

senses.note: Fare giardinaggio = to do gardening.

etymology: Borrowed from French jardin, of Germanic origin (compare Franconian gardo, German Garten).

fact.text: Came via French jardin from Frankish *gardo, 'enclosure'. It is related to English 'garden' and 'yard', which go back to the same Germanic root.

senses.note: giardino zoologico = zoo; giardino d'infanzia = kindergarten.

etymology: From Latin [ars] gymnastica (“gymnastic [art]”).

fact.text: From Greek gymnos (naked), because athletes in ancient Greece trained naked. English gymnasium and gym come from the same root.

senses.note: Fare ginnastica = to exercise or work out. At school it also means PE.

etymology: From Late Latin genuculum, alteration of Latin geniculum, diminutive of genū (“knee”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu.

fact.text: It comes from a Latin diminutive of genu, 'knee'. That word shares an ancient root with English knee and also gives English genuflect, to bend the knee.

senses.note: Masculine singular (il ginocchio); usual plural is feminine le ginocchia. In ginocchio = kneeling.

etymology: Inherited from Latin iocārī. By surface analysis, gioco (“game”) + -are. Cognate with Sicilian jucari.

fact.text: From Latin iocari 'to joke, jest', from iocus 'joke'. English joke and jocular come from the same Latin word, so playing began as joking.

senses.note: Used for games and sports: giocare a calcio. For instruments use suonare: suonare il piano.

etymology: From giocare + -tore. Compare French joueur, Piedmontese giugador and giugheur, Portuguese jogador, Romanian jucător, Spanish jugador.

fact.text: It comes from giocare, from Latin iocari, 'to jest', from iocus, 'joke'. Latin iocus is also the source of English 'joke' and 'jocular'.

senses.note: Feminine: la giocatrice. A musician who plays an instrument is a suonatore or musicista.

etymology: Diminutive of gioco (“game”).
Inherited from Latin iocus. Compare English joke.

fact.text: Comes from Latin iocus, 'joke, jest', which is also where English joke comes from. The older Latin word for game, ludus, faded away.

senses.note: Also 'play' in general: per gioco = for fun. Hunted game is selvaggina.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French joie, from Late Latin gaudia, from Classical Latin gaudium. Doublet of gaudio. Cognate with Sicilian gioja.

fact.text: Latin gaudia, the plural of gaudium (joy), came to be treated as a feminine singular. It reached Italian through Old French joie, the same source as English 'joy'.

senses.note: Also used as a term of endearment: gioia mia = my darling.

etymology: From Latin diurnālis (with influence from giorno (“day”)), from Latin diurnus, from Latin diēs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (“heaven, sky”). Originally an adjective meaning "daily" (modern giornaliero) as a modifier for foglio giornale.

fact.text: Same root as English journal: both come from Latin diurnalis, 'daily', from dies, 'day'. It began as an adjective, as in foglio giornale, a 'daily sheet'.

senses.note: Also 'newspaper office'. Giornalaio = newsagent; edicola = newsstand.

etymology: From giornale + -ista.

fact.text: From giornale 'newspaper', from giorno 'day'. A newspaper was a daily record, and English journal comes from the same 'day' word.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: il/la giornalista. Plural: i giornalisti, le giornaliste.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French jornee. Documented from 1230–50. Derivable from giorno + -ata.

fact.text: Comes from Old French jornee, 'a day's span'. That same word gave English 'journey', which first meant a day's travel or a day's work.

senses.note: Giornata = the day as it is spent (Buona giornata!). Giorno = the day as a calendar unit.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin diurnum. Doublet of diurno, a borrowing.

fact.text: From Late Latin diurnum 'daily (portion)'. Via French jour, the same word gave English journal (a daily record) and journey (originally a day's travel).

senses.note: Plural giorni. Un giorno = one day; buongiorno = good morning.

etymology: Inherited from Latin iuvenis. Cognate with Sicilian jùvini.

fact.text: Comes from Latin iuvenis, the source of English juvenile, and further back from the same Indo-European word that gave English young.

senses.note: Same form for both genders. Also a noun: un/una giovane = a young person; i giovani = young people.

etymology: Inherited from Latin iuvenis. Cognate with Sicilian jùvini.

fact.text: Comes from Latin iuvenis, the source of English juvenile, and further back from the same Indo-European word that gave English young.

etymology: Inherited from Latin Jovis diēs or Iovis diēs, variant of diēs Iovis (“day of Jupiter”).

fact.text: Means 'Jupiter's day' (Giove). English Thursday is 'Thor's day', because Germanic peoples matched the thunder god Thor with Jupiter, the Roman god of thunder.

senses.note: Not capitalised. Plural unchanged. Il giovedì = on Thursdays; giovedì = this Thursday.

etymology: From Latin gȳrāre.

fact.text: From Latin gyrare, from Greek gyros 'circle', the same source as English gyrate, gyroscope and the spinning-spit gyros sandwich.

senses.note: gira a destra = turn right; also 'to wander around': girare per la città.
girare un film / una scena = to shoot a film / a scene

etymology: From Latin gȳrus, from Ancient Greek γῦρος (gûros).

fact.text: Comes from Greek gyros (circle) by way of Latin gyrus, the same root as English 'gyroscope' and 'gyrate'. The Giro d'Italia cycling race is literally the 'Tour of Italy'.

senses.note: Also a lap in a race. Fare un giro = to go for a walk or ride; in giro = around.

etymology: Reminescence of the Central Italian verb gire (“to go”), derived from Latin īta, feminine of ītum, ultimately from Latin īre. Cognate with Sicilian juta. Cf. the regional use of gimo (“we go, let's go”).

fact.text: Comes from the old Central Italian verb gire (to go), which goes back to Latin ire, 'to go'. So a gita is literally 'a going'.

senses.note: Fare una gita = to go on a trip. Gita scolastica = school trip.

etymology: From Latin jūdicāre, iūdicāre (“to pass judgement”).
From Latin iūdicem.

fact.text: From Latin iūdicem ('judge'), from iūdicium ('judgment'). The same root as English 'judge' and 'judicial'.

senses.note: A judicial officer or umpire; invariable for gender (giudice for male/female).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin jūdicium, iūdicium.
Inherited from Latin Iūnius.

fact.text: From Latin Iunius, the Roman month most often linked to the goddess Juno, though some ancient writers tied it to the Junius family instead.

senses.note: Months are lowercase in Italian: a giugno = in June.

etymology: Inherited from Latin iungere (“to join”), from Proto-Italic *jungō, from Proto-Indo-European *yunégti ~ *yungénti, from the root *yewg-, whence also Romanian ajunge.
From Latin jūrāre, iūrāre (“to swear or take an oath”), itself from the root *h₂yew- (“justice”, “law”).

fact.text: From Latin iurare 'to take an oath', linked to ius 'law'. English 'jury' comes from the same verb by way of Old French jurer, and so do 'juror' and 'perjury'.

senses.note: Only for oaths. To swear (curse) = bestemmiare or dire parolacce. Lo giuro! = I swear!

etymology: Borrowed from French jury, from English jury. Same etymon as giurì.

fact.text: Borrowed from French, which took it from English jury. The word traveled back and forth between languages during the medieval period as the jury system spread across Europe.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin iūstitia. Doublet of giustezza.

senses.note: Also the justice system: rivolgersi alla giustizia = to go to the law.

etymology: Inherited from Latin iūstus.

fact.text: From Latin iustus, which also gave English 'just' and 'justice'. The Italian word keeps both meanings: fair and correct.

senses.note: Also means 'fair, just'. Used as a tag question: '…, giusto?' = '…, right?'

etymology: Inherited from Latin iūstus.

senses.note: A tag question at the end of a sentence. 'Vero?' is an alternative.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin iam (“already, now”).
Cognate with Portuguese já and Spanish ya.

fact.text: As a one-word reply, già! means 'yeah' or 'exactly'. It comes from Latin iam ('already, now'), which is also the source of Spanish ya.

senses.note: Means 'yet' in questions: hai già mangiato? On its own, già! means 'yeah, right'.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin iūsum~iōsum, from Classical Latin deorsum.

senses.note: essere giù = to feel down. su e giù = up and down.

etymology: From Latin illī (dative masculine singular of ille). Cognate with Sicilian ci.

senses.note: Used before a vowel, s + consonant, z, gn, ps: gli amici, gli studenti, gli zii.
Plural, with a plural verb: gli Stati Uniti sono… For 'in the US', say negli Stati Uniti.
Always plural: gli occhiali. 'Da' shows what something is for.
Elided glielo/gliela before a vowel or h-: gliel'ho detto = I told him/her.

etymology: Univerbation of glie + lo.

senses.note: gli + lo merged into one word, also used for formal 'you'. Before ho it usually becomes gliel'ho.

etymology: From globalizzare + -zione.
Learned borrowing from Latin glōria.

fact.text: From nocca, meaning 'knuckle'—gnocchi were so named because their shape resembles knuckles. The word reflects how Italian cuisine names dishes after their appearance.

senses.note: Usually treated as plural; singular gnocco is rarely used

etymology: Uncertain.

senses.note: Also means awkward or inelegant. Synonym: impacciato.

etymology: From Latin gula, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷel- (“throat”).

fact.text: From Latin gula, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷel- meaning 'throat'. Cognates appear in Sanskrit (gala), Persian (galu), and Russian (glotka).

senses.note: The anatomical passage for swallowing and breathing.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English golf.

fact.text: Unadapted borrowing directly from English 'golf'. Italian kept the English word unchanged, unlike many Romance languages that adapted it differently.

senses.note: Invariable noun; also means cardigan or jumper in some contexts

etymology: From Late Latin gumma, from Latin cummi, gummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi).

fact.text: From Latin gummi, ultimately from Greek kómmi. English "gum" and Italian gomma share this Greek origin, tracing back to ancient trade routes.

senses.note: Feminine. Plural: gomme. Also means 'rubber', 'tyre/tire', 'gum' depending on context.

etymology: Borrowed from Venetan góndoła, probably from Byzantine Greek κοντοῦρα (kontoûra, “small tail”).

fact.text: Borrowed from Venetan góndoła, likely from Byzantine Greek kontoûra meaning "small tail" — possibly referring to the boat's shape or stern.

senses.note: The iconic narrow boats of Venice, traditionally poled through canals.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin gunna (“leather garment”).

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin gunna, a fur or leather garment. English gown comes from the same word through Old French goune.

senses.note: Minigonna = miniskirt.

etymology: From Latin gubernātōrem.

fact.text: From Latin gubernātor (one who steers). The same root gives English 'govern' and 'gubernatorial'—all trace back to Ancient Greek kubernáō, to pilot a ship.

etymology: From the verb governare or from Latin gubernum. Compare Portuguese governo, Spanish gobierno.

fact.text: Comes from Latin gubernare, 'to steer a ship', which Latin borrowed from Greek kybernan. The same Greek root later gave English 'cybernetics'.

senses.note: Il governo italiano. Related verb: governare (to govern).

etymology: From Latin gradus.

fact.text: From Latin gradus, 'step'. That root also gave English grade, gradual and graduate, and degree itself comes via Old French from de- + gradus.

senses.note: Used for temperatures, angles and level or extent. A university degree is la laurea. Essere in grado di = to be able to.

etymology: Borrowed from Lombardic *krapfo, from Proto-West Germanic *krappō.

fact.text: English graffiti comes from Italian graffito, from graffiare (to scratch). Early graffiti were literally scratched into walls.

senses.note: Plural graffi. From graffiare, to scratch.

etymology: From Latin gramma from Ancient Greek γράμμα (grámma, “a twenty-fourth of ounce”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek gramma, which meant a letter or written mark and also a small weight. The same Greek word is behind English grammar and telegram.

senses.note: Masculine: un grammo, due grammi. Abbreviated g. At the deli, un etto = 100 grams.

etymology: Inherited from Latin grandem, of unclear origin.

fact.text: From Latin grandis 'big', which also gave English 'grand'. Some scholars have linked it to English 'great', but where grandis comes from is still unclear.

senses.note: Often shortened to gran before a consonant: un gran giorno. Before a noun it can mean 'great'.
mio fratello più grande = my older brother. i grandi = adults.

etymology: Borrowed from Proto-West Germanic *krappō (“hook”).

fact.text: Grappa was born of thrift. It is distilled from pomace, the skins, seeds and stalks left over after pressing grapes for wine, so nothing from the harvest went to waste.

senses.note: Called grappa in English too. Also means a metal clamp or staple, a much rarer sense.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin grassus. Doublet of crasso.

fact.text: From Late Latin grassus, a variant of crassus 'thick', which gave English crass. The last day of Carnival is martedì grasso, 'Fat Tuesday', like French Mardi Gras.

senses.note: Also 'fatty, greasy' of food. As a noun, il grasso = fat.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Latin grātīs.

fact.text: Latin gratis is a shortened form of gratiis, 'for thanks': something given for nothing but thanks. The same root gives grazie.

senses.note: Invariable. Can also act as an adjective: ingresso gratis = free entry. More formal: gratuito.

etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *gʷreh₂-
Proto-Indo-European *-us
Proto-Indo-European *gʷréh₂us
Proto-Italic *gʷraus
Latin gravis
Italian grave
Inherited from Latin gravis. Doublet of greve.

fact.text: From Latin gravis (heavy, serious). Cognate with Ancient Greek barus (heavy), Sanskrit guru, and English 'grave'. The sense extends from physical weight to emotional and moral weight.

senses.note: Can also mean heavy, solemn, or (in music) low-pitched. Gender: same form for all genders.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin gravitātem. By surface analysis, gravi- + -ità.

senses.note: Covers both physical gravity and seriousness, as in la gravità della situazione. Same form in the plural.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin grātia (“favour/favor; goodwill; charm”).

fact.text: Grazie, the everyday 'thank you', is just this word in the plural, literally 'graces' or 'favours', like Spanish gracias.

senses.note: The plural grazie is the everyday 'thank you'.

etymology: Plural of grazia (“grace”), from Latin grātia, as used in the phrase grātiās agō (“to thank; to express thanks”). Compare Sicilian grazzi and Spanish gracias.

fact.text: Literally 'graces', from Latin gratia. It shares a root with English 'grace', 'gratitude' and 'gratis'.

senses.note: grazie mille = thanks a lot. Reply: prego (you're welcome).

etymology: Literally, “a thousand graces”.

senses.note: Very common. 'Grazie tante' and 'molte grazie' mean much the same.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *crītāre with irregular voicing.

senses.note: Can be transitive or intransitive; from Vulgar Latin with irregular voicing.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French or Old Occitan, both from Frankish *grīs, from Proto-Germanic *grīsaz (“grey”). Akin to Old High German grīs (“grey”) (German greis) and Dutch grijs (“grey”). More at grizzle. Cognate with Sicilian grisu/griciu.

fact.text: It comes from Frankish *gris, 'grey', via Old French gris. The same French word gave English 'grizzled' (greying), and the grizzly bear is named for its grey-tipped fur.

senses.note: Plurals: grigi (m), grigie (f). It can also mean dull or dismal: una giornata grigia.

etymology: Borrowed from French grille. Doublet of graticola.

fact.text: Borrowed from French grille, which descended from Latin crāticula. The word entered Italian through Romance trade and cultural contact, becoming essential to Mediterranean cooking terminology.

etymology: From griglia + -are, modelled on French griller.

fact.text: From Italian griglia (grill) plus the verb suffix -are, modelled on French griller. The grill itself ultimately derives from Latin craticula.

senses.note: transitive verb; commonly used for grilling meat or vegetables
A grilled meat dish or social gathering with grilled food.

etymology: From Latin grossus.

fact.text: It shares a Latin root with English 'gross' (grossus), but it never means disgusting. That is 'schifoso'. Think of 'gross' as in 'gross weight' instead.

senses.note: Often means bulky or thick. Un pezzo grosso = a big shot.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *cruppus, (cf. Renaissance Latin grupus).

fact.text: English group comes from this word through French groupe. It started out as an art term for a cluster of figures in a painting or sculpture.

senses.note: General word: un gruppo di amici (a group of friends).
A rock or pop band is un gruppo (or una band). La banda is a brass or marching band.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *wadaniāre, of Germanic origin; from Frankish *waiþanōjan, *waiþanōn (“to hunt, graze”) (a calque of Latin petere). Compare French gagner, Catalan guanyar, Portuguese ganhar, Galician gañar, Galician ganar, Galician gadaña, Galician gadañar, cf. also Spanish ganar and Spanish guadañar.

fact.text: A Germanic loan: it comes from a Frankish verb meaning 'to hunt, graze'. French gagner and Spanish ganar come from the same source.

senses.note: Also 'to gain': guadagnare tempo = to gain time.

etymology: Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *wai (“expression of grief”). Alternatively from Ancient Greek οὐαί (ouaí), from the verse in Revelation 8:13. Compare English woe, German Weh, Latin vae.

fact.text: Its origin is uncertain, but it is probably related to English 'woe', either from Germanic wai or via the biblical cry 'ouai' (woe!).

senses.note: Often plural: essere nei guai = to be in trouble. Che guaio! = what a mess!

etymology: From Old Occitan, from Old French guant, from Frankish *want, from Proto-Germanic *wantuz (“glove, mitten”), from Proto-Indo-European *wondʰnú- (“glove”), from the root *wendʰ- (“to wind, wrap”). Cognates include French gant, Catalan guant, Sicilian nguanta and Spanish guante.

fact.text: From Frankish *want. Germanic w- often became gu- in Italian, as in guerra 'war' and guardare, which is related to English ward.

senses.note: Usually plural: i guanti. Colloquially also means 'condom'.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin wardāre.

fact.text: Comes from a Germanic word, the same root as English 'ward' and 'guard'. To guard something is to keep watching it.

senses.note: Takes a direct object with no 'at': guardo la TV.
Reflexive verb; 'guardarsi da' means to be careful of or avoid something.

etymology: From guardare, of Germanic origin, possibly corresponding to Frankish *warda or Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐍂𐌳𐌾𐌰 (wardja), all ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to watch, notice, give heed”). Compare French garde, Spanish guarda.

fact.text: Germanic w- became gu- in Italian, so this word is a cousin of English ward and warden. The same shift links guerra to war.

senses.note: Always feminine, even for a male guard: lui è una guardia. Di guardia = on duty.

etymology:
From Frankish *warjan, possibly through the intermediate of a Late Vulgar Latin *warīre, *uarīre.
Compare French guérir, Occitan garir, Catalan and Spanish guarir.

fact.text: Comes from Frankish *warjan (to protect). Like guerra (war), it shows how a Germanic w- became gu- in Italian. French guérir has the same root.

senses.note: Intransitive with essere (la ferita è guarita). Transitive: to cure someone.

etymology: From the short past participle of guastare (“to ruin”) in Tuscan; compare the Standard Italian participle guastato. Cognate with Piedmontese guast.

senses.note: Un guasto al motore = an engine fault. As an adjective: broken, out of order.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin werra, from Frankish *werʀu (“confusion; quarrel”).

fact.text: Not from Latin bellum but from Frankish werra, 'quarrel', the same Germanic root as English 'war'. Germanic gu- for w- shows up again in guardia (ward) and Guglielmo (William).

etymology: From guidare. Compare French guide, Spanish guía. Doublet of ghia.

senses.note: Feminine even for a male guide. Also guidebook and driving (scuola guida = driving school).

etymology: From Old Occitan guidar, of Germanic origin; e.g. Frankish *witan, Proto-Germanic *witaną, possibly through a Medieval Latin intermediary. Compare French guider, Spanish guiar.

fact.text: It came into Italian through Old Occitan from a Germanic verb, Frankish *witan. That verb is related to Old English witan 'to know', the ancestor of English 'wit'.

senses.note: Also to guide or lead a person: lo stai guidando = you're guiding him.

etymology: From Hindi गुरू (gurū, “teacher”).

fact.text: From Hindi गुरू (gurū), meaning 'teacher'. The word entered Italian through English.

senses.note: Religious or spiritual leader; influential person.

etymology: From Latin gustāre. Compare gusto.

fact.text: From Latin gustāre. Related to English 'gusto'—both capture the idea of enjoying flavor and experiencing something fully.

senses.note: Also 'to enjoy'; can be transitive (gusto il vino) or reflexive.

etymology: From Latin gustus (“taste”), from Proto-Italic *gustus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus.

fact.text: English borrowed this Italian word as 'gusto', meaning enthusiasm. The same Latin root, gustus, also gives us 'disgust', which literally means 'bad taste'.

senses.note: Ice-cream flavours are gusti: che gusti vuoi? Also 'taste' as in style: buon gusto.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English hobby.

senses.note: Invariable: gli hobby.

etymology: Borrowed from French hôtel, from Middle French hostel (“hostel”, “inn”), from Old French ostel (“shelter”), from Latin hospitālis (“pertaining to hospitality”). Doublet of ospedale and ospitale.

fact.text: Italian borrowed this from French hôtel, but it has a native twin: ospedale (hospital). Both come from Latin hospitalis, 'relating to guests and hosts'.

senses.note: Invariable: un hotel, due hotel. The h is silent. Albergo is a common native synonym.
Lit. 'fruits of the forest'; common on Italian menus
Italian delicacy; 'funghi' (mushrooms) is plural
Di + noun often works like an English noun modifier: prodotti di bellezza.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin idea, from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”), from εἴδω (eídō, “to see”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek idea, 'form, look', from a verb meaning 'to see'. That makes an idea literally the way something looks to the mind.

senses.note: Feminine, but takes l' before the vowel: l'idea, le idee.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin ideālis.
From Renaissance Latin identicus + -ficare.
inherited from Latin identitās

senses.note: Same form in the plural (le identità). Carta d'identità = ID card.

etymology: From ideo- + -logia.
Borrowed from Latin idiōta, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “layman”) from ἴδιος (ídios, “private”).

fact.text: From Ancient Greek idiotes, 'private person, layman', from idios 'one's own'. Originally meant someone apart from public life; only later came to mean foolish or ignorant.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: un idiota, un'idiota. Also an adjective: idiotic.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin idiōta, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “layman”) from ἴδιος (ídios, “private”).

fact.text: From Ancient Greek idiotes, 'private person, layman', from idios 'one's own'. Originally meant someone apart from public life; only later came to mean foolish or ignorant.

etymology: From Latin hydraulicus, from Ancient Greek ὑδραυλικός (hudraulikós, “of a water organ”), from ὕδραυλις (húdraulis, “water organ”), from ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + αὐλός (aulós, “pipe”). Cognate with Piedmontese idràulich.

fact.text: Goes back to the Greek hydraulis, an ancient water organ, from hydor (water) and aulos (pipe). English hydraulic comes from the same source.

senses.note: Also an adjective meaning hydraulic (impianto idraulico = plumbing system).

etymology: Inherited from Latin heri.

fact.text: From Latin heri, from the same Proto-Indo-European root as the 'yester-' in English yesterday, so the two words are distant cousins.

senses.note: L'altro ieri = the day before yesterday. Ieri sera = last night.

etymology: From earlier 'l, a reduced form of lo. The initial i- is a svarabhakti vowel added in order to make the pronunciation easier. Proof of this is De scriptura nigra (a work in Old Lombard) only employing il to mean “the”, and el to mean “he/him”. Also, works in 1400’s Tuscan showing both “il” and “el”, yet with no forms such as “de Roma” instead of “di Roma” appearing, prove that il does not originate as a pretonic evolved form of el. Compare, by the way, Sicilian lu ~u, representing both the definite masculine singular article, and also iḍḍu (“he”) ḍḍu (“that”) and chiḍḍu (“that”); all cognates from the same source.

senses.note: Use lo before s+consonant, z, gn, ps; l' before a vowel. Plural: i (gli for lo/l').
Irregular plural: le dita dei piedi. The big toe is "l'alluce".
duomo is the main church; cattedrale is also correct
Masculine here: il fine settimana. 'Il weekend' is also common.
"La band" and "il complesso" are also common. Plural: i gruppi musicali.
listino can also mean menu (in a restaurant context)
Usually pasta, risotto or soup, served before the main course (il secondo). 'Piatto' is often left out.
Masculine/feminine forms provided
Nel tempo libero means 'in my spare time'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin illūmināre (“to illuminate”). Compare alluminare.

senses.note: Means to shed light on something. To light a fire is accendere: accendere un falò.

etymology: From Latin imitārī.

fact.text: From Latin imitārī, meaning to copy or mimic—the same root as English 'imitate'.

etymology: From Latin imāginārī (“to imagine, to conceive”), from imāginem (“a copy, likeness, image”).

senses.note: Also 'to suppose': immagino di sì = I suppose so. Immaginati! / Si immagini! = Don't mention it!

etymology: From Latin imāginem (“image, imitation”), from Proto-Italic *imā (“copy”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eym- (“copy”). Doublet of imago, and also the now-archaic mania.

senses.note: Feminine noun. Plural: le immagini. Note the double m.

etymology: From immediato + -mente.

senses.note: Shorter everyday synonyms: subito, all'istante.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin immōbilis (“immobile, immovable”).

fact.text: From Latin immobilis (im- 'not' + mobilis 'movable'). English 'mobile' and 'immobile' share the same root.

senses.note: Legal/technical term for real estate and buildings; invariably masculine.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *imparāre, from in- + parāre. Compare French emparer (“to seize”).

fact.text: Built from in- + Latin parare 'to prepare', the same verb behind English 'prepare'. Its French relative emparer went a different way and means 'to seize'.

senses.note: Imparare a + infinitive: imparo a nuotare = I'm learning to swim.

etymology: From im- + pasta + -are.

fact.text: Literally 'to make into pasta (dough)'. Painters' impasto, paint laid on thickly with visible strokes, was borrowed from the related Italian noun.

senses.note: Also to mix (cement, plaster). The resulting dough or mixture is l'impasto.

etymology: From Latin impatientem.

senses.note: Impaziente di + infinitive = eager to: sono impaziente di vederti.

etymology: From im- + pazzo (“crazy, mad”) + -ire.

fact.text: It is built from pazzo (crazy). Italian cooks use it for mayonnaise that splits: la maionese è impazzita, literally 'the mayonnaise has gone mad'.

senses.note: Takes essere and adds -isc- in some forms: impazzisco. Impazzire per = to be crazy about.

etymology: Inherited from Latin impedīre.
From im- + pegno + -are.

senses.note: impegnarsi = to commit oneself; essere impegnato = to be busy. Can also mean to pawn.

etymology: Deverbal from impegnare + -o.

senses.note: Also a prior engagement: ho un impegno = I have something on. Also effort: con impegno.

etymology: From im- + pensabile; cognate with Piedmontese impensàbil.
Borrowed from Late Latin impermeābilis. Compare Piedmontese impermeàbil.

fact.text: In Italian a raincoat is simply 'the impermeable': the adjective for waterproof, English 'impermeable', became the everyday word for the coat.

senses.note: Masculine noun, takes l'. As an adjective it means waterproof.
Impianto elettrico = wiring; impianto di riscaldamento = heating; impianto stereo = stereo system.
Usually an office or white-collar worker. Feminine: l'impiegata.

etymology: From importare + -ante.
From Medieval Latin importantia.
From Latin importāre.

fact.text: Latin importare, from in + portare (to carry in), also gave English 'import'. English 'import' can mean importance too, as in 'a matter of great import'. In Italian, importare can also mean to import goods.

senses.note: Works like piacere: mi importa = it matters to me. Non importa = never mind. Takes essere.

etymology: From Late Latin impossibĭlis, im- + possibile.
From imprendere + -tore.

fact.text: Built from imprendere (to undertake), the Italian match of French entreprendre, which gave English 'entrepreneur'. Both literally mean 'one who undertakes'.

senses.note: Also businessman or contractor. Feminine: imprenditrice.

Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of imprendere, a less common alternative for intraprendere (“to undertake”).
Cognate with Sicilian mprisa.
Compare French entreprise for a similar construction.

fact.text: Formed like French 'entreprise'—from imprendere (to undertake). English 'enterprise' has a parallel construction from the same Latin root.

etymology: From Latin impressio, impressionis from impressus

senses.note: avere l'impressione che... = to have the feeling that... (usually followed by the subjunctive)

etymology: From im- + prevedibile.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural imprevedibili.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin improbābilis. By surface analysis, in- + probabile.

senses.note: Colloquially also means 'outlandish': un vestito improbabile = a ridiculous outfit.

etymology: From improntare.
From improvviso + -mente.

fact.text: Built on improvviso, 'sudden', from Latin improvisus, 'unforeseen'. That is the source of English 'improvise': doing something with no time to prepare.

senses.note: Synonyms: all'improvviso, di colpo.

etymology: From Latin improvisus (“unforeseen”).

fact.text: From Latin improvisus, 'unforeseen'. English 'improvise' came via French from Italian improvvisare, which is built on this word: you improvise when something sudden happens.

senses.note: All'improvviso = suddenly, all of a sudden.

etymology: Inherited from Latin in.

senses.note: Merges with articles: nel, nello, nella, nei, negli, nelle. Used with countries: in Italia.

etymology: Literally, “in the wolf's mouth”.

fact.text: Literally 'into the wolf's mouth'. The usual reply is 'Crepi (il lupo)!', meaning 'may the wolf die!'. Answering 'grazie' is traditionally thought to bring bad luck.

senses.note: Literally 'into the wolf's mouth'. The usual reply is 'Crepi (il lupo)!'
'In offerta' means a special promotion. For seasonal sales, use 'in saldo' / 'i saldi'.
Mostly in 'stare in pena per qualcuno' (to be worried sick about someone). 'Suffering' is a loose gloss.

etymology: Akin to Sicilian in ritardu.

senses.note: Essere in ritardo = to be late (behind schedule). For 'late in the day', use tardi.
Used with essere/andare: sono in vacanza, vado in vacanza.

etymology: Deverbal from incaricare.

From Late Latin incastrāre, likely derived from castrum (“fortress”). Cognate with French encastrer, Spanish encastrar.
Unrelated to Italian castrare (“to castrate”).
Borrowed from Latin incendium.

fact.text: From Latin incendium, from incendere 'to set on fire'. English incendiary comes from the same verb, and so does incense, the stuff you burn.

senses.note: A fire that destroys things (house, forest). A fire you light on purpose is il fuoco.

fact.text: Don't say accidente for an accident. Accidenti! is a mild curse, roughly 'Damn it!', and un accidente can be a curse or a stroke of bad luck.

senses.note: Often a crash: incidente stradale = road accident. Avere un incidente = to have an accident.

etymology: From Latin incīnctus, past participle of incingō. Compare French enceint, Spanish encinto.

fact.text: From Latin incinctus, past participle of incingere, 'to gird'. Isidore of Seville already argued it meant 'ungirded', because pregnant women loosened their belts.

senses.note: In practice almost always feminine: incinta. Essere incinta di tre mesi = be three months pregnant.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin inclūdere. Doublet of inchiudere, which was inherited.

fact.text: From Latin inclūdere (to shut in), same root as English 'include'. The past participle incluso is used as an adjective, like English 'included'.

senses.note: irregular past participle: incluso

etymology: Borrowed from Latin inclūsus. Cf. chiuso.

senses.note: Agrees with the noun: inclusa, inclusi, incluse. 'Me incluso' = me included.

fact.text: Made from in- + colpa 'fault, blame', from Latin culpa, the same root as English 'culpable'.

senses.note: incolpare qualcuno di qualcosa = to blame someone for something.

etymology: From in- + cominciare.

senses.note: Means the same as cominciare. Takes avere with an object and essere without one: Il film è incominciato.

etymology: Derived from Late Latin incontrā. By surface analysis, incontro (adverb) + -are. Compare Portuguese and Spanish encontrar, French rencontrer.

fact.text: Built on Late Latin incontra, 'against, facing'. English 'encounter' has the same origin, via Old French encontrer.

senses.note: Used for meeting by chance or by arrangement. For meeting someone for the first time, use conoscere.

etymology: Deverbal from incontrare + -o.
Borrowed from Latin incrēdibilis. By surface analysis, in- + credibile.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural incredibili.
Also crossing or junction. In biology, a cross between breeds or varieties.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin incubus.

fact.text: Same word as English 'incubus', from Latin incubare 'to lie upon': bad dreams were blamed on a demon that sat on the sleeper's chest. 'Incubate' shares the root.

etymology: From Latin indāgō (“investigation”).

senses.note: Also means research, survey, or legal hearing.

etymology: From Late Latin indiānus, from India.
From Latin indicāre.

senses.note: Stress on the first syllable: ÌNdico, ÌNdica. Adds -h- before i/e: indichi, indicherò.

etymology: From in- + dietro. Compare Romanian îndărăt, and Sicilian 'n 'arreri.

senses.note: tornare indietro = to go back; essere indietro = to be behind.
Mi è indifferente = I don't mind / it's all the same to me.

etymology: From in- + dimenticabile.

senses.note: The list glosses 'India' but the noun forms and dictionary senses primarily mean 'Native American' or 'indium'. Treating as proper noun per the list gloss requested.

etymology: Deverbal from indirizzare + -o.

senses.note: Also an email address (indirizzo email). In schools it can mean a course stream or track.

etymology: From in- + dispensabile.
From in- + dosso + -are.

fact.text: Built from in + dosso 'back' (from Latin dorsum): to wear something is literally to put it 'on your back'. Compare addosso, 'on oneself'.

senses.note: Also 'to put on'. More formal than portare, which is everyday 'to wear'.

etymology: From in- + Latin divināre.
Borrowed from Latin industria.

fact.text: Latin industria first meant diligence or hard work. That older sense survives in English 'industrious', which means hardworking.

etymology: From Latin īnfantia.

fact.text: From Latin infantia, related to 'infant' in English. Both refer to the inability to speak (in- not + fari to speak).

senses.note: The period of being a child; from Latin infantia.

fact.text: English 'in fact' can introduce a correction, but this word only confirms or backs up what was said. For 'actually' in the sense of 'contrary to what you think', Italians say 'in realtà'.

senses.note: Confirms or explains what was just said. Infatti! = Exactly! To contradict someone, use in realtà.

etymology: From Latin īnferiōrem, comparative form of īnferus (“low, deep”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)n̥dʰér.

fact.text: From Latin īnferiōrem, comparative of īnferus ('low, deep'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)n̥dʰér.

etymology: From infermo (“invalid”, “infirm”) + -iere (“-er”, “-or”).

fact.text: Built on infermo, 'sick, infirm', so it is literally the person who looks after the infirm. English 'infirmary' is related.

senses.note: Feminine: l'infermiera. The hospital sick bay is l'infermeria.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin īnfernus, īnfernum (“the depths of the earth”), noun use of īnfernus (“of the lower regions”), derived from īnferus (“low”).

fact.text: Dante's Divine Comedy has three parts: Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso. In English, inferno means a blazing fire, but in Italian it is simply 'hell'.

senses.note: The ordinary word for hell. Common expressions: Va' all'inferno! (Go to hell!)

etymology:
Borrowed from Latin in fīne.
By surface analysis, univerbation of in + fine.

senses.note: Use it for the last item in a sequence. For a relieved 'at last!', say finalmente.

etymology: From Latin īnfōrmāre.

senses.note: informare qualcuno di qualcosa. Reflexive informarsi = to find out, to enquire.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin īnfōrmātiōnem (“idea, concept”).

fact.text: Unlike in English, this word is countable, so Italians freely say 'informazioni'. A sign reading Informazioni is an information desk, and asking for 'un'informazione' is perfectly normal.

senses.note: Countable in Italian: un'informazione (a piece of information), delle informazioni.

etymology:
From ingegno + -ere (agentive suffix).
Compare French ingénieur.

fact.text: Built from ingegno (talent, ingenuity). In Italy, Ingegnere is a real form of address: people greet engineers as 'Ingegnere' the way English speakers say 'Doctor'.

senses.note: Also used as a title: 'Buongiorno, ingegnere!' Before a name it becomes ingegner: l'ingegner Rossi.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French engleis.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian. L'inglese = the English language; in inglese = in English.

etymology: From Latin ingredientem (“entering”), from ingredior (“to enter”).

fact.text: From Latin ingrediens (entering). Identical root as English 'ingredient', from ingredior (to enter or go into), referring to what enters a mixture.

etymology: From Latin ingressus.

senses.note: Can also mean ticket or admission fee in commercial contexts

etymology: Borrowed from Latin initiāre. Cf. also cominciare.

senses.note: Takes avere with an object (ho iniziato il libro) and essere without one (il film è iniziato).
Both take 'a' + infinitive: iniziare a/cominciare a lavorare.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin initium.

fact.text: It comes from Latin initium, 'a beginning', the same source as English initial, initiate and initiative.

senses.note: All'inizio = at the beginning; dall'inizio = from the start.
Use di for the person: innamorarsi di qualcuno. Takes essere.

etymology: Univerbation of innanzi + tutto.

senses.note: Also written as two words: innanzi tutto. Prima di tutto means the same.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin innoc|ēns, ~entis (“harmless, inoffensive”). Cognate with Sicilian nnucenti.

fact.text: From Latin innocens (harmless), formed with in- (not) + nocens (harming). The same root gives English 'innocuous' and 'nuisance'.

etymology:
From Latin in ultrā.
By surface analysis, univerbation of in + oltre.
Compare French en outre.

senses.note: Usually goes at the start of a sentence to add a point. Similar to per di più.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin inquilīnus.

fact.text: From Latin inquilinus (inhabiting, dwelling in). The root in- (in) + colere (to dwell) literally means one who lives in a place—compare English 'cultivate' and 'colony' from the same Latin root.

etymology: From inquinare + -mento.

fact.text: From Latin inquinare (to soil, make unclean) plus -mento (result of action). The root inquinare is the source of 'inquinate' in English, though the Italian noun is far more common.

etymology: From insalato, which is an adjective derived from the verb insalare (“to salt”).

fact.text: Literally 'salted': it comes from insalare, 'to salt', because greens were seasoned with salt. English 'salad' comes from the same root.

senses.note: Also means lettuce. Figuratively a jumble or mishmash.

fact.text: Comes from insegnare 'to teach', from Vulgar Latin insignare 'to mark, point out', built on signum 'sign'. So a teacher is literally someone who points things out to you.

senses.note: Same form for men and women: l'insegnante, un/un'insegnante. From insegnare (to teach).

etymology: From Vulgar Latin īnsignāre (also present in Medieval Latin), from Latin signāre. For sense 3 compare Spanish enseñar.

fact.text: It comes from Latin signare 'to mark', the same root as English 'sign'. Teaching was originally 'marking' something on the mind. An insegna is a shop sign.

senses.note: insegnare qualcosa a qualcuno; insegnare a fare qualcosa. Don't confuse it with imparare (to learn).

etymology: From Latin īnsequī, remodeled after Italian seguire (“to follow”).

senses.note: Also figurative: inseguire un sogno = to chase a dream.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin īnsectus.

fact.text: Borrowed from Latin īnsectus (literally 'cut into' or 'segmented'), the same root as English insect. Both words reflect the divided body structure of insects.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *īnsemel, which is a combination of Latin īnsimul and semel. See also French ensemble, Catalan ensems and Neapolitan nzieme.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin *insemel, which also gave French ensemble. English borrowed that French word for a group performing together.

senses.note: Insieme a / con = together with. As a noun, l'insieme = the whole, or a set.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin īnsipidus (“tasteless”), from in- (“not”) + sapidus (“savory”).

senses.note: Used for food that lacks salt or flavour, and for dull people or things.

etymology: From Latin īnsistere, from in + sistō.

senses.note: Takes 'su' (insistere su qualcosa) or 'a' + infinitive (insiste a dire...).

etymology:
Univerbation of in (“in”) + somma (“sum; essence”), a calque of Latin in summā.
Compare French en somme.

fact.text: Said as a one-word reply to 'How are you?' it means 'so-so'; snapped impatiently, it means 'Oh, come on!' or 'For heaven's sake!'

senses.note: Also a filler like 'well...'; as a reply to Come stai? it means 'so-so'.

etymology: Univerbation of in + tanto.

fact.text: Formed by combining 'in' and 'tanto' (so much). Over time, these two words fused into a single adverb, a linguistic process called univerbation.

senses.note: also: in the meantime; used to introduce a contrasting point
Same form for masculine and feminine; plural intelligenti.

etymology: Inherited from Latin intendere.

fact.text: From Latin intendere (in- + tendere, to stretch), literally 'to stretch toward'. Same origin as English intend and intent, all from the sense of directing attention.

senses.note: Irregular verb. Passato remoto: intesi. Also means 'to intend', 'to hear', or 'to mean'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin intentiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin intentiōnem, derived from intendō (to stretch toward, aim). English 'intention' and 'intend' share the same Latin root; both preserve the sense of directing effort or purpose.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; the plural is interessanti.

etymology: From interesse + -are.

fact.text: From the noun interesse (interest, stake) + the verb-forming suffix -are. The root ultimately traces to Latin inter- (between) + esse (to be), so 'interest' literally meant 'it matters/it is between'.

senses.note: transitive: interesting to someone; also reflexive interessarsi (to be interested in)
Interessarsi di/a qualcosa. Uses essere: mi sono interessato di arte.
Takes 'a': interessato a qualcosa. It can also mean self-interested: un consiglio interessato.
Can mean concern/attention, or financial interest/profit. Plural interessi often used for business/money matters.

etymology: From inter- + nazionale.

fact.text: Milan's football club Inter is short for Internazionale. It was founded in 1908 by members who broke away from AC Milan because they wanted to welcome foreign players too.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural internazionali.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English internet.

senses.note: Usually used without an article: su internet, navigare in internet.

etymology: From Latin internus.

fact.text: On Italian flat door labels and phone systems, 'interno' (often abbreviated int.) specifies the apartment or extension number. For example, 'interno 23' means apartment 23 or extension 23.

senses.note: In Italian addresses, interno (abbr. int.) denotes the flat number; on phones, interno 23 means extension 23.

etymology: From Latin internus.

fact.text: On Italian flat door labels and phone systems, 'interno' (often abbreviated int.) specifies the apartment or extension number. For example, 'interno 23' means apartment 23 or extension 23.

senses.note: 'All'interno' means inside. Also used for a phone extension or a flat number.

etymology: From Latin interrumpere.

fact.text: From inter- (between) + rumpere (to break). English 'interrupt' shares the same Latin root: inter + rupt (broken).

senses.note: transitive; also means break off, disconnect, or switch off

etymology: From Latin intervenīre (“to intervene”).

fact.text: From Latin intervenire (inter- between + venire to come). English intervene shares the same Latin root.

senses.note: Irregular verb

etymology: Calque of English interview, from inter- + vista. Compare Spanish and Portuguese entrevista.

fact.text: Borrowed from English 'interview' (inter- + vista, 'between' + 'view'). Calque also adopted in Spanish (entrevista) and Portuguese (entrevista).

etymology: Inherited from Latin intēnsus. Doublet of intenso.

senses.note: Past participle of intendere. Inteso? = Understood? / Got it? Siamo intesi = we're agreed.

etymology: From in + torno.

senses.note: Followed by a it works as a preposition: intorno alla casa = around the house.

etymology: Borrowed from French entrevoir, from Vulgar Latin *intervidēre.

fact.text: Literally 'to see between' (intra + vedere), like French entrevoir. English interview comes from French entrevue, from the same verb: a quick look at each other.

senses.note: Conjugated like vedere. Past participle: intravisto (or intraveduto).
Reflexive of intrecciare (to braid); related to treccia, braid. Le corde si intrecciano.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin intrōductiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin intrōductiō (leading in), sharing the same root as English 'introduce'. Both words literally mean 'to lead in'.

senses.note: Can also be used as a noun: un introverso = an introvert.

etymology: From Latin inūtilis, from in- + ūtilis.

senses.note: Also 'unnecessary': è inutile... = there's no point...

etymology:
Univerbation of in + vece.
Compare Venetan invéze.

fact.text: Literally 'in place': in + vece, from Latin vicem (turn, place). The same Latin root gives English vice-president, vicar and vicarious.

senses.note: Invece di + noun or infinitive = instead of. On its own it can also mean 'whereas' or 'on the other hand'.

fact.text: Literally 'in place': in + vece, from Latin vicem (turn, place). The same Latin root gives English vice-president, vicar and vicarious.

senses.note: Invece di + noun/infinitive = instead of. Also 'whereas': io lavoro, lui invece dorme.

etymology: From Latin inventum, the supine form of inveniō (“find, discover”).

fact.text: Latin invenire meant 'to find, to come upon'. So inventing was originally finding something, not creating it from scratch.

senses.note: Also means to make up (a story or an excuse): inventare una scusa.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin inventiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin invenire 'to come upon, find'. To invent was originally to find something, not to create it.

senses.note: Feminine, like most nouns in -zione: l'invenzione, le invenzioni.

etymology: From Late Latin hībernum, reanalyzed as in- + verno, for which cf. Emilian invêren, Sicilian mmernu, Spanish invierno, Portuguese inverno.

fact.text: From Late Latin hibernum 'wintry', the same root as English hibernate. Speakers later reanalysed it as in + verno, which is how the n got into the word.

senses.note: d'inverno / in inverno = in winter.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin investīre.

fact.text: Shares Latin root investīre with English 'invest'. The core sense is to clothe or cover; financial investing wraps capital into ventures.

senses.note: transitive; can mean spend money/time or formally confer authority

etymology: From Late Latin inviāre, which is derived from Latin via (“path, road”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese enviar, French envoyer.

fact.text: From Late Latin inviare, built on via 'road': to put something on its way. French envoyer is from the same source, and so is English 'envoy', a person sent.

senses.note: A bit more formal than mandare: inviare un'email, un pacco.

etymology: From Late Latin invīsibilis.

fact.text: From Late Latin invīsibilis. Shares the root with English 'invisible'—both mean 'not able to be seen'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin invītāre.

senses.note: Pattern: invitare qualcuno a + infinitive or noun, as in 'Ti invito a cena'.

etymology: Deverbal from invitare.
Inherited from Late Latin eo, from Classical Latin egō̆.

fact.text: Descends from Latin ego, worn down to eo in Late Latin. It is the same word English borrowed as 'ego'.

senses.note: Usually dropped (sono = I am); used for emphasis or contrast: Sono io = It's me. Not capitalised.
Proper noun; typically capitalized.

etymology: From Irland(a) (“Ireland”) + -ese.

fact.text: Formed from Irlanda (Ireland) with the suffix -ese, used in Italian for nationality adjectives like francese (French) and tedesco (German).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ironia, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνεία (eirōneía).

fact.text: Greek eirōneía meant 'feigned ignorance', the pose Socrates took when he pretended to know nothing in order to expose his opponents.

senses.note: ironia della sorte = irony of fate. fare ironia = to be ironic.

etymology: From iscrivere + -si.

senses.note: Reflexive verb; can also mean to enroll, join. Takes auxiliary essere.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin īnscrīptiōnem. By surface analysis, inscrivere + -zione.

fact.text: From Latin īnscrīptiō (inscription). English 'inscription' shares the same root—both refer to writing recorded or marked.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *isula, from classical Latin īnsula.

fact.text: English 'isolate' comes, via French, from Italian isolato, meaning 'made into an island'. Latin insula also gave 'insulate' and 'peninsula' ('almost an island').

senses.note: Isola pedonale = pedestrian zone.

etymology: From Latin īnspectōrem.

fact.text: Directly related to English 'inspector'—both from Latin inspicere ('to look into'), from in- + specere ('to look').

senses.note: A person who inspects or supervises.

etymology: From Latin īnstantem, from īnstō.

fact.text: From Latin īnstantem (standing on, pressing upon). English 'instant' and Italian istante share the same root, both referring to an urgent, present moment.

senses.note: instant, a very brief time

etymology: From Latin īnstitūtum.

senses.note: Also a type of secondary school: istituto tecnico, istituto professionale.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin Italia, from Ancient Greek Ῑ̓ταλίᾱ (Ītalíā), from Oscan 𐌅𐌝𐌕𐌄𐌋𐌉𐌞 (víteliú, “land of bulls”), a name for the southwestern tip of the boot of Italy; usually assumed to be a cognate of vitulus (“calf”).

fact.text: Probably from Oscan Víteliú, 'land of bulls', first used only for the toe of the boot. A link to Latin vitulus, 'calf', is usually assumed but not certain.

senses.note: Always capitalized: Italia. Takes the article: l'Italia, in Italia.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin italiānus (“Italian”). By surface analysis, Itàlia (“Italy”) + -àno (“-an”, derivational suffix).

fact.text: From Latin italiānus, the direct ancestor of English 'Italian'. Both languages inherited this word unchanged from Rome.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin italiānus (“Italian”). By surface analysis, Itàlia (“Italy”) + -àno (“-an”, derivational suffix).

fact.text: From Latin italiānus, the direct ancestor of English 'Italian'. Both languages inherited this word unchanged from Rome.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian. Feminine: italiana. L'italiano also means the Italian language.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English killer.

fact.text: Direct English borrowing, unchanged in Italian. The word entered Italian from English 'killer' and retains the same form and meaning across both languages.

senses.note: Unadapted English borrowing, invariable
Elided lo/la before a vowel: l'amico, l'acqua. Plurals don't elide: gli amici, le acque.
Lit. 'accommodation with family'

etymology: From Latin illa(m), feminine form of ille.

senses.note: Becomes l' before a vowel: la casa, but l'amica.
Often just "la camera". Plural: le camere da letto.
Italian 'cioccolata' is the drink; 'cioccolato' is the candy
dell' = di + l'. Fermata comes from fermare, 'to stop'.
Can be person (la guida) or guidebook
"La fotocamera" is a common synonym. A video camera is "la videocamera".
'Metro' is the informal shortening
Italian dessert (cream + gelatin); panna = cream, cotta = cooked
Lit. 'mounted cream'; used in desserts
For younger children, use 'maestro/a'
Feminine and invariable: la serie, le serie.
Lit. 'orange juice squeezed'; fresh-squeezed style
Both terms common; 'via' also used in addresses
Usually a language course abroad. Plural: le vacanze studio.
Lit. 'guided visit'

etymology: Inherited from Latin labrum, related to labium, from the Proto-Indo-European root *leb- (“to hang down”).

fact.text: Shares the Proto-Indo-European root *leb- 'to hang down' with English lip, and with Latin labium, which gives English labial.

senses.note: Irregular plural: il labbro → le labbra (lips). Labbri is used for rims or edges.

etymology: From Latin labōrātōrium.

fact.text: Same root as English laboratory: both from Latin laborātōrium. The Italian word dropped one syllable over time.

etymology: From Latin lacrima.

fact.text: Old Latin said dacrima. The d later became l, just as in lingua. It comes from the same ancient root as Greek dakry and English tear.

senses.note: Often plural: in lacrime = in tears. Also spelled lagrima (literary).

etymology: From earlier latro, from Latin latrō (“mercenary; thief; robber”) (nominative form). Doublet of ladrone, from the Latin accusative latrōnem.

fact.text: From Latin latro, which first meant a hired soldier or mercenary and later a robber. Its relative ladrone (bandit) comes from the accusative form latronem.

senses.note: Feminine: la ladra. Also an adjective for a crook: quel commerciante è ladro.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English lady.

fact.text: Unadapted English loanword meaning a titled or highborn woman. It remains invariable in Italian while English 'lady' has regular plural 'ladies'.

senses.note: Invariable English loanword; refers to titled or highborn women

etymology: Univerbation of là + giù.

senses.note: Also used loosely for 'over there'. Opposite: lassù (up there).

etymology: Inherited from Old Italian laco, from Latin lacus (“lake”), from Proto-Indo-European *lókus (“lake, pool”).

senses.note: Plural: i laghi. Il Lago di Como = Lake Como.

fact.text: From Latin lamentari (to wail), related to English 'lament'. The reflexive form emphasizes the personal expression of sorrow or grievance.

senses.note: reflexive verb; commonly used to express dissatisfaction

etymology: From Latin lampada, from lampas.

senses.note: A light bulb is la lampadina, a diminutive of this word.
Diminutive of lampada 'lamp'.

etymology: Borrowed from Gallo-Italic, compare Piedmontese àmpola, Lombard ampon, Venetan ampoma, ampómola, with the initial l- by concretion of the definite article.

fact.text: Borrowed from Gallo-Italic languages. The initial 'l' developed through the concretion of the definite article 'la' merging with the root (compare Piedmontese àmpola, Lombard ampon). Related to the Proto-Germanic word for 'raspberry.'

etymology: From Latin lāna.

fact.text: From Latin lana. English lanolin, the grease taken from sheep's wool, gets its name from the same Latin word.

senses.note: Di lana = woollen, e.g. un maglione di lana (a wool sweater).

etymology: From Late Latin lanceāre, from Latin lancea. Compare Catalan llançar, French lancer, Occitan and Portuguese lançar, Spanish lanzar, English launch (via Northern Old French).

fact.text: From Late Latin lanceare, from lancea 'lance': it first meant hurling a lance. English launch comes from the same word via Northern Old French.

senses.note: Also 'to launch': lanciare un prodotto. lanciarsi = to throw oneself, to dive in.

etymology: From lanciare.

senses.note: Invariable: i laptop. Il portatile (computer portatile) is just as common.

etymology: From Latin largus.

fact.text: False friend: it means wide or broad, not large. A large pizza is una pizza grande, while una strada larga is a wide road.

senses.note: Also means loose-fitting, for clothes. 'Large' in Italian is grande.

etymology: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *lasania, from Latin lasanum (“cooking pot”), from Ancient Greek λάσανον (lásanon, “trivet or stand for a pot”).

fact.text: The word traces back through Latin lasanum (cooking pot) to Ancient Greek lásanon (trivet), making it one of many culinary terms that travelled from ancient cooking vessels to modern dishes.

etymology: Inherited from Latin laxāre.

fact.text: From Latin laxare, 'to loosen', which is related to English 'lax' and 'relax'. Leaving something is letting go of it.

senses.note: Leaving something or someone, unlike partire (to depart). Also 'to let': lasciami andare.

etymology: Univerbation of là + su.

fact.text: From là (there) + su (up), combined into one word—a univerbation common in Italian adverbials.

etymology: From Latin laterālis.

senses.note: Often translated as 'side': porta laterale = side door, effetti laterali = side effects.

etymology: From latino- + americano.

From Latin lātus (“side”, “flank”).
Compare Spanish lado and Portuguese lado.

fact.text: From Latin latus, lateris 'side, flank'. It's the same root as English lateral and bilateral.

senses.note: 'Da un lato... dall'altro' means 'on the one hand... on the other'.

etymology: From Late Latin lactem, accusative of Late Latin lactis.

fact.text: Order 'un latte' in an Italian bar and you'll get a glass of milk. English latte is short for caffellatte, so ask for that or a cappuccino.

senses.note: Usually uncountable. caffellatte = coffee with milk.

etymology: From Latin lacticīnium.

fact.text: From Latin lacticinium (dairy-related product), derived from lac (milk). The Italian form shows the evolution of the Latin root through Romance languages.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin laurea.

fact.text: From Latin laurus, 'laurel', the same root as 'poet laureate'. Italian graduates still wear a laurel wreath on the day they graduate.
