senses.note: Laurearsi = to graduate; un laureato = a graduate.

fact.text: Comes from laurea, a degree, named after the laurel (lauro) crown of ancient victors. Italian graduates still wear a laurel wreath on graduation day.

senses.note: Only for university degrees, and it takes essere: mi sono laureata. For finishing high school, use diplomarsi.

etymology: From the town of Lavagna, near Genoa, known for slate quarries in the nearby mountains.

fact.text: It is named after Lavagna, a town near Genoa whose nearby mountains were quarried for slate, the stone that school blackboards were once made from.

senses.note: Also means whiteboard (lavagna bianca) and the stone slate.

etymology: From lavanda + -eria.

senses.note: The shop or room, not the clothes. 'Lavanderia a gettoni' = laundromat.
Bathroom washbasin or kitchen sink; a kitchen sink is also called il lavello.

etymology: From Latin lavāre (“to wash”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃- (“to wash”).

fact.text: From Latin lavare 'to wash', which also gave English lavatory (originally a washing place) and, via Old French, laundry.

senses.note: Reflexive lavarsi = to wash oneself (mi lavo le mani = I wash my hands).

etymology: Verb-object compound, composed of lava (“to wash”) + stoviglie (“dishes, crockery”).

senses.note: Feminine and invariable: la lavastoviglie, le lavastoviglie.

etymology: From lavare + -trice.

fact.text: Built from lavare, 'to wash', plus -trice, an ending for female agents or machines. English 'lavatory' comes from the same Latin verb, lavare.

senses.note: A dishwasher is lavastoviglie.

etymology: From Latin labōrāre.

fact.text: From Latin laborare, 'to toil', the same root as English 'labor' and 'laboratory', which was originally a place of work.

senses.note: Regular -are verb. Also used for working a material or kneading dough.
Means 'of or related to work'; often used in set phrases.

etymology: From Latin labōrātōrem. By surface analysis, lavorare + -tore. Compare Portuguese lavrador, Spanish labrador, cf. also Aromanian lãlãtoari.

fact.text: The Portuguese cognate lavrador ('farmer, landholder') is thought to be behind the name Labrador, after the explorer João Fernandes Lavrador.

senses.note: Feminine: la lavoratrice. From lavorare (to work).

etymology: Deverbative from lavorare; perhaps corresponding to Latin labor.

fact.text: Comes from lavorare, from Latin laborare, 'to toil'. That is the same root as English labour and laboratory.

senses.note: Masculine: il lavoro. Che lavoro fai? = What do you do for a living?

etymology: From Latin illas, which is the accusative plural feminine of ille. Cognate with Sicilian li~i.

senses.note: Used with all feminine plural nouns: le case, le amiche.
'Macchina' is the everyday word for car. 'Auto' is also common.
Plural form; used when requesting directions
Lit. 'gym shoes'; also 'le tennis' or 'le ginnastica'

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English leader.
From Latin ligāmen (“bandage, band, tie”). Compare Sicilian ligama.
Inherited from Latin ligāre.

fact.text: From Latin ligare, 'to bind', the same root as English ligament and ligature.

senses.note: legare con qualcuno = to bond with / get along with someone.

etymology: From Latin lēgem.
Inherited from Latin legere.

fact.text: From Latin legere, 'to read' (originally 'to gather'). English 'legend' comes from Latin legenda, 'things to be read', and 'lecture' comes from the same verb.

senses.note: Irregular: letto (past participle), lessi (passato remoto). Cominciare A leggere, not 'per'.

etymology: From leggero + -ezza; cognate with Piedmontese legerëssa.

fact.text: Italo Calvino gave the first of his famous 'Six Memos for the Next Millennium' (Lezioni americane) the title Leggerezza, praising lightness as a literary virtue.

senses.note: Also means frivolity or carelessness. Una leggerezza is a thoughtless mistake.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French legier, from Vulgar Latin *leviārius, from Latin levis.

fact.text: Borrowed from Old French legier (modern léger). English has the same word in 'legerdemain', from French léger de main, 'light of hand', meaning sleight of hand.

senses.note: Also mild or slight. Musica leggera = pop music. Older spelling: leggiero.

etymology: Inherited from Latin lignum. Cognates include Spanish leño, Romanian lemn.

fact.text: From Latin lignum, possibly from a root meaning 'to collect', i.e. wood gathered for the fire. English lignite and ligneous share the same Latin source.

senses.note: Wood as material; a forest or the woods is il bosco. di legno = wooden.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin illaei.
The formal address Lei appears in the 16th century in connection with Signoria (“Lordship”), Eccellenza (“Excellency”), Santità (“Holiness”) and Magnificenza, alongside Voi.

fact.text: Formal 'you' (Lei) is literally 'she'. From the 1500s people were addressed through feminine titles like Vostra Signoria (Your Lordship), and the pronoun followed the title.

senses.note: Also 'her' after prepositions (con lei). Capitalised Lei = formal 'you', used with 3rd-person verbs.

etymology: From lento (“slow”) + -mente.

fact.text: Comes from lento, 'slow', which musicians worldwide use as a tempo marking for a slow passage.

senses.note: Also piano: vai piano = go slowly.

etymology: Inherited from Latin lentus.

fact.text: Latin lentus first meant soft or pliant and is probably related to the word for the linden tree, whose wood is soft. 'Slow' came later.

senses.note: Adverb: lentamente or piano. Also 'loose' of a knot or screw.

etymology: From Latin linteolum, from linteum, nominal form of linteus (“linen”), from linum (“linen; flax”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin linteolum, 'a small linen cloth', from linum 'flax, linen'. Sheets were once made of linen.

senses.note: Usual plural is feminine: le lenzuola (a set of sheets). I lenzuoli is also possible.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin leōnem.

fact.text: The winged lion is the symbol of Venice and Saint Mark. The top prize at the Venice Film Festival is the Leone d'Oro, the Golden Lion.

senses.note: Female: la leonessa. Capitalized, Leone is the zodiac sign Leo.

etymology: From Latin littera.

fact.text: At Italian universities, Lettere (literally 'letters') is the name for the humanities: literature, classics and related subjects.

senses.note: Means both a letter you post and a letter of the alphabet. alla lettera = literally.

etymology: From Latin litterātūra.

senses.note: Spelled with a double t: letteratura.

etymology: From Latin lectus (“bed”). Compare French lit, Galician and Portuguese leito and Catalan llit.

senses.note: Andare a letto = to go to bed. Also the past participle of leggere: ho letto = I have read.

etymology: Inherited from Latin levāre.
Borrowed from Latin lectiōnem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin lectio, 'a reading', from legere 'to read'. English lesson and lecture come from the same word, since teaching once meant reading texts aloud.

senses.note: Also a class or lecture at school or university. Fare lezione = to teach a class.

etymology: From Latin illī, nominative masculine plural of ille.

senses.note: Direct object pronoun for masculine or mixed groups; feminine is 'le'. Goes before the verb: li vedo.

etymology: From Latin lībra.

fact.text: It comes from Latin libra (scales, pound). That is why the English abbreviation for pound is 'lb', and the £ sign is a stylized L for libra.

senses.note: Only the unit of weight. The British pound (money) is la sterlina.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin līberāre. See also Old Italian liverare, livrare (“to finish”).

fact.text: From Latin liberare (to set free). The English word 'liberate' is a direct cognate, both preserving the Latin root liber (free).

senses.note: Transitive. Can mean to free from constraint, clear/vacate a space, or deliver someone.

etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ-
Proto-Indo-European *-teros
Proto-Indo-European *h₁léwdʰeros
Proto-Italic *louðeros
Old Latin loeber
Latin līberumlbor.
Italian libero
Learned borrowing from Latin līberum.

fact.text: English borrowed the word for sport. A libero is the free-roaming sweeper in football, and the specialist defensive player in volleyball.

senses.note: Sei libero? = Are you free? For 'free of charge', Italian usually says gratis or gratuito.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin lībertātem.

fact.text: From Latin libertātem. Related to English liberty and liberal, both rooted in the Latin concept of freedom.

senses.note: Invariable noun; does not pluralize.

etymology: From libro + -eria.

fact.text: False friend warning: this is not a library! It means a bookcase or a bookshop. If you want to borrow books, look for a biblioteca.

senses.note: Also means 'bookshop'. A library is una biblioteca.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin librum (“book”).

fact.text: Latin liber first meant the inner bark of a tree, an early writing material. That is why the word still means phloem in botany. English 'library' comes from the same root.

senses.note: Masculine: il libro, i libri. A library is una biblioteca; a libreria is a bookshop.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin licentiāre. Compare French licencier.
From Latin Lycēum.

fact.text: Named after the Lyceum, the Athens gymnasium where Aristotle taught. It took its name from a nearby temple of Apollo Lykeios.

senses.note: An academic upper secondary school, e.g. liceo classico, scientifico, linguistico.

etymology: From Latin līmitem.

senses.note: Essere al limite = to be at one's limit. Limite di velocità = speed limit.

etymology: From limone (“lemon”) + -ata, following the same formation of aranciata (“orange juice”), cedrata (“citron juice”), citronata (“lemonade”). Compare French limonade, Venetan łimonada.

fact.text: From limone (lemon) plus -ata, the Italian suffix for fruit drinks. The same pattern builds aranciata (orange juice) and cedrata (citron juice).

etymology: From Arabic لَيْمُون (laymūn).

senses.note: Masculine, unlike most fruit names. The same word is used for the fruit and the tree.

etymology: From Latin līnea (“line, thread”), from līnum (“flax”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin linea (a linen thread), from linum (flax). English line and linen share that root.

senses.note: Mantenere la linea = to keep your figure. In linea = on the line or online.

etymology: From earlier lengua, from Latin lingua.

fact.text: English 'tongue' shares the same Indo-European root. Old Latin had 'dingua'; the d probably became l partly through association with lingere, 'to lick'.

senses.note: Lingua madre = mother tongue. Plural: le lingue.
Mostrare la lingua = to stick out your tongue.

etymology: From Latin liquidus.

senses.note: Can also mean 'runny'. As a noun: il liquido = a liquid.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin lyricus, from Ancient Greek λυρικός (lurikós).

fact.text: Comes from Greek lurikós, 'of the lyre'. Lyric poems were first sung to the lyre, which is also why song words are called 'lyrics'.

senses.note: Also means 'opera': cantante lirico = opera singer. The noun la lirica = lyric poetry or opera.

etymology:
From Vulgar Latin *līsius, from Ancient Greek λισσός (lissós, “smooth”). Or, from *lixus, derived from *lixāre (“to clean, boil”), presumably related to lixa (“lye”).
Compare Portuguese and Spanish liso, French lisse, Catalan llis, Sicilian lisciu, Friulian, Lombard, and Provençal lis, Romansh glisch.

senses.note: Andare liscio = to go smoothly. Of drinks: neat. Acqua liscia = still (not sparkling) water.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *lista, of Germanic origin, from either Frankish *līsta or Lombardic līsta, both from Proto-West Germanic *līstā.

fact.text: Germanic origin, from Proto-West Germanic *līstā 'strip, edge'. Italian still uses it for 'strip, stripe'. A list started out as a narrow strip of paper with names on it.

senses.note: Fare la lista = to make a list; lista della spesa = shopping list.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin lītigāre. Compare Spanish lidiar and Portuguese lidar.

fact.text: Despite looking like English litigate, in everyday Italian it just means to argue or fight, for example with your partner or siblings. No lawyers needed.

senses.note: Litigare con qualcuno = to argue with someone. Takes avere: ho litigato.

etymology: From French litre.

fact.text: Came through French from Greek litra, which was a Sicilian coin and a unit of weight. So a modern metric unit has roots in ancient Sicily.

etymology:
Deverbal from livellare (“to level, to make level”) + -o.
Alternatively, from Vulgar Latin *lībellus.

senses.note: Curve di livello = contour lines. Livello del mare = sea level.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *(il)lu, from Latin illum, illud, by dropping il- and -m. Cognate with Sicilian lu.

fact.text: Latin illum ('that one') gave Italian both this article and the object pronoun lo ('him, it'), as in lo vedo, 'I see him'.

senses.note: Masculine singular before s+consonant, z, gn, ps, x, y: lo zaino, lo studente. Plural: gli.

etymology: From Late Latin locālis, from Latin locus. Cognate with Sicilian lucali.

fact.text: Much like British English calling a neighbourhood pub 'the local', Italian uses this word for any bar, club or restaurant you go out to.

senses.note: Un locale = a bar, club or restaurant. In flat ads, locali = rooms (trilocale = 3 rooms).

etymology: From Latin logicus.

fact.text: From Latin logicus, borrowed from Greek logikos. The word travels across European languages nearly unchanged: English 'logical', French 'logique', German 'logisch'.

etymology: From the Vulgar Latin *longitānus, from Latin longe; cognate with French lointain, Sicilian luntanu, Friulian and Romansch lontan, Dalmatian luntun.

senses.note: Also an adverb: abito lontano = I live far away. Lontano da = far from.

etymology: From the Vulgar Latin *longitānus, from Latin longe; cognate with French lointain, Sicilian luntanu, Friulian and Romansch lontan, Dalmatian luntun.

senses.note: Lontano da = far from. As an adjective it agrees: una città lontana.

etymology: Borrowed from English lord.

fact.text: From Old English hlāfweard ('loaf-ward'), originally 'the bread keeper' in a household. Borrowed into Italian unchanged.

senses.note: Invariable; borrowed from English.

etymology: Uncertain; often suggested to be from derived from Latin lūridus (“sallow, pale”), via Late Latin lurdus, making it a doublet of lurido.

fact.text: The commercial sense comes from Old French 'gros' (large, whole). English 'gross' in commerce also comes from French. Both derive ultimately from Latin grossus.

senses.note: Opposite of netto (net); used in commerce and finance.

etymology: Inherited from Latin illōrum, genitive plural of ille, illud (“that”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin illorum, 'of those'. Because it began as a genitive (meaning 'of'), the possessive 'their' never changes for gender or number.

senses.note: Invariable; usually takes an article: il loro, la loro, i loro, le loro.
Subject pronoun; also 'them' after prepositions (con loro).

etymology: Inherited from Latin illōrum, genitive plural of ille, illud (“that”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin illorum, 'of those'. Because it began as a genitive (meaning 'of'), the possessive 'their' never changes for gender or number.

senses.note: As a subject it is usually left out: (loro) parlano.
Never changes form, and usually takes the article: i loro nomi, la loro casa.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin lucta, from Latin lūctāre (“to wrestle”). Compare French lutte. By surface analysis, lottare (“to fight”) + -a.

fact.text: Comes from Latin luctari, 'to wrestle'. English 'reluctant' has the same root, from reluctari, 'to struggle against'.

senses.note: Also 'fight' and the sport of wrestling (lotta libera). Verb: lottare.

etymology: Inherited from Latin luctārī.
From Old French lot, from Frankish *hlot, from Proto-Germanic *hlutą.

fact.text: The Lotto game started in 16th-century Genoa, where people bet on which citizens would be drawn for public office. English borrowed the name lotto from Italian.

senses.note: Il Lotto is Italy's national numbers game. Lotto also means a batch or a plot of land.

etymology: From Latin lūcem (“light”), from Proto-Italic *louks, from the Proto-Indo-European root *lewk- (“bright; white”). Doublet of the borrowed lux.

fact.text: From Latin lux, like English lucid. Even English light goes back to the same Indo-European root, *leuk- 'bright'.

senses.note: accendere/spegnere la luce = turn on/off the light. dare alla luce = to give birth.

etymology:
From Latin iūlius, through a process of dissimilation; compare also the obsolete regional variant form giuglio. Alternatively, derived from a Vulgar Latin root *lūlius, along with other Italo-Romance and Rhaeto-Romance cognates; compare Corsican lugliu, Neapolitan lùglio, Sicilian lugghiu, Venetan lujo, Romansh lügl, Friulian Lui, Ladin lugio, Ligurian lûggio, Emilian and Romagnol lój, Lombard luj. Gallo-Roman town name Juliobona (nowadays in Normandy, France) evolved into its modern French name Lillebonne following the same process.
Doublet of Giulio.

fact.text: Named after Julius Caesar, from Latin Iulius. The sound changed from Iu- to L- over time, so it shares its origin with the name Giulio.

senses.note: Written in lower case: a luglio = in July.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin illui.

fact.text: The accent changes everything: with an accent, luì is a small warbler bird such as the chiffchaff. Without one, lui just means he or him.

senses.note: Also 'him' after prepositions (con lui). Subject pronouns are often dropped unless stressed.

etymology: From Luna, from Latin lūna, from Old Latin losna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂, derived from the root *lewk- (“bright”). Cognates include Armenian լուսին (lusin), Spanish luna, Portuguese lua, Romanian lună, Russian луна́ (luná).

fact.text: Monday in Italian is lunedì, from Latin lunae dies, 'day of the moon'. English Monday, 'moon day', is named the same way.

senses.note: Idiom: avere la luna storta = to be in a bad mood.

etymology: From Latin Lūnae dīēs, variant of dīēs Lūnae (“day of the Moon”).

fact.text: Like English Monday ('Moon's day'), it comes from Latin Lunae dies, 'day of the Moon'. Luna is still the Italian word for moon.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian and invariable: il lunedi, i lunedi. Il lunedi = on Mondays.

etymology: From Latin longus (“long, extended”), from Proto-Indo-European *dlongʰos (“long”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin longus, and both go back to the same Proto-Indo-European root as English 'long'. So the Italian and English words are distant cousins.

senses.note: Also a preposition, 'along': lungo il fiume. Un caffè lungo = a weaker, longer espresso.

etymology: From earlier luoco < loco, from Latin locus.

fact.text: From Latin locus 'place', the same root as English local, locate and location.

senses.note: Common phrases: avere luogo 'to take place', luogo comune 'cliché'.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lūpum, from Latin lŭpum. Doublet of lupus and lovo.

fact.text: Italians wish good luck by saying In bocca al lupo (into the wolf's mouth). The traditional reply is Crepi! (may it die), never grazie.

senses.note: The feminine is la lupa, as in the she-wolf of Rome's founding legend.

etymology: From Latin luxus.

fact.text: Lusso derives directly from Latin luxus, which originally meant 'excess' or 'indulgence' and shares roots with the English word 'luxurious'.

etymology:
From Latin illāc. Compare Spanish allá, Portuguese lá, French là, Sicilian ḍḍà.
The original geminated -ll-, though lost in the standard language, is still found in most regional Italian varieties.

senses.note: The accent tells it apart from the article la. Often a bit farther or vaguer than lì.

etymology:
From Latin illic. Compare Spanish allí, Portuguese ali.
The original geminated -ll-, though lost in the standard language, is still found in most regional Italian varieties.

senses.note: The accent matters: lì = there, but li = them. là also means there.

etymology: Inherited from Latin magis.

fact.text: Comes from Latin magis, 'more', the same word behind Spanish más. The sense moved from 'more, rather' to 'but'.

senses.note: Also used for emphasis: Ma dai! = Come on! / No way!

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *macla, from Latin macula. Doublet of macula, a borrowing.

fact.text: A caffè macchiato is coffee 'stained' with a little milk. The word also means scrubland, and French maquis (the WWII Resistance) comes from its Corsican form.

senses.note: Also a spot, or a stain on someone's name. Another meaning is scrubland or bush.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin machina (“engine, device, mill”), from Ancient Greek μαχανά (makhaná). Compare the inherited doublet macina (“grindstone”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin machina, from Doric Greek mākhanā 'device', the same source as English 'machine'. In everyday Italian it usually means a car.

senses.note: Also means 'machine', e.g. macchina fotografica = camera.

etymology: From Macedonia, probably referring to the great ethnic variety that distinguished that region.

fact.text: Named after Macedonia, the region whose ethnic diversity inspired the metaphor of mixed ingredients in a salad—just as a macedoine is a medley in French cuisine.

etymology: From Latin mea domina (“my lady”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin mea domina, 'my lady'. English 'madam' has the same origin, via French ma dame.

senses.note: Madonna! shows surprise or annoyance. Some consider it mildly irreverent. La Madonna = the Virgin Mary.

etymology: From the older form matre, from Latin mātrem, from Proto-Italic *mātēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.

fact.text: Goes back to Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr, the same ancestor as English mother, so the two words are distant relatives rather than borrowings.

senses.note: Mamma is the everyday word. The possessive has no article: mia madre.

etymology: From Latin magistrum. Doublet of mastro.

fact.text: From Latin magister, built on magis (more): the 'greater one'. Its opposite, minister, was the 'lesser one'. The same root gives English master and magistrate.

senses.note: Feminine: maestra. Also means a master of an art, or a music conductor.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin maiestātem.

senses.note: Invariable noun (same form singular and plural); typically capitalized when referring to a royal title.

etymology:
Borrowed from Greek μακάρι (makári, “I wish”), which is derived from Ancient Greek μακάριος (makários, “blessed, happy”).
Compare Sicilian macari, Portuguese macar (“although”, conjunction), Spanish maguer (“although”, conjunction) and Romanian măcar (“even”, adverb).

fact.text: A rare Greek loan in everyday Italian: from Greek makári 'I wish', from Ancient Greek makários 'blessed, happy'. Spanish maguer 'although' shares the root.

senses.note: Reply showing you'd love something to be true: 'Vai in vacanza?' 'Magari!'
Adverb use: Magari vengo domani = Maybe I'll come tomorrow.

etymology:
Etymology tree
Arabic خَزَنَ (ḵazana)der.
Arabic مَخْزَن (maḵzan)
Arabic مَخَازِن (maḵāzin)bor.
Italian magazzino
From Arabic مَخَازِن pl (maḵāzin), plural of مَخْزَن (maḵzan, “storeroom, storehouse”), noun of place from خَزَنَ (ḵazana, “to store, to stock, to lay up”). Compare Sicilian magasenu.

fact.text: From Arabic makhzan (storeroom), plural makhazin. The word spread through Mediterranean trade languages, with cognates in many European languages.

etymology: From Latin Maius.

fact.text: Il primo maggio (1 May) is Labour Day, a national holiday in Italy, and Rome holds a huge free open-air concert that day.

senses.note: Italian months take a small letter: a maggio = in May.

etymology: From Latin maiōrem /majjoːrɛ̃/, accusative case of maior, from Proto-Italic *magjōs, from Proto-Indo-European *m̥ǵh₂yós, from *méǵh₂s (“big”, “great”).

fact.text: From Latin maior, 'greater', which also gave English both major and mayor. The town's mayor is literally its 'greater' man.

senses.note: Comparative of grande. La maggior parte = most (of).
La sorella maggiore = older sister. Il maggiore = the eldest.

etymology: From Late Latin magia, from Ancient Greek μαγεία (mageía).

fact.text: From Ancient Greek mageía (mageía), the same root gives English 'magic'. The Magi were the wise men of ancient Persia.

etymology: From maglia + -etta.

senses.note: A diminutive of maglia (jersey or sweater).

etymology: From maglia + -one.

fact.text: Built from maglia (knitwear, jersey) plus -one, an ending that makes things bigger. Literally it's a 'big knit', while the -etta ending in maglietta (T-shirt) makes things smaller.

senses.note: Also called a jumper or pullover. A T-shirt is 'maglietta'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin magnificus.

fact.text: Lorenzo de' Medici, ruler of Florence and patron of Botticelli and Michelangelo, was known as Lorenzo il Magnifico. The word comes from Latin magnus 'great' + -ficus 'making', so literally 'doing great things'.

senses.note: Also used to mean 'wonderful, superb'. Historically a title, as in Lorenzo il Magnifico.

etymology: From Latin macrum, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós.

fact.text: It comes from Latin macer 'thin', which also gave English 'meager' via French. The word 'emaciated' comes from the same Latin root.

senses.note: Also used for lean meat and low-fat food: yogurt magro.

etymology: From ma (“but”).

fact.text: This shrug-word grew out of 'ma' (but): a 'but...' left hanging turned into a one-word sigh of doubt, roughly 'Who knows?'

senses.note: Shows doubt or a resigned shrug, e.g. 'Mah, non lo so.'

etymology: Inherited from Latin magis.

fact.text: Surprisingly, it comes from Latin magis, 'more'. Non... mai first meant 'not any more'. The same Latin word gave Spanish más and French mais ('but').

senses.note: After a verb it needs non: Non l'ho mai visto. In questions it means ever: Sei mai stato a Roma?

etymology: From Latin maiālis, from the goddess Maia.

fact.text: Latin maialis was a castrated pig, said to be the animal sacrificed to the goddess Maia. Her name is also behind the month of May (maggio).

senses.note: Also used as an insult for a dirty or lecherous person.
Carne di maiale = pork; also just 'maiale' on menus.

etymology: Borrowed from Spanish maíz.

fact.text: One of the first words Europe took from the Americas: Taíno mahisi came into Spanish as maíz after Columbus's voyages, and English 'maize' comes from the same source.

senses.note: Invariable and usually uncountable. A corn cob is 'pannocchia'.
Apocopic (shortened) form of male (evil). Used in fixed expressions.
Also a noun: un malato = a sick person, a patient. essere malato = to be ill.

etymology: Cognate with Catalan malaltia, English malady, French maladie, Sicilian malatìa, Portuguese maladia.

fact.text: Comes from malato 'sick', traced to Latin male habitus 'in poor condition'. English 'malady' is a close cousin, borrowed through French maladie.

senses.note: Covers illness and disease. Related: malato = ill, sick.

etymology: From Latin male.

fact.text: Not English 'male' (that's maschio)! It comes from Latin male, 'badly', which is also behind the English prefix mal-, as in malfunction and malnutrition.

senses.note: Opposite: bene. Sto male = I feel bad/ill. As a noun, il male = harm, evil, pain.

etymology: From Latin maledictus.

fact.text: From Latin maledictus, 'spoken ill of' (male 'badly' + dicere 'to say'). Its opposite benedetto, 'blessed', and English malediction and benediction share these roots.

senses.note: Common in exclamations (Maledetto traffico!). Can sound strong; the opposite is benedetto.

etymology: From Latin maledictiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin maledictiōnem, meaning 'evil speech'. The root 'male' (badly) and 'dicere' (to speak) combine in both Italian and related languages like English 'malediction'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mamma.

senses.note: An affectionate everyday word. The neutral word is madre. Mamma mia! = good grief!

etymology: Borrowed from English manager.

fact.text: A round trip: English manage probably comes from Italian maneggiare, 'to handle' (horses in particular). Italian later borrowed the word back as manager.

senses.note: An English loanword. It does not change in the plural: i manager.

etymology: From mancare.

senses.note: Also: shortage, deficiency, absence, fault, or defect.

etymology: From manco (adjective) + -are, or from a Vulgar Latin *mancāre, from Latin mancus.

fact.text: From Latin mancus, 'maimed, defective'. Its French cousin manquer gave English 'manqué', as in 'a poet manqué', someone who never became what they could have been.

senses.note: Works backwards: mi manchi = I miss you (lit. 'you are lacking to me').
Manca il sale = the salt is missing. mancare di = to lack.
senses.prompt: to be lacking, to be missing

etymology: Probably from Old French manche (“sleeve”).

fact.text: Probably from Old French manche, 'sleeve'. In the Middle Ages a lady might give a knight her sleeve as a token, so the word came to mean a small gift.

senses.note: Dare/lasciare la mancia = to leave a tip.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mandāre.

fact.text: From Latin mandare, 'to entrust, to order', which also gave English mandate. To send someone was once to give them a task.

senses.note: Mandare via = to send away; mandare un messaggio = to send a text.

etymology: From Latin mandātum.

fact.text: From Latin mandatum (command, task), past participle of mandare (to commit, entrust). Root mand- means 'hand over' (manus = hand).

etymology: Borrowed from Old French mangier, from Latin mandūcāre (“to chew, (coll.) eat”). Doublet of manducare, manicare, and manucare.

fact.text: It came via Old French mangier, from Latin manducare, 'to chew'. The French word also gave English 'manger', a feeding trough for animals.

senses.note: Regular -are verb; keeps the soft g: mangio, mangiamo. 'Mangiamo fuori' = we eat outside.

etymology: Borrowed from English mango, from Portuguese manga, from Malay mangga, from Tamil மாங்காய் (māṅkāy) from மா (mā, “mango species”) + காய் (kāy, “unripe fruit”).

fact.text: From Portuguese manga, via Malay mangga, ultimately from Tamil meaning 'mango tree' + 'unripe fruit'. The fruit traveled west along Portuguese trade routes.

etymology: Inherited from Latin manica.

fact.text: Italians call the English Channel la Manica, 'the Sleeve', because of its shape. French does the same with La Manche.

senses.note: A maniche corte = short-sleeved. Plural: maniche.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French maniere, from manere.

fact.text: From Old French maniere, meaning 'manner' or 'method'. The word entered French from manere, and spread through Romance languages. Related to English 'manner' through the same Old French root.

etymology: Inherited from Latin manus (whence also English manual, etc.), from Proto-Italic *manus, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂- (“to beckon”), or perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *mon-u- (see the Proto-Italic entry).

fact.text: Latin manus (hand) appears in many English words: manual, manuscript (written by hand), manicure and manufacture (originally made by hand).

senses.note: Feminine even though it ends in -o. The plural is irregular: le mani.

etymology: From Late Latin manūtenēre (“to support”), from Latin manū (“with the hand”) + teneō (“to hold”). By surface analysis, mano + tenere. Compare French maintenir, Spanish mantener, Portuguese manter.

fact.text: From manū tenēre (to hold in one's hand): manū (with the hand) + tenēre (to hold). The 'by hand' sense evolved into 'maintain' and 'support'.

senses.note: Also: keep, support, uphold, defend, respect (a commitment).

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin manuāle.

fact.text: Manuale comes from Late Latin manuāle, related to manus (hand), literally referring to a handbook—something held in hand.

etymology: Disputed, maybe from a pre-Latin (possibly Illyrian) root. Compare Albanian mëz, and Romanian mânz, Aromanian mãndzu, which might be from the same source.

senses.note: Also the live animal (a steer or young ox). Often 'carne di manzo'.

etymology: From Latin mappa, of possibly Semitic origin.

fact.text: Latin mappa meant 'napkin, cloth', and Quintilian said it was a Punic word. Medieval world maps drawn on cloth were called mappa mundi, which gave us 'map'.

senses.note: For road or tourist maps, Italians often say la cartina instead.

fact.text: Named after Marathon, Greece, site of a 490 BCE battle. The modern race commemorates a soldier's run from Marathon to Athens to announce victory.

etymology: Of Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *marką or Proto-Germanic *markō.

fact.text: Comes from a Germanic root meaning 'mark' or 'border', related to English mark and march (a border region). The Italian region Le Marche takes its name from medieval border marches.

senses.note: Di marca = branded or designer. Marca da bollo = a revenue stamp on official documents.

etymology: From marcare + -tore.

senses.note: In sport it also means goalscorer: il miglior marcatore = the top scorer.

etymology: From marcia + piede.

fact.text: Built from marcia (march, walk) plus piede (foot), so roughly 'walking on foot'. It is the strip of the street meant for pedestrians.

senses.note: Masculine, with plural marciapiedi. Also the platform alongside a railway track.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mare, from Proto-Italic *mari, from Proto-Indo-European *móri.

fact.text: Comes from Latin mare, which gave English marine and maritime. Its Indo-European ancestor *mori also gave Old English mere 'sea, lake', which survives in mermaid.

senses.note: 'Al mare' means at or to the seaside.

etymology: From earlier margarita, from Latin margarīta, from Ancient Greek μαργαρίτης (margarítēs), from a loanword of Eastern origin.

fact.text: From Latin margarīta via Greek margarítēs, from an Eastern loanword meaning pearl. Also the Italian name for Margaret, famous as the queen of Daisy. The flower was named after pearls for its resemblance.

senses.note: Formerly meant pearl (obsolete).

etymology: Inherited from Latin marītus.

fact.text: From Latin maritus, 'husband'. Its verb maritare, 'to marry', is the source of English marry, and it also gave us marital.

senses.note: mio marito takes no article: possessive plus a singular family noun.

fact.text: From Portuguese marmelada (quince preserve), from marmelo (quince). Italian, French, and English all borrowed variants of this Portuguese word for the preserve itself.

etymology: Originally Tuscan, from Byzantine Greek μάραον (máraon, “sweet chestnut”), ultimately from Proto-Celtic *māros (“great”), referring to the size of the nut, related to Welsh mawr and Cimbrian môr, a borrowing.

fact.text: At first it meant a large sweet chestnut, as in French marron glacé, and the colour was named after the nut. It still means chestnut as a noun.

senses.note: Plural is marroni. For brown hair or eyes, use castano.

etymology: From Latin Martis dīēs, variant of dīēs Martis (“day of Mars”).

fact.text: It means 'day of Mars', the Roman war god. English Tuesday is named after Tiw, a Germanic war god who was matched with Mars, so both names honour a war god.

senses.note: Lowercase and invariable (i martedì). Il martedì = on Tuesdays.

etymology: Inherited from Latin (mēnsis) mārtius.

fact.text: Named after Mars, Roman god of war, like English March. In the earliest Roman calendar it was the first month of the year, when the season for war and farming began.

senses.note: Months are lowercase and usually take no article: a marzo, in marzo.

etymology:
Etymology tree
Late Latin mascara
Latin *mascra
Proto-Indo-European *mesg-der.
Proto-Germanic *maskwǭ
Proto-West Germanic *maskābor.
Latin masca
Italian maschera
Inherited from Late Latin mascara, *mascra, masca. Doublet of mascara.
From maschio.

senses.note: Used for grammar and for men's things: nome maschile, abbigliamento maschile. Its opposite is femminile.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin masclus, contracted form of Latin masculus. Doublet of mascolo and masculo.

fact.text: It comes from Latin masculus, which also gave English 'masculine' and, through Old French masle, the English word 'male' itself.

senses.note: Also means 'boy, son': hanno due maschi. As an adjective: maschio/maschia.

etymology: Borrowed from French massage, derived from masser (“to massage”), from Arabic مَسَّ (massa, “to feel, touch”).

fact.text: Massaggio comes via French massage from Arabic massa (to feel, touch), traveling westward to become the Italian and English word for therapeutic touch.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin maximus.

fact.text: From Latin maximus (greatest). English maximum is the direct borrowing; Italian adapted it. Both trace to Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂s (great).

senses.note: Al massimo = at most. Also a noun: il massimo = the maximum, the best.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin maximus.

fact.text: From Latin maximus (greatest). English maximum is the direct borrowing; Italian adapted it. Both trace to Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂s (great).
In Italy a 'master' is usually a postgraduate professional course. The degree that matches an English-style master's is the laurea magistrale.

senses.note: A loanword from English and invariable: i master. It usually means a postgraduate professional course.
Singular in Italian: la matematica. Also means a female mathematician.

etymology: Latinization of older matera, from Latin māteria.

fact.text: Latin materia first meant timber or building wood, then any material. English gets both 'matter' and 'material' from the same word.

senses.note: Also means a school subject: 'Qual è la tua materia preferita?' (What's your favourite subject?)

etymology: From Latin māteriālis.

senses.note: Also an adjective: material, physical (danni materiali = material damage).

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin māternitātem.

senses.note: Invariable feminine noun. Also refers to a maternity ward or hospital.

etymology: From ematite (“hematite”). Rods of hematite ore were once used as pencils.

fact.text: From ematite 'hematite': rods of this iron ore were once used for drawing, and the word for the stone became the word for the pencil.

senses.note: Matita colorata = coloured pencil. A pen is una penna.

etymology: From Late Latin mātrīnea, from māter (“mother”) + -īneus (“relative suffix”). Compare Late Latin mātrīna (“stepmother, godmother”); alternatively from Late Latin mātrigna, after the model of prīvignus (“stepson”).

fact.text: From Latin māter (mother) plus a relative suffix. The form reflects mātigna, possibly influenced by prīvignus (stepson).

etymology: From matrimonio + -ale.

senses.note: Also means 'double' (of a bed) or 'master' (of a bedroom).

etymology: From Latin mātrimōnium.

fact.text: From Latin matrimonium, built on mater, 'mother'. In Roman thinking, marrying was tied to a woman becoming a mother. Compare patrimonio, built on pater, 'father'.

senses.note: The institution or state of being married.
The ceremony: andare a un matrimonio = to go to a wedding.

etymology: From Latin [hōra] mātūtīna.

fact.text: Comes from Latin hora matutina 'morning hour', named after Matuta, the Roman goddess of dawn. English 'matins', the early morning prayer, has the same origin.

senses.note: Di mattina = in the morning; stamattina = this morning. Also il mattino.

etymology: From Latin matutinus (“early”).

fact.text: From Latin matutinus 'of the morning', which also gave English matins, the early-morning prayer service.

senses.note: mattina is more common in everyday speech. mattino appears in set phrases like alle 9 del mattino.

etymology: From Late Latin mattus (“drunk, intoxicated”), itself either from a contraction of a form *madĭtus (as a past participle of Latin madeō), or madidus (“drunk, tipsy”). Cognate to French mat (“matte, pale”).

fact.text: From Latin mattus (drunk), the word originally meant intoxicated. Related to Sanskrit matta and French mat. The sense shifted from drunk to crazy over time.

etymology: The origin is uncertain, perhaps from Latin maltha (“cement”).

fact.text: Italians call a tedious, heavy book or film 'un mattone', a brick. 'Il mattone' can also mean the real-estate market: investire nel mattone means to invest in property.

senses.note: Colloquially, un mattone is something heavy and boring, like a dull book or film.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin mātūritātem.

senses.note: invariable noun (no plural form)

etymology: From Latin mē.

senses.note: Stressed form, used after prepositions (con me, per me) or for emphasis. Unstressed form: mi.
Also an adjective: mechanical. A trained engineer is 'ingegnere'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin media.

fact.text: From Latin media, feminine of medius ('middle'), the feminine form used to denote the middle value or average in mathematics.

senses.note: In statistics, education, and general use; media as mass media is masculine invariable.

etymology: From Latin medicina.

senses.note: Means both the drug and the field. A doctor is il medico.

etymology: Inherited from Latin medicus. Compare Neapolitan miedeco.

senses.note: Il dottore is also common in speech. Female: la medico or la dottoressa. Also an adjective: medical.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin medius, whence also Italian mezzo (an inherited doublet).

fact.text: Comes from Latin medius by the learned route. The same Latin word also passed down naturally through everyday speech and became mezzo (half), so the two are doublets.

senses.note: Statura media = average height; taglia media = medium size; dito medio = middle finger.

etymology: From Latin meditātiōne(m), case form of meditātiō (“thinking, contemplation”). By surface analysis, medita(re) (“to meditate”) + -zione (“-ation”).

fact.text: From Latin meditatio via the suffix -azione. Shares the same root as English 'meditation' and 'meditate', making it a perfect cognate across languages.

etymology: From Latin melius. Cognate with Sicilian megghiu.

senses.note: Adverb (and 'best'). The adjective 'better' is usually migliore.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin mēla, from mēlum, from Latin mālum, likely from Doric Greek μᾶλον (mâlon, “apple”); compare Attic μῆλον (mêlon).

fact.text: From Latin malum 'apple', which looked almost the same as malum 'evil'. This pun is often given as the reason the forbidden fruit of Eden is shown as an apple.

senses.note: The apple tree is 'il melo' (masculine). Colloquially, 'mela' can also mean a buttock.

etymology: From Arabic بَاذِنْجَان (bāḏinjān), from now archaic Persian بادنگان (bâdengân), from Sanskrit भण्डाकी (bhaṇḍākī) or वातिगगम (vātigagama, “eggplant, aubergine”), reshaped under the influence of mela (“apple”). Compare Greek μελιτζάνα (melitzána), Sicilian milinciana and Medieval Latin mēlongēna.

fact.text: From Arabic bāḏinjān, from Persian bâdengân, ultimately from Sanskrit bhaṇḍākī. The name was influenced by the Italian word mela (apple), creating melanzana.

etymology: From Late Latin mēlōnem, shortening of Latin mēlopepō, from Ancient Greek μηλοπέπων (mēlopépōn, “melon”).

fact.text: From Ancient Greek mēlopépōn (melon fruit), shortened in Latin to melo. The word travelled west on Mediterranean trade routes, reaching English and other European languages.

etymology: From Latin membrum (“member; limb”), from Proto-Indo-European *memso-, *mems-ro (“flesh”).

fact.text: From Latin membrum (member, limb), from Proto-Indo-European *memso- (flesh). English membrane shares the same root.

senses.note: One who belongs to a group; an element of a set.

etymology: Inherited from Latin memoria.

fact.text: Imparare a memoria means to learn by heart. Italians memorize poems this way at school, often Dante or Leopardi.

senses.note: Also computer memory. A single memory you recall is more often un ricordo.

etymology: Derived from Latin minus.

fact.text: The everyday phrase meno male, literally 'less bad', means 'thank goodness' or 'just as well'.

senses.note: Also 'minus' in maths: dieci meno tre.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin mēnsa (“table”), although some sources disagree.

fact.text: Latin mensa means 'table'. The high-IQ society Mensa took its name from it, suggesting a round table where everyone is equal.

senses.note: A school, university or workplace cafeteria: mangiare in mensa.
Also an adjective meaning 'monthly' (rata mensile). It comes from mese, 'month'.
A single wall-mounted shelf. A bookshelf unit is una libreria or uno scaffale.

etymology: From Latin mentha, from Ancient Greek μίνθη (mínthē).

fact.text: From Latin mentha via Greek mínnthē. The word traveled through languages as the plant itself spread along trade routes—mint became one of antiquity's most valued herbs.

etymology: From Latin mentem, from Proto-Indo-European *méntis (“thought”).

fact.text: The -mente ending on Italian adverbs is this word. Latin lenta mente meant 'with a slow mind', which became lentamente, 'slowly'. English -ly has a similar origin, from a word for 'body'.

senses.note: 'Avere in mente' means 'to have in mind'. 'Venire in mente' means 'to come to mind' or 'to occur to someone'.

etymology: From Latin mentīrī.

fact.text: From Latin mentiri, built on mens 'mind', as in English mental. The idea moved from being inventive with your mind to making things up, and so to lying.

senses.note: Lying down is sdraiarsi. Present tense: mento, menti, mente.

etymology:
Inherited from Late Latin dum interim (“while”).
Akin to Spanish mientras.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin dum interim, 'while meanwhile', which was squeezed down over the centuries. Spanish mientras shares the same origin.

senses.note: Can also contrast two things, like 'whereas': io lavoro, mentre lui dorme.
Also spelled menu. Invariable: i menù.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mīrābilia.

fact.text: From Latin mīrābilia (marvelous things), related to English 'miracle' and 'mirror' (both from mirari, to wonder). The 'Seven Wonders of the World' uses this same root.

senses.note: Feeling of awe and astonishment; also means a wonderful or marvelous thing

etymology: From meraviglia + -oso.

fact.text: Built from meraviglia 'wonder', which comes from Latin mirabilia 'wonderful things'. That is the same source as English 'marvel' and 'marvellous'.

senses.note: From meraviglia (wonder, marvel). Che meraviglia! = How wonderful!

etymology: Inherited from Latin mercātus.

fact.text: English 'market' comes from the same Latin word, mercatus, via Old North French. 'Merchant' and 'mercantile' are from the same family.

senses.note: Also the economic sense: il mercato del lavoro = the job market.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mercem (“merchandise”, “goods”).

fact.text: Descended from Latin merx (merchandise). The word Mercurius (Mercury), the Roman god of trade, likely shares the same economic root, making our modern 'merchant' a distant cousin.

senses.note: fem. noun; plural merci

etymology: From Latin Mercuriī diēs, variant of diēs Mercuriī (“day of Mercury”).

fact.text: Italian keeps the Latin 'day of Mercury'. English 'Wednesday' is Woden's day: Germanic peoples swapped in Woden, the god the Romans equated with Mercury.

senses.note: Lowercase and invariable. 'Il mercoledì' = on Wednesdays.

etymology: Inherited from Latin merda, from Proto-Italic *(s)merdā, from Proto-Indo-European *smerd-h₂- (“stench”).

fact.text: From Latin merda, which goes back to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning 'stench'. It is related to Slavic words for 'stink', such as Russian smorod.

senses.note: Common as an exclamation (Merda!) and as an insult. Avoid in polite company.

etymology: From Latin merenda (“light evening meal”). Compare Galician and Portuguese merenda, Spanish merienda.

fact.text: It comes from Latin merenda, related to merere (to earn or deserve). It was originally a light meal you had earned. Compare Spanish merienda.

senses.note: Typically the mid-afternoon snack, especially for children. Fare merenda = to have a snack.

etymology: From Latin meritāre, from meritus.

fact.text: From Latin meritāre, derived from meritus (deserved, earned). The English word merit shares the same Latin root.

etymology: From Latin meritum (“merit”, “deserts”), from a noun use of the neuter form of meritus.

fact.text: Shares the Latin root meritus with English 'merit' and 'deserve'. In modern Italian, merito is common in phrases like 'per merito' ('by merit').

senses.note: Now marked obsolete or literary; from merito ('merit, deserving').

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin misculāre, derived from Latin miscēre (“mix”). Doublet of mischiare.

fact.text: Goes back to Latin miscere, 'to mix', which is also the source of English mix and miscellaneous.

senses.note: Also means to stir (a sauce) or to shuffle (cards).

etymology: From Latin mēnsem (“month”). Compare Catalan mes, French mois, Portuguese mês, Romansh mais, Spanish mes.

fact.text: From Latin mensis, month, which also gave English 'menstrual'. It goes back to an ancient word for 'moon', the same source as English 'month' and 'moon'.

senses.note: Masculine: il mese, i mesi. Al mese = per month.

etymology: From Late Latin missa, from Latin missum.

fact.text: From the Latin dismissal phrase 'ite missa est' (go, the dismissal is made). The word literally means 'a sending away' or 'dismissal', capturing the moment the priest released the congregation.

senses.note: Often capitalized: la Messa.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French message, from Early Medieval Latin missāticum, derived from Latin mittere (“send”).

fact.text: Goes back to Latin mittere 'to send', like English message. The same root gives English mission, missile and transmit: a message is literally something sent.

senses.note: Also a text message: mandare un messaggio = to send a text.

etymology: From Messico + -ano.

fact.text: The name Mexico comes from Nahuatl Mexihco, possibly meaning 'place of the Mexica people' or derived from Mexitli, an alternate name for the Aztec war god Huitzilopochtli.

senses.note: Proper noun; the country in North America.

etymology: From Latin metallum (“metal, mine, quarry, mineral”), from Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon, “mine, quarry, metal”).

fact.text: The Greek word it comes from, métallon, first meant 'mine' or 'quarry'. Only later did it mean the material dug out of one.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin methodus, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos).

fact.text: From Latin methodus, from Ancient Greek méthodos (way, path). Both English and Italian inherited this learned word directly from Greek.

etymology: From Latin metrum (“a measure”), from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron).

fact.text: Gender changes the meaning: il metro is a metre (from Greek metron, 'measure'), while la metro is the subway, a shortening of la metropolitana.

senses.note: Masculine: il metro, i metri. Can also mean a measuring tape or a yardstick (criterion).
In this sense it is feminine and does not change in the plural: la metro, short for la metropolitana.

etymology: From Latin mētropolis.

fact.text: Comes via Latin from Greek mētropolis, 'mother city' (mētēr 'mother' + polis 'city'). It first meant a city that founded colonies.

senses.note: Feminine and invariable: la metropoli, le metropoli.

etymology: From metterci + -la.

senses.note: Compound: mettere + ce + la (to put there it)
senses.prompt: to put one's all into it

etymology: Inherited from Latin mittere, probably from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange, remove”). Cognate with French mettre, Spanish meter, Occitan metre, and English mission.

fact.text: Comes from Latin mittere, 'to send, let go', which also gave English mission, missile, emit, submit and transmit. In Italian the meaning drifted from 'sending' to 'putting'.

senses.note: Very versatile: also to place, to set. mettersi = to put on (clothes) / to start to.

etymology: From mettere + -si.

senses.note: Reflexive verb; also means to position oneself or begin.

etymology: From Late Latin medietātem, from Latin medius. Compare medietà, a borrowed doublet.

fact.text: It comes from Late Latin medietatem. The same word passed through French to give the rare English word moiety, meaning a half or a share.

senses.note: Used as a noun: la metà di = half of; a metà = halfway. The adjective is mezzo.

etymology: From mezza (“half; mid”) + notte (“night”), or directly from Latin mediam noctem.

fact.text: In literary Italian it can also mean 'north', just as mezzogiorno (noon) means 'south'. That is why southern Italy is called il Mezzogiorno.

senses.note: A mezzanotte = at midnight (no article). Usually used in the singular.

etymology: From Latin medius, whence also Italian medio (a borrowed doublet).

fact.text: Comes from Latin medius, 'middle', which gave English medium and median. It goes back to the same Indo-European root as native English mid and middle.

senses.note: Before a noun it agrees: mezza mela. After a noun it is often left unchanged: l'una e mezzo. As a noun, mezzo also means 'means'.

etymology: From Latin medius, whence also Italian medio (a borrowed doublet).

fact.text: Comes from Latin medius, 'middle', which gave English medium and median. It goes back to the same Indo-European root as native English mid and middle.

senses.note: 'I mezzi (di trasporto)' means 'means of transport' or 'vehicles'.
'Nel mezzo di' means 'in the middle of'. As an adjective, mezzo means 'half'.

etymology: From mezzo- + giorno. Compare Catalan migjorn, Romanian miazăzi.

fact.text: Means 'midday', and because the sun stands due south at noon it also means south. Il Mezzogiorno is the usual name for southern Italy.

senses.note: A mezzogiorno = at noon. Capitalised, il Mezzogiorno means southern Italy.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mē and, as an indirect object pronoun, possibly in part from Latin mihi.

senses.note: Also means 'to me': mi piace = I like it (literally, it pleases me). Goes before the verb.
Formal (Lei). Shop staff often say it to mean 'How can I help you?'
Use it for regret or sympathy. To apologise for something small, 'scusa/scusi' is more common.
scusa (informal, to one person); scusi (formal); mi dispiace (more empathetic)

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *melem m or f, from Latin mel n. Compare Sicilian meli, Romanian miere.

fact.text: From Latin mel, the same root as English 'mellow'. Also related to ancient Greek meli and Sanskrit madhu, showing this word for honey is ancient across Indo-European languages.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mīlliārium.

fact.text: Unique: the singular is masculine (il migliaio) but the plural is feminine (le migliaia). It derives from Latin milliarium ('thousand paces').

senses.note: Singular masculine, but plural migliaia is feminine. Used for approximation (about a thousand) or 'thousands' in plural.

etymology: Back-formation from the plural miglia, from Latin mīlia n pl (“thousand”) in the phrase mīlia passuum (“thousand paces”). Doublet of mille.
Inherited from Late Latin meliōrāre, a verb based on Latin meliārī (“better”). By surface analysis, migliore + -are.

fact.text: Built on Latin melior, 'better', the same root as English 'ameliorate' (via French améliorer). Migliore, 'better', is its Italian sibling.

senses.note: Uses avere when transitive and essere when it means 'to get better': è migliorato.

etymology: Inherited from Latin meliōrem, from Proto-Indo-European *mélyōs, from *mel- (“strong, big”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin melior 'better', the same root as English 'ameliorate' (to make better). In Latin, melior took the place of the regular form bonior as the comparative of bonus 'good'.

senses.note: Irregular comparative of buono. With the article it means 'the best': il/la migliore.

fact.text: The everyday Italian word for a billion (a thousand million) is miliardo, not bilione. Bilione is rare and has traditionally meant a million million.

senses.note: Takes di before a noun: un miliardo di persone.

fact.text: English 'million' was borrowed from Italian milione (via French). The Italian word is mille 'thousand' + the augmentative -one, so it is literally 'a big thousand'.

senses.note: Masculine, plural milioni. Takes di before a noun: un milione di euro.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin mīlitāris.

fact.text: From Latin mīlitāris (military). Root mīles (soldier) evolved into this adjective that also functions as a noun for a military person.

senses.note: can be noun or adjective; as noun refers to a person

etymology: From Latin mīlle, from Proto-Italic *smīɣeslī, from Proto-Indo-European *smih₂ǵʰéslih₂ (“one thousand”). Doublet of miglio.
From mille (“a thousand”) + foglie (“leaves, layers”), modeled on French mille-feuille.

fact.text: Italian calque of French mille-feuille, meaning literally 'a thousand leaves' (mille + foglie). The name refers to the many thin pastry layers.

senses.note: Puff pastry and custard cake; invariable singular.

etymology: From mille + uno.
From milli- (“a thousandth”) + metro (“metre”).

senses.note: Unit of measurement; also spelled millimetre.

etymology: From Latin minācia (“threat”), a noun based on mināx (“threatening”).

fact.text: From Latin minacia ('threat'), based on minax ('threatening, menacing'), from minari ('to threaten').

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *mināciāre, from Latin minācia, from mināx (“threatening”). Or, by surface analysis, minaccia + -are.
From minestrare (“to serve, prepare (as in soup)”), from Latin ministrāre.

fact.text: Comes from minestrare, 'to serve food', from Latin ministrare. That is the same root as English minister and administer, since a minister was originally a servant.

senses.note: Usually a soup with pasta or rice. Zuppa is a thicker soup, often served with bread.

etymology: From minestra (“soup”, ultimately from Latin ministrō) + -one (augmentative suffix).

fact.text: An augmentative form of minestra (soup), formed with the suffix -one. The word comes from Latin ministrō (to serve). Minestrone literally means 'big soup'.

senses.note: Thick Italian vegetable soup, often uncountable

etymology: Borrowed from English minibar. By surface analysis, mini- + bar.

fact.text: Borrowed directly from English in the 1960s as the hotel minibar concept became popular. The word is identical in both languages and is invariable in Italian (no plural change).

senses.note: Small refrigerated cabinet in hotels or homes

etymology: Derived from Latin minimus.

fact.text: From Latin minimus, the irregular superlative of parvus (small). English minimum, minimal, and minimize all derive from this same Latin root.

senses.note: Non ho la minima idea = I haven't the slightest idea. As a noun, il minimo = the minimum.

etymology: Derived from Latin minimus.

fact.text: From Latin minimus, the irregular superlative of parvus (small). English minimum, minimal, and minimize all derive from this same Latin root.

senses.note: The least or lowest point; minimum settings or idle speed.

etymology: From Latin ministrum.

fact.text: From Latin ministrum, meaning 'servant' (from minus, 'less' + comparative suffix -teros). A minister originally was one who served, a meaning still present in 'minister to someone's needs.'

etymology: From Latin minōrem.

senses.note: Comparative of piccolo. Also used in music: in la minore = in A minor.
Il fratello minore = younger brother. Il minore = the youngest.

fact.text: Related to English 'minuscule'. From Latin minusculus (rather small). In typography, minuscolo means lowercase, contrasting with maiuscolo.

senses.note: Also: minuscule, minute. In typography, lowercase.

etymology: From Latin minūtus. Doublet of menu.

fact.text: From Latin minutus, 'made small'. English 'menu' comes from the same word via French: originally a small, detailed list of dishes.

senses.note: Masculine noun: il minuto, i minuti. Un minuto! = Just a minute! As an adjective it means tiny or fine.

etymology: From Latin minūtus. Doublet of menu.

fact.text: From Latin minutus, 'made small'. English 'menu' comes from the same word via French: originally a small, detailed list of dishes.

senses.note: As an adjective, minuto means tiny or petite.
Usually with the article (il mio libro), but not with singular family: mia madre.

etymology: From Old Italian meo, from Latin meus, from Proto-Italic *meos.

senses.note: Usually with the article (il mio libro), but not with a singular family member: mia madre, mio padre.

etymology: From Old Italian meo, from Latin meus, from Proto-Italic *meos.

senses.note: Usually takes the article (il mio libro), but not with singular relatives (mio padre). Forms: mia, miei, mie.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin mīrāculum, from mīror.

fact.text: From Latin miraculum (wonder), from mirari (to admire). English 'miracle' and Italian 'miracolo' share the same Latin origin—a perfect cognate pair.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin myrtillus.

fact.text: From Medieval Latin myrtillus, which comes from Ancient Greek myrtus (myrtle). The word travelled from Greek through Latin across Romance languages.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin miseria (“misery”). By surface analysis, mìsero + -èria.

fact.text: Derives from Latin miseria, the direct ancestor of English 'misery' — both languages inherited this word for wretchedness and hardship from the same Roman source.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin missiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin missio, based on mittere (to send). The word's root traces back through Proto-Italic and Proto-Indo-European, literally meaning a sending or dispatch — fitting for a task or assignment someone is sent to accomplish.

etymology: From Latin mixtus.

fact.text: From the same Latin mixtus root as English 'mixed', 'mix', and 'mixture'. A direct cognate across Romance and Germanic languages.

etymology: From Latin mixtus.

fact.text: From the same Latin mixtus root as English 'mixed', 'mix', and 'mixture'. A direct cognate across Romance and Germanic languages.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin mītem (“mild, mature”).

fact.text: From Latin mitis, 'mild, soft', which also gave English 'mitigate', to make something milder. It has nothing to do with the tiny English bug!

senses.note: The same form for masculine and feminine; plural miti. E.g. 'un clima mite', 'una persona mite'.

etymology: From mito + -logia.
From Latin mittentem, present active participle of mittō.

fact.text: From Latin mittens (from mittere 'to send'). English 'transmit' and 'emit' share the same Latin root.

senses.note: Of letters or messages; also used in postal/official contexts.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin mōbilis.

fact.text: Not a mobile phone (that is il cellulare). From Latin mobilis, 'movable': furniture is property you can move. Real estate, which cannot be moved, is gli immobili.

senses.note: Countable: un mobile = one piece. 'Furniture' in general is i mobili (plural) or l'arredamento.
di moda / alla moda = fashionable; fuori moda = out of fashion.

etymology: From a variant of Late Latin modulus.

fact.text: From Latin modulus, 'small measure', a diminutive of modus. English model, module and mould (mold) all come from the same Latin family.

senses.note: Means a template, like a sewing pattern. A decorative pattern is usually 'motivo'. Also means 'model'.

etymology: From Late Latin modernus; from Latin modo (“just now”).

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin modernus, built on modo, 'just now'. So something modern is literally 'of just now'. English modern has the same origin.

etymology: From Latin modus, from Proto-Indo-European *modós, derived from the root *med- (“to measure”).

fact.text: From Latin modus, 'measure, manner', from a root meaning 'to measure'. English mode, model, modest and moderate come from the same source.

senses.note: in questo modo = this way; ad ogni modo = anyway. Not a physical path (that's strada).

etymology: From Latin modulus.

fact.text: From Latin modulus, 'small measure', a diminutive of modus. English module and model come from the same root, but in daily Italian life it's mostly the form you fill in.

senses.note: compilare un modulo = to fill in a form. Also means 'module'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mulier (nominative). The alternative forms reflect the Latin accusative mulierem.

fact.text: It comes from Latin mulier, meaning 'woman'. The Spanish word mujer comes from the same root and still means both 'woman' and 'wife'.

senses.note: Irregular plural: le mogli.

etymology: From molle (“soft”) + -are.
Borrowed from Latin multiplicāre.

fact.text: Latin multiplicare is the source of English multiply, multiple, and multiplication.

senses.note: Transitive verb; takes a direct object (multiply something).

fact.text: From Latin multus 'much, many', which also gave English the prefix multi- and words like multiply and multitude.

senses.note: As an adjective it agrees: molta acqua, molti libri.
As an adverb it never changes: molto bello, molto belle.

etymology: Derived from Latin multus, from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥tos (“crumbled, crumpled”, past passive participle). Compare Portuguese muito, Romanian mult, Catalan molt.

fact.text: From Latin multus 'much, many', which also gave English the prefix multi- and words like multiply and multitude.

senses.note: As an adverb it never changes (molto bello); as an adjective it agrees (molte persone).

etymology: Derived from Latin multus, from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥tos (“crumbled, crumpled”, past passive participle). Compare Portuguese muito, Romanian mult, Catalan molt.

fact.text: From Latin multus 'much, many', which also gave English the prefix multi- and words like multiply and multitude.

senses.note: Agrees as a determiner (molti soldi, molta gente). As an adverb meaning 'very' it never changes: molto bello.
'Benissimo' is a one-word alternative.

etymology: From Latin mōmentum.

fact.text: Latin momentum, from movere ('to move'), meant movement, such as the tiny shift that tips a scale. That is why English has both moment and momentum.

senses.note: Un momento! = Just a moment! / Hang on!

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin monachus.

fact.text: From Greek monachos, 'solitary', from monos, 'alone' (as in monologue). Munich, named after the monks, is called Monaco di Baviera in Italian.

senses.note: Plural monaci (with a hard c sound changing to ch-less 'ci'). Nun = suora or monaca.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mundus (“world”).

fact.text: From Latin mundus 'world', the source of English mundane, which originally meant 'earthly' as opposed to spiritual.

senses.note: in tutto il mondo = all over the world. Also used in exclamations like mondo cane!

etymology: From Latin monēta. Compare Spanish moneda and Portuguese moeda.

fact.text: Rome's mint was beside the temple of Juno Moneta, so moneta came to mean coin. The same word gave English both 'money' and 'mint'.

senses.note: Also currency: la moneta unica = the single currency (the euro).

etymology: From mono- + locale.

fact.text: Built from mono-, one, and locale, room. Italian flat ads count rooms this way, so a bilocale has two rooms and a trilocale three. Bathrooms are not counted.

senses.note: Common in housing ads, along with bilocale (two rooms) and trilocale (three rooms).

etymology: From Latin monopōlium.

fact.text: From Latin monopōlium, combining Greek monos (alone) and pōlein (to sell). The board game named after the concept was first called The Landlord's Game.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin montānia, a collective based on Latin montem.

senses.note: 'In montagna' = in/to the mountains. 'Una montagna di…' = a mountain of / loads of.

etymology: From Latin monumentum, possibly a borrowing.

fact.text: Comes from Latin monēre, 'to remind', so a monument is literally a reminder. The same root gives English admonish and monitor.

senses.note: Also a historic building or sight: visitare i monumenti = to see the sights.

etymology: Inherited from Latin morbidum (“sick”), from Latin morbus (“disease, illness”); as sickness makes one feeble, in Italo-Romance the meaning evolved into “limp, flabby”, and thence into “tender”, “delicate”.

fact.text: Not 'morbid'! It comes from Latin morbidus (sick). Illness makes you limp, so in Italian the meaning drifted to flabby and then to soft and tender.

senses.note: Soft to the touch (un cuscino morbido). 'Morbid' in Italian is morboso.

etymology: Inherited from Latin morbidum (“sick”), from Latin morbus (“disease, illness”); as sickness makes one feeble, in Italo-Romance the meaning evolved into “limp, flabby”, and thence into “tender”, “delicate”.

fact.text: Not 'morbid'! It comes from Latin morbidus (sick). Illness makes you limp, so in Italian the meaning drifted to flabby and then to soft and tender.

senses.note: An adjective that agrees with its noun: aghi morbidi, una coperta morbida.

etymology: Inherited from Latin morī(rī).

fact.text: Shares its Latin root with 'mortal' and even 'mortgage', from Old French mort gage, literally a 'dead pledge'.

senses.note: Irregular (muoio, muori, muore); takes essere: è morto. morire di fame = to starve.

etymology: From Latin mortālis.

senses.note: Also 'fatal, deadly': un incidente mortale. As a noun: noi semplici mortali = us ordinary mortals.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mortem, from Proto-Indo-European *mér-tis (“death”), from *mer- (“to die”).

fact.text: From Latin mors, mortis. English shares the root in mortal and mortuary, and also in mortgage: from Old French, literally a 'dead pledge'.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *mortus, from Classical Latin mortuus, from Proto-Italic *mortwos, from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥twós, derived from the root *mer- (“to die; to disappear”).

fact.text: From Latin mortuus (also behind English mortal and mortuary). The root *mer- ('to die') appears in English murder too.

senses.note: Also the past participle of morire: è morto = he died. Un morto = a dead person.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *mortus, from Classical Latin mortuus, from Proto-Italic *mortwos, from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥twós, derived from the root *mer- (“to die; to disappear”).

fact.text: From Latin mortuus (also behind English mortal and mortuary). The root *mer- ('to die') appears in English murder too.

etymology: From mosso.

senses.note: A move in a game or plan: fare la prima mossa. 'Move!' as a command is Muoviti!

etymology: Deverbal from mostrare + -a.

fact.text: It comes from mostrare, 'to show', from Latin monstrare. English gets 'demonstrate' from the same root, and 'monster' from the related word monstrum.

senses.note: Mettere in mostra = to show off or display.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mōnstrāre (“to show”). Cognate with Spanish mostrar, Occitan muishar and French montrer.

fact.text: Comes from Latin monstrare 'to show', which is related to monstrum, an omen or something shown as a warning. That is where English 'monster' comes from, and 'demonstrate' shares the root.

senses.note: Mostrare qualcosa a qualcuno = to show someone something.

etymology: From the older form monstro, from Latin mōnstrum.

fact.text: From Latin monstrum, originally meaning 'a portent or sign sent by the gods', later 'a misshapen creature'. The sense narrowed from divine omen to physical deformity to modern 'monster'.

etymology: From Late Latin mōtīvus.

senses.note: Per quale motivo? = For what reason? Also means a tune or a decorative pattern.

etymology: Shortened form of motocicletta.

fact.text: Feminine despite the -o ending, because it is short for la motocicletta (like la foto from fotografia). Il moto, masculine, is a different word meaning motion or movement.

senses.note: Feminine and invariable: la moto, le moto.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin mōtōrem.

senses.note: Also means 'motor'. Motore di ricerca = search engine.

etymology: From motore + -ino (diminutive suffix).

senses.note: Literally 'little motor'; the everyday word for a moped or small scooter.

etymology: From muovere + -mento, perhaps based partly on Medieval Latin mōvimentum, from Latin moveō. Compare French mouvement.

fact.text: English "movement" comes from the same Latin root muovere/movēō. Both languages use this word for physical motion, musical sections, and organized groups of people.

etymology: Diminutive of mozza (“a type of cheese”), related to the verb mozzare. Originally of southern Italian origin. Compare Neapolitan muzzarella.

fact.text: Named from a Neapolitan verb mozzare meaning to cut; the cheese was traditionally cut from a larger mass of curds. The name reflects the cheese-making method.

senses.note: Soft, mild Italian cheese, commonly used on pizza

etymology: Uncertain, possibly from Alemannic German Mugg, itself derived from or related to the verb muggire (“to moo, low”).

fact.text: Origin uncertain: possibly from an Alemannic German dialect word, Mugg, perhaps linked to the Italian verb muggire, 'to moo'. If so, it's basically a 'moo-er'.

senses.note: The everyday word for a cow; 'vacca' also exists but can be an insult.

etymology: From Latin mūtulus, syncopated to *mutlus, or from cumulus, transposed to a Vulgar Latin form *muculus > *muclus. Based on the first etymology, mutulo is a doublet, and based on the second, cumulo and cumolo are.

senses.note: 'Un mucchio di' often just means 'a lot of' (colloquial).

etymology: From Late Latin molīnum, from molīnus, from Latin molō.

fact.text: From Latin molere 'to grind'. Mola, a millstone, from the same family, gave English molar: the teeth that grind your food.

senses.note: Mulino a vento = windmill; mulino ad acqua = watermill.

etymology: From Latin multa.

senses.note: A monetary penalty imposed for breaking the law.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin mungere, from Classical Latin mulgēre (“to milk”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *h₂melǵ-.

fact.text: It goes back to the Proto-Indo-European root *h₂melǵ- 'to milk', which is also the ancestor of the English word 'milk' itself.

senses.note: Can also mean to milk someone, i.e. exploit them or squeeze money out of them. Past participle: munto.

etymology: From Latin municipium.

fact.text: From Latin municipium, derived from municeps (citizen of a municipality). The same root gives English "municipal."

senses.note: Also: town council, local government office.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *movĕre, from Latin movēre.

senses.note: Muoversi = to move (yourself). Muoviti! = Hurry up! Past participle: mosso.

fact.text: From Latin movēre (to move). English move shares the same Latin root. The reflexive form muoversi reflects the Italian tendency to use reflexives for intransitive meanings.

senses.note: Reflexive form; often means to move oneself, hurry, or leave.

fact.text: Italian has two plurals for muro: i muri (general walls, masculine plural) and le mura (fortification walls, feminine). Mura is specifically for city walls or battlements.

senses.note: Plural form (feminine); singular is il muro.

etymology: From Late Latin mūrāre (“to provide or surround with walls”). By surface analysis, muro + -are.

fact.text: Built on muro, from Latin murus 'wall', the same root as English 'mural', a painting done on a wall.

senses.note: Murare vivo = to wall someone up alive.

etymology: From murare + -tore.

senses.note: Comes from muro (wall), through murare (to wall up).

etymology: From Latin mūrus, from Old Latin *moerus, *moiros, from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to strengthen”).

fact.text: Has two plurals: i muri are the walls of a room, while le mura (feminine!) are the defensive walls around a city, as in le mura di Lucca. English mural and intramural share the Latin root murus.

senses.note: Plural muri for ordinary walls. City walls are le mura (feminine).

fact.text: Comes through Latin from Greek mouseion, 'seat of the Muses', the goddesses of the arts. The most famous was the Mouseion of Alexandria, a centre of learning.

senses.note: Plural musei. Stress falls on the e: mu-SE-o.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin mūsica, from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ, “of a Muse”).

fact.text: Comes via Latin from Greek mousike, 'of a Muse', meaning the art of the Muses. English 'museum', a place of the Muses, shares the same root.

senses.note: Plural: le musiche (the ch keeps the hard 'k' sound).

etymology: From Medieval Latin mūsicālis, derived from Latin mūsica.

senses.note: E.g. strumento musicale = musical instrument.

etymology: From Latin mūtus.

fact.text: From Latin mutus, the direct source of English mute. Both languages share the same ancient root.

senses.note: Can describe a person who cannot speak, or (in linguistics) a consonant requiring tight airflow restriction.

etymology: From Latin mūtuum (“loan”), from a noun use of the neuter form of mūtuus (“lent”, “borrowed”).

fact.text: From Latin mutuum 'loan', from mutuus 'borrowed, exchanged', the source of English 'mutual'. As an adjective, mutuo still means mutual in Italian.

senses.note: Any long-term bank loan, usually for a house. Accendere un mutuo = to take out a mortgage.

etymology: Inherited from Latin nascere.

fact.text: Comes from the same Latin root as English nascent, native, nation and nature, all tied to the idea of being born.

senses.note: Takes essere; past participle nato: sono nato nel 1990.

etymology: Cognate with Sicilian nàscita.

senses.note: Related to nascere (to be born). 'Data di nascita' = date of birth.

etymology: From Late Latin inabscondere, from Latin abscondere.

fact.text: It goes back to Latin abscondere, 'to hide away'. English 'abscond' comes from the same verb and means to slip away in secret, often with someone else's money.

senses.note: Irregular past participle: nascosto. Use nascondersi for 'to hide oneself'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin nāsus, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s.

senses.note: Ficcare il naso = to poke your nose (into something). Avere naso = to have a flair for something.

etymology: From Old High German nestila (“belt, strap, thong”), from Proto-West Germanic *nastilu.

fact.text: From Old High German nestila meaning belt or strap, the same root gave us English 'nestle'—both suggesting something binding or nestled together.

etymology: From Latin nātālis (“natal”).

fact.text: From Latin natalis, 'of birth', as in dies natalis, 'birthday': Christmas is literally Christ's birthday. English natal and prenatal come from the same root.

senses.note: Capitalised: Natale. Buon Natale! = Merry Christmas! Lowercase natale = birth, birthday.

etymology: From Latin nātūra.

fact.text: Italian calls a still-life painting a natura morta, literally 'dead nature'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin nātūrālis.

fact.text: Order water in an Italian restaurant and you will likely hear 'naturale o frizzante?' Here naturale means still water, as opposed to sparkling.

senses.note: acqua naturale = still water (vs acqua frizzante = sparkling).

etymology: From Latin nāvem, from Proto-Italic *naus ~ *nāwis, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us, derived from the root *(s)neh₂- (“to swim, float”).

fact.text: From Latin navis, the source of English navy and naval. The related Greek naus gave nausea, which originally meant seasickness.

senses.note: Feminine despite the -e ending: la nave. Nave spaziale = spaceship.

etymology: From Latin nāvigāre (“to sail, cruise”).

fact.text: Latin navigare combines navis (ship) with agere (to drive). To navigate was literally to drive a ship. The same navis gives English navy and naval.

senses.note: Also: navigare in Internet = to surf the web.

etymology: From nazionale + -ità.

senses.note: Same form in the plural: le nazionalità.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin nātiōnem.
