fact.text: Comes from Latin natio, built on nasci, 'to be born'. A nation was literally 'the people you were born among'. English 'native' and 'natal' have the same root.

senses.note: Le Nazioni Unite = the United Nations.

etymology: From Latin inde (“thence, from that place; from that person, of them”). Compare French en (adverb, pronoun).

fact.text: From Latin inde, 'from there, of them'. It does the same job as French en, as in il y en a (there are some).

senses.note: Replaces di + noun and is often left untranslated: ce n'è uno = there's one (of them).

etymology: Univerbation of né + anche.

senses.note: Neanche io = me neither. After a verb it needs non: non lo so neanche io. Synonyms: nemmeno, neppure.

etymology: From Latin nebula, through a contracted Vulgar Latin form *nebla. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos (“cloud”). Compare Sicilian negghia, Venetan nebia, Spanish niebla, Romanian negură and Aromanian negurã. Doublet of nebula, which was borrowed.

fact.text: It comes from Latin nebula, 'mist', which English borrowed directly as nebula. Piedmont's Nebbiolo grape is named after the fog too.

senses.note: C'è nebbia = it's foggy. The Po Valley is famous for it.

etymology: From Latin necessārius.

senses.note: Non è necessario = it's not necessary / there's no need.

etymology: From Latin negātīvus.
Borrowed from Latin negōtium, possibly a semi-learned term. First attested 14th century.

fact.text: From Latin negotium 'business', literally nec + otium, 'not leisure'. English negotiate comes from the same root.

senses.note: Also 'store'. Fare un affare = to make a deal; negozio can also mean a business deal.
in + il, before masculine singular nouns: nel paese = in the village.

etymology: From Latin inimīcus, with the loss of the first syllable.

fact.text: From Latin inimīcus (in- 'not' + amīcus 'friend'). Literally 'not a friend.' The first syllable dropped in Italian, giving nemico.

etymology: Univerbation of né + meno, but may also continue Latin nē minimum (quidem) (literally “not even a little”), with the superlative replaced by the comparative, and nec minus (literally “nor any less, and just as much > and even”)).

senses.note: Same as neanche and neppure. Nemmeno io = me neither. Before a verb, add non: non riesco nemmeno.

etymology: From neo- + nato.

fact.text: It literally means 'new-born': neo- (new) + nato (born, the past participle of nascere). The neo- is the same Greek prefix as in English neonatal.

senses.note: Feminine: la neonata. A baby or child in general is il bambino.

etymology: From Latin nigrum.

fact.text: In nero means off the books: lavoro in nero is undeclared work paid cash in hand. It's like English 'black market', which in Italian is mercato nero.

senses.note: Umore nero = a dark, bad mood. Feminine: nera; plurals: neri, nere.

etymology: From Latin nervōsus.

fact.text: Not quite a false friend, but a tricky one: Italians often use it to mean irritable or cranky rather than anxious. To say you're anxious before an exam, 'agitato' or 'in ansia' is often clearer.

senses.note: Often means irritable or on edge: 'Oggi sono nervoso' = I'm in a bad mood today.

fact.text: In Italian versions of the Odyssey, Ulysses tells the Cyclops his name is Nessuno ('Nobody'). When the blinded giant cries that Nobody is hurting him, no one comes to help.

senses.note: After a verb it needs non: Non ho sentito nessuno. As an adjective it means 'no, not any': nessun problema.

etymology: From Latin nē (“not”) + ipse (emphatic, literally “himself”) + ūnus (“one”), by surface analysis “not even one”. Cognate with Neapolitan nisciuno, Sardinian nisciunu, Friulian nissun, Ligurian nisciǜn, and Old French neisune. Compare Spanish ninguno and Romanian niciun.

fact.text: In Italian versions of the Odyssey, Ulysses tells the Cyclops his name is Nessuno ('Nobody'). When the blinded giant cries that Nobody is hurting him, no one comes to help.

senses.note: Before a verb it needs non: Non c'è nessuno. Also an adjective: nessun libro, nessuna parte.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *nittus, a syncopation of Latin nitidus. Doublet of nitido, which is borrowed.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin *nittus, a syncopation of Latin nitidus ('bright, shining'). Doublet of nitido.

senses.note: Also means 'net' (e.g. net weight).

etymology: From neuro- + -logo.

fact.text: From neuro- (nerve) + -logo (one who studies). The -logo suffix comes from Greek logos, meaning word or study, the same root as in English 'logic' and 'biology'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin nivem, from Proto-Italic *sniks, from Proto-Indo-European *snígʷʰs. Compare Portuguese neve, Spanish nieve.

fact.text: English snow and Italian neve come from the same Proto-Indo-European word, *snígʷʰs. Latin dropped the initial s-, which is why the two words look so different.

senses.note: Uncountable, like in English. Slang: also cocaine.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nivicāre, a verb based on Latin nivem (“snow”, noun). By surface analysis, neve + -icare. Cognate with Sicilian nivicari.

senses.note: Impersonal: nevica = it's snowing. Past tense takes avere or essere: ha/è nevicato.
Shortened form of niente used before a vowel, as in nient'altro (nothing else).

etymology:
From an earlier neente, either from Latin ne gentem (“no person, no one”), nec entem, ne entem, or ne inde. Compare Old Catalan nient, Sicilian nenti, Piedmontese gnente, Occitan neient, French néant.
The regional pronunciation with initial self-gemination of /nj-/ is by speakers who try to correct the /ɲ-/ because of the orthography, but keep the syllable structure, and thus gemination, of the original /ɲ-/.

fact.text: Its origin is debated. It may come from Latin ne gentem 'no person' or nec entem 'not a being'. French néant 'nothingness' is a close relative.

senses.note: Needs non when it comes after the verb: non vedo niente. Means the same as nulla.

etymology:
From an earlier neente, either from Latin ne gentem (“no person, no one”), nec entem, ne entem, or ne inde. Compare Old Catalan nient, Sicilian nenti, Piedmontese gnente, Occitan neient, French néant.
The regional pronunciation with initial self-gemination of /nj-/ is by speakers who try to correct the /ɲ-/ because of the orthography, but keep the syllable structure, and thus gemination, of the original /ɲ-/.

fact.text: Its origin is debated. It may come from Latin ne gentem 'no person' or nec entem 'not a being'. French néant 'nothingness' is a close relative.

senses.note: After a verb it needs non: Non ho visto niente = I didn't see anything. Synonym: nulla.

etymology: From Latin nepōtem, from Proto-Italic *nepōts, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *népōts. Compare French neveu, Romanian nepot, Catalan and Occitan nebot, Sicilian niputi and Persian نوه.

fact.text: It comes from Latin nepos. English 'nepotism' comes from Italian nepotismo, coined for popes who gave posts to their 'nephews', who were sometimes really their sons.

senses.note: Il nipote = nephew, la nipote = niece. The same word also means grandchild.
Il/la nipote = grandson/granddaughter. Context tells it apart from nephew/niece.

etymology: Inherited from Latin nōn.

senses.note: Also a tag at the end of a sentence: Vieni, no? = You're coming, right?

etymology: Borrowed from English no.

senses.note: Borrowed from English.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *nuceola, from nuceus (“of nuts”), from Latin nux (“nut”). Compare Ligurian nisêua, Sicilian nuzzola, Venetan noxeła, Romansh nitschola, and also French noisette.

fact.text: From Latin nux (nut), the same root as English 'nut'. The word traveled through Romance languages: French noisette, Spanish avellana. The -nut ending in English filbert varieties comes from the same stem.

senses.note: Invariable; typically used with masculine nouns.

etymology: Inherited from Latin nucem. Cognate with Sicilian nuci.

fact.text: The word comes from an ancient root *knu- shared by Celtic and Germanic languages too. English 'nut' and Italian 'noce' are cousins from the same ancestral word.

etymology: From Latin nōs, from Proto-Italic *nōs.

senses.note: Subject pronoun; often dropped because the verb shows the person: (noi) siamo = we are. Also 'us' after prepositions.

etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan enojos.

fact.text: It came in from Old Occitan enojos. That word family goes back to Latin in odio ('in hatred'), which also gave English 'annoy' and the French loanword 'ennui'.

senses.note: Can also mean annoying. 'Che noia!' = how boring!

etymology: From nolo (“hire”) + -eggiare.

fact.text: Comes from nolo, 'hire' or 'freight', which traces back through Latin naulum to Greek naûlon, 'passage money', from naûs, 'ship'. Hiring once meant chartering a ship.

senses.note: Used for cars, bikes, boats and gear; for houses Italians usually say affittare.

etymology: From Latin nōmen.

fact.text: Comes from Latin nomen, which is related to English 'name'. Latin nomen also gave English 'noun', 'nominate' and 'nominal', which is why the Italian word also means 'noun'.

senses.note: Also means 'first name' (vs cognome = surname) and, in grammar, 'noun'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin nōn.

senses.note: Goes right before the verb. Double negatives are normal: non vedo niente = I see nothing.
A set reply to 'Come stai?' meaning 'not too bad'.
'Non so' is also used. 'Lo' refers to the fact you don't know.
Literally 'I don't see the hour'. Add 'di' + infinitive: non vedo l'ora di partire.

etymology: From Late Latin nonna.

fact.text: It comes from Late Latin nonna, a respectful word for an older woman that the Church also used for nuns. English 'nun' comes from the same Latin word.

senses.note: Grandfather is il nonno, and grandparents are i nonni.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin nonnus.

fact.text: From Late Latin nonnus, probably a child's word, which also came to mean monk. Its feminine nonna gave English nun as well as Italian nonna, grandmother.

senses.note: Plural i nonni = grandparents. Grandmother = la nonna.

etymology: Univerbation of non + ostante. Compare Portuguese não obstante, Spanish no obstante, French nonobstant.

fact.text: A univerbation (fusion) of non + ostante (from Latin obstans, standing against). Literally 'not standing against', it means concession or opposition does not prevent something. Paralleled in Spanish, Portuguese, and French.

senses.note: Preposition or conjunction.

etymology: Via Spanish and French, ultimately from Old English norþ.

fact.text: It isn't from Latin. It came via French from Old English norþ, so it's a cousin of English north. Sud, est and ovest also came from Germanic through French.

senses.note: Al nord = in the north. Literary synonym: settentrione.

etymology: From Latin nōrmālis.

fact.text: From Latin norma, a carpenter's square. 'Normal' first meant 'at right angles', which is why a 'normal' in geometry is still a perpendicular line.

etymology: Borrowed from New Latin nostalgia, coined from Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos, “returning home”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”).

fact.text: Swiss doctor Johannes Hofer coined the word in 1688 for a medical condition: the homesickness of soldiers far from home. He built it from Greek nostos (return home) + algos (pain).

senses.note: Also homesickness. 'Avere nostalgia di casa' = to be homesick.

fact.text: The Sicilian Mafia's name for itself, Cosa Nostra, simply means 'our thing'.

senses.note: Usually takes the article: la nostra casa. No article with singular family nouns: nostro padre.

etymology: From Latin nostrum, from Proto-Italic *nosteros.

fact.text: The Sicilian Mafia's name for itself, Cosa Nostra, simply means 'our thing'.

senses.note: Forms: nostro, nostra, nostri, nostre. Usually with the article: la nostra casa.

etymology: From Latin nostrum, from Proto-Italic *nosteros.

fact.text: The Sicilian Mafia's name for itself, Cosa Nostra, simply means 'our thing'.

senses.note: Agrees with the thing owned: è il nostro, sono le nostre.
Works for written notes and musical notes. 'Prendere nota' = to take note.
The alternative form 'swim' is Tuscan regional usage.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin nōtitia.

fact.text: It looks like English 'notice', but it means news. A notice is un avviso. Both words come from Latin notitia, meaning knowledge or acquaintance.

senses.note: Le notizie = the news. Chiedere notizie di qualcuno = to ask after someone.

etymology: From the Latin nōtus (“known; notorious”).

fact.text: From Latin notus 'known', the root of English notorious. But noto is usually neutral or positive, so don't translate it as notorious.

senses.note: Neutral, not negative: un noto scrittore = a well-known writer.

etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts
Proto-Italic *nok⁽ʷ⁾ts
Latin nox
Italian notte
Inherited from Latin nox, from Proto-Italic *nok⁽ʷ⁾ts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.

fact.text: Goes back to Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts, the same ancestor as English 'night', German 'Nacht' and Latin 'nox' (as in 'nocturnal' and 'equinox').

senses.note: Feminine. Buona notte = good night; stanotte = tonight / last night.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *nōvāgintā, from Latin nōnāgintā (blended with novem (“nine”)), from earlier *nūnāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥(d)ḱomt (“nine tens”).
From novanta (“ninety”) + cinque (“five”).
From novanta (“ninety”) + due (“two”).
From novanta (“ninety”) + nove (“nine”).
From novanta (“ninety”) + quattro (“four”).
From novanta (“ninety”) + sei (“six”).
From novanta (“ninety”) + sette (“seven”).
From novanta (“ninety”) + tre (“three”).
From novanta (“ninety”) + otto (“eight”).
From novanta (“ninety”) + uno (“one”).

fact.text: As a noun, il novantuno can mean the Carcano Model 1891, Italy's standard rifle in both World Wars. A later Carcano carbine was the rifle used in the 1963 assassination of John F. Kennedy.

etymology: From Latin novem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Cognate with Portuguese nove, Spanish nueve.

senses.note: Don't confuse it with nuovo/nuove ('new').

etymology: From Latin novem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Cognate with Portuguese nove, Spanish nueve.
From nove (“nine”) + cento (“hundred”).
Inherited from Latin novembrem.

fact.text: From Latin novem, 'nine'. It was the ninth month of the early Roman calendar, which began in March. That's why the 'ninth' month is now the eleventh.

senses.note: Italian does not capitalise month names: a novembre = in November.

etymology: From earlier novitade, novitate, from Latin novitātem (“newness, novelty”).

senses.note: Invariable: le novità. Also means news: Ci sono novità? = Any news?

etymology: From Latin nūbilis.

fact.text: From Latin nūbilis, related to nūbere ('to marry'). The root also appears in English 'nubile,' which now usually refers to physical attractiveness rather than marital status.

senses.note: Applies to both masculine and feminine; now primarily literary or formal.

etymology: From nucleo + -are.

senses.note: Centrale nucleare = nuclear power plant.

etymology: Inherited from Latin nūlla, feminine singular and neuter plural (collective) of nūllus.

fact.text: Inherited from Latin nullus (not any). The Italian form nulla preserves the feminine singular form used as a neuter noun meaning 'nothing', a pattern seen in Romance languages.

etymology: Inherited from Latin nūlla, feminine singular and neuter plural (collective) of nūllus.

fact.text: Inherited from Latin nullus (not any). The Italian form nulla preserves the feminine singular form used as a neuter noun meaning 'nothing', a pattern seen in Romance languages.

senses.note: After a verb it needs non: non cambia nulla. Same meaning as niente.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin numerus, whence also Italian novero (an inherited doublet).

senses.note: Also used for shoe size: Che numero porti? (What size do you take?)

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *nŏra, from Late Latin nura, from Classical Latin nurus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *snusós.

fact.text: Goes back to Latin nurus and a very old Indo-European root, *snusós. Old English also had a word from this root, snoru, meaning daughter-in-law.

senses.note: Son-in-law is genero.

etymology:
From older notare, from Vulgar Latin *notāre, from Latin natāre. Compare Corsican nutà, Romanian înota.
The original Italian notare had no diphthong in the infinitive, but it did have conjugations such as nuota (“swims”), reflecting the regular diphthongization of Latin /ŏ/ in a stressed open syllable. Eventually the diphthong spread to all forms of the verb, including the infinitive.
Doublet of natare.

fact.text: Old Italian said notare. The uo sound first appeared only in stressed forms like nuota, then spread to the whole verb, including the infinitive.

senses.note: 'I used to swim' = nuotavo (imperfetto).

etymology: From nuotare.

senses.note: The activity/sport. The verb 'to swim' is nuotare.

etymology: Inherited from Latin novus, from Proto-Italic *nowos, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos, from the root *new-.

fact.text: Italian nuovo and English new go back to the same Proto-Indo-European word, *néwos. The Latin form novus also gave English novel, novice and innovate.

senses.note: Di nuovo = again (facciamolo di nuovo = let's do it again).

etymology: Inherited from Latin nūtrīre.

fact.text: From Latin nutrire 'to suckle, nourish'. Its relative nutricia 'wet nurse' became English nurse, and the verb itself gave nutrition and nutrient.

senses.note: Also figurative: nutrire speranze/dubbi = to harbour hopes/doubts.

etymology: From a Latin nūbila, noun use of the feminine of nūbilus (“cloudy”), from nūbēs. Cognate with Sicilian nuvula. Compare Catalan núvol.

fact.text: It comes from Latin nubes, 'cloud'. The French form, nue, gave the verb nuer, 'to shade', which is where English 'nuance' comes from.

senses.note: Also used for 'the cloud' in computing (il cloud is common too). Nube is the literary word.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin nūbilōsus, from Latin nūbilus. By surface analysis, nuvola + -oso.

senses.note: Used for the sky and weather: oggi è nuvoloso = it's cloudy today.

etymology: From Latin nec.

senses.note: né... né = neither... nor. The accent tells it apart from the pronoun ne.

etymology: From Latin aut.

senses.note: o... o... = either... or... Sometimes written od before a vowel.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin obligāre.

fact.text: From Latin obligāre (to bind, tie to). English 'oblige' and 'obligation' share this root, all centered on binding or duty.

senses.note: transitive; can mean to obligate or do a favor
Synonym: compulsory. E.g. 'La cintura è obbligatoria.'

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin obiectīvus.

senses.note: Can mean a goal/target or the objective lens in optical instruments.

etymology: From Latin obsolētus.

senses.note: Also means 'outdated' in general, not only for technology.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin occāsiōnem, whence also Italian cagione (an inherited doublet).

fact.text: Not just 'occasion': in shops un'occasione is a bargain, and d'occasione means second-hand or cut-price, so un'auto d'occasione is a used car.

senses.note: Also means 'occasion'. In shops it means 'bargain'.

etymology: From occhio (“eye”) + -ale.

senses.note: Almost always plural: gli occhiali. Occhiali da sole = sunglasses.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *oculāta, ultimately from Latin oculus (“eye”). Or by surface analysis, occhio + -ata.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin oculāta (related to oculus, 'eye'). The -ata suffix often signals a female agent or a single action, so occhiata literally means 'a looking' or 'a glance' — a moment of using one's eyes.

senses.note: A quick or casual look

etymology: From Vulgar Latin oclus, syncopated from Latin oculus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃okʷ-, *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”). Doublet of oculo, a borrowing.

fact.text: Literally 'Eye!'. Italians often say it while pulling down the lower eyelid with a finger, a gesture that means 'stay alert'.

senses.note: Plural occhi. Aprire gli occhi = to open one's eyes (to the truth).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin occupāre.

senses.note: Occuparsi di = to take care of, to deal with. Occupato = busy or engaged (a phone or toilet).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ōceanus, from the name of the deity Ōceanus, from Ancient Greek Ὠκεᾰνός (Ōkeănós).

fact.text: It is named after Okeanos, a Greek Titan. The Greeks pictured him as a giant river flowing in a ring around the whole flat world.

senses.note: Stressed on the E: o-CE-a-no. L'Oceano Atlantico = the Atlantic Ocean.

etymology: From odio (“hatred”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).

senses.note: Present tense: odio, odi, odia… Odio = I hate, and also the noun 'hatred'.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin odium (“hate”), whence also uggia, inherited through Vulgar Latin.

fact.text: Comes from Latin odium, which English kept almost unchanged in 'odium' and 'odious'.

senses.note: Odio is also 'I hate' (from odiare): Odio il traffico.

etymology: From Latin odōrāre (“to perfume, make fragrant”), derived from odor (“smell”).

senses.note: Both to sniff something and to give off a smell: odorare di rose. Everyday speech often uses sentire l'odore.

etymology: From Latin odōrem, from an archaic form odōs, from Proto-Italic *odōs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃édos, derived from the root *h₃ed- (“to smell, stink”). Doublet of aulore and olore.

fact.text: It comes from the same Indo-European root (*h3ed-, 'to smell') as English 'odour' and, through Greek ozein, 'to smell', the word 'ozone'.

senses.note: Neutral word for any smell, good or bad. At the greengrocer, gli odori means herbs.

etymology: From the feminine of the past participle of offrire, or from Medieval Latin or Late Latin offerta, ultimately from Latin offerō. Compare Spanish, Portuguese, Catalan, and Sardinian oferta; Friulian ufierte; Romansh offerta; Sicilian ufferta.

fact.text: Comes from Latin offerre, 'to bring before' (ob- 'toward' + ferre 'to carry'). English 'offer' comes from the same Latin verb, so the two words are close cousins.

senses.note: Also a bid, tender or donation. 'In offerta' = on special offer.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *offerīre, from Latin offerre.

senses.hint: most common; also means treat/pay for
senses.note: Also 'to treat/pay for': Offro io! = My treat! Past participle: offerto.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin obiectum.

fact.text: Look at the top of an Italian email: the subject line is labelled 'Oggetto', not 'soggetto'. In grammar, though, the object of a sentence is also called oggetto.

senses.note: In letters and emails, oggetto is the 'subject' line (Oggetto: ...).

etymology: Inherited from Latin hodiē.

fact.text: Comes from Latin hodie, which was squeezed together from hoc die, 'on this day'. Spanish hoy has the same origin, and so does the 'hui' in French aujourd'hui.

senses.note: 'Oggi come oggi' means 'as things stand today'.

etymology: From oggi (“today”) + giorno (“day”).

fact.text: Literally today-day: from oggi (today) + giorno (day). A compound that evolved from the phrase meaning at the present day.
Comes from Latin omnis, 'all, every'. The same root gives English omnipresent, omnivore and omnibus ('for everyone'), which was later shortened to bus.

senses.note: Never changes form and is always followed by a singular noun: ogni giorno = every day.

etymology:
Inherited from Old Italian onne~onni (with /ˈɔ-/ per the Latin etymon), from Latin omnis.
The development of palatalized /-ɲ-/ and closed /ˈo-/, already attested in the thirteenth century (ógne, later ógni), are due to the word being frequently unstressed. Variants with /ˈɔ-/ still survive in much of Tuscany and Central Italy.

fact.text: Comes from Latin omnis, 'all, every'. The same root gives English omnipresent, omnivore and omnibus ('for everyone'), which was later shortened to bus.

senses.note: Invariable, always followed by a singular noun: ogni giorno = every day.

etymology: From ogni (“each, every”) + uno (“one”).

fact.text: Built from ogni (each, every) + uno (one), so literally means 'each one'.

etymology: Onomatopoeic; compare Latin ō.

senses.note: Shows surprise. In casual speech it is also used to get someone's attention, like 'hey!'
An English loanword, also written ok. Native options: va bene, d'accordo.

etymology: From Latin oleum, from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion).

fact.text: Comes through Latin oleum from Greek elaion, meaning olive oil specifically. English oil has the same origin, so all 'oil' was once olive oil.

senses.note: Plural: gli oli (also olii). Olio d'oliva = olive oil.

etymology: From Latin olīva, from Etruscan 𐌄𐌋𐌄𐌉𐌅𐌀 (eleiva) or from Proto-Hellenic *elaíwā (compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀁𐀨𐀷 (e-ra-wa), Ancient Greek ἐλαίᾱ (elaíā)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁loywom.

fact.text: The word travelled from Ancient Greek through Latin olīva, possibly via Etruscan. The same root gave English 'olive', making it a true linguistic ambassador of Mediterranean agriculture.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin ultra, from ulter.
Cognate with French outre, from Old French oltre.

fact.text: It comes from Latin ultra, 'beyond', which English borrowed as the prefix ultra- (ultraviolet). It is related to 'ultimate', from Latin ultimus, 'farthest'.

senses.note: Oltre a = besides, apart from (oltre a me = apart from me). Also a preposition: oltre il fiume.

etymology: From Latin umbra, probably from Old Latin *omra, possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *h₂mr-u-, *h₂mrup-.
Variant of ombrella.

fact.text: English took 'umbrella' from Italian ombrella around 1600. It goes back to Latin umbra, 'shade', so the first umbrellas were for blocking the sun, not the rain.

senses.note: Masculine: un ombrello. A beach or sun umbrella is l'ombrellone.

etymology: From Latin homicīdium.

senses.note: Also the legal term 'homicide'. 'Omicidio colposo' means manslaughter.

etymology: From Latin unda, from nasalized form of Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ (“water”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin unda ('wave'), which is hidden in English 'undulate', 'inundate' and 'abundant' (from Latin abundare, 'to overflow').

senses.note: Andare in onda = to go on air (radio or TV).

etymology: From Latin honestus, from honor.

senses.note: Can also mean fair or reasonable: un prezzo onesto = a fair price.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin honestātem.

fact.text: From Latin honestātem. Related to English honest, both meaning 'having integrity and truthfulness'.

senses.note: Invariable noun; does not pluralize.

etymology: Inherited from Latin honōrem.

senses.note: Note: British spelling used (also honor in US English)

etymology: Inherited from Latin opera.

fact.text: Latin opus 'work' had the plural opera, which was later reread as a feminine singular. English took 'opera' from Italian: a musical 'work'.

senses.note: Opera d'arte = work of art. It also means opera, and an institution or charity (opera pia).

etymology: From Latin operārius. By surface analysis, from operare + -aio

fact.text: From Latin operarius, from opera (work), which is the root of English operate. Italian opera, the musical art form, originally just meant 'a work'.

senses.note: A manual or blue-collar worker; feminine l'operaia. Office workers are impiegati.

etymology: From Latin operātiōnem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin operātiōnem, which gave English the word 'operation'. Both languages share the same Latin root meaning 'work' or 'working'.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin opīniōnem.

senses.note: Secondo la mia opinione = in my opinion. Cambiare opinione = to change your mind.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin opportūnitātem.

fact.text: From Latin opportunitas. English opportunity and Italian opportunità are cognates from the same source.

senses.note: Invariable noun in Italian (opportunità), same form singular and plural.

etymology: From Latin opportūnus.

senses.note: Means opportune, timely, fitting—not the same as English appropriate (suitable for purpose).

etymology: Univerbation of o + pure; compare Lombard opur, Piedmontese opura.

senses.note: A fuller alternative to o; common when offering options: Tè oppure caffè?

etymology:
Derived from Latin hōrā, ablative case of hōra (“hour”).
Compare Old French ore, Spanish ahora and Portuguese agora.

fact.text: It comes from Latin hora, from Greek hora, which also gave English 'hour'. The adverb ora (now) comes from Latin hac hora, 'at this hour'.

senses.note: Also a noun, l'ora = hour/time: è ora di… = it's time to…

etymology: Inherited from Latin hōra (“hour”), from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “hour”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin hora, from Greek hora, which also gave English 'hour'. The adverb ora (now) comes from Latin hac hora, 'at this hour'.

senses.note: Che ora è? / Che ore sono? = What time is it? The adverb ora means 'now'.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin hōrārium. Cognate with Piedmontese orari.

senses.note: Also means hours: orario di apertura = opening hours. In orario = on time.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ōrdināre.

fact.text: From Latin ordinare, which also gave English 'ordain' by way of Old French. Italian keeps that church sense too: ordinare un prete means to ordain a priest.

senses.note: Used for ordering food or goods and for giving orders. It can also mean to tidy or arrange.

etymology: From Latin ōrdinem.

senses.note: In ordine = tidy, in order. Also used for a command and for a religious order.

etymology: From orecchia f.

fact.text: A masculine noun with a feminine plural: one ear is l'orecchio, but two ears are usually le orecchie. Several body parts work this way, like ginocchio and braccio.

senses.note: Masculine singular (l'orecchio). Usual plural is feminine: le orecchie (orecchi also exists).

etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin organizāre (“to organize”).

senses.note: Regular -are verb with double z: organizzo, organizzi. Reflexive organizzarsi = to get organized.

etymology: From organizzare + -zione.

fact.text: From organizzare + -zione. Shares the same root as English 'organize', both ultimately from Greek órganon (instrument, tool).

senses.note: Also: arrangement, planning, an organized entity.

etymology: From orizzonte (“horizon”) + -ale.

fact.text: From orizzonte (horizon) + -ale (adjective suffix). The word's structure mirrors English 'horizon' + '-al', both ultimately from Greek horizein (to limit or bound), making it the 'limit-forming' direction.

etymology: From ora (“now”) + mai (“ever, never”). Compare Piedmontese oramai, French désormais.

senses.note: Often suggests it is too late to change things: ormai è tardi = it's too late now.

etymology: From Latin aurum, from earlier ausum, from Proto-Italic *auzom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éh₂usom (“glow”), derived from the root *h₂ews-.

fact.text: It comes from Latin aurum, which is why gold's chemical symbol is Au. The word likely goes back to a root meaning 'to dawn, glow', the same root behind Aurora, the goddess of dawn.

senses.note: Also gold medal: vincere l'oro. D'oro = golden, made of gold.

etymology: From Latin hōrologium, from Koine Greek ὡρολόγιον (hōrológion).

fact.text: From Greek horologion, from hora 'hour' plus a root meaning 'to tell', so an 'hour-teller'. English 'horology', the study of timekeeping, has the same origin.

senses.note: Means both wall clocks and wristwatches. orologio da polso = wristwatch.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin horribĭlis.

senses.note: Also 'awful, dreadful'. Same form for masculine and feminine; plural orribili.

etymology: From Latin urtīca. Compare Sicilian ardìcula.

fact.text: Comes from Latin urtica, the source of urticaria, the medical name for hives. That rash feels like a nettle sting.

senses.note: Plural ortiche. Nettles are used in Italian cooking, e.g. risotto alle ortiche.

etymology: From Late Latin ausāre, frequentative from Latin audēre.

fact.text: It goes back through Late Latin ausare to Latin audere, 'to dare'. The same root gives English 'audacious' and 'audacity'.

senses.note: Non osare! = Don't you dare! Osare + infinitive: Come osi parlare così?

etymology: From earlier *ospetale, from Late Latin hospitāle (“hospice, shelter, guesthouse”), substantivization of Latin hospitālis (“hospitable; pertaining to a host or guest”). Doublet of ospitale and hotel, which were borrowed from Latin and French respectively.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin hospitale, 'guesthouse', from hospes, 'host or guest'. English hospital, hostel, hotel and hospitality all come from the same root.

senses.note: In ospedale = in/to hospital (no article).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin hospitālitātem.

fact.text: Latin hospes meant both 'host' and 'guest', and Italian kept the ambiguity: ospite can mean either the person hosting or the one being hosted.

senses.note: Invariable: plural is also ospitalità.

etymology: From Latin hospitem. Cognate to Italian oste (“innkeeper, landlord”).

fact.text: One word means both guest and host, just like its Latin source hospes. Hospes also gave English 'host', 'hospital' and 'hotel'.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: l'ospite. It can also mean host.

etymology: From Latin observāre.

senses.note: Also means to point out or remark, and to keep (rules or a fast).

etymology:
From Latin ossum, popular variant of os, ossis, from Proto-Italic *ōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ésth₁ (“bone”), *h₂óst.
Compare Catalan, French, and Romanian os; Portuguese osso; Corsican, Sardinian, and Sicilian ossu; Spanish hueso.

fact.text: Latin os, ossis 'bone' lives on in English ossify (to turn into bone) and ossuary, a place where bones are kept.

senses.note: Plural: le ossa (bones of a body), gli ossi (loose bones, e.g. for dogs).

etymology: Borrowed from Old French ostel, from Latin hospitālis (“pertaining to hospitality”). Doublet of ospitale.

fact.text: English 'hostel' comes from the same Latin root (hospitālis). It's a doublet of Italian 'ospitale' (hospital), both meaning 'hospitable' or 'relating to hospitality'.

etymology: From Latin octāgintā, variant of octōgintā (“eighty”), from Proto-Indo-European *oktōḱomt, from earlier *oḱto(w)-dḱomt (“eight-ten”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + cinque (“five”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + due (“two”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + nove (“nine”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + quattro (“four”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + sei (“six”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + sette (“seven”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + tre (“three”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + otto (“eight”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + uno (“one”).
From Latin obtinēre, probably a semi-learned borrowing.

fact.text: From Latin obtinēre, a semi-learned borrowing. The verb entered Italian through scholarly channels rather than as a natural phonetic evolution.

senses.note: Takes object. Semi-learned from Latin.
The singular is the same for both genders: lui/lei è ottimista. Also a noun: an optimist.

etymology: From Latin optimus.

fact.text: From Latin optimus 'best', the superlative of bonus 'good'. English gets optimum, optimal and optimist from the same word.

senses.note: Also works as the superlative of buono (good → best/very good): un ottimo vino.

etymology: From Latin octō.

fact.text: It comes from Latin octo, also behind octopus-style 'oct-' words and October. October was the eighth month of the early Roman year.

senses.note: Takes the elided article: l'otto.

etymology: From Latin octō.

fact.text: It comes from Latin octo, also behind octopus-style 'oct-' words and October. October was the eighth month of the early Roman year.

etymology: From Latin Octōbrem.

fact.text: From Latin octo, 'eight'. October was the eighth month of the early Roman calendar, which began in March.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian. Usually no article: a ottobre = in October.

etymology: From otto (“eight”) + cento (“hundred”).
From Medieval Latin ovālis.
Originated as an incorrect reading of a borrowing from French ouest, from Old English west. Doublet of vespro.

fact.text: It began as a misreading of French ouest, since u and v were once written the same way. The French word itself was borrowed from Old English 'west'.

senses.note: Takes the elided article: l'ovest.

etymology: From ovvio + -mente.

senses.note: Also used on its own as a reply meaning 'of course!'

etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin obvius.

fact.text: From Latin obvius, from ob viam, 'in the way': something obvious is literally lying in your path. English obvious comes from the same Latin word.

senses.note: Ovviamente = obviously. 'È ovvio!' = of course!

etymology: Borrowed from Middle Dutch pack (whence modern Dutch pak), from Old Dutch pac, *pakko, from Frankish *pakkō, from Proto-Germanic *pakkô (“bundle”).

fact.text: Borrowed from Middle Dutch 'pak', from a Germanic word for 'bundle'. That same Germanic root gave English 'pack'.

senses.note: Also 'parcel'. Colloquially 'fare/tirare un pacco' = to swindle someone or stand them up.

etymology: From Latin pācem (“peace”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-.

fact.text: Latin pax comes from a root meaning 'to fasten': peace was an agreement that bound two sides together. The same root gave English pact.

senses.note: lasciare in pace = to leave alone: Lasciami in pace! = Leave me alone!

etymology: From earlier *patella, from Latin patella, diminutive of patera or patina.

fact.text: From Latin patella, 'small dish'. English uses the same Latin word for the kneecap, the patella, because of its shallow, dish-like shape.

senses.note: Idiom: dalla padella nella brace = out of the frying pan into the fire.

etymology: Derived from Old Italian patre, from Latin patrem, from Proto-Italic *patēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr.

fact.text: A true cousin of English father: both go back to Proto-Indo-European *ph2ter. Germanic languages turned the p into f (Grimm's law), which is why Latin pater and English father differ.

senses.note: No article with a singular possessive: mio padre, not il mio padre.

etymology: From earlier *patrone, from Latin patronus. Doublet of patron. Compare Sicilian patruni.

fact.text: From Latin patronus, which comes from pater (father). English patron comes from the same word, so a padrone was originally a father-like protector.

senses.note: Also boss or employer. Padrone di casa = landlord or host. Feminine: padrona.

etymology: From paese + -aggio, based on French paysage. Compare also Spanish paisaje, Portuguese paisagem, Piedmontese paisagi, Sicilian pajisaggiu.

fact.text: From paese ('country') + -aggio (borrowed from French -age). Related to English 'landscape' via Romance languages; compare Spanish paisaje and French paysage.

senses.note: A view or natural scenery; also a landscape painting or style.

etymology: From Late Latin pāgēnsis (“inhabitant of a district”), from Latin pāgus (“village; district”). Compare Catalan, Portuguese, and Spanish país; French pays; Venetan pajès; Friulian paîs; Istriot and Piedmontese pais; Sicilian pajisi.

fact.text: From Latin pāgus, 'village, district'. The same root gave 'pagan', originally a country dweller, and, through French pays and paysan, 'peasant'.

senses.note: il mio paese = my country (or my home town, depending on context).
Typical small Italian town; a city is una città.

etymology: Deverbal from pagare (“to pay”) + -a.

senses.note: Usually refers to wages or salary in modern usage.

etymology: From pagare + -mento.

fact.text: Comes from pagare, from Latin pacare 'to pacify', because paying a creditor calmed them down. English 'pay' has the same origin.

etymology: From earlier *pacare, inherited from Latin pacāre, from pax, pacis (“peace”). Doublet of pacare, a borrowing.

fact.text: It comes from Latin pacare, meaning to pacify, from pax (peace). Paying a creditor was a way to keep the peace. English pay comes from the same source through French.

senses.note: No 'per' needed: pagare il conto = to pay for the bill.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pāgina. Doublet of pania.

senses.note: 'A pagina 10' = on page 10. A web page is 'pagina web'.

etymology: Back-formation as a masculine noun from the plural paia, from Latin paria (“even, equal”, neuter plural of pār). Cognate with Sicilian paru.

fact.text: The singular was formed from the plural, not the other way round. Plural 'paia' comes from Latin paria, 'equal things', and the masculine singular was created from it later. That is why the plural looks feminine.

senses.note: Irregular plural is feminine: un paio → due paia. 'Un paio di' can also mean 'a couple of'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pāla (“shovel, spade”).

fact.text: Direct inheritance from Latin pāla (shovel, spade). The same root appears in French pelle and other Romance languages.

etymology: Inherited from Latin palātium (“palace, large residence”), from Palātium (“Palatine”), one of the seven hills of Rome. Cognate to English palace, French palais, Spanish palacio, Portuguese paço, palácio, see more at palātium.

fact.text: Named after the Palatine Hill in Rome, where the emperors built their homes. English 'palace' comes from the same hill.

senses.note: An everyday word for any large apartment or office building.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin palaestra, from Ancient Greek παλαίστρα (palaístra, “wrestling school”).

fact.text: It goes back to Ancient Greek palaístra, a 'wrestling school', from pálē, meaning wrestling. Today's gym is named after a place where ancient Greeks trained to wrestle.

senses.note: Andare in palestra = to go to the gym.

etymology:
From Medieval Latin balla, palla, bala, from Frankish *ballu, from Proto-Germanic *balluz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoln- (“bubble”), from *bʰel- (“to blow, swell, inflate”).
Alternatively, via Lombardic *palla, from Proto-Germanic *ballô, from the same ultimate origin. Compare Sicilian baḍḍa.

fact.text: 'Che palle!' (literally 'what balls!') is a very common, mildly vulgar way to say 'what a drag!'. Something boring is 'una palla'. The word is Germanic, like English 'ball'.

senses.note: In the plural it is also vulgar slang for testicles.

etymology: Calque of English basketball, from palla + canestro.

fact.text: A word-for-word copy of English 'basketball': palla (ball) + canestro (basket). Italians also simply borrow the English word and say 'il basket'.

senses.note: Colloquially often just 'il basket'. No plural.

etymology:
Univerbation of palla + a + volo, literally “ball on flight”.
The pronunciation with -vv-, though usually proscribed, is very common, as it respects the syntactic gemination of a.

fact.text: A fusion of palla a volo, literally 'ball in flight'. That's why many Italians say 'pallavvolo' with a double v.

senses.note: Invariable: la pallavolo. Giocare a pallavolo = to play volleyball.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin pallidus, derived from palleō (“to be pale”).

senses.note: Also figurative: un pallido ricordo = a faint memory.

etymology: From pancia (“belly”) + -etta.

fact.text: Pancetta and bacon are not the same: pancetta is cured pork belly that is air-dried, not smoked, and eaten in thin slices. English bacon often includes the loin.

senses.note: In Italian, pancetta is specifically cured pork belly, not smoked bacon.

etymology: From Latin panticem.

fact.text: From Latin pantex, 'belly'. The same Latin word reached English through Old French and became 'paunch'.

senses.note: Everyday word for tummy. Mal di pancia = stomach ache. Plural pance.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pānem, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to feed, to graze”).

fact.text: Latin panis is hidden in English companion: from Latin com- 'with' + panis, someone you share bread with. Italian compagno has the same origin.

senses.note: Usually uncountable: compro il pane. The plural pani means loaves or kinds of bread.

etymology: From pane + -eria.

senses.note: A shop selling bread. The baker is il panettiere / la panettiera.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin panicus, from Ancient Greek πανικός (panikós, “pertaining to Pan”), from Πάν (Pán, “Pan”).
From pane (“bread”) + -ino (“small”).

fact.text: Literally 'little bread' (pane + -ino). English 'panini' is the Italian plural, so in Italy one sandwich is un panino, and 'paninis' sounds odd.

senses.note: It's a filled roll and doesn't need to be grilled. A sliced-bread sandwich is a tramezzino.

etymology: From panno, because the cream covers milk like a cloth, or from Latin patina (> *patna), because the cream forms a patina on the surface of milk. If the latter, a doublet of patina.

fact.text: Named after Pantalone, the old Venetian merchant of the commedia dell'arte who wore long, tight breeches. His name came from Saint Pantaleone. It reached Italian again by way of French pantalon.

senses.note: Usually plural: i pantaloni. The singular il pantalone is also used, mostly in shops.

fact.text: Named after Pantalone, the old Venetian merchant of the commedia dell'arte, who wore long tight trousers. English pantaloons, and so pants, come from the same character.

senses.note: Always plural, like in English: i pantaloni. The singular pantalone is rare.

etymology: From Latin papa, from Ancient Greek πάππας (páppas).

fact.text: Watch the accent: papa (stress on the first syllable) is the Pope, and papà is dad. Both go back to the same baby-talk word that imitates a baby's lips.

senses.note: Often capitalised: il Papa. Stress on the first syllable; papà means dad.

etymology: Named after Coriolano Paparazzo, the name of a character in Federico Fellini's film La dolce vita. By surface analysis, Paparo + -azzo.

fact.text: Named after Coriolano Paparazzo, a character in Federico Fellini's 1960 film La dolce vita. The character's name became synonymous with celebrity photographers.

senses.note: Singular: paparazzo

etymology: From various North Italian dialects.

senses.note: Stress on the last syllable. The plural is the same: i papà. Babbo is the Tuscan word.

etymology: From Latin paradīsus, from Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos).

fact.text: Comes through Greek parádeisos from an Old Iranian word for a walled garden or enclosed park. So paradise was originally a royal garden.

senses.note: Also means paradise. Il cielo can mean heaven too, but it is mainly 'sky'.

etymology: Deverbal from parcheggiare + -o.

senses.note: Also the act of parking, or a single parking space. Plural: i parcheggi.

etymology: From Old French parc. First attested in the 14th c.

senses.note: As an adjective, parco means 'frugal, sparing'.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin pariculus, diminutive of Latin pār. Doublet of pareglio and pariglio, both borrowed via Old French pareil. Compare Spanish parejo.

fact.text: From Late Latin pariculus, a diminutive of pār (equal). English 'parity' and Italian pareggio (tie, draw) share the same Latin root.

senses.note: Can modify nouns (parecchia gente = quite a few people) or stand alone.

etymology: From Latin parentem.

fact.text: False friend: it does not mean 'parent'. It means any relative, such as an aunt or a cousin. Your mum and dad are i genitori.

senses.note: Il/la parente. Parents are i genitori.

etymology: From Late Latin parenthesis, from Ancient Greek πᾰρένθεσῐς (părénthesĭs).

fact.text: From Greek parenthesis (a placing in beside), from para- (beside) + en- (in) + thesis (placing). The English and Italian words are cognates, both borrowed directly from the Greek grammatical term.

senses.note: Invariable noun (same in singular and plural).

etymology: Inherited from Latin pārēre, from Proto-Italic *pāzēō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-s- (“watch, see”), s-present of *peh₂- (“protect”).

fact.text: From the same Latin root parere as English 'appear'. Its past participle parso suggests an older sense of 'to come into sight'.

senses.note: A mio parere = in my opinion. Chiedere un parere = to ask for an opinion or advice.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pārēre, from Proto-Italic *pāzēō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-s- (“watch, see”), s-present of *peh₂- (“protect”).

fact.text: From the same Latin root parere as English 'appear'. Its past participle parso suggests an older sense of 'to come into sight'.

senses.note: Irregular verb; often impersonal with dative (mi pare = it seems to me)

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin parētem, from Latin parietem m.

fact.text: From Latin paries 'wall'. English kept it in anatomy: the parietal bones form the side walls of your skull.

senses.note: Parete is an inside wall or wall surface; muro is a structural or outdoor wall.

etymology: From parlare (“to speak”) + -mento (verbal action suffix).

fact.text: From parlare (to speak) + -mento (verbal action suffix). Cognate with English parlement via Norman French.

senses.note: The institution, its members, or meeting place

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin parabolāre.

fact.text: From Late Latin parabolare, from parabola, 'speech' or 'parable'. Through French parler, it is related to English parliament and parlour, and also to parable.

senses.note: parlare a/con qualcuno = to talk to/with someone. parlare di = to talk about.

etymology: From Parma + -igiano. Compare Sicilian parmisanu and parmicianu.

fact.text: From the Italian place name Parma + the suffix -igiano (meaning 'native of' or 'from'). The word entered English as 'Parmesan' and is now primarily used for the cheese, though it originally denoted a person from Parma.

senses.note: Often used as uncountable; countable plural exists but uncommon for cheese.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *paraula, from Late Latin paravola, from Latin parabola (“comparison; later, speech”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of parabola, a borrowing. Compare with French parole, Catalan paraula, Sicilian palora and parola, Spanish palabra.

fact.text: Comes from Latin parabola, used for the Gospel parables, so it shares a root with English parable. Its French cousin parole gave English parole, release on one's word.

senses.note: Also 'one's word' as a promise: ti do la mia parola.

etymology: Inherited from Latin partem, from Proto-Italic *partim.

senses.note: Feminine. d'altra parte = on the other hand; da parte = aside.

etymology: From Latin participāre.

fact.text: It can also mean to announce formally. Italian wedding announcements are called partecipazioni, because they share the news with you.

senses.note: Takes a: partecipare a una riunione = to take part in a meeting.

etymology: From partire + -enza.

senses.note: Shown as Partenze on station and airport boards. Opposite: arrivo.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin particulāris.

fact.text: It never means fussy or picky, as in 'a particular eater'. For that, Italians say schizzinoso. Una persona particolare is an unusual or quirky person.

senses.note: in particolare = in particular. Also means unusual or special. As a noun, il particolare = detail.

etymology: From particolare + -mente.
Inherited from Latin partīre (“to divide”), from pars (“part”).

fact.text: From Latin partire, 'to divide', from pars (part). Leaving was originally separating yourself from others, like English 'to part' and 'parting'.

senses.note: Takes essere: sono partito. a partire da domani = starting tomorrow.

etymology: From partito, past participle of partire, from Latin partīre. Compare the similar development of French partie (“part; party, game”, etc.) from Old French partie (“party, gathering, group”, literally “part, section, division”), from Medieval Latin partīta.

fact.text: In Italy 'partita IVA' is your VAT number. Having one means you're self-employed, so 'sono una partita IVA' means 'I'm a freelancer'.

senses.note: Also a game of cards or chess. Not the match you strike to make fire, which is fiammifero.

etymology: partire + -ito

fact.text: From partire (to depart/divide)—a political party is a group that departs from or divides from others.

etymology: Borrowed from English partner.

fact.text: English loanword: partner comes from Old French parcener (joint heir), ultimately from Latin partitio (portion). Both English and Italian adopted the same word from French.

senses.note: Invariable in Italian; same form for singular and plural

etymology: From pascolo + -are.

senses.note: Transitive (pascolare le pecore = to graze the sheep) or intransitive (le mucche pascolano).

etymology: Inherited from Latin pāscuum.

fact.text: Latin pascuum comes from pascere, 'to feed (animals)'. That verb is also the root of English pasture and pastor, which first meant a shepherd.

senses.note: Also 'grazing': portare al pascolo = to take out to graze.

fact.text: A well-known proverb: 'Natale con i tuoi, Pasqua con chi vuoi', meaning Christmas with your family, Easter with whoever you like. Easter Monday (Pasquetta) is for picnics.

senses.note: Capitalised: Pasqua. Buona Pasqua! = Happy Easter! Pasquetta = Easter Monday.

etymology: From passare + -aggio, or from Old French passage.

fact.text: 'Mi dai un passaggio?' is the everyday Italian way to ask 'Can you give me a lift?', so the word covers car rides as well as corridors.

senses.note: Dare un passaggio a qualcuno = to give someone a lift.

etymology: Verb-object compound, composed of passa (“to pass”) + porto (“port”).

fact.text: A compound of passa 'pass' + porto 'port': the document that lets you pass through a port. English passport has the same origin.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *passāre, derived from Latin passus (“step”, noun).

fact.text: From Latin passus, 'a step'. The Roman mile was mille passuum, 'a thousand paces', and passus also gave English 'pace'.

senses.note: Takes essere when intransitive: il tempo è passato. Passato also means 'past'.
Only for time: passare le vacanze. For money, use spendere.

etymology: From passare (“to pass; to rub”).

fact.text: From passare: the tomatoes are passed through a sieve. The same noun means a quick once-over, as in dare una passata, to give something a quick wipe.

senses.note: Raw strained tomatoes, the base for sauces, not a finished sauce. Also 'a quick wipe or once-over'.

etymology: From passare.

senses.note: In passato = in the past. Also a past tense (passato prossimo) and a purée (passato di pomodoro).

etymology: From passo + -eggiare. Cognate with Sicilian passijari.

fact.text: Built from passo, 'step'. The related noun passeggiata is a beloved Italian ritual: a slow evening stroll through town to see people and be seen.

senses.note: A leisurely walk, not walking to get somewhere (that is camminare).

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of passeggiare (“to walk, stroll”). Cognate with Sicilian passijata.

fact.text: In many Italian towns, 'la passeggiata' is an evening ritual. People dress up and stroll slowly along the main street or piazza to see and be seen.

senses.note: Fare una passeggiata = to go for a walk. Colloquially also 'a piece of cake'.
A small kitchen sieve. In much of Italy, colino is the more common word.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin passiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin patior, 'to suffer', so passion first meant suffering, as in the Passion of Christ. The same verb gives English patient: someone who suffers or endures.

senses.note: Avere la passione per = to be passionate about. La Passione = the Passion of Christ.

etymology: From Latin passus (“a step”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin passus 'step', which also gave English 'pace'. The Roman mile was mille passus, 1,000 paces, and that is where 'mile' comes from.

senses.note: tenere il passo = to keep pace, keep up; passo also = mountain pass.
