Inherited from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá).

fact.text: From Greek 'pastá', from a verb meaning 'to sprinkle'. Through Late Latin 'pasta', the same word gave English 'paste' and 'pastry'.

senses.note: Also dough, paste or a pastry: 'una pasta' = a small cake or pastry.

etymology: From pasticcio + -eria.
Inherited from Latin pāstus (“pasture, food”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin pastus, 'pasture, food'. The same root is behind English 'pasture' and the old word 'repast', meaning a meal.

senses.note: Don't confuse with pasta. 'Lontano dai pasti' = between meals (on medicine labels).

etymology: Borrowed from Spanish patata.

fact.text: Comes from Spanish patata, from Taíno batata, which first meant the sweet potato. English 'potato' comes from the same Caribbean word.

senses.note: Also vulgar slang for female genitals. 'Patata bollente' = hot potato.

etymology: From patata + -ina.

senses.note: British: crisps; American: French fries (smaller, for dipping)

etymology: From Latin patentem.

fact.text: Not a patent (that's brevetto). From Latin patens, 'open': royal 'letters patent' were open documents granting rights, and English 'patent' comes from the same word.

senses.note: prendere la patente = to get your driver's license.

etymology: From Latin patria (“fatherland”).

fact.text: Short for Latin terra patria, 'the land of the fathers', from patrius, 'paternal'. English 'patriot' and 'patriotic' come from the same root.

senses.note: Carries emotional or patriotic weight. For a neutral 'country', use paese.

etymology: From Late Latin patrīneus, from pater (“father”) + -īneus (“relative suffix”). Compare Medieval Latin patrīnus (“godfather”); alternatively from Late Latin patrignus, after the model of prīvignus (“stepson”).

fact.text: Built from Latin pater (father) + a relative suffix, similar to how 'padrino' (godfather) was formed. The 'step-' relationship was codified in Late Latin as patrignus.

etymology: From Latin pactum from pacisci (“to make an accordance”).

fact.text: From Latin pactum, from pacīscī (to negotiate/agree). Related to pax (peace) through the same Proto-Indo-European root *peh₂k- (to fix, settle).

senses.note: An agreement or accord; from Latin pactum.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin pavor, with the ending replaced by -ura.
Compare French peur.

senses.note: Avere paura (di) = to be afraid (of). Ho paura = I'm scared.

etymology: From Latin pausa.

senses.note: pausa pranzo = lunch break; fare una pausa = to take a break

etymology: Borrowed from Latin pavīmentum. Doublet of Old Italian palmiento, inherited.

fact.text: False friend: it does not mean 'pavement'. It is the floor inside a room. A pavement or sidewalk is 'marciapiede'.

senses.note: The surface you walk on indoors. A storey of a building is 'piano'.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin patientem, present active participle of patior (“to suffer”).

fact.text: From Latin patiens, 'suffering', from patior 'to suffer'. So a patient is literally 'one who suffers'. The same root gives English passion.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: il/la paziente. As an adjective it also means patient (calm).

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin patientia, derived from patiēns, present active participle of patior (“to suffer”).

fact.text: From Latin patientia, from patior 'to suffer'. The same root gives English 'patient': the hospital patient was originally 'one who suffers'.

senses.note: avere pazienza = to be patient

etymology: From pazzo (“crazy”) + -esco.

fact.text: From pazzo (crazy) plus the suffix -esco, which creates adjectives meaning resembling or having the quality of something.

etymology:
Uncertain. Perhaps a Lombardic or Carolingian era borrowing from Old High German barrezzen (“to hate”) or maybe from French page (“page, serving boy”), probably via Neapolitan pazzo (compare French adage “être effronté comme un page”).
Alternatively from Latin patiēns (“suffering”). Compare Sicilian pacciu.

fact.text: Origin uncertain: possibly from Old High German barrezzen (to hate), French page (serving boy), or Latin patiens (suffering). Multiple plausible sources remain unresolved.

senses.note: Andare pazzo per = to be crazy about. Also used as a noun: un pazzo = a madman.

etymology:
Uncertain. Perhaps a Lombardic or Carolingian era borrowing from Old High German barrezzen (“to hate”) or maybe from French page (“page, serving boy”), probably via Neapolitan pazzo (compare French adage “être effronté comme un page”).
Alternatively from Latin patiēns (“suffering”). Compare Sicilian pacciu.

fact.text: Origin uncertain: possibly from Old High German barrezzen (to hate), French page (serving boy), or Latin patiens (suffering). Multiple plausible sources remain unresolved.

etymology: Inherited from Latin peccātum (“sin”).

fact.text: From Latin peccatum, 'sin'. A small sin in Spanish is a pecadillo, which English borrowed as peccadillo: a minor fault.

senses.note: Che peccato! = What a shame! Sarebbe un peccato = It would be a pity.

etymology: From pedo- + -iatra.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: il/la pediatra. Plurals: i pediatri, le pediatre.

etymology: From pedone + -ale.

senses.note: Zona pedonale = pedestrian zone; strisce pedonali = zebra crossing. A pedestrian person is il pedone.

etymology: From Latin peius, from peior, peiōris.

fact.text: Comes from Latin peior, 'worse', which also gives English 'pejorative', a word that makes something sound worse.

senses.note: Adverb, the comparative of 'male'. The adjective is usually 'peggiore'.

etymology: From Late Latin peiōrāre (“worsen”), from Latin peiōrem (“worsen”). By surface analysis, peggiore + -are.

fact.text: Built on Latin peior, 'worse', which also gave English 'pejorative', a word that makes something sound worse.

senses.note: Takes avere with an object, essere when something gets worse by itself: 'è peggiorato'.

etymology: From Latin peiōrem, from Proto-Indo-European *ped-yōs (“to the ground, downward”).

fact.text: From Latin peior, 'worse', which also gave English 'pejorative', meaning a word that makes something sound worse.

senses.note: Il/la peggiore = the worst. Don't confuse it with the adverb peggio (worse): sto peggio.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pellis, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to cover, wrap; skin, hide; cloth”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin pellis, 'skin, hide'. It shares an ancient root with Old English fell, 'animal hide', and is probably related to English pelt.

senses.note: Also means leather: una giacca di pelle (a leather jacket).

etymology: From Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ).

fact.text: From Latin poena, from Greek poinē 'blood money, penalty'. The same root gives English pain, penalty, punish and penance.

senses.note: Pena di morte = death penalty. Scontare una pena = to serve a sentence.
Distress or pity, not physical pain (dolore). Vale la pena = it's worth it. Che pena! = how sad!

etymology: From pendere.

fact.text: Comes from pendere (to hang), the same Latin root as English pendant and pendulum. A slope seems to hang down the hillside.

senses.note: In pendio = sloping. Masculine, stressed on the i: pen-DI-o.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pēnis.
From Latin penna and pinna, from Proto-Italic *petnā, from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ ~ pth₂én- (“feather, wing”).

fact.text: People once wrote with feather quills, which is why penna means both 'feather' and 'pen'. Penne pasta is named after the slanted cut of a quill tip, and English 'pen' comes from the same Latin word.

senses.note: Also means 'feather'. A ballpoint pen is una penna a sfera.
English loanword; no Italian definition provided in source.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pēnsāre (“weigh carefully”), frequentative of pendere. Doublet of pesare.

fact.text: From Latin pensare, 'to weigh carefully', so thinking is weighing things up. Its doublet is pesare (to weigh), and via French penser it also gave English 'pensive'.

senses.note: pensare a = to think about; pensare di + infinitive = to plan to; penso di sì = I think so.

etymology: Borrowed from Provençal pensier, from Latin pēnsāre. Compare Sicilian pinzeri.

fact.text: It goes back to Latin pensare, 'to weigh', so thinking was pictured as weighing things up. English 'pensive' comes from the same root.

senses.note: Stare in pensiero = to be worried. Verb: pensare.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin pēnsiōnem. Doublet of pigione, which was inherited.

fact.text: From Latin pensio, 'payment', from pendere, 'to weigh out', because money was once weighed. Its inherited twin word, pigione, means rent.

senses.note: Andare in pensione = to retire. Also a small guesthouse. Mezza pensione = half board.

etymology: From a Vulgar Latin *pinta, alternative form of Latin picta (“painted [pot]”), feminine perfect passive participle of pingō (“to decorate; to paint”), from the custom of decorating crocks and pots by painting them.

fact.text: Probably from Vulgar Latin *pinta, 'painted (pot)', from pingere 'to paint', after the custom of decorating cooking crocks and pots with paint.

senses.note: Cooking pot or saucepan. A plant pot is 'un vaso'.

etymology: From Latin piper, from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi, “pepper”), via Middle Persian from an Indo-Aryan source.

fact.text: Careful: peperoni in Italian means bell peppers, not salami. If you order a pizza ai peperoni in Italy, you get peppers. Spicy salami is salame piccante.

senses.note: The spice only. Bell pepper = peperone; chili = peperoncino.

etymology: From Latin piper (“pepper”).

fact.text: From Sanskrit pippali (long pepper) via Latin piper. The -one suffix is a standard Italian diminutive/augmentative marker, making it literally a larger pepper-type plant.

etymology: From Latin per, taking many roles from Latin pro.

senses.note: Very versatile: also 'through', 'by', 'per'. Partire per Roma = to leave for Rome.
Followed by an infinitive: per portare = (in order) to bring.
Literally 'for (a) favour'. Per piacere and per cortesia mean the same.
After prepositions use the stressed pronouns: me, te, lui, lei, noi, voi, loro.
Usually used with non: non mi piace per niente. It can also mean 'for nothing'.

etymology: Literally, “for first thing”.

senses.note: Alternatives: 'prima di tutto', 'innanzitutto'.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *pira, from the plural of Latin pirum, reanalyzed as a feminine singular.

fact.text: Latin pirum (pear) was neuter, and its plural 'pira' was later taken for a feminine singular. That's why the fruit is feminine but the tree, il pero, is masculine.

senses.note: The tree is il pero. In slang, 'farsi una pera' = to shoot up drugs.

fact.text: From Latin per centum (by the hundred), the source of English percent. Both languages adopted this phrase to express ratios.

etymology: Univerbation of per (“for”) + che (“which”), probably inherited from Vulgar Latin. Compare Neapolitan pecché, Sicilian pirchì, and further Romance parallels such as Sardinian pro chite, French pourquoi, Spanish porque/por qué, Portuguese porque/por que.

fact.text: Italian uses one word for both 'why' and 'because', so a child's 'Why? Just because!' becomes 'Perché? Perché sì!' Literally 'for what', from per + che.

senses.note: Perché? = Why? Written with an acute accent: é.
Same word as 'why': Perché piove = because it's raining.

etymology: Univerbation of per (“for”) + che (“which”), probably inherited from Vulgar Latin. Compare Neapolitan pecché, Sicilian pirchì, and further Romance parallels such as Sardinian pro chite, French pourquoi, Spanish porque/por qué, Portuguese porque/por que.

fact.text: Italian uses one word for both 'why' and 'because', so a child's 'Why? Just because!' becomes 'Perché? Perché sì!' Literally 'for what', from per + che.

senses.note: Also 'so that' when followed by the subjunctive.
One word asks and answers: Perché? – Perché sì!

etymology: Univerbation of per (“for”) + che (“which”), probably inherited from Vulgar Latin. Compare Neapolitan pecché, Sicilian pirchì, and further Romance parallels such as Sardinian pro chite, French pourquoi, Spanish porque/por qué, Portuguese porque/por que.

senses.note: 'Perché' also means 'because'. Note the acute accent: é.

etymology: Univerbation of per + ciò.

senses.note: Means 'so' or 'that's why'. Also classed as an adverb. Literally per + ciò = 'for this'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin percursus.

senses.note: Also a figurative path: percorso di studi = course of study.

etymology: Inherited from Latin perdere. The variant past participle perso was created by analogy with preso, etc.

senses.note: Also 'to miss' (perdere il treno) and 'to waste' (time). Past participle: perso or perduto.

etymology: From Latin perdita, the feminine of perditus. Compare French perte, Portuguese perda, and Spanish pérdida.

senses.note: Can also mean leak or leakage.

etymology: From Late Latin perdōnāre.

fact.text: From Late Latin perdōnāre (per- + dōnāre 'to give, donate'). Attested 350–500 CE. Possibly influenced Germanic languages as *fragebaną, or vice versa.

senses.note: Transitive; also used intransitively with 'a' (perdonare a qualcuno).

etymology: Deverbal from perdonare (“to forgive”) + -o.

senses.note: Past participle of perdere. Perso is more common in everyday speech; perduto sounds more emphatic or literary.

etymology: From Latin perfectus.

fact.text: From Latin perfectus, from per- 'thoroughly' + facere 'to make', so it first meant 'completely made, finished' rather than flawless.

senses.note: 'Perfetto!' alone is an everyday 'Great!' or 'Fine!'

etymology: Univerbation of per + fino.

fact.text: Literally 'per fino' (to the end), a univerbation showing how compound words form over time. Related to fino (fine/thin/far).

senses.note: univerbation of per + fino (to + far)

etymology: Borrowed from Latin perīculum. Doublet of the archaic inherited periglio.

fact.text: It comes from Latin periculum, which also gave English 'peril' (through French). Think 'perilous' and pericoloso, 'dangerous', is easy to remember.

senses.note: In pericolo = in danger. Pericoloso = dangerous.

etymology: Probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin periculōsus. By surface analysis, pericolo + -oso.
From peri- + feria.

fact.text: Not quite 'suburbs': in Italy, la periferia often means poorer high-rise districts on the edge of a city, while wealthier people tend to live in the centre.

senses.note: Often suggests working-class or run-down districts rather than leafy suburbs.

etymology: From Latin periodus, from Ancient Greek περίοδος (períodos, “circuit, period of time, path around”), from περι- (peri-, “around”) + ὁδός (hodós, “way”).

fact.text: From Greek períodos, made of peri- (around) and hodós (way, path). A period was literally a 'way around', a full circuit that comes back to where it began.

senses.note: A span of time. A full stop is punto, and a menstrual period is usually il ciclo.

fact.text: Italians say 'Permesso?' (literally 'permission?') when stepping into someone's home or office, and when squeezing past people in a crowd.

senses.note: Also a permit: permesso di soggiorno = residence permit.

etymology: From Latin permittere.
Univerbation of per + sino.

fact.text: Formed from per + sino, 'up to'. So 'persino i libri' is literally 'right up to the books', meaning it went as far as that.

senses.note: Perfino is a common synonym. Persino lui = even him.

etymology: From Latin persōna (“person”), of Etruscan origin.

fact.text: Latin persona first meant the mask an actor wore on stage. It probably comes from Etruscan phersu, a masked figure. English 'persona' kept the mask idea.

senses.note: Always feminine, even when it refers to a man. Plural persone, though 'people' is usually gente.

etymology:
Borrowed from French personnage; persona + -aggio.
Compare Piedmontese përsonagi.

fact.text: From French personnage (from personne + -age suffix). A 'character' is literally a distinct 'person-age' or personified role. The unusual -aggio suffix (not -agge) marks it as borrowed from Romance languages.

senses.note: In narrative, drama, or film.

etymology: From Latin persōnālis.

senses.note: Can also mean 'personal' or 'private' when used as an adjective.

etymology:
Borrowed from Late Latin persōnālitātem, from Latin persōna (“mask; character”), from Etruscan 𐌘𐌄𐌓𐌔𐌖 (φersu), from Ancient Greek πρόσωπον (prósōpon, “face; mask”).
Cognate with Piedmontese përsonalità.

fact.text: From Late Latin persōnālis, derived from persōna (mask; character). The Etruscan origin phersu originally meant 'mask', echoing how personality is the 'face' you present.

etymology: From personale + -mente.

senses.note: adverb formed from personale + -mente suffix

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin per hoc (“for this reason”, literally “through this”). The original meaning of però was “for this reason, therefore”. Cognate with Spanish pero, Old Franco-Provençal enperoi.

fact.text: From Late Latin per hoc 'through this', which first meant 'therefore'. Over time it flipped to 'however'. Spanish pero shares the same origin.

senses.note: Stress on the final o. Can end a sentence: È caro, però buono.
Can also mean tedious or tiresome: un film pesante, una persona pesante.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pēnsāre (“weigh, hang”), whence also the doublet pensare (“to think”). Compare French peser.

fact.text: Both pesare and pensare (to think) come from Latin pensare, 'to weigh'. Thinking meant weighing things up. English 'pensive' comes from the same root.

senses.note: Quanto pesi? = How much do you weigh? Also 'to weigh on': mi pesa = it's a burden to me.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *pessica (cf. Medieval Latin pesca), from Late Latin persica, from Latin persicum (“peach”, literally “fruit from Persia”). Compare French pêche.

fact.text: From Latin persicum, meaning 'fruit from Persia'. Ancient Romans called peaches 'Persian apples' because they imported them from the East via Persia.

senses.note: Also refers to the color (pale orange); from Latin persicum meaning 'Persian fruit'

etymology: From Latin piscārī.

fact.text: The noun pesca means both 'fishing' and 'peach'. They are different words: the fruit comes from Latin persica, meaning the Persian fruit.

senses.note: andare a pescare = to go fishing. Colloquially also 'to dig out, find'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin piscem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peysk-.

fact.text: An April Fool's prank in Italy is a 'pesce d'aprile'. Children traditionally try to stick paper fish on people's backs without them noticing.

senses.note: Pesce is both the live animal and the fish you eat. Pescare = to fish.

etymology: From pesce + -eria.

senses.note: Fishmonger's shop

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *pēsum, from Latin pēnsum.

fact.text: Formed from the verb pesare 'to weigh', from Latin pensare. The Spanish currency peso is a relative: it was first a coin of a fixed weight of silver.

senses.note: Prendere peso = to put on weight. Pesi = weights at the gym.
Singular is pessimista for both genders; also a noun: un/una pessimista = a pessimist.

etymology: From Latin pessimus.

fact.text: Latin pessimus meant 'worst', the superlative of malus 'bad'. English 'pessimist' comes from the same word: someone who always expects the worst.

senses.note: Superlative of cattivo, so don't say 'molto pessimo'. Opposite: ottimo.

etymology: From Latin pistus (“crushed, pounded”), from Latin pīnsō (“to pound, beat, crush”), whose frequentative also gave Italian pestare (“to pound”).

fact.text: From Latin pistus ('crushed, pounded'), the past participle of pīnsō. The name describes how basil, garlic, and pine nuts are crushed together.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pectinem.

fact.text: It comes from Latin pecten (comb). Scallops are named Pecten in biology because their ridged shells look like a comb.

senses.note: Pettinare = to comb. Also the name of some scallops.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pectus, from Proto-Italic *pektos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peg- (“breast”). Compare Catalan pit, Portuguese peito, Romanian piept, Spanish pecho.

fact.text: From Latin pectus. Cognate with Spanish pecho, Portuguese peito, and Catalan pit; all descended from Proto-Italic *pektos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peg- 'breast'.

senses.note: anatomical; also applied to poultry breast

etymology: Variant of pezza.

fact.text: A variant of pezza, from Medieval Latin pettia, probably a Gaulish word. The same root reached English through French pièce, giving us 'piece'.

senses.note: Un pezzo di pane = a piece of bread; pezzo grosso = big shot.

fact.text: Named after Fön, an early German hairdryer trademark, which took its name from the Föhn, a warm, dry wind that blows down the Alps.

senses.note: Also spelled fon. Invariable: i phon. More formal synonym: asciugacapelli.

etymology: Inherited from Latin placēre. Compare Romanian plăcea, French plaire, Occitan plaser.

fact.text: From Latin placere, 'to please', which also gave English please, pleasure and placid. On its own, Piacere! means 'Nice to meet you'.

senses.note: Mi piace la pizza = I like pizza (literally, pizza pleases me). Takes essere: mi è piaciuto.
Masculine noun: il piacere. Piacere! = Nice to meet you. Piacere mio = My pleasure.

etymology: From piace(re) (“to be liked, to please”) + -evole.

senses.note: The same for masculine and feminine; the plural is piacevoli.

etymology: Derived from Late Latin planēta.
Inherited from Latin plangō, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂k-. Compare Spanish plañir, Catalan plànyer, Romanian plânge, French plaindre.

fact.text: From Latin plangere, to beat one's breast in mourning. Through French plaindre, the same root gave English 'complain', 'plaintive' and 'plangent'.

senses.note: Irregular: piansi, pianto. For 'to cry out, shout', use gridare.

etymology: Inherited from Latin plānus. Compare Sicilian chianu.

fact.text: From Latin planus, 'flat, smooth'. English piano is short for pianoforte, 'soft-loud', because unlike the harpsichord it could play both quietly and loudly.

senses.note: Also 'softly, quietly'. Piano piano = little by little.

etymology: Inherited from Latin plānum, derived from plānus.

fact.text: From Latin planus, 'flat, smooth'. English piano is short for pianoforte, 'soft-loud', because unlike the harpsichord it could play both quietly and loudly.

senses.note: 'Piano terra' is the ground floor. 'Primo piano' is the first floor above it.
'Quali sono i tuoi piani?' means 'What are your plans?'

etymology: From piano + forte.

fact.text: It literally means 'soft-loud', because unlike the harpsichord it could play both softly and loudly. English piano is a shortened form of this word.

senses.note: In everyday speech Italians often just say il piano. To play the piano: suonare il pianoforte.

etymology: From Latin planta, from Proto-Italic *plāntā, from Proto-Indo-European *pléh₂-n̥t-eh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”).

fact.text: Latin planta originally meant the sole of the foot. Italian keeps that sense (pianta del piede), and so does English plantar, as in plantar fasciitis.

senses.note: Also means floor plan or city map (pianta della città) and sole of the foot.

etymology: From Latin plantāre. By surface analysis, pianta (“plant”) + -are. Compare Sicilian chiantari.
From Vulgar Latin *plattus, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad, flat”). Doublet of chiatto.

fact.text: From Greek platys, 'broad, flat', through Vulgar Latin plattus. English 'plate' comes from the same root, and so does 'platypus', which means 'flat foot'.

senses.note: Flat as in level: una superficie piatta. Also figurative: dull, flat.
Noun, masculine: il piatto. Also a course: primo piatto, secondo piatto.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *plattus, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad, flat”). Doublet of chiatto.

fact.text: From Greek platys, 'broad, flat', through Vulgar Latin plattus. English 'plate' comes from the same root, and so does 'platypus', which means 'flat foot'.

senses.note: Also a course of a meal: primo piatto (first course). As an adjective, piatto means flat.

etymology: From Latin platea, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa). Doublet of platea. Cognate with Portuguese praça, Spanish plaza, French place, German Platz.

fact.text: From Greek plateia hodos, 'broad way'. The same root gave Spanish plaza, German Platz and French place, which English borrowed as 'place'.

senses.note: The main public square of an Italian town, and the centre of its social life.

etymology: Borrowed from Middle French, whence French piquant.

fact.text: Borrowed from French, the same source as English 'piquant'. Both come from the idea of 'pricking' or stinging the tongue.

senses.note: Formaggio piccante = strong, sharp cheese. It can also mean racy or risqué.

etymology: Onomatopoeic, related to picca, piccare.

senses.note: Picchiare qualcuno = to beat someone up. Il sole picchia = the sun is beating down.

etymology: Borrowed from Neapolitan piccione, from Latin pīpiōnem. Doublet of pippione.

fact.text: From Neapolitan piccione, from Latin pīpiōnem, an onomatopoeia imitating the bird's cooing sound. A doublet of Italian pippione.

etymology:
Uncertain. Possibly from:
* An onomatopoeic root or children's/nursery word *pikk-, *picc-.
* From Vulgar Latin *pikk (“little”), related to *piccāre (“to pierce”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew-, *bu- (“to make a dull, hollow sound”).
* From picca (“point”).
* From Vulgar Latin pittitus (“small, worthless”), which is linked to French petit and English piece.

fact.text: English borrowed the name of the small, high-pitched flute, the piccolo, from Italian flauto piccolo, 'small flute'. Where the Italian word itself comes from is still uncertain.

senses.note: Can also mean 'young': da piccolo = as a child. Feminine: piccola.

etymology: From Latin pedem (“foot”), from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds. Compare Catalan peu, French pied, Piedmontese pé, Latvian pēda, Lithuanian pėdės, Portuguese pé, Sardinian pei, Spanish pie.

fact.text: Latin pedem and English foot both come from the same Proto-Indo-European root, *pōds. The Latin side also gave English pedal and pedestrian.

senses.note: a piedi = on foot; in piedi = standing.

etymology: From earlier *piecare, from Latin plicāre, from Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ- (“to plait, to weave”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin plicare 'to fold', the same root as English pliable, ply and complicate, which literally means 'folded together'.

senses.note: piegare i vestiti = to fold clothes
piegare un ramo = to bend a branch; piegarsi = to bend over or give in

etymology: Inherited from Latin plēnus, from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”). Compare Catalan ple, French plein, Portuguese cheio, Romanian plin, Sardinian prenu, Sicilian chinu, Spanish lleno.

fact.text: At a petrol station, 'il pieno, per favore' means 'fill it up, please'. Fare il pieno = to fill the tank.

senses.note: Pieno di = full of. Sono pieno = I'm full (after eating).

etymology: Inherited from Latin petra, from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, “stone, rock”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek petra, meaning rock. It's the same root as English petrify and petroleum ('rock oil'), and as the name Peter, 'the rock'.

senses.note: pietra preziosa = gemstone; mettere una pietra sopra = to let bygones be bygones.

etymology: From Latin petrōsus or from pietra + -oso. Doublet of petroso.

senses.note: terreno pietroso = stony ground.

etymology: Inherited from Old Italian pietade, pietate, from Latin pietātem (“piety”, “pity”). By surface analysis, pio (“pious”) + -età (“-ity”).

fact.text: Michelangelo's Pietà, the famous marble sculpture in St Peter's Basilica showing Mary cradling the dead Christ, is named after this word, expressing the profound compassion in the scene.

senses.note: compassion or feeling for suffering

etymology: Probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin pigrum. See also peritarsi, which was inherited from a derivative verb pīgritārī.

senses.note: Pigrizia = laziness. Fare il pigro = to laze about.

fact.text: Named after Joseph Pilates, who developed the exercise method in the early 20th century.

senses.note: The exercise method. Invariable noun.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin pilula, pillula.

fact.text: Like English pill, it comes from Latin pilula, 'little ball', a diminutive of pila, 'ball'. So a pill is really just a tiny ball.

senses.note: La pillola also means the contraceptive pill. Figuratively: a little nugget of information.

etymology: From earlier pedota, pedotta, from Byzantine Greek *πηδώτης (*pēdṓtēs, “helmsman”), from Ancient Greek πηδόν (pēdón, “oarblade, oar”). The pil- forms are probably influenced by pileggiare (“to sail, navigate”).

fact.text: English 'pilot' was borrowed from this Italian word. It goes back to a Byzantine Greek word for 'helmsman', from a word for an oar blade. The first pilots steered ships.

senses.note: il pilota for a man, la pilota for a woman. Plural: piloti (m), pilote (f).
Used for racing drivers. An ordinary driver is l'autista or il conducente.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plo(v)ia. Doublet of ploia; piecewise doublet of piova.

senses.note: The verb is piovere: piove = it's raining. Sotto la pioggia = in the rain.

etymology: Inherited from Latin plumbum.

fact.text: Comes from Latin plumbum, 'lead'. That's why lead's chemical symbol is Pb, and why English has 'plumber': Roman water pipes were made of lead.

senses.note: Only the metal. A lead climber is a capocordata. Gli anni di piombo = Italy's violent 1970s.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *plovere, from Classical Latin pluere.

senses.note: Usually impersonal: piove = it's raining. Past: è piovuto or ha piovuto (both are fine).

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *pipa, from Latin pipō (“to pip”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin pipare, 'to chirp or peep', a sound word. English pipe comes from the same root, and it first meant a simple musical pipe that made that kind of sound.

senses.note: Only a tobacco pipe; a water or gas pipe is 'il tubo'.

etymology: Child speak, similar to French pipi.
Borrowed from Latin piscīna.

fact.text: Latin piscina meant 'fishpond', from piscis 'fish'. The Romans also used it for bathing pools, and that meaning won out in Italian.

senses.note: 'Andare in piscina' = to go to the pool. Can also mean a fishpond.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *pisellum, diminutive of Latin pisum, from Ancient Greek πίσον (píson).

senses.note: Careful: also common slang for penis. For the food you usually say 'piselli' (plural).

etymology: Variant of pesta (“footprint”), technical senses influenced by French piste.

fact.text: From the Italian word pesta meaning footprint. The technical uses (racetrack, ski run) were influenced by French piste, which shares the same Latin root via Old Occitan.

senses.note: Can mean physical track, ski run, or racetrack depending on context.
Song or recording track, e.g., on an album or cassette.

etymology: From Latin pistacium (possibly through Latin *pistaculum), from Ancient Greek πιστάκιον (pistákion). Of Iranian origin. See also πιστάκη (pistákē).

fact.text: From Ancient Greek pistákion, ultimately from Iranian. The word traveled from the Persian Empire through Greek into Italian and English — the same word across Mediterranean trade routes.

senses.note: The nut and the tree

etymology: Borrowed from French pistole, from Czech píšťala (“firearm”, literally “tube, pipe”).

fact.text: Probably from Czech píšťala, 'whistle, pipe', which came to mean a firearm and reached Italian via French. The origin is not fully certain.

senses.note: Also a spray gun (pistola a spruzzo). Firearm in general = arma da fuoco.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pictōrem.

fact.text: From Latin pictor 'painter', from pingere 'to paint', the same root as English picture, depict and pigment.

senses.note: Feminine: la pittrice. A house painter is usually un imbianchino.

etymology: From Latin pictūra.

senses.note: A single painting is usually un quadro or un dipinto. Also means paint: pittura fresca = wet paint.

etymology: Univerbation of più + (archaic) tosto (adverb). Compare French plutôt and Catalan més aviat.

fact.text: Built from più + old tosto 'soon', so literally 'more soon', i.e. 'sooner'. French plutôt (plus + tôt) was put together the same way.

senses.note: Also 'instead': piuttosto che = rather than.

etymology:
First attested in 1590, as Neapolitan pizza (Velardiniello, La storia de cient'anne arreto). Likely related to Byzantine Greek πίτα (píta, “cake, pie”) (12th century);
the origin of the Greek word is itself uncertain. Also possibly from Lombardic bizza (also pizza or bizzo (pizzo), which would rather suggest a north-to-south spread of the word. See the English and Greek entries for more detail.

fact.text: In casual speech it can also mean something boring: 'Che pizza!' means 'What a drag!' First recorded in Naples in 1590.

etymology: From pizza + -eria.

senses.note: English also uses 'pizzeria'.

etymology: From pizza + -etta.

fact.text: From pizza plus the diminutive suffix -etta, which Italian adds to nouns to indicate something small or cute—like libro (book) becoming libretto.

senses.note: Appetizer served at parties

etymology: Deverbal from pizzicare + -o.

fact.text: It comes from the verb pizzicare, 'to pinch'. That verb also gave music the term pizzicato, where string players pluck the strings instead of using the bow.

senses.note: Un pizzico di sale = a pinch of salt. Also an insect bite or sting.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin plūs, from Old Latin *plous, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁-, *pelh₁u- (“many”).
The initial autogemination, though lost in standard pronunciation, is still found in most varieties of regional Italian. The gemination occurs predictably before the palatalization of the original liquid -l-, compare doppio, orecchio, etc.

fact.text: Comes from Latin plus, the same word as English 'plus'. In Italian the maths sign + is read as this word: due più due = two plus two.

senses.note: 'Più…, più…' = the more…, the more…; 'non… più' = no longer, not anymore.

etymology: From the adjective plastico (“plastic”), from Latin plasticus (“pertaining to moulding/molding or shaping”).

senses.note: Feminine noun: la plastica. Also short for plastic surgery.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin plūrālis.

senses.note: Also a masculine noun: il plurale (the plural). Singular is singolare.

etymology: From Latin pneumaticus, from Ancient Greek πνευματικός (pneumatikós, “relating to wind or air”), from πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, air, breath, spirit”), from πνέω (pnéō, “to blow, breathe”).

fact.text: From Greek pneuma, meaning 'air' or 'breath', because the tire is filled with air. It shares a root with English pneumatic and pneumonia.

senses.note: Traditionally 'lo pneumatico', but 'il pneumatico' is common too. Also called la gomma informally.

fact.text: Written with an apostrophe, not an accent, because it is a clipped form of poco. The apostrophe marks the missing -co. Writing 'pò' is a classic spelling mistake.

senses.note: Usually in un po': un po' di pane = a bit of bread.

fact.text: In 'un po'' (a bit), the shortened form takes an apostrophe, not an accent, because the end of poco was cut off. Writing it as 'pò' is a classic spelling mistake.

senses.note: Agrees with the noun: poca attenzione, pochi soldi (little money). Plural pochi/poche = few.

etymology: From Latin paucus, from Proto-Italic *paukos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ukos, derived from the root *peh₂w- (“few”, “little”). Compare French peu, Portuguese pouco, Spanish poco.

fact.text: In 'un po'' (a bit), the shortened form takes an apostrophe, not an accent, because the end of poco was cut off. Writing it as 'pò' is a classic spelling mistake.

senses.note: un po' (short for un poco) = a bit. Also an adjective that agrees: poca acqua, pochi soldi.
Agrees with its noun: poco profonda/i/e. "Basso" is also used for shallow water.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English podcast.

fact.text: From English 'podcast,' blending 'iPod' and 'broadcast.' Italian adopted it unchanged as a masculine noun, typical of tech terms entering Romance languages.

senses.note: Masculine; invariable in plural (il podcast, i podcast)

etymology: Borrowed from Latin poesis.

fact.text: Comes through Latin from Greek poiesis, meaning 'making' or 'composition'. To the ancient Greeks, a poet was literally a 'maker'.

senses.note: Una poesia = a poem; la poesia = poetry in general.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin poēta, from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs).

fact.text: From Greek poiētḗs, 'maker', from poiein, 'to make'. To the Greeks, a poet was literally someone who makes things with words.

senses.note: Masculine even though it ends in -a: il poeta, i poeti. A female poet is la poetessa.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *pos, from Classical Latin post. Compare Portuguese pois, Spanish pues, French puis, and Romanian apoi / Romanian poi (archaic păi).

senses.note: Means 'then, afterwards, later'. E poi? = And then? / So what?

etymology:
Univerbation of poi + che.
Compare French puisque.

fact.text: Formed from poi (then) + che (that), creating a univerbation. Compare French puisque, which has the same structure and meaning.

senses.note: Causal conjunction (why/because) and temporal (from that time).

etymology: Inherited from Latin polenta.

fact.text: The word is Latin. Romans used it for porridge made from hulled barley, long before maize came from the Americas. Today Italian polenta is usually made from cornmeal.

senses.note: Usually uncountable. A staple of northern Italy, served soft or set and grilled.
Uncountable; to say 'policies' use le politiche

etymology: From Latin polīticus, from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós).

fact.text: From Ancient Greek politikos, meaning relating to the state or citizen. The same root gives English political.

etymology: From Late Latin polītīa, from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía).

fact.text: Goes back to Greek politeia 'citizenship, government', from polis 'city'. English police, policy and politics all share this root.

senses.note: Takes a singular verb: la polizia è arrivata. A police officer is un poliziotto.

etymology: From polizia + -otto.

fact.text: From polizia (police) + the diminutive suffix -otto. The -otto suffix originally conveyed smallness or endearment but became a standard way to create agent nouns in Italian.

senses.note: Common informal term for a police officer.

etymology: From Medieval Latin apodissa (“receipt for money”), from a Byzantine Greek *ἀπόδειξα (*apódeixa), from Ancient Greek ἀπόδειξις (apódeixis, “proof”). Doublet of the learned borrowing apodissi.

fact.text: From Byzantine Greek apodeixa (proof, receipt). The word travelled through Medieval Latin and arrived in Italian with a narrowed meaning for insurance contracts.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pollicem.

fact.text: Its first meaning is 'thumb'. The inch was originally about a thumb's width, so Italian uses one word for both, just as French uses pouce.

senses.note: Also the everyday word for 'thumb'. A TV of 50 pollici is a 50-inch TV.

etymology: From Latin pullus, from Proto-Indo-European *polH- (“animal young”).

fact.text: From Latin pullus, 'young animal, chick'. Through French it also gave English pullet and poultry.

senses.note: Also slang for a gullible person, a sucker. A live hen is una gallina.

fact.text: Probably built from polpa, 'flesh, pulp', plus the suffix -accio, which often makes things bigger or coarser. So roughly 'the fleshy lump' of the leg.

senses.note: The back of the lower leg. A young cow is il vitello.

etymology: From poltro (“bed”).

fact.text: Related to poltrone 'lazybones', from the same root poltro 'bed'. Through French, poltrone became the English word 'poltroon', meaning a coward.

senses.note: Also a theatre seat in the front rows, or figuratively a cushy position of power.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pulverem, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“dust; flour”). Doublet of polve, from the Latin nominative pulvis. Akin to Sicilian prùvula.

fact.text: It comes from Latin pulvis, pulveris (dust). The same word reached English twice: as 'powder', via Old French poudre, and as 'pulverize', to grind something to dust.

senses.note: Also 'powder': latte in polvere = powdered milk. Polvere da sparo = gunpowder.

etymology: Inherited from Latin post merīdiem (“after noon”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin post meridiem, 'after midday'. That's the same phrase behind the English abbreviation p.m.

senses.note: 'Di pomeriggio' or 'nel pomeriggio' = in the afternoon.

etymology:
Univerbation of pomo (“apple”) + d' (“of”) + oro (“gold”), literally “golden apple”. Possibly owing to the fact that the first varieties of tomatoes arriving in Europe and spreading from Spain to Italy and North Africa were yellow. Earliest attestation (of the archaic plural form pomi d'oro) goes back to Matthiolus (1544).
A red strain was later developed in Moorish Africa, which came to be known in Italy as pomo dei mori (“apple of the Moors”).

fact.text: Literally means 'golden apple' (pomo d'oro). The first tomatoes to reach Italy in the 1500s were probably yellow, not red.

etymology: From pompa (“pump”) + -iere.

fact.text: Literally 'pump man': it comes from pompa 'pump' plus -iere, after the hand pumps early firefighters used to spray water.

senses.note: The official service is i vigili del fuoco. Pompiere is the everyday word.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin pontem.
Compare French, Dutch, and Catalan pont, Romanian punte, Romansh punt, Portuguese ponte, Spanish puente.

fact.text: Italians 'fare il ponte' (make the bridge): they take off a workday that falls between a holiday and the weekend, turning it into a long break.

senses.note: Also means a ship's deck, and a long weekend: fare il ponte.
Borrowed from English and never changes form: il pop, la musica pop.

etymology: From Latin populus, from Proto-Italic *poplos (“army”).

fact.text: From Latin populus, which originally meant 'army' in Proto-Italic. The idea of a people as a collective body evolved from the military sense of assembled forces.

etymology: From Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos.

fact.text: From Proto-Italic *porkos, related to English 'farrow' (young pig). Originally meant 'pig'; the insult sense derives from the animal.

senses.note: Used as a curse or swearword.

etymology: Inherited from Latin porrigere.

fact.text: From Latin porrigere, literally 'to reach forward' (por- 'forth' + regere 'to direct'). This root regere gave English 'regiment' and 'region'.

senses.note: Literary or formal; less common than 'offrire'

etymology: Inherited from Latin pōnere (“to put, place”), with pōnō > *ponjo> *pogno > pongo subsumed to the 'L-pattern' of vengo (cf. Old Italian vegno, vegnamo, vegnono) in a much-debated process of 'velar allomorphy'. This is mirrored in Spanish pongo, vengo, but with an opposite outcome in Portuguese ponho, venho.

fact.text: From Latin ponere (to put, place), whose past participle positus lies behind English 'position', 'compose', 'deposit' and 'impose'.

senses.note: Irregular: pongo, posi, posto. Porre una domanda = to ask a question.

etymology: Inherited from Latin porta, from the Proto-Indo-European root *per- (“to pass through”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin porta, which is also the source of English 'portal' and 'porch'. Its Latin doublet portus gave English 'port'. Both go back to a root meaning 'to pass through'.

senses.note: Also used for a city gate, e.g. Porta Romana.
This is the goal frame or net. To score a goal is segnare un gol.

etymology: Verb-object compound, composed of porta (“to carry”) + foglio (“sheet of paper”).

fact.text: Portafoglio is a verb-object compound: porta (to carry) + foglio (sheet of paper), literally 'paper carrier'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin portāre (“to bring, carry”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“go, traverse”).

fact.text: From Latin portare 'to carry', the root of English portable, porter, transport, import and export.

senses.note: Also 'to wear': porto gli occhiali = I wear glasses.

etymology: From Latin portus, from Proto-Italic *portus, from Proto-Indo-European *pértus (“crossing”), from the root *per- (“to go forth”, “to cross”).

fact.text: From Latin portus, from a Proto-Indo-European word for 'crossing'. The same root gives English 'ford' and Old Norse fjord: all places where you cross water.

etymology: Borrowed from Catalan [taronja de] Portugal, possibly via Neapolitan portogallo. Compare also Sicilian partugaḍḍu.

fact.text: Originally from China, sweet oranges were brought to Europe by Portuguese sailors, hence the Italian name meaning 'orange from Portugal'.

senses.note: The word literally means 'orange from Portugal'.

etymology: Sense “free rider” from the expression fare il portoghese, from spectacles organized by the Portuguese embassy in Rome that were free for anyone declaring to be Portuguese (18th c.).

senses.note: Relating to Portugal or its people/language.

etymology: Verb-object compound, composed of posa (“to put, to lay”) + cenere (“ash”).

fact.text: A verb-plus-object compound: posa (puts down) + cenere (ash), so literally a 'put-ash'. Italian builds many words this way, e.g. portafoglio (wallet, 'carry-sheet').

senses.note: The plural usually stays the same: i posacenere.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin pausāre, perhaps influenced in meaning by Latin pōnere. Compare French poser.

fact.text: From Late Latin pausare, 'to stop or rest', from pausa. That makes it a cousin of English 'pause', and through French poser, of 'pose'.

senses.note: Posare mattoni = to lay bricks. Also means to pose for a photo or portrait.

etymology: From posare.

senses.note: The plural le posate = cutlery (knives, forks and spoons).

etymology: From Latin positīvus.
From Latin positiōnem.

senses.note: Used for your location on a map or phone, and also for a stance or job position.

etymology: Inherited from Latin possidēre.

fact.text: From Latin possidēre. Related to English 'possess'. The root sed- means 'to sit', so it originally meant 'to sit on' or occupy.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin possibilis.

senses.note: il più possibile = as much as possible

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin possibilitātem.

senses.note: Invariable plural: le possibilità. Also means 'chance' or 'means': 'non ho la possibilità'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin posita, feminine singular of positus, past participle of pōnō (“to put”). Originally, "post for horses or for mooring ships", then "stopping place for coaches on a journey, way station". Doublet of posta (feminine past participle of porre).

fact.text: English post (mail) comes from this Italian word through French poste. It first meant a relay station where couriers changed horses.

senses.note: Also 'post office' (andare alla posta). Email = posta elettronica.

etymology: From posta.

fact.text: Il Postino (1994) is a well-loved Italian film about a shy island mailman who befriends the exiled Chilean poet Pablo Neruda.

senses.note: Female form: la postina.

etymology: From Latin postus, from positus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin positus, 'placed', the same root as English post (as in a job or position), position and deposit. Italian kept all those meanings in one word.

senses.note: Also seat, room/space, or job: un posto di lavoro. A posto = in order, fine.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin potēre, regularization of Latin posse.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin potere, a regularised form of Latin posse. The same family gave English potent, potential and possible, and il potere also means 'power'.

senses.note: Irregular: posso, puoi, può, possiamo, potete, possono. Followed directly by an infinitive: posso venire.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin potēre, regularization of Latin posse.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin potere, a regularised form of Latin posse. The same family gave English potent, potential and possible, and il potere also means 'power'.

senses.note: Irregular. Posso...? = Can I...? / May I...?
Diminutive and affectionate; expresses sympathy.

etymology: From Latin pauperem. Given that the expect native reflex would have been *popere, this form was likely among the early borrowings into Italian from Gallo-Italic.

senses.note: After the noun = without money (un uomo povero); before it = pitiable (povero ragazzo!).

etymology: From Latin pauperem. Given that the expect native reflex would have been *popere, this form was likely among the early borrowings into Italian from Gallo-Italic.

senses.note: I poveri = the poor. Feminine: la povera.

etymology: From Latin paupertātem. By surface analysis, povero + -tà.

fact.text: From Latin paupertatem (poverty). By surface analysis: povero (poor) + -ta (suffix forming abstract nouns).

senses.note: Invariable noun (no plural)

etymology: From pranzo + -are.

senses.note: Regular -are verb with avere: ho pranzato. Comes from il pranzo = lunch.

etymology: Inherited from Latin prandium, whence also Dalmatian prinz and Romanian prânz. Ultimately of Proto-Indo-European origin.

fact.text: From Latin prandium. One theory says it originally meant 'first meal', from Indo-European roots for 'first' and 'eat'.

senses.note: Traditionally the main meal of the day. 'Pranzo di Natale' = Christmas lunch/dinner.

etymology: Noun use of the feminine form of the adjective pratico.

senses.note: In practice = in pratica. In offices it also means a file or case: la mia pratica è in corso.

etymology: From pratico + -mente.

senses.note: Very common filler in speech, like 'basically'.

etymology: From Medieval Latin prāctica (“practical affairs, business”), from Ancient Greek πρᾱκτική (prāktikḗ, “practice, experience”), from πρᾱκτικός (prāktikós, “practical”), from πρᾱ́σσω (prā́ssō, “I do”).

senses.note: Wide range of meanings: to practise a profession/sport, to perform medical procedures, to pierce/bore holes, to frequent places, to associate with people.

etymology: From Late Latin practicus, from Ancient Greek πρᾱκτῐκός (prāktĭkós, “pertaining to an action”), derived from πρᾱγ- (prāg-), the root of πρᾱ́σσω (prā́ssō, “to do”) + -τῐκός (-tĭkós, verbal adjective suffix).

senses.note: 'Essere pratico di' means to know well or be familiar with: Sei pratico della zona?

etymology: Inherited from Latin prātum (“meadow”).

senses.note: Covers both a wild meadow and a mown lawn. Vietato calpestare il prato = keep off the grass.

etymology: From precedere with substantive senses under the influence of English precedent and French précédent.

senses.note: Same form for both genders. As a noun, un precedente = a precedent; precedenti penali = criminal record.

etymology: From precedere + -enza.
Borrowed from Latin praeferre, with a change in conjugation.

senses.note: -isc- verb: preferisco, preferisci, preferisce... but preferiamo, preferite.
Goes after the noun: il mio film preferito. Also the past participle of preferire.

etymology: From Late Latin praefixum, from Latin praefixus.

senses.note: Also a telephone area/dialling code, e.g. il prefisso di Roma è 06.

etymology: From earlier precare, from Latin precārī.

fact.text: The everyday reply 'Prego!' (you're welcome) literally means 'I pray/beg you'. English 'pray' comes from the same Latin verb, precari, via Old French preier.

senses.note: Also 'to beg'. Prego (lit. 'I pray') means 'you're welcome' or 'please, go ahead'.

fact.text: Literally 'I pray' or 'I beg', from pregare and Latin precari, 'to pray'. English pray and precarious (once meaning 'obtained by begging') come from the same root.

senses.note: Also said by shop staff to mean 'Can I help you?'
Used to let someone go first or to invite them in or to sit down.

etymology: From Latin premere.

senses.note: Premere il pulsante = to press the button. Mi preme = it matters to me.

etymology: From Latin praemium.

fact.text: From Latin praemium, literally 'what is obtained before or better than others', from prae- (before) + emō (acquire). English premium shares the same root.

senses.note: An award won for achievement in competition.

etymology: Inherited from Latin prēndere, from earlier prehendere, from prae- (“before”) + *hendere (“take, seize”) (not attested without a prefix), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed-.

fact.text: Comes from Latin prehendere, 'to seize'. English took the same root in apprehend, comprehend and prehensile (a 'grasping' tail), and also in prison, via French.

senses.note: Very common: prendere il treno (take the train), prendere un caffè (have a coffee).
Used for catching a thief, a ball or a cold: prendere il raffreddore.

etymology: Literally, “to take the sun”. Compare French prendre le soleil.

senses.note: Literally 'to take the sun'.
Pronominal reflexive verb; typically expressed with object pronoun (me la, te la, etc.)
prendersi cura di = to take care of; prendersela = to get upset.

etymology: From Latin praenotāre.

fact.text: From Latin praenotare, 'to note down beforehand'. Booking something means getting your name written down first.

senses.note: prenotare un tavolo = to book a table; la prenotazione = the booking.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin praenotātiōnem, form of praenotātiō.

senses.note: Fare una prenotazione = to make a booking. Verb: prenotare.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin praeoccupāre.

senses.note: Preoccupare = to worry someone; preoccuparsi (di) = to be worried (about).

fact.text: False friend: English 'preoccupied' usually means lost in thought or distracted, but Italian preoccupato means worried or anxious.

senses.note: Reflexive: mi preoccupo. Non preoccuparti! = Don't worry! Preoccuparsi di/per = to worry about.

fact.text: Not quite English 'preoccupied'. In Italian it mainly means worried or anxious, not lost in thought. 'Sono preoccupato' = I'm worried.

senses.note: Essere preoccupato per qualcosa = to be worried about something.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin praeoccupātiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin praeoccupātiōnem, literally 'pre-occupying' (prae- + occupatio). The prefix suggests something that occupies the mind beforehand, exactly matching the modern meaning of worry.

senses.note: Can also mean preoccupation or concern.

etymology: From Latin praeparāre (“to make ready in advance”), from prae- (“pre-”) + parō (“to make ready”).

senses.note: Prepararsi = to get ready. Preparare la cena = to make dinner.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin praepositiōnem.

senses.note: Preposizioni articolate combine with the article: di + il = del, in + la = nella.

etymology: From Latin praesentāre (“to present, show”).

senses.note: Also 'to introduce' someone: Ti presento Marco = Let me introduce Marco.

etymology: From presentare + -zione.

senses.note: Also: slideshow, introduction, the act of presenting.

etymology: Inherited from Latin praesentem.

fact.text: From Latin praesentem (before, in front). Same root as English 'present', 'presence', 'presentiment'.

senses.note: Also: appearing, this (in formal contexts).

etymology: From Latin praesentia.

fact.text: From Latin praesentia (being present). Prae (before) + esse (to be). English 'present' shares the same Latin root.
From Latin praeses 'one who sits in front, a guardian', from prae + sedere 'to sit'. It is related to English 'preside' and 'president'.

senses.note: Il/la preside (same form for both). At university, preside di facoltà = dean.

etymology: From Latin praesidentem.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: il presidente / la presidente. It also means the chair of a board.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin pressiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin pressio, derived from premere 'to press'. The physical sense evolved in Italian alongside chemical and social meanings, with 'pressione sanguigna' (blood pressure) becoming standard medical terminology.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pressō, from Latin presse (“narrow, short”). Cognate with Walloon and French près.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin pressō, derived from Latin presse (narrow, short). French près (near) is a cognate; both preserve the sense of proximity from an older meaning of 'close/narrow'.

senses.note: Rare adverbial use; more commonly seen in formal expressions like 'presso la sede' (at the office).

etymology: Inherited from Latin praestāre (“to provide, supply, offer, bestow”).

senses.note: To borrow is prendere in prestito. Prestare attenzione means to pay attention.

fact.text: Italian usually says 'borrow' and 'lend' with this noun: prendere in prestito means to take on loan, and dare in prestito means to give on loan.

senses.note: Also means 'loanword'. Dare in prestito = to lend; prendere in prestito = to borrow.

etymology: From Late Latin praestus, from the Latin praestō (“at hand”, adverb). Compare Catalan prest, French prêt.

fact.text: From Latin praesto 'at hand'. Music uses it as the tempo mark for 'very fast', and English magicians borrowed it for 'Hey presto!'

senses.note: A presto! = See you soon!
svegliarsi presto = to wake up early. Opposite: tardi.

etymology: From Latin praesūmō.
From Old Italian preite, from Vulgar Latin *previter, from Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros). Compare French prêtre, Romanian preot.

fact.text: Comes through Latin presbyter from Greek presbyteros, 'elder'. English priest and Presbyterian come from the same source.

senses.note: The everyday word for a Catholic priest. Il sacerdote is more formal.

etymology: From Latin praevidēre.

fact.text: Made of pre + vedere, 'see before', just like English foresee. A weather forecast is 'le previsioni del tempo'.

senses.note: 'Prevedere di fare' means 'to plan to do'. Can also mean 'to forecast' or, for rules, 'to provide for'.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin praevīsiōnem, from Latin praevideō.

senses.note: The weather forecast is usually plural: le previsioni del tempo.

etymology: A syncope of earlier pretosemolo, with metathesis from petrosemolo, from a cross of Latin petroselīnum and sēmen (thus "stone seed") as in Sardinian perdusèmene. The Latin word borrowed from Ancient Greek πετροσέλῑνον (petrosélīnon), from πέτρα (pétra, “stone”) + σέλῑνον (sélīnon, “celery”).

fact.text: Like English 'parsley', it comes from Greek petroselinon, 'rock celery'. Italians call someone who turns up everywhere 'come il prezzemolo', like parsley in every dish.

etymology: From Latin pretium, whence also Italian pregio, a doublet. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *préti (“back”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin pretium (price, worth), which is also behind English price, praise and precious, and Italian pregio (merit).

senses.note: Quanto costa? / Qual è il prezzo? A metà prezzo = half price.

etymology: From earlier priscione, possibly via Old French prison, from Latin prehēnsiōnem (“the act of seizing”), from prehendō (“to seize, grab”). Doublet of prensione.

fact.text: From Latin prehensio, 'a seizing', from prehendere, 'to grab'. English 'prison' (via Old French) and 'apprehend' come from the same root: a prison is where the seized are kept.

senses.note: 'Carcere' is a common synonym. 'In prigione' means 'in prison'.

etymology: See primo.

senses.note: Can also mean 'first' (prima mangiamo). 'Prima di' + noun/infinitive; 'prima che' + subjunctive.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin prīma vēra (“early spring”), derived from vēr (“spring”). Compare Spanish primavera, French primevère.

fact.text: It comes from Late Latin prima vera, 'early spring'. The same phrase gave French primevère, 'primrose', which is also a meaning of the Italian word.

senses.note: in primavera = in spring

etymology: From Latin prīmus, from earlier prīsmos < *prīsemos < Proto-Italic *priisemos.

fact.text: On an Italian menu, il primo (the first course) is the pasta, risotto or soup dish. It comes after the antipasto and before il secondo, the meat or fish course.

senses.note: Usually comes before the noun: il primo giorno = the first day.

etymology: Derived from Latin principālis. By surface analysis, principe + -ale.

senses.note: Can also be used as an adjective meaning 'principal' or 'main'.

etymology: From Latin prīncipem (“chief”) (compare principio (“principle”) from the meaning "first").

fact.text: From Latin princeps (chief, first)—the same root as English prince, principal, and principle, all meaning 'first' or 'foremost'.

etymology: From principe (“prince”) + -essa (“-ess”); compare French princesse, Sicilian principissa.

fact.text: The -essa suffix is Italian's equivalent of English -ess, as in 'princess'. Both derive from Latin -issa.

etymology: From Latin prīvātus.

fact.text: From Latin prīvātus, the same root as English 'private', 'deprive', and 'privilege' (which originally meant 'private law').

etymology: Borrowed from Latin probābilis.

senses.note: È probabile che + subjunctive: è probabile che piova = it will probably rain.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin probābilitātem. By surface analysis, probabile + -ità.

fact.text: From Latin probābilitās. Shares the root with English 'probable'—both trace back to Latin probare (to test, approve).

etymology: From probabile + -mente.

Borrowed from Latin problēma, from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma, “obstacle”), from προβάλλω (probállō, “to throw or lay something in front of someone, to put forward”), from prefix προ- (pro-, “in front of”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw, to cast, to hurl”).

fact.text: Masculine despite ending in -a, like many Greek-origin words such as il tema and il sistema. Greek problema meant something 'thrown in front of you', an obstacle.

senses.note: Masculine despite the -a ending: il problema, i problemi. Nessun problema = no problem.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prōcēdere.
From Latin processus, possibly borrowed.

fact.text: Comes from Latin processus, the past participle of prōcēdō meaning 'to advance or proceed.' The root is also shared by English 'proceed' and 'process.'

etymology: From Latin prōcūrātōrem.

senses.note: Someone who holds power of attorney; also a historical term for a Roman procurator.

etymology: From Latin productus.

senses.note: Also the past participle of produrre (produced). Prodotti tipici = local specialities.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prōdūcere.

fact.text: Its infinitive is a shortened form of Latin producere, 'to lead forward'. That is why the full stem produc- returns when you conjugate it. Tradurre, condurre and ridurre follow the same pattern.

senses.note: Conjugates from the stem produc-: produco, producevo. Past participle: prodotto.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prōductōrem, from Latin prōductus.

senses.note: Feminine: produttrice. Also used for a manufacturer or a grower.

etymology: From professione + -ista.
Learned borrowing from Latin prŏfessōrem.

fact.text: Not only a university professor: in Italy, every middle and high school teacher is called professore or professoressa. Primary school teachers are maestro or maestra.

senses.note: Used for middle school, high school and university teachers. Feminine: professoressa.

etymology: Deverbal from profilare.
From Latin profundus.

fact.text: Shares its root with English 'profound': Latin profundus, from pro- + fundus 'bottom'. Something deep goes far towards the bottom.

senses.note: Un respiro profondo = a deep breath. Also figurative: profound.
Used for any pleasant smell, e.g. food: Che profumo! (That smells great!)

etymology: Borrowed from French projet, derived from projeter (“to plan”).

senses.note: Can also mean a plan or a design: 'progetti per il futuro' means 'plans for the future'.

etymology: From Late Latin programma, from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma).

fact.text: It is masculine despite ending in -a, because it comes from a Greek neuter noun in -ma. The same goes for il problema, il tema and il sistema.

senses.note: A TV show, a schedule of events or a computer program.
Often plural: Che programmi hai per stasera? = What are your plans for tonight?

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prōgressus.

senses.note: Countable in Italian: 'fare progressi' = to make progress.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prohibēre.

fact.text: From Latin prohibere (pro- + habeo, to have). The formation parallels Old English forhealdan.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōiectilis (“projectile”), from Latin prōiectus, perfect passive participle of prōiciō (“throw forth; extend; expel”). By surface analysis, proietto + -ile.

fact.text: From Latin proiectus (thrown forward), past participle of proicere. The word shares the same Latin root as English 'project' and 'trajectory'.

etymology: From Medieval Latin, Vulgar Latin promissa (“promise”), from Latin prōmissum (“promise”), from promittō (“to send forth; to promise”).

senses.note: Mantenere una promessa = to keep a promise. Also: a promising talent (una giovane promessa).

etymology: From Latin prōmittere.

fact.text: From Latin prōmittere, 'to send forth' (pro- 'forward' + mittere 'to send'). The same verb is behind English 'promise', 'mission' and 'emit'.

senses.note: Promettere di + infinitive. Past participle: promesso. Promette bene = it looks promising.

etymology: From Latin prōmovēre (“to promote”).

fact.text: Italian students who pass the school year are 'promossi' (promoted). Students who fail are 'bocciati' and have to repeat the year.

senses.note: Irregular: promosso, promossi. 'Essere promosso' also means to pass a school year or exam.

etymology: Inherited from Latin prōnōmen.

senses.note: Masculine: il pronome, i pronomi.

etymology: From Latin prōmptus.

fact.text: Italians answer the phone with 'Pronto?', literally 'Ready?', as if saying 'I'm ready to talk'. It comes from Latin promptus, which also gave English 'prompt'.

senses.note: Agrees with the noun: pronto, pronta, pronti, pronte.
Used only on the phone; for greeting in person use ciao or buongiorno.

etymology: From Latin prōmptus.

fact.text: Italians answer the phone with 'Pronto?', literally 'Ready?', as if saying 'I'm ready to talk'. It comes from Latin promptus, which also gave English 'prompt'.

senses.note: Only for answering the phone, usually as a question: Pronto? As an adjective it means 'ready'.

etymology: Deverbal from pronunciare (“to pronounce, utter”) + -a.

senses.note: Related verb: pronunciare = to pronounce.

etymology: Derived from Latin prōpōnere (“to set forth; to propose; to declare”).

senses.note: Irregular like porre: propongo, proposi, proposto.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prōpositum (“plan, intention”, literally “that which is proposed”), neuter form of prōpositum, perfect passive participle of prōpōnō.

fact.text: From Latin propositus, the past participle of proponere (to propose, set forth). The English word 'proposal' shares the same Latin root.

senses.note: Common in phrases like a proposito (on purpose) and a tal proposito (on that subject).

etymology: From Latin prōposita.
From Latin proprietārius.

senses.note: Feminine: la proprietaria. Also used for a landlord.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prŏprietātem. By surface analysis, proprio + -età.

senses.note: Invariable noun (same form singular and plural)

etymology: Borrowed from Latin proprius.

fact.text: From Latin proprius, source of English proper and property. Still retains the 'own' sense in modern Italian: propria casa literally means one's own house.

senses.note: Possessive adjective, agrees with noun: proprio libro (one's own book), propria casa (one's own house).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin proprius.

fact.text: From Latin proprius, source of English proper and property. Still retains the 'own' sense in modern Italian: propria casa literally means one's own house.

senses.note: Also means just or exactly: proprio lì = right there; proprio ora = just now.

etymology: From asciutto (“dry”), with a change of prefix, or perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *perexsūctus, from Latin per + exsūctus. Compare Portuguese presunto.

fact.text: In English, 'prosciutto' means dry-cured ham, a sense its root asciutto ('dry') fits. In Italy the word covers any ham, so ask for crudo or cotto.

senses.note: prosciutto crudo = cured ham; prosciutto cotto = cooked ham.

etymology: From Prosecco in Trieste, Italy.

fact.text: Named after the town of Prosecco near Trieste in northeastern Italy, where the grapes originated. Now produced mainly in the Veneto region.

senses.note: Italian sparkling wine from Veneto/Friuli Venezia Giulia regions.

etymology: Inherited from Latin proximus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin proximus 'nearest', the root of English 'proximity' and 'approximate'. As a noun, il prossimo means 'your neighbour', as in ama il prossimo tuo, 'love thy neighbour'.

senses.note: La settimana prossima = next week. Usually comes before the noun: il prossimo treno.

etymology: From Ancient Greek πρωταγωνιστής (prōtagōnistḗs).

fact.text: From Greek prōtos 'first' + agōnistēs 'contestant, actor': in ancient Greek drama, the protagonist was literally the first actor.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: il/la protagonista; plurals i protagonisti, le protagoniste.

etymology: From Latin prōtegere, from prō- + tegō.

fact.text: From Latin prōtegere (pro- 'forward' + tegō 'to cover'). Shares an ancestor with English protect.

senses.note: Irregular verb; past participle protetto.

etymology: From Late Latin prōtectiōnem.
Either deverbal from provare (“to try; to test; to prove; to feel”) + -a, or from Late Latin proba, from Latin probō.

fact.text: Related to provare (to try/test/prove). The shift from 'to test' to 'test' as a noun is natural; the same root appears in English 'proof'.

senses.note: Versatile noun: exam, experiment, attempt, rehearsal, or evidence

etymology: From Latin probāre. Compare French prouver, Portuguese provar.

fact.text: Comes from Latin probare, 'to test, to prove', the same source as English prove and probe. So in Italian, trying something out and proving it are the same verb.

senses.note: Also: to try on (clothes), to feel (an emotion). Provare a + infinitive = to try to do something.

etymology: From Latin prōvenīre (“to originate, arise”).

fact.text: From Latin provenire, 'to come forth, arise'. Through French provenir, the same root gives English provenance, the documented origin of an artwork or object.

senses.note: Takes essere and conjugates like venire: provengo, provieni. Used with da: proviene da Roma.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prōvincia.

fact.text: Directly from Latin prōvincia, the same source as English 'province': originally meant an area placed under Roman rule.

senses.note: Administrative division; in Italian, also used generically for regions around major cities.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *prūnea, from Vulgar Latin *prūna, feminine singular formed from the neutral plural of Latin prūnum, from Ancient Greek προῦμνον (proûmnon). Cognate with Sicilian prunu.

fact.text: From Latin prūnum via Vulgar Latin, borrowed from Ancient Greek. The word traveled westward through Romance languages from Greek agriculture.

etymology: From Latin prūrītus m .

senses.note: Ho prurito = I'm itchy. Figurative: an urge or craving.

etymology: Borrowed from English pub.

fact.text: Pub is a direct English loanword, short for 'public house', showing how Italians adopted the English term alongside native culture.

etymology: From Latin pūblicāre.

senses.note: Also means to post online: pubblicare una foto.

etymology: From French publicité.

senses.note: The plural is unchanged. It also means advertising or publicity in general.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin pūblicus. Doublet of piuvico, which is inherited.

fact.text: English "public" comes from the same Latin pūblicus. The word entered both languages directly from Latin, making them true cognates.

etymology: From Latin pugnus, from Proto-Italic *pugnos, from Proto-Indo-European *puǵnos, from *pewǵ- (“prick, punch”).

fact.text: From Latin pugnus via Proto-Indo-European *pewǵ- (prick, punch). Related to Ancient Greek pugmē (fist) and English pugilism and pugnacious.

etymology: Inherited from Latin polīre (“to polish, to smooth”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin polire, 'to polish, to smooth', which is also the source of English polish and polite (originally meaning 'polished').

senses.note: An -isc- verb: pulisco, pulisci, pulisce, puliscono. Pulirsi = to clean oneself.

etymology: From Latin polītus. Cf. the doublet polito.

fact.text: From Latin politus, 'polished', the same word that gave English 'polite'. Italian also kept the doublet polito, meaning 'polished, refined'.

senses.note: Colloquially it also means broke, with no money.
Fare le pulizie = to do the (house) cleaning, usually in the plural.

fact.text: This animal name came into European languages from Quechua, the Inca language of the Andes, by way of Spanish.

senses.note: Masculine and invariable: il puma, i puma.

etymology: From Late Latin puncta, from the feminine of Latin punctus.
From Latin punctum.

fact.text: From Latin punctum, 'a prick, a small hole', from pungere 'to prick'. It's related to English punctuation, puncture and punctual.

senses.note: Also dot and full stop (period). a un certo punto = at a certain point.

etymology: Univerbation of pur(e) + che.

fact.text: Univerbation of pure (pure) and che (that), literally 'pure that'. Compare French à condition que and Spanish con tal que.

senses.note: Conjunction requiring subjunctive: purché tu venga (provided that you come).

etymology: Inherited from Latin pūrē, the adverb of pūrus.
