senses.note: Agrees: quello, quella, quelli, quelle. Before nouns it changes like the article: quel, quello, quell', quei, quegli.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin quaestiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin quaestio (a questioning, inquiry). The root quaerere means to seek or ask, so literally a questione is something asked about or investigated.
From Vulgar Latin eccum iste, roughly 'look, that one!'. The eccum part also survives in Italian ecco, 'here it is / there you go'.

senses.note: Agrees with the noun: questo, questa, questi, queste. Before a vowel: quest'anno.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *eccum iste, from Latin eccum (deictic) + iste (“that”), the former surviving also as Italian ecco and the latter as esto.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin eccum iste, roughly 'look, that one!'. The eccum part also survives in Italian ecco, 'here it is / there you go'.

senses.note: Forms: questo, questa, questi, queste. Also a pronoun: questa è la tua idea.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *eccum iste, from Latin eccum (deictic) + iste (“that”), the former surviving also as Italian ecco and the latter as esto.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin eccum iste, roughly 'look, that one!'. The eccum part also survives in Italian ecco, 'here it is / there you go'.

senses.note: Agrees with what it refers to: questo, questa, questi, queste. Also used before nouns: questa casa.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin quaestūra.

fact.text: Named after the Latin quaestura, the office of a Roman quaestor. Today the questura is also where foreigners in Italy apply for their residence permit (permesso di soggiorno).

senses.note: The main State Police office in each province, run by the questore.

etymology:
From Vulgar Latin *eccum hīc (with apocope), from Latin eccum + hīc.
The original geminated -cc-, though lost in the standard language, is still found in most regional Italian varieties.

senses.note: Qui and qua both mean 'here' and are mostly interchangeable.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *eccum inde. The regular outcome of the stressed vowel should have been */e/. The actual /i/ may have been taken by analogy from quinci (< *eccum hince), with which quindi forms a natural pair, and where stressed /i/ is expected due to the following /ntʃ/ triggering anaphonesis.

senses.note: Very common in speech as a filler 'so...': Quindi, cosa facciamo?

etymology: From Latin quīndecim.
From Late Latin quintale, from Arabic قِنْطَار (qinṭār), ultimately from Latin centēnārium.

fact.text: From Arabic qinṭār via Late Latin quintale. The word traveled from Arabic into European languages as trade expanded, originally derived from Latin centēnārium (hundred).

senses.note: A unit of mass equal to 100 kilograms, used mainly in commerce.

etymology: From Latin quīntus, from quīnque.

fact.text: Latin quintus is also in English 'quintessence', literally the 'fifth essence': a fifth element that medieval thinkers believed made up the heavens.

etymology: From Latin quotīdiānus, from quot (“as often as”) + diēs (“day”).

fact.text: From Latin quotidianus, from quot 'as often as' + dies 'day', so 'every day'. English 'quotidian' (everyday, ordinary) comes from the same Latin word.

senses.note: Also an adjective: la vita quotidiana = daily life. Giornale is the general word for newspaper.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin rabia, from Classical Latin rabiēs.

fact.text: From Latin rabiēs, which also meant both anger and the rabies disease, reflecting the connection between fury and the violent symptoms of infected animals.

senses.note: Also means rabies (the disease).

etymology: Borrowed from French raquette.

fact.text: Comes from French raquette, possibly from Arabic rāḥat al-yad, 'palm of the hand'. Early tennis was played by hitting the ball with the palm. English 'racket' has the same root.

senses.note: Also a table-tennis bat or paddle.

etymology: From Latin recolligere. Compare Sicilian ricògghiri.

senses.note: Also to collect, pick up, harvest. Irregular: raccolgo, raccolsi, raccolto.

etymology: From ra- + accomandare. Compare Spanish recomendar.

senses.note: Reflexive verb (raccomandarsi); also means to beg or appeal.

etymology: ellipsis of posta raccomandata

fact.text: Short for posta raccomandata, from raccomandare 'to entrust, to recommend', a relative of English 'recommend'. The idea: a letter specially entrusted to the post.

senses.note: Short for lettera/posta raccomandata. With proof of delivery: raccomandata con ricevuta di ritorno (A/R).

etymology: From ra- + contare.

fact.text: Built from ra- + contare, 'to count'. English recount works the same way: it can mean counting again or narrating. Bank tellers and story tellers come from the same idea.

senses.note: Used for telling stories or events: raccontare una storia. To tell someone to do something uses dire.

etymology: Inherited from Latin rādīcem.

fact.text: It comes from Latin radix, 'root', which also gave English 'radical' (going to the root) and 'radish', literally a root vegetable.

senses.note: Also a figurative root or source. Radice quadrata = square root.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin radius. Doublet of raggio, razzo, and rai, the first two of which were inherited from Latin, while the last was borrowed from Occitan.

fact.text: Gender changes the meaning: la radio is the radio you listen to, but il radio is the radius bone in your forearm, or the chemical element radium.

senses.note: Feminine and invariable: la radio, le radio. Ascoltare la radio = to listen to the radio.

etymology: From raffreddare + -ore.

senses.note: Prendere il raffreddore = to catch a cold. For cold weather, Italian uses il freddo.

etymology: The feminized version of the masculine ragazzo (“boy; boyfriend”) from Vulgar Latin *ragatius, from Ancient Greek ῥάκος (rhákos, “rag, tatter”, suggesting the clothing).

fact.text: Watch the context: 'la mia ragazza' normally means 'my girlfriend', not just 'my girl'. In the same way, 'il mio ragazzo' means 'my boyfriend'.

senses.note: Boy is il ragazzo. With a possessive it usually means girlfriend: la mia ragazza.

etymology: From ragazzo + -ino.

fact.text: The -ino suffix is a diminutive, making ragazzino the small or young version of ragazzo (boy). Common in Italian for affectionate or diminishing reference.

etymology:
Uncertain. Possibly
* from Arabic رَقَّاص (raqqāṣ, “courier, delivery boy”).
* alternatively, from Ancient Greek ῥάκος (rhákos, “rag, tatter”, suggesting the clothing).

fact.text: Its origin is uncertain. One theory traces it to Arabic raqqas, 'courier, errand boy'. Another links it to Greek rhakos, 'rag', after the boys' ragged clothes.

senses.note: Also 'boyfriend': il mio ragazzo. Plural ragazzi = guys / kids, also mixed groups.

etymology: Inherited from Latin radius. Doublet of razzo, radio, and rai, which were respectively inherited from Latin, borrowed from Latin, and borrowed from Occitan.

fact.text: From Latin radius. English 'radius', 'radial', and 'radiant' all descend from the same root. Italian raggio is a direct heir to the Latin term.

senses.note: of light; also spoke of a wheel or radius of a circle

etymology: From ra- + giungere.

fact.text: From ra- (intensive prefix) + giungere (to arrive). The prefix ra- intensifies, so raggiungere means 'to arrive at thoroughly', conveying the sense of catching up or joining someone.

senses.note: Takes direct object (transitive).

etymology: From Latin ratiōnem, whence also razione (a borrowed doublet). The natural outcome would have been razzone [rat'tsone] (which is attested in some archaic works in Roman vernacular); the reason why the modern form shows a g is that Tuscan literates mistook Northern rason as an outcome of non-existent Latin **rasione~**raseone—whose -sj- indeed evolves regularly into tuscan [ʃ]~[ʒ] and non-tuscan [s]<s> (compare fagiolo from Latin phaseolum, and compare the pronunciation of English vision as "vizhun"—indeed, approvvigionare ultimately comes from Latin visionem with the same assimilation of -sj- into a palatal voiced fricative). Compare other terms ending in -gione. Furthermore, the reason why it’s nowadays pronounced with an affricate rather than a fricative (together with all Italian terms having as the corresponding etymological clusters being -tj- or -sj-, or even -cj- through Gallic languages—see crogiolo) is due to hyper-correction of Tuscan gorgia, i.e. the merging of ungeminated fricatives and affricates into the first ones. Indeed, older spellings with sci or sgi tried to reproduce the ungeminated fricative before the gorgia took place (once it happened, it was more convenient, with merged sounds, to merge the spellings, despite being unetymological).

fact.text: Comes from Latin ratio, 'calculation, reason', the source of English reason and ration. Italian also has a borrowed twin from the same Latin word: razione, 'ration'.

senses.note: avere ragione = to be right (Ha ragione = He's right). dare ragione a qualcuno = to agree with someone.

etymology: Borrowed from French ragoût, from Middle French ragoûter (“to awaken the appetite”), from goût (“taste”), from Latin gustus. See also gusto (“taste”) and its derivations.

fact.text: From French ragoût, which comes from Middle French ragoûter (to awaken the appetite). Related to English 'gusto', both ultimately from Latin gustus (taste).

senses.note: A meat and vegetable stew; invariable noun

etymology: From ra- + allentare.

fact.text: Musicians already know its gerund. Rallentando (rall.) is a score marking that means gradually slowing the tempo.

senses.note: Takes avere when transitive. When intransitive it can take essere or avere.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arāmen, variant of Late Latin aerāmen, derived from Latin aer-.

senses.note: Usually uncountable. I rami can mean copper pots and pans.

etymology: From Latin rapīna.

fact.text: From Latin rapina (plunder, robbery). Related to English rapine and rapacious.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *rapīre, from Latin rapere, from Proto-Italic *rapiō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rp-i-, from *h₁rep- (“to snatch”).
Deverbal from rapportare + -o.

fact.text: From rapportare (to bring back, report). Related to English 'report', 'rapport'—all sharing the Latin root portare (carry).

senses.note: Wide range of meanings: personal ties, official reports, mathematical ratios, even intimate relations.

etymology: From Latin repraesentāre.
From raro + -mente.
From Medieval Latin rata, from the Latin phrase pro rata parte (“according to the proportional share”), from ratus (“reckoned”), past participle of the verb reor (“to think over, deem, reckon”).

fact.text: From Medieval Latin 'pro rata parte' (according to the proportional share). English 'rate' comes from the same Latin ratus (reckoned).

senses.note: A periodic payment; plural often used in payment plans.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin rattus (“rat”), from Proto-Germanic *rattaz.

fact.text: Shares roots with Germanic languages—the word traveled from Proto-Germanic through Latin, reaching Italian and English through different routes.

etymology:
c. 1300, as masculine razzo, the feminine razza is from the early 14th century. The etymology of this word is uncertain, with a large number of controversially discussed suggestions.
Among the most widely accepted suggestions is the one embraced by Französisches Etymologisches Wörterbuch (1922), but was proposed earlier, among others by L. Spitzer (Z. rom. Philol. t. 53, pp. 300–301), which derives the word from Latin ratiō (the nominative, as opposed to ragione, from the accusative ratiōnem, which nonetheless was attested with a similar sense to razza in the late Middle Ages; ratio also came to mean “idea” or “conception of something” in Ecclesiastical Latin) likely via a Vulgar Latin variant *ratia, and underwent a change of gender later from an original form *razzo, or else derived ultimately from generātiō through apheresis.
Another likely origin is from the Latin racēmus, meaning a “cluster or bunch of grapes, berries or similar fruits”, from which the French “raisin” is derived.
Other suggestions include, Lombardic *raiza (compare Old High German reiza (“line”)), Latin rādīx (“root”) or Ancient Greek ῥίζα (rhíza, “root”), Arabic رَأْس (raʔs, “head”), or Old French haraz (“culture of horses”).

fact.text: English 'race' in this sense came from Italian razza by way of French race. Where razza itself comes from is still debated: Latin ratio and generatio are among the suggestions.

senses.note: Used mainly for animal breeds (razza canina). Used of people it is sensitive, so 'etnia' is often preferred.

etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ-
Proto-Indo-European *-s
Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs
Proto-Italic *rēks
Latin rēx
Italian re
Inherited from Latin rēx, via the nominative singular, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs (“ruler, king”). Doublet of rege, which was borrowed from Latin via the accusative rēgem.

fact.text: It comes from Latin rex, regis, 'king'. The same root gives English regal, regent and reign (Latin regnum), and royal comes from it too, through French.

senses.note: The plural is the same as the singular: il re, i re.

etymology: From re- + agire (“act”).
From reale + -izzare. The sense “to become aware of” is a semantic loan from English realize.

fact.text: Realizzare means both 'to achieve' and 'to realize/become aware'—the latter is a semantic loan from English, so it behaves similarly but has a distinct Italian identity.

senses.note: Also means 'to realize' in the sense of becoming aware, influenced by English 'realize'.

etymology:
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin reālitātem, from Late Latin reālis (“real”), from Classical Latin rēs (“thing”) + -ālis.
Doublet of realità, which is a learned borrowing.

fact.text: The very common phrase 'in realtà' means 'actually' or 'in fact', and it often corrects what was just said, as in 'In realtà, non è vero'.

senses.note: Has the same form in the plural: le realtà.

etymology: From Latin reāctiō.
From recente + -mente.

senses.note: Synonyms: di recente, ultimamente.
Rare. The adjective reciproco/reciproca ('mutual') is far more common.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin recitāre.
Deverbal from reclamare + -o.

fact.text: Derived from the Latin verb reclamare (to cry out against), related to English 'reclaim' and 'acclaim'—all share the root clamare (to shout).

senses.note: Formal written or official complaint; also a claim or grievance.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin recuperāre.
Probably borrowed from Spanish regalar.

fact.text: Despite the look, it has nothing to do with regal or kings. It probably goes back to French régaler (to treat), which is related to English regale and gala.

senses.note: Related noun: il regalo (gift). Mi ha regalato un libro = he gave me a book (as a present).

etymology: From French régal or Spanish regalo .

fact.text: It looks royal, but it doesn't come from Latin rex 'king'. It came through French régal 'feast, treat', which is also the source of English regale.

senses.note: fare un regalo a qualcuno = to give someone a present.

etymology: Inherited from Latin rēgīna; cognate with Spanish reina.

senses.note: Also used for the queen in chess and cards, and for the queen bee (l'ape regina).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin regiōnem, case form of regiō (literally “direction, line”), derived from regō (“to rule, govern”). Compare rione, an inherited doublet.

fact.text: Italy has 20 regioni. Five of them have special autonomous status: Sicily, Sardinia, Valle d'Aosta, Trentino-Alto Adige and Friuli-Venezia Giulia.

senses.note: Also the name for Italy's top-level administrative units, e.g. la regione Lazio.

fact.text: Coined in 1932 by the linguist Bruno Migliorini to replace the French régisseur. English football later borrowed it for a deep-lying playmaker who 'directs' play.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: il/la regista (pl. i registi, le registe). A company director is direttore.

etymology: From registro + -are.
From Latin rēgnum.
Borrowed from Latin rēgula as a semi-learned term. Compare Spanish regla, Portuguese regra, French règle.

fact.text: Comes from Latin regula, 'straight stick, ruler', which also gave English 'rule' (via Old French) and 'regular'. A rule was first a tool for drawing straight lines.

senses.note: In regola = in order, above board; di regola = as a rule.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin rēgulāris. By surface analysis, regola (“rule”) + -are (“-ar”, adjective-forming derivational suffix).

fact.text: Borrowed from Late Latin regularis. 'Regular' and 'regola' (rule) share the same Latin root regula.

etymology: From Latin relātiōnem.

fact.text: It can catch you out: at school or work, 'fare una relazione' means writing or giving a report, not starting a relationship.

senses.note: Often means a romantic relationship or an affair. It can also mean a report: una relazione scritta.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin religiōnem (“piety”, “superstition”).
Borrowed from Latin religiōsus.

fact.text: Borrowed from Latin religiōsus. English 'religious' comes from the same Latin root via Old French.

etymology: From Late Latin rendere, from Latin reddere. The past participle was contaminated by Latin prehensus (of unrelated prehendere), with the past historic altered by analogy to prendere (past historic presi).

fact.text: English 'render' and 'rent' both come from this word's Old French relative rendre. Latin reddere, 'to give back', turned into rendere under the influence of prendere.

senses.note: Rendere + adjective = to make something X (renderlo bello). Also 'to give back'.
A section of a shop, firm or factory. Also a hospital ward (reparto di cardiologia) or a military unit.

etymology: From earlier republica, from Latin rēspūblica, rēs pūblica (literally “the public thing”).

fact.text: Repubblica comes from Latin rēs pūblica (literally 'the public thing'), the same root as English 'republic'—a shared concept and word across Romance and Germanic languages.

etymology: From Latin reputātiōnem.
From Medieval Latin residentia, from Latin residēns (“residing”), from resideō (“to reside”), from re- + sedeō (“to sit”).

fact.text: From Latin residentia (from residēns, residing). Shares the root with English "reside" and "residential."

senses.note: Formal term; often used of official residences or formal addresses.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin resistere, from re- + sistō.
Latinized form of older rispirare, inherited from Latin respīrāre.

fact.text: From Latin respirare, re- 'again' + spirare 'to breathe'. That breathing root also gives English respiration, inspire, and spirit.

senses.note: Il respiro = the breath; fare un respiro profondo = take a deep breath.

etymology: Deverbal from respirare + -o.

senses.note: Fare un respiro profondo = to take a deep breath.

etymology: Borrowed from French responsable, assimilated to the native suffix -abile. Cognate with Piedmontese responsàbil.

fact.text: Borrowed from French responsable. Cognate with English "responsible"—both trace back to the same Romance root meaning accountability.

senses.note: Adj/noun; can mean responsible person or person in charge.

etymology: From responsabile + -ità, modeled after similar formation of French responsabilité and English responsibility in the late 18th century.

fact.text: A fairly young word: it was formed in the late 18th century from responsabile, modelled on French responsabilité and English responsibility.

senses.note: Invariable: le responsabilità. Also means legal liability or blame.

etymology: From Latin restāre, from re- + stō.

fact.text: From Latin restare, 're-' plus 'stare' (to stand). Through French rester it gave English 'the rest', meaning what remains.

senses.note: Takes essere: sono restato. Mi resta poco = I have little left.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin rēstituere (“to replace, restore”), with change of conjugation.

senses.note: An -isc- verb: restituisco, restituisci. Also used for refunding money.

etymology: Deverbal from restare + -o.

fact.text: Not 'rest' as in relaxing (that's riposo). Resto is whatever remains, including the change you get back at the till.

senses.note: Tenga il resto = keep the change.
il resto = the rest; del resto = besides, after all.

etymology: From Latin rēte (“net”).

fact.text: From Latin rete 'net', which is also behind English retina (the net-like layer of the eye) and reticulated.

senses.note: In football it also means a goal: segnare una rete = to score a goal.
rete wifi, rete stradale (road network), in rete = online.

etymology: Inherited from Latin retrō.

fact.text: Don't confuse it with retrò (stress at the end), an adjective from French meaning vintage or old-fashioned in style.

senses.note: Invariable noun. 'Sul retro' means on the back or round the back. For direction, use 'indietro'.

etymology: From rettangol(o) (“rectangle”) + -are (“-ar”, adjective-forming suffix).

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine. Plural: rettangolari.

etymology: Derived from Latin rēctōrem (“guide, tutor”).

fact.text: From Latin rector, 'guide, ruler', from regere, 'to steer, to rule'. The same root gives English 'regent', 'regime' and 'correct'.

senses.note: In Italy, the head of a university, roughly a UK vice-chancellor or a US president.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin revīsiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin revideō (to see again), related to English video and revise; the Latin -tiō suffix creates abstract nouns from verbs.

senses.note: Can mean checking/inspection generally; in Italy often refers to vehicle inspection (MOT equivalent).

etymology: From ri- + assumere.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle riassunto, which also means 'a summary'. Can also mean to rehire.

etymology: From ri- + avere.
From ricco + -ezza.

fact.text: Derived from ricco (rich) plus the suffix -ezza (used to form abstract nouns from adjectives), similar to how English creates nouns from adjectives.

etymology: From Latin ēricius (“a hedgehog”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰḗr (“to bristle”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin ericius, 'hedgehog', the animal with bristly spikes. The same Latin word, through Old French, gave English 'urchin', first meaning hedgehog and later sea urchin.

senses.note: Capelli ricci = curly hair. As a noun, il riccio = a curl, or a hedgehog.

etymology: Borrowed from Lombardic rīhhi (possibly through a Vulgar Latin or Late Latin *riccus, *ricus), from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz.

fact.text: A Germanic loan, not a Latin word: it came from Lombardic rīhhi, from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz. The same root gives English 'rich' and German 'reich'.

senses.note: Also 'rich in': ricco di vitamine = rich in vitamins.

etymology: Deverbal from ricercare + -a.

fact.text: Deverbal from ricercare (to search, investigate) + -a. The suffix -a turns the verb into a feminine noun, similar to how English -ing can nominalize verbs.

etymology: From Latin recepta, feminine of receptus (“received”), from perfect passive participle of recipiō (“to receive”). Compare Sicilian rizzetta.

fact.text: It comes from Latin recepta, 'received', which is also the source of English 'receipt'. In older English, 'receipt' could mean a recipe or a medical prescription too.

senses.note: Also means a doctor's prescription (ricetta medica).

etymology: From Latin recipere. Possibly borrowed from a Gallo-Italic language, where Latin /-p-/ > /v/ is a regular change, unlike in Italian. Compare the doublet recepire.

fact.text: From Latin recipere (to take back). The Italian form may have been influenced by Gallo-Italic languages where Latin -p- regularly became -v-, creating ricevere instead of the expected recepire.

etymology: From ricevere (“to receive”).
From Vulgar Latin *requaerere, from Latin requīrere with dissimilation of /r–r/ to /d–r/, from re- with quaerere, from Proto-Indo-European.

fact.text: From Latin requaestio (inquiry), which gave English 'request' and 'question'. The Italian path went through Old French requeste.

etymology: From ri- + cominciare.
From Latin recognōscere.

fact.text: From Latin recognoscere (re- + cognoscere, to know). The same root gives English 'cognition' and 'cognitive'.

senses.note: Transitive verb; often used with objects like faces, voices, or situations.

etymology: From Latin recordārī.

fact.text: From Latin recordari: re- 'back' + cor 'heart, mind'. To remember was to bring something back to the heart, like the English 'learn by heart'. English record has the same origin.

senses.note: ricordare qualcosa a qualcuno = to remind someone of something (Gli ricordava... = It reminded him...).

etymology: Deverbal from ricordare + -o. Compare Sicilian rigordu.

fact.text: Comes from ricordare, from Latin recordari, which is built on cor ('heart'). The ancients thought memory lived in the heart, which is why we still learn 'by heart'.

senses.note: Means a single remembered thing. The ability to remember is memoria. Can also mean souvenir.

etymology: From ri- + costruire.

senses.note: An -isc- verb: ricostruisco, ricostruisci. Also used for reconstructing events or facts.

etymology: Literally, “cooked again”, from Latin recocta. See ricuocere.

fact.text: Literally 'cooked again' from Latin recocta. Ricotta is made by reheating the whey left behind from mozzarella or other cheese production, giving it its name.

senses.note: Soft whey cheese, made from leftover whey after making other cheeses

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin rīdere, from Latin rīdēre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin ridere, to laugh, which also gave English 'ridiculous' and 'deride'. Its past participle riso also means 'laughter'. Riso meaning 'rice' is an unrelated word.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle riso, passato remoto risi. To laugh at someone = ridere di qualcuno.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin rīdiculus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin rīdiculus, the same root as English 'ridicule'. Both mean 'worthy of laughter or mockery'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin redūcere (“to reduce”).
From ri- + entrare (“to enter”).
From Latin referre (“to bear or bring back”).

fact.text: Shares its Latin root referre with English 'refer' and 'reference' — all mean to bring something back or point to it.

etymology: Inherited from Latin refūtāre (“to oppose, refute”). The -i- was an influence by fiutare (“to sniff”). Doublet of refutare.

fact.text: From Latin refūtāre (to oppose, refute). The -i- was influenced by fiutare (to sniff), creating the sense of 'turning away'.

senses.note: transitive; reflexive form rifiutarsi also exists

etymology: Borrowed from Latin reflectere. By surface analysis, ri- + flettere.

fact.text: From Latin reflectere (re- + flectere, to bend), giving English reflect and reflection. The physical sense of light bending led to the mental sense of thinking.

senses.note: Irregular past participle: riflesso. Transitive or intransitive depending on meaning.

etymology: From Latin refugium.

fact.text: In the Alps and Dolomites, a rifugio is a staffed mountain hut that serves meals and offers beds to hikers and climbers, often at high altitude.

senses.note: In the mountains, a rifugio is a mountain hut.

etymology: From ri- + guardare. Compare French regarder.

fact.text: Composed of ri- (again) and guardare (to look), the literal sense of looking again evolved to mean to regard or concern oneself with something.
Built just like English regard: ri- plus guardare, 'to look'. Both go back to a Germanic word for watching, the source of English ward and guard.

senses.note: a riguardo = about it; riguardo a = regarding, about.

etymology: From Latin relaxāre.

senses.note: Transitive: rilassare i muscoli. To relax yourself, use rilassarsi. Fare rilassare qualcuno = to help someone relax.

fact.text: From Latin relaxare, 'to loosen again'. English 'release' comes from the same Latin verb, through Old French.

senses.note: Rilassati! = Relax! Takes essere: mi sono rilassato.

etymology: From Late Latin relevium, from Latin relevō (“to raise”).

senses.note: In geography, rilievi are hills or mountains. Mettere in rilievo = to emphasize.

etymology: From Latin remanēre, from re- + maneō.

fact.text: From Latin remanere, the same source as English 'remain'. Its root manere, 'to stay', also gave English 'mansion' and 'manor', which were originally places where you stay.

senses.note: Irregular: rimango, rimasi, rimasto. Takes essere in compound tenses.
Reflexive verb with essere. Also means to recover from illness.

etymology: From rin- + fresco + -are.

fact.text: The related noun rinfresco means a small reception or buffet with drinks and snacks, the kind served after a wedding or a christening.

senses.note: Takes avere when it has an object (rinfrescare la stanza), essere for weather: è rinfrescato = it got cooler.

etymology: From rin- + grazie + -are.

fact.text: Built on grazie ('thanks'), which comes from Latin gratia, the source of English 'grace' and 'gratitude'.

senses.note: Takes a direct object: ti ringrazio. For the reason, use per/di: grazie per l'aiuto.

etymology: From Latin renovāre.

fact.text: From Latin renovare, made from re- 'again' and novus 'new'. English 'renovate' comes from the same verb, and 'novel' and 'nova' share the novus root.

senses.note: Used for renovating a place and for renewing documents: rinnovare il passaporto.

etymology: From Latin renuntiāre (“to reject, retract, revoke”).

fact.text: From Latin renuntiāre, composed of re- (back) and nuntiāre (to announce). The same root gives English 'nuncio' (papal ambassador).

senses.note: Often used with 'a' (rinunciare a): to give up or abandon something.

etymology: Inherited from Latin reus. Compare Romanian rău (“bad”), Dalmatian ri (“bad”). Doublet of the borrowed Italian reo.

senses.note: Archaic/poetic. Not to be confused with the noun rio (stream; a small canal in Venice).

etymology: Inherited from Latin reparāre.

fact.text: Italian schools used to hold esami di riparazione: September resit exams for students who had failed subjects, literally 'repair exams'.

senses.note: Also: to shelter. Ripararsi dalla pioggia = to take shelter from the rain.

etymology: From Latin repetere.

senses.note: Ripetere l'anno = to repeat a school year (be held back).

etymology: Alteration of rapido (“fast”) influenced by ripa (“shore”).

fact.text: An altered form of rapido (fast), reshaped under the influence of ripa (bank, shore), as if describing a steep riverbank.

senses.note: Una salita ripida = a steep climb.

etymology: From ri- + pieno.
From Latin reportāre.

senses.note: Also: to report (news) and to suffer (riportare ferite = to sustain injuries).

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin repausāre, from Latin pausāre. By surface analysis, ri- + posare.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin repausare, 're-pause', which also gave English 'repose' (via French). It goes back to Greek pausis, the source of English 'pause'.

senses.note: Also used reflexively: riposarsi = to have a rest. Riposi in pace = rest in peace.

etymology: Deverbal from riposare + -o. Compare French repos, Spanish reposo, Portuguese repouso, Romanian repaus.

senses.note: giorno di riposo = day off; in riposo = retired; Riposo! = At ease! (military)

etymology: From Latin reprehendere.

fact.text: From Latin reprehendere, which also gave English 'reprehend'. Italian kept that meaning too: riprendere can mean to scold someone.

senses.note: Riprendere il lavoro = to go back to work. Can also mean to film or to scold.
Riprendi quello che hai detto! = Take back what you said!

etymology: From ri- + pristino + -are.

fact.text: Built from ri- (again) + pristino (original state) + -are. Pristino is a cousin of English 'pristine', so the word literally means to make pristine again.

senses.note: To return something to its earlier state. Also used in tech: ripristinare il sistema (restore the system).

etymology: From riscaldare + -mento.

senses.note: Also a sports warm-up: fare riscaldamento = to warm up.

etymology: From rischio + -are.

From Old Italian risco, from Vulgar Latin *resecum or deverbal from resecare, via risicare and later riscare, rischiare, both from Latin resecō (“to cut off”). Compare Sicilian rìsicu.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin *resecum via Old Italian risco. The term entered Italian through maritime trade, possibly influenced by Arabic 'rass' (headland/cape), though the Latin derivation from resecare 'to cut off' is primary.

etymology: From rischio + -oso.

fact.text: From rischio (risk) + -oso (suffix meaning 'full of'), following the same pattern as English 'risky' from risk.

senses.note: Can also mean check, confirmation, or reply.

etymology: From Latin rīsus.

fact.text: Italian has two words spelled riso: 'rice', from Greek oryza like English rice, and 'laughter', from Latin risus. Only the laughter one has the odd feminine plural le risa.

senses.note: Usually uncountable: il riso. Don't confuse it with riso meaning 'laughter' (plural le risa).

etymology: From Latin resolvere, possibly a semi-learned borrowing.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle risolto, passato remoto risolsi. Also 'to resolve, to settle'.

etymology: From riso + -otto.

fact.text: From riso (rice) + the diminutive suffix -otto. Risotto is a creamy rice dish typical of northern Italy, especially the Piedmont and Lombardy regions.

etymology: From ri- + sparmiare, the latter (now archaic) from Late Latin sparmiāre, from a Germanic source, likely Lombardic *sparōn (“to spare, save”) (compare Old High German sparōn, German sparen), from Proto-Germanic *sparōną. The development of the -m- in the Late Latin form (instead of the expected -n- or -r-) is traditionally attributed to the influence of Frankish *waidanjan (“to earn, gain”) (which also yielded guadagnare). Cognate with French épargner, Occitan esparnhar, and English spare. Related to sparagnare.

fact.text: Cognate with English 'spare': both trace to Germanic *sparōn via different Romance and English paths, meaning to set aside or preserve.

senses.note: Transitive: to save money, economize, put by.

etymology: From Latin respectāre.
From Latin respectus.

fact.text: From Latin respectus. English 'respect' is cognate—both derive from the idea of 'looking back at' or regarding someone with consideration.

etymology: From Late Latin respondere, from Latin respondēre.

fact.text: From Latin respondere, 're-' + spondere 'to pledge', so literally 'to pledge back'. Spondere also gave English sponsor and spouse.

senses.note: rispondere a qualcuno/qualcosa. Irregular: risposi, risposto.

etymology: From rispondere, corrupted by posta, feminine past participle of porre. Compare Asturian and Spanish respuesta; Catalan, Galician, and Portuguese resposta.

senses.note: Dare una risposta = to give an answer. Plural: le risposte.

etymology: Noun use of present participle of ristorare (“to restore”)

fact.text: It literally means 'restoring', from ristorare, 'to restore'. In 18th-century France a restaurant was first a restorative broth, and the name later passed to the places that served it.

senses.note: A trattoria or osteria is usually simpler and cheaper than a ristorante.

etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin resultāre, from resiliō.

senses.note: Also used for a match score: il risultato della partita.

fact.text: The musical term ritardando, meaning gradually slowing down, comes from the related verb ritardare, 'to delay'.

senses.note: essere in ritardo = to be late; il treno è in ritardo = the train is late.

etymology: From ri- + tirare.

senses.note: Also 'to collect, pick up' (ritirare un pacco). Ritirarsi = to retreat or to retire.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin rhythmus, from Ancient Greek ῥυθμός (rhuthmós), from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”).

fact.text: From Greek rhythmos, from rheo 'to flow', so rhythm was originally a 'flow'. The same Indo-European root probably also gave English stream.

etymology: From Latin retornāre, corresponding to ri- + tornare.

senses.note: Uses essere for 'go back' (sono ritornato) and avere for 'give back'. Very close to tornare.
Biglietto di andata e ritorno = return (round-trip) ticket. In sport also 'second leg'.

etymology: From ri- + trovare. Compare French retrouver.

senses.note: Ritrovarsi = to meet up again, or to end up somewhere.

etymology: From ri- + uscire. Compare French réussir, borrowed via riuscita.

fact.text: Literally ri- + uscire, 'to go out again', so 'to come out well'. French réussir ('to succeed') was borrowed from this Italian word.

senses.note: riuscire a + infinitive. Takes essere. Non riesco = I can't (manage).

etymology: From riuscire.

fact.text: From riuscire (to succeed, to turn out), itself from ri- (again) + uscire (to exit/leave)—literally a way out or successful conclusion.

etymology: Inherited from Latin revidēre. By surface analysis, ri- + vedere.

fact.text: From Latin revidēre. Composed of ri- (again, from re-) + vedere (to see), literally 'to see again'. English "review" follows the same path.

senses.note: Transitive, irregular. Past participle: rivisto. Also means 'to see again' or 'to return to'.

fact.text: Watch out: Italian magazzino means warehouse or storeroom, not magazine. A magazine you read is una rivista.

senses.note: Can also mean a military review or a variety stage show (revue).

etymology:
From Vulgar Latin rauba, of Germanic origin, via Gothic or Frankish *raub, all from Proto-Germanic *raubaz.
Cognate with Sicilian robba, English robe, rob, and reave; and Scots reif (“robbery, stolen goods”).

fact.text: It shares a Germanic root with English rob and robe. The word first meant plunder, and clothing was a common kind of loot.

senses.note: An uncountable singular noun: la mia roba = my stuff. Che roba! = What a thing!

etymology: Borrowed from French robot, borrowed from Czech robot, from robota (“drudgery, servitude”), from Old Czech robota, from Proto-Slavic *orbota, from *orbiti + *-ota.
Borrowed from Old French roche, from Early Medieval Latin rocca, of uncertain origin. Doublet of rocca.

fact.text: It has a twin: 'rocca', from the same Medieval Latin rocca, which means a fortress on a crag. That's why so many Italian towns are called Rocca something.

senses.note: Plural rocce (no i). For a small stone use 'sasso' or 'pietra'.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English rock.

senses.note: Only the music genre. A rock or stone is roccia or sasso.

etymology: Borrowed from English romantic.

fact.text: Borrowed from English romantic, which comes from the medieval 'romances': tales written in the Romance vernacular rather than Latin. So the word traces back to Roma. Related: Italian romanzo means 'novel'.

senses.note: Also used for the Romantic movement (Romanticismo), e.g. i poeti romantici. Plural: romantici, romantiche.

etymology:
Borrowed from Old French romanz, which stems from the Latin expression romanice loqui (“to speak in the Roman way”).
Cognate with English romance (noun).

fact.text: Means a novel, not a romance. Medieval stories got the name because they were written in the everyday Romance language ('in the Roman manner') instead of Latin.

senses.note: Masculine: il romanzo giallo = crime novel. A love affair is usually 'storia d'amore'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin rumpō, rumpere (“to break”).

fact.text: From Latin rumpere, also behind rupture and interrupt. English bankrupt comes from Italian banca rotta, a 'broken bench' of a failed money-changer.

senses.note: Past participle rotto. Colloquially rompere (le scatole) = to annoy someone.

etymology: From Latin rosa.

fact.text: Pink is the colour of Italian cycling. La Gazzetta dello Sport is printed on pink paper, and the Giro d'Italia leader wears the maglia rosa (pink jersey).

senses.note: Never changes its ending: le camicie rosa. Also means romantic or gossip (cronaca rosa).

etymology: From Latin rosa.

fact.text: Pink is the colour of Italian cycling. La Gazzetta dello Sport is printed on pink paper, and the Giro d'Italia leader wears the maglia rosa (pink jersey).
From rosso 'red' plus the diminutive -etto, so literally 'a little red one'.

senses.note: Mettersi il rossetto = to put on lipstick.

etymology: From Latin russus. Cognate with Sicilian russu.

fact.text: Comes from Latin russus, which goes back to the same Proto-Indo-European root, *h₁rewdʰ-, as English red.

senses.note: Also used for red or ginger hair: capelli rossi.
Feminine of rotondo: una pancia rotonda = a round belly. As a noun, la rotonda = roundabout.

etymology: Inherited from Latin rotundus; otherwise an assimilated or relatinized form of Old Italian ritondo, from Late Latin retundus, variant of the classical term.

fact.text: It comes from Latin rotundus, which also gave English rotund and rotunda, a round domed building like the Pantheon.

senses.note: Also used for people: plump, chubby. Una tavola rotonda = a round table.

etymology: Inherited from Latin rupta [via], compare French route.

fact.text: From Latin rupta (via), literally 'broken way'. The same root gave French route and Spanish ruta, all referring to a path that was 'broken' or cleared through the land.

senses.note: Primarily nautical/aviation usage; also means defeat, rout.

etymology: Borrowed from French roulotte.

fact.text: Borrowed from French. It goes back to Old French ruele, a little wheel, so the name basically means 'the thing on little wheels'.

senses.note: A French loanword, invariable: la roulotte, le roulotte. A desert caravan is carovana.

etymology: From earlier ruina, from Latin ruīna.

senses.note: Also a run-down place. In the plural, le rovine means ruins or remains.

etymology: From Latin ruīnāre (“to ruin”). By surface analysis, rovina + -are. Compare Spanish ruinar, arruinar, French ruiner, Piedmontese ruiné, ruviné.

fact.text: From Latin ruina, from ruere, 'to fall down'. Ruins were literally things that had fallen, which is why this verb can also mean to collapse.

senses.note: Takes avere when transitive (to ruin, to spoil). With essere it means to collapse or crash down.
Also the past participle of rovinare (to ruin). Used of things, plans, and people who are financially ruined.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin raubāre, from Proto-West Germanic *raubōn.

fact.text: Comes from a Germanic verb meaning 'to plunder', the same source as English 'rob'. It is also related to 'robe': stolen clothing was some of the most common loot.

senses.note: Rubare qualcosa a qualcuno = to steal something from someone.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English rum.
From Latin rūmōrem ("rustle," "murmur").

fact.text: False friend: this means 'noise', not 'rumour'. Both words come from Latin rumor, 'murmur, rustle'. For a rumour, Italians say una voce ('a voice') or una diceria.

senses.note: Fare rumore = to make noise. A 'rumour' is una voce or una diceria.

etymology: From rumore + -oso; cognate with Piedmontese rumoros.

fact.text: Built on rumore, 'noise', not 'rumour' (in Italian that is voce or diceria). Both words come from Latin rumor, which meant common talk or murmuring.

senses.note: Used for places and people: vicini rumorosi. For a loud voice or loud music, use forte or alto.

etymology: From Latin rota

fact.text: From Latin rota, 'wheel', which also gives English 'rotate', 'rotary' and 'rotation'.

senses.note: Ruota panoramica = Ferris wheel; ruota di scorta = spare wheel.

etymology: From Latin rūgidus, from ruga (“wrinkle”). Cognate with Piedmontese rùvid.

fact.text: From Latin rūgidus, from ruga ('wrinkle'). The connection is physical: wrinkles and rough texture go together, so the word for 'wrinkled' came to mean 'rough' or 'coarse'.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin sabbatum. Compare English Sabbath.

fact.text: Most Italian weekdays are named after planets and gods, but this one comes from Hebrew shabbat via Latin sabbatum, the same source as English 'Sabbath'.

senses.note: Written in lowercase. Il sabato = on Saturdays; sabato = this Saturday.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *sabla, from a contraction of Latin sabula, plural of sabulum, variant of sabulō. Compare French sable, Occitan sabla.

senses.note: Le sabbie mobili = quicksand.

etymology: Inherited from Latin saccus, from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos, “sack, bag; sackcloth”), from Semitic.

fact.text: This word started in a Semitic language and passed into Greek sákkos and Latin saccus. English 'sack' comes from the same source, so it is one of the oldest travelling words.

senses.note: Un sacco di = a lot of (colloquial): un sacco di formaggio = loads of cheese.

etymology: From Late Latin exagium, from Latin exigō (“to examine”).

fact.text: From Late Latin exagium, related to the root meaning to weigh or test; reflects the essay's role as a test of thought.

senses.note: A written composition of moderate length.

etymology: Borrowed from Lombardic *sala (“hall”), from either Proto-Germanic *saliz or *salą (both meaning "house, hall").

fact.text: This Germanic loanword is related to German Saal. Its Italian augmentative salone went into French as salon, which gave English both 'salon' and 'saloon'.

senses.note: Used for big or public rooms: sala da pranzo (dining room), sala d'attesa (waiting room).

etymology: From sale (“salt”).

fact.text: English borrowed the Italian plural 'salami' and uses it as a singular. The word comes from sale (salt), because the meat is cured with salt.

senses.note: Singular salame, plural salami. Colloquially also 'fool' (che salame!); vulgar slang for penis.
Informally also means pricey: un conto salato = a steep bill.

etymology: Deverbal from saldare + -o.

senses.note: Il saldo del conto = the account balance.
In this sense usually plural: i saldi (estivi/invernali) = the (summer/winter) sales.

etymology: Inherited from Latin salem.

senses.note: 'Sale e pepe' = salt and pepper. Plural 'sali' mostly means chemical salts or smelling salts.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin salīre.
Cognate with Spanish salir (“to go out”) and French saillir (“to stick out”).

fact.text: From Latin salire 'to jump', the root of English 'salient' and 'sally'. Its Spanish cognate salir means 'to go out'. Don't mix them up: 'to go out' in Italian is uscire.

senses.note: Irregular: salgo, salgono. Uses essere (sono salito), but avere with an object: ho salito le scale.

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of salire (“to go up”).

senses.note: In salita = uphill; the opposite is la discesa. Also a rise (of prices).

etymology: Inherited from Latin salmōnem.

fact.text: From Latin salmōnem, which also gave English 'salmon'. The word entered European languages from a pre-Latin Mediterranean source, possibly Basque.

senses.note: Masculine; plural 'salmoni' (countable), though uncountable when referring to color.

etymology: From sala + -otto; cognate with Piedmontese salòt.

senses.note: Can also mean a literary or social salon, e.g. salotto letterario.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *salsa, noun use of the feminine of Latin salsus (“salted”), from saliō, from sal.

fact.text: From Latin salsus, 'salted', from sal, 'salt'. English 'sauce' comes from the same Latin word via French, so a sauce was once simply something salted.

senses.note: Pasta sauce is often called 'sugo' (sugo al pomodoro).

etymology: Inherited from Latin saltāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin saltare, which meant both 'to jump' and 'to dance'. It is a frequentative of salire 'to leap', a verb that means 'to go up' in Italian.

senses.note: Also 'to skip' (saltare la colazione) and 'to blow up' or 'be cancelled'.

etymology: From Latin saltus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin saltus 'leap'. English 'somersault' comes from Old French, ultimately from Latin supra 'over' + saltus 'leap'.

senses.note: Fare un salto = to jump; also 'to pop over' (faccio un salto da te).

etymology: From Latin salūtāre.

fact.text: It comes from Latin salutare, from salus (health), so a greeting first meant wishing someone good health. English salute comes from the same root.

senses.note: Also used for saying goodbye. Salutami Marco = say hi to Marco for me.

etymology: From Latin salūtem, from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“whole, completed”).

fact.text: Italians say 'Salute!' both when making a toast and when someone sneezes, wishing them good health. It comes from Latin salus, the same root as English 'salute' and 'salutary'.

senses.note: Said when raising a glass. Cin cin! is also common.
Said to someone who has just sneezed.

etymology: From Latin salūtem, from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“whole, completed”).

fact.text: Italians say 'Salute!' both when making a toast and when someone sneezes, wishing them good health. It comes from Latin salus, the same root as English 'salute' and 'salutary'.

senses.note: Salute! is used both as a toast ('Cheers!') and after a sneeze ('Bless you!').

etymology: From salutare.

fact.text: It comes from salutare, from Latin salus, 'health'. A greeting was a wish for good health. English salute and salutary come from the same source.

senses.note: 'Saluti' or 'cari saluti' at the end of a letter = regards / best wishes.

etymology: From Late Latin salvāre (“to save”), from Latin salvus. Compare French sauver, Portuguese and Spanish salvar.

fact.text: Related to English 'safe' and 'salvation' via Latin salvus (safe, whole). Spanish 'salvar', French 'sauver', and Portuguese 'salvar' share the same root, making it one of the most stable Romance words.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin salvē.

fact.text: This was how the ancient Romans greeted each other. Latin salve means 'be well', from salvere 'to be in good health'.

senses.note: A polite greeting that works with strangers. It sits between casual ciao and formal buongiorno.

etymology: Ultimately from Sanskrit चन्दन (candana).

fact.text: Two unrelated words that look the same: the shoe comes from Greek sandalion, while the fragrant wood comes from Sanskrit candana via Persian and Arabic. The same is true of English sandal and sandalwood.

senses.note: Usually plural: i sandali. The same word also means sandalwood (the tree).

etymology: From Late Latin sanguem, alteration of Classical Latin sanguinem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sh₂-én-, oblique stem of *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”). Compare French sang, Romanian sânge.

fact.text: Latin sanguis gave English sanguine. It first described a ruddy, blood-dominated temperament, which medieval medicine linked to a cheerful, optimistic mood.

senses.note: Mostly uncountable; the plural sangui is rare. A sangue freddo = in cold blood.

etymology: From Latin sānus, from Proto-Indo-European *swā-n- (“healthy; whole; active; vigorous”).

fact.text: From Latin sanus, 'healthy, whole', which also gave English 'sane' and 'sanitary'. In Italian it is mostly about the body, not the mind.

senses.note: For people and food: cibo sano. Sano e salvo = safe and sound.
Masculine: santo. Used before female saints' names (Santa Maria). As an adjective it means 'holy'.

etymology: Derived from Latin sānctus.

senses.note: Also functions as an adjective (santo/santa = holy). As a noun, refers to a saint.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sapēre, from Latin sapĕre (“taste, know”).

fact.text: Latin sapere first meant 'to taste', then 'to be wise', hence Homo sapiens, 'wise man'. Italian keeps the taste sense too: sa di fragola means 'it tastes of strawberry'.

senses.note: Used for facts and skills (so nuotare = I can swim). For knowing people or places, use conoscere.

etymology: From Latin sāpōnem, from Proto-Germanic *saipǭ.

fact.text: Latin borrowed sapo from Germanic *saipo, the same word that became English 'soap'. So the Italian and English words are cousins, with the Romans as the borrowers.

senses.note: Countable for bars: 'un sapone'; uncountable for the substance.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sapōrem (“taste, flavor”).

fact.text: From Latin sapor, from sapere 'to taste, to be wise'. The same verb gives Italian sapere 'to know', English 'savor', and the sapiens in Homo sapiens.

senses.note: Sapere di = to taste of: sa di fragola (it tastes of strawberry).

fact.text: From French, named after Adolphe Sax, the Belgian inventor who patented it in 1846. The instrument's name is one of the few where we know exactly who it's named after.

etymology: From s- + bagliare (see also abbagliare). See bagliore. Compare Sicilian sbagghiari for more.

senses.note: sbagliarsi = to be mistaken. With an object it means to get wrong: sbagliare strada = take the wrong road.

etymology: Deverbal from sbagliare (“to make a mistake”) + -o.

senses.note: Per sbaglio = by mistake. Fare uno sbaglio = to make a mistake.

etymology: The prefix im- (“into, in”) of imbarazzare (formerly meaning "to impede") is replaced with s- (“remove, reverse”), resulting in a meaning “to remove the obstacle”.

fact.text: Made by swapping the im- of imbarazzare (once 'to hinder') for s- ('undo'), so it means 'to un-hinder'. English 'embarrass' comes from the same root and first meant 'to obstruct'.

senses.note: Mostly reflexive: sbarazzarsi di qualcosa. Without si: to clear (a table, a room).

etymology: From s- + battere, or possibly a Vulgar Latin *exbattere, from Latin battuere.

senses.note: Sbrigati! = Hurry up! Uses essere: mi sono sbrigato. Note -gh- before e/i.

etymology: From s- + buccia + -are.

fact.text: It is built from s- (removing) plus buccia, 'peel, skin', so it literally means 'to un-skin'.

senses.note: Sbucciare una mela = to peel an apple. Sbucciarsi un ginocchio = to scrape your knee.

etymology: Derivative of scaffa.

senses.note: Can mean a single shelf or a whole bookcase/shelving unit; also supermarket shelves.

etymology: Inherited from Latin scāla (“stair, staircase, ladder”).

fact.text: Milan's La Scala opera house is named after the church of Santa Maria alla Scala, which once stood on its site. The church was named after Beatrice Regina della Scala of the Scaligeri family.

senses.note: Often plural: le scale = the stairs. Also means ladder and scale (musical, map).

etymology: From scalare + -tore.

senses.note: Also used in cycling for a rider who is strong on climbs. Feminine: scalatrice.

From Vulgar Latin *excappāre, a verb based on Late Latin cappa (“cloak”).

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin excappāre, based on cappa (cloak) — originally meant to slip out of one's cloak to escape a pursuer.

senses.note: or escape, flee

etymology: From Latin scarabaeus, from Ancient Greek κάραβος (kárabos, “beetle”).

fact.text: From Ancient Greek kárabos (beetle), the same root that gave the English word 'scarab'. The scarab was sacred in ancient Egypt and appears as a protective amulet.

etymology: From s- + caricare.

fact.text: Made from s- (reversal) + caricare (to load), so it literally means to unload. Downloading a file is 'unloading' it onto your device.

senses.note: Also means to unload (goods) or to vent. Scaricarsi = to go flat (of a battery).

etymology: From s- + carico.

senses.note: Also means empty, flat (battery), or run-down (clock).

From Gothic *𐍃𐌺𐌰𐍂𐍀𐌰 (*skarpa) or *𐍃𐌺𐌰𐍂𐍀𐍉 (*skarpō), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skarpaz.

fact.text: A Germanic loanword, probably from Gothic, ultimately linked to Proto-Germanic skarpaz, which gave English sharp. Its 'sloping wall' sense gave English scarp and escarpment.

senses.note: Usually plural: le scarpe. Scarpe da ginnastica = trainers or sneakers.

etymology: Metathesised form of Early Medieval Latin castula (“basket”), diminutive of a term borrowed from a Germanic language, *kasto, whence also Italian castone, German Kasten. Compare Sicilian scàtulu.

fact.text: Rompere le scatole (literally 'to break the boxes') means to annoy someone. It is a polite stand-in for a much ruder expression.

senses.note: Also a tin or can: una scatola di pomodori. Scatola nera = black box.

etymology: From Latin excavāre.

fact.text: From Latin excavare, the source of English 'excavate'. The ruins of Pompeii are signposted in Italian as gli Scavi di Pompei, 'the Pompeii excavations'.

senses.note: Gli scavi = excavations or archaeological digs.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exēligere, from Latin ex (“out of, from”) + ēligere.

fact.text: From ex + Latin eligere 'to pick out'. Eligere also gave English elect and eligible.

senses.note: Irregular: scelgo, scelgono, scelsi, scelto.

etymology: From scegliere.

senses.note: Fare una scelta = to make a choice. A scelta = of your choice. From scegliere.

etymology: From scemare.

fact.text: Derives from 'scemare' (to diminish). The idea is that a fool has diminished sense or judgment.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin scēna, from Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ).

fact.text: From Ancient Greek skēnḗ meaning 'tent' or 'stage building'. The same root gave English scene, scenery, and obscene.

etymology: From a reduction of the prefix in discendere, from Latin dēscendere.

fact.text: A shortened form of discendere, from Latin descendere, which also gave English 'descend'. Italian simply dropped the first syllable.

senses.note: Takes essere: sono sceso. Scendere dal treno = to get off the train.

etymology: Borrowed from English sheriff.

fact.text: Borrowed from English 'sheriff', which comes from Old English scīrgerēfa 'shire reeve'. The Italian word reflects the English pronunciation, not the Arabic sharif (despite the spelling similarity).

etymology: Deverbal from schermire (“to protect”) + -o.

fact.text: Originally a shield, from schermire 'to protect', from Germanic *skirmjan. Via French, that root also gave English skirmish, and Italian scherma (fencing).

senses.note: A TV, computer or cinema screen. Grande schermo = the big screen (cinema).

etymology: Borrowed from Lombardic *skerzan (“to jump merrily, enjoy oneself, jest”) from Proto-Germanic *skertaną (“to hop, jump”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerd- (“to dance, jump”). Akin to Middle High German scherzen (“to frolic, jump merrily, hop up and down”) (German scherzen (“to joke”); Scherz (“joke, sport”)), Norwegian skjerta (“to joke”). More at scherzo.

fact.text: Same root as the musical 'scherzo', a lively, playful movement. Both come from a Germanic verb meaning to jump merrily, related to German Scherz, 'joke'.

senses.note: Non sto scherzando = I'm not kidding. Scherzi? = Are you kidding?

etymology: Deverbal from scherzare (“to joke, play, jest”) + -o, from Old Italian scherzare, borrowed from Lombardic *skerzan (“to jump merrily, enjoy oneself, jest”) from Proto-Germanic *skertaną (“to hop, jump”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerǝd- (“to dance, jump”). Akin to Middle High German scherzen (“to frolic, jump merrily, hop up and down”) (German scherzen (“to joke”); Scherz (“joke, sport”)), Norwegian skjerta (“to joke”).

fact.text: From Lombardic *skerzan 'to jump merrily'. Related to German Scherz and Scherzen. The musical meaning (scherzo) came later, borrowed back into Italian from its use in German music terminology, though the root is Germanic.

etymology: Probably onomatopoeic; the figurative sense influenced by French écraser. Compare Galician escachar. Cognate with Sicilian scacciari.

fact.text: Tuscany's schiacciata, a flat olive-oil bread, literally means 'squashed', named after dough pressed flat by hand.

senses.note: Also to press: schiacciare un pulsante. Colloquial: schiacciare un pisolino = take a nap.

etymology: From Lombardic skina, related to Old Saxon skina, German Schiene and English shin.

fact.text: It comes from the Lombards' Germanic word skina, which is related to German Schiene and to English shin. A shin bone ended up naming the whole back!

senses.note: Mal di schiena = backache. Not used for 'back' meaning the rear of something (that's retro).

etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan esquiera, from Old French eschiere, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skarō, whence also Old English sċearu, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to part; split; cut off; sever; divide”). Compare German Schar (“troop”), Danish skare (“host", "crowd”).

fact.text: A Germanic loanword related to German Schar, 'troop'. It comes from a root meaning 'to cut or divide', which also gave English 'share' and 'shear'.

senses.note: Also a troop or host of people: una schiera di fan. Schierarsi = to line up, or to take sides.

etymology: From Old French eschiu (“shy, timid”) (cf. eschiver), from Frankish *skeuh (“shy, timid, fearful”), from Proto-Germanic *skeuhaz (“shy, frightened”). Cognate with English shy, Sicilian schifiju (“disgust, mess”). More at shy, eschew.

fact.text: Goes back to a Germanic word meaning 'shy, fearful', the same root as English shy and eschew. What started as shying away from something came to mean disgust.

senses.note: Che schifo! = how gross! Fa schifo = it's disgusting or it sucks (colloquial).

etymology: From schifo + -oso.

senses.note: Comes from schifo (disgust): Che schifo! = How gross! Also used loosely for 'lousy' or 'awful'.

etymology: Borrowed from Norwegian ski.

fact.text: Italian and English both took the word from Norwegian ski, which comes from Old Norse skíð, 'stick of wood' or 'snowshoe'.

senses.note: It takes lo because it starts with the sc sound. Fare sci = to go skiing.
The plural doesn't change: gli sci = the skis.

etymology: From sci + -are

fact.text: Italian spells ski as sci, pronounced like English 'she'. The word reached Italian from Norwegian via French ski.

senses.note: Note the forms io scio, tu scii, noi sciamo. Andare a sciare = to go skiing.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin scientia.

fact.text: Latin scientia simply meant knowledge, from sciens, 'knowing'. Coscienza (conscience, consciousness) comes from the same root: con- + scientia, 'knowing together'.

senses.note: Scienze (plural) is also the school subject. Uomo di scienza = man of science, scientist.

etymology: From earlier scimia, Latin sīmia, from Ancient Greek σῑμός (sīmós, “snub-nosed”). For more examples of initial s- palatalized to sci-, see scialiva, scempio, sciringa (doublet of siringa). Compare Sicilian scìmia.

fact.text: From Greek sīmós (snub-nosed), the literal physical description. The initial s- softened to sci- in Italian, a common sound shift seen in scialiva and sciringa.

senses.note: Feminine. Plural: scimmie. From Greek sīmós (snub-nosed).

etymology: From Latin exsolvere (“to unloose, release, free; to unbind, untie, undo”). Compare Sicilian sciògghiri.

fact.text: From Latin exsolvere 'to loosen, release', a relative of solvere, which gives English solve, dissolve and solution. That is why it can mean both to melt and to untie.

senses.note: Irregular: sciolgo, sciolto. For something melting by itself, use sciogliersi: la neve si scioglie.
Feminine past participle of sciogliere (to melt, to untie): la neve si è sciolta.

etymology: Deverbal from scioperare + -o.

fact.text: Comes from the verb scioperare, usually traced to Vulgar Latin *exoperare, 'to be without work' (ex- + operare). The word first meant simply being idle, long before it meant an organised walkout.

senses.note: Fare sciopero = to go on strike; essere in sciopero = to be on strike; sciopero generale = general strike.

etymology: From Medieval Latin siruppus, syrupus, from Arabic شَرَاب (šarāb, “a drink, beverage, wine, coffee, syrup”), from شَرِبَ (šariba, “to drink”).

fact.text: Comes from Arabic šarāb, 'a drink', from šariba, 'to drink'. The same Arabic root gave English sherbet and Italian sorbetto, so syrup and sorbet are distant cousins.

senses.note: Also used for medicine: sciroppo per la tosse = cough syrup.

etymology:
The word is probably of onomatopoeic origin.
From Latin exsībilāre. .
Also possibly a portmanteau of sci (“ski”) + volare (“to fly”), which is perhaps a folk etymology.

senses.note: Takes essere when you slip: sono scivolato/a.

etymology: From s- + commettere.

fact.text: From s- (a prefix denoting separation) plus commettere (to commit/put together). The sense evolved from 'to set aside' to 'to wager', reflecting how a bettor risks or separates themselves from money.

senses.note: transitive verb

etymology: From s- + comodo.

senses.note: Also inconvenient (un orario scomodo). Opposite: comodo.

etymology: From s- + comparire (“to appear”). Cognate with Sicilian scumpàrriri.

senses.note: Takes essere: è scomparso. Irregular: scompaio, scomparve. Also a gentle way to say someone died.

etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan esconfire, from Latin *excōnficiō, from ex- + cōnficiō.

fact.text: From Old Occitan esconfire, via Latin *exconficio (to undo thoroughly). The past participle sconfitto is irregular.

senses.note: Irregular verb

etymology: Deverbal from scongiurare + -o.

fact.text: Where English speakers knock on wood, Italians touch iron (tocca ferro) or make the horns gesture with index and little finger to ward off bad luck.

senses.note: 'Fare gli scongiuri' = to knock on wood. 'Ti scongiuro' (I beg you) is the verb scongiurare.

etymology: From s- (“un-”) + conosciuto (“known”).

senses.note: Feminine: la sconosciuta. Also an adjective meaning unknown: un posto sconosciuto.

etymology: From Latin discomputus (literally “calculated off”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin discomputus, meaning 'counted off'. English 'discount' has the same origin, via Old French.

senses.note: fare uno sconto = to give a discount. Example: uno sconto del 20%.

etymology: From scontrare + -ino.

fact.text: Italian businesses must issue a receipt for every sale as an anti-tax-evasion measure, so you'll be handed one even for a single espresso.

senses.note: The till slip. A formal invoice is 'la fattura'; a written receipt is 'la ricevuta'.

etymology: From Late Latin scōpāre (“to brush or sweep away”), from Latin scōpae (“broom”).
