From Late Latin scopus (“target”).

fact.text: From Late Latin scopus, borrowed from Ancient Greek skopós ('target, mark'). The root originally meant 'to look at'—a target is what you look toward.

etymology: From s- + coprire (“cover”).

fact.text: It is s- plus coprire, 'to cover', so it literally means 'un-cover'. English dis-cover works exactly the same way.

senses.note: Irregular past participle: scoperto. Also means to uncover. La scoperta = a discovery.

etymology: From Latin excursus.

fact.text: This is the past participle of scorrere, 'to flow, run by' (Latin excurrere). L'anno scorso is literally the year that has run past.

senses.note: l'anno scorso = last year. For 'last' meaning final, use ultimo.

etymology: Inherited from Latin scrīptōrem.

senses.note: The feminine form is la scrittrice.

etymology: From scrivano + -ia.

fact.text: Built from scrivano, 'scribe or clerk', + -ia, so it was originally the clerk's place. It shares its root with scrivere, 'to write'.

senses.note: A writing or office desk. A school desk is 'il banco'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin scrībere.

senses.note: Irregular past participle: scritto (ho scritto).

etymology: From Latin sculptōrem. Cognate with Friulian scultôr, Lombard scultor, Piedmontese scultor.

senses.note: Takes lo because it starts with s + consonant. The feminine is la scultrice.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin sculptūra (“act of carving; sculpture”), derived from sculpō (“to carve”) + -tūra (“-ing, -ure”, action noun suffix).

senses.note: Means both the art form and a single work. A sculptor is lo scultore.

etymology: Inherited from Latin schola. First attested in the 14th century. Compare Sicilian scola.

fact.text: Comes from Latin schola, which came from Greek scholē. Oddly, scholē first meant 'leisure': time free for discussion and learning. It is the same root as English 'school'.

senses.note: Andare a scuola = to go to school (no article). Scuola media = middle school.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *exquatere, *excotere, a remodelling of Latin excutere on simplex quatere. Compare Romanian scoate (“remove”). Cf. also escutere, a borrowed doublet.

fact.text: Goes back to Latin excutere, built on quatere 'to shake', the same root behind English concussion and percussion.

senses.note: Irregular: scossi, scosso. scuotere la testa = to shake one's head.

etymology: From oscuro, from Latin obscūrus.

fact.text: A shortened form of oscuro, from Latin obscurus, which also gave English 'obscure'. The first o simply dropped off over time.

senses.note: With colours: blu scuro = dark blue. Figuratively also gloomy or grim.
Chiedere scusa = to apologize. On its own, Scusa! = Sorry! (informal; Scusi! is formal).
Scusa is informal (tu). Scusi is formal (Lei).

etymology: From Latin excūsāre.

senses.note: Scusa (informal), Mi scusi (formal), Scusate (to a group) = Excuse me / Sorry.
Reflexive verb; used with reflexive pronouns (mi, ti, si, ci, vi)
This is the formal (Lei) form of scusare. With friends, say scusa.

etymology: Probably inherited from Vulgar Latin *exdēradiāre.

fact.text: A deck chair or sun lounger is a 'sdraio', short for 'sedia a sdraio'. That is the chair you lie back on at an Italian beach, next to the ombrellone (beach umbrella).

senses.note: To lie down yourself is reflexive: sdraiarsi (mi sdraio). Plain sdraiare means to lay someone down.

etymology: From sdraiare + -si.

fact.text: An Italian beach staple is la sdraio, the deckchair, short for sedia a sdraio, 'a chair for lying down'. Rows of them fill every stabilimento balneare.

senses.note: Takes essere: mi sono sdraiato. Sdraiati! = lie down!

etymology: From Latin sī (“if”) or from Late Latin se(d), from Latin sī and quid ("what").

senses.note: Also means 'whether'. Don't confuse it with sé (oneself), which has an accent.

etymology: Univerbation of se (“if”) + bene (“well”).

fact.text: Formed by combining se (if) and bene (well) into one word. The compound univerbation reflects how "if well" transformed into a causal conjunction over time.

etymology: From Latin siccus, from Proto-Indo-European *seyk-.

fact.text: Comes from Latin siccus. The same root gave French sec and, through 'wyne sack' (vin sec), the old English word 'sack' for dry fortified wines like sherry.

senses.note: Also 'dried' (fichi secchi) and 'very thin'. Vino secco = dry wine.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin saeculum.

fact.text: From Latin saeculum, 'lifetime, age'. The same word gave English 'secular': things of this worldly age rather than eternal or religious.

senses.note: Plural: i secoli. Il Novecento = the 20th century. Da secoli = for ages.

etymology: From Latin secundus (“he who follows, second”), from sequor (“to follow”). Cognate with Sicilian sicunnu.

fact.text: From Latin secundus, from sequor 'to follow': the second is literally 'the one that follows'. Latin secundus could also mean 'favourable', from the idea of a wind that follows your ship.

senses.note: Also a noun (un secondo = a second of time) and a preposition: secondo me = in my opinion.

etymology: From Latin secundus (“he who follows, second”), from sequor (“to follow”). Cognate with Sicilian sicunnu.

fact.text: From Latin secundus, from sequor 'to follow': the second is literally 'the one that follows'. Latin secundus could also mean 'favourable', from the idea of a wind that follows your ship.

senses.note: Un secondo! = just a second!
Usually meat or fish, served after the primo (pasta or rice).
Means 'according to me'. 'Secondo te' = 'in your opinion'. The source gloss mixes me/you.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sēdēs.

fact.text: From Latin sēdēs ('seat, abode'). The word reflects the original sense of a physical location or 'seat' of authority or an organization.

etymology: From Latin sedēre, from Proto-Italic *sedēō, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.

fact.text: From Latin sedēre. The past participle seduto is used in many Romance languages; English sedentary shares the same Latin root.

senses.note: Can be intransitive (to sit) or transitive (to seat someone).
Irregular present: mi siedo, ti siedi, si siede. Takes essere: mi sono seduto. Si sieda! = please sit down (formal).

etymology:
From sedere.
The initial auto-gemination found in some regional Italian varieties seems to be unetymological.

fact.text: Comes from sedere, 'to sit', the same Latin root as English 'sedentary' and 'sediment'.

senses.note: sedia a rotelle = wheelchair; seggiovia = chairlift.

etymology: From Latin sēdecim.
Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of sedere, sedersi (“to sit”).

fact.text: From the feminine past participle of sedere (to sit) — the word literally captures the idea of sitting as an event or gathering.

senses.note: Common in institutional/political contexts, like parliamentary sessions.

etymology: From Late Latin signāle < signālis, from Latin signum.

senses.note: segnale stradale = road sign; un segnale = a signal or sign that something happens.

etymology: From Latin signum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”) or *sekʷ- (“to follow”).

fact.text: From Latin signum, derived from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (to cut) or *sekʷ- (to follow)—literally something marked or distinguished by cutting.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin sēcrētārius, from Latin sēcrētus. By surface analysis, segreto (“secret”) + -ario (“-ary”).

fact.text: From Medieval Latin secretarius, from secretus 'secret'. A secretary was originally a person trusted with confidential matters, a keeper of secrets.

senses.note: Female: la segretaria. Il segretario del partito is the leader of a political party.

etymology: From segretario + -eria.

fact.text: La segreteria telefonica is an answering machine or voicemail, so a recorded message is literally the 'telephone secretary's office'.

senses.note: Also a secretariat or administration office, e.g. at a school or university.

etymology:
* adjective: From Latin sēcrētus (perfect passive participle of sēcērnō)
* noun: From Latin sēcrētum (noun form of secretus)

fact.text: From Latin secretus, past participle of secernere meaning 'to separate or set apart'. A secret is something kept separate. English 'secrete' (to hide or produce in secret) comes from the same Latin root.

senses.note: As a noun it is masculine: il segreto, i segreti. As an adjective: un passaggio segreto = a secret passage.

etymology:
* adjective: From Latin sēcrētus (perfect passive participle of sēcērnō)
* noun: From Latin sēcrētum (noun form of secretus)

fact.text: From Latin secretus, past participle of secernere meaning 'to separate or set apart'. A secret is something kept separate. English 'secrete' (to hide or produce in secret) comes from the same Latin root.

etymology: From Latin sequentem.

senses.note: Il giorno seguente = the next day. Often comes after the noun.
Seguì (accented) = he/she followed, passato remoto. Segui (no accent) = you follow / follow!

etymology: From earlier *sequire, from Vulgar Latin *sequīre of deponent Classical Latin sequī, from Proto-Italic *sekʷōr, from Proto-Indo-European *sékʷetor, derived from the root *sekʷ- (“follow”).

fact.text: From Latin sequi, 'to follow', which also gave English sequel, sequence and consequence.

senses.note: Also means 'to take' a course or 'to keep up with': seguire un corso = to take a course.

etymology: Deverbal from seguitare + -o.

fact.text: From seguitare (to follow) + -o. Literally 'what follows', same root as English 'sequel' from Latin sequi.

senses.note: Can mean continuation of a story or the people following someone.

etymology: From Latin sex, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.

fact.text: One spelling, two common words: 'six' and 'you are' (from essere). 'Sei stanco?' means 'Are you tired?', but 'sei mele' means 'six apples'. The context always tells you which.

senses.note: This is the tu form of essere: (tu) sei, 'you are'.

etymology: From Latin sex, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.

fact.text: One spelling, two common words: 'six' and 'you are' (from essere). 'Sei stanco?' means 'Are you tired?', but 'sei mele' means 'six apples'. The context always tells you which.

etymology: From Latin sescentī (“six hundred”).

Borrowed from Old Occitan salvatge, from Vulgar Latin *salvāticus, from Latin silvāticus (“of the woods”). Doublet of the inherited selvatico. Compare Sicilian sarbaggiu, Spanish salvaje, Portuguese selvagem, Catalan salvatge, Piedmontese salvaj.

fact.text: From Latin silvaticus, 'of the woods' (silva = forest). English 'savage' comes from the same word through French, so a savage was first just someone from the forest.

senses.note: Used for animals, land and people: animali selvaggi, una costa selvaggia.

etymology: Borrowed from French sémaphore.

fact.text: From Greek sema 'sign' + -phoros 'carrier', just like English 'semaphore'. In Italian the old signalling word became the everyday name for traffic lights.

senses.note: Al semaforo = at the lights. Semaforo rosso/verde = red/green light.

etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan semblar, from Late Latin similāre, a verb based on Latin similis (“similar”). More or less a doublet of somigliare.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin similare, which is based on similis ('similar'). English 'semblance' and 'resemble' come from the same source by way of French.

senses.note: Takes essere: è sembrato. mi sembra = it seems to me / I think.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sēmen, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₁mn̥.

fact.text: Comes from Latin semen 'seed', which English kept as 'semen'. It is also behind 'seminar' and 'seminary', from Latin seminarium, a seed plot or nursery.

senses.note: Also a suit in playing cards (e.g. 'seme di cuori', hearts).

etymology: From Latin semestris (“six months”), from sex (“six”) + mensis (“month”).

fact.text: From Latin semestris: literally six months (sex = six, mensis = month). The same root structure appears in English semester.

etymology: Attested from ca. 1261. A cross of inherited sempice, semprice with Latin simplicem, from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together, one”) + *pleḱ- (“to plait, to weave”). Compare duplice, molteplice. Partial doublet of scempio.

fact.text: From Latin simplex, roughly 'one-fold' (sem- 'one' + a root for folding or weaving). Compare duplice, 'twofold', and English duplex.

senses.note: Can also mean 'plain' or 'ordinary': un semplice impiegato = just an ordinary clerk.

etymology: From semplice + -mente.

senses.note: Formed from semplice + -mente, like English -ly.

etymology: Inherited from Latin semper; compare Catalan and Portuguese sempre, Spanish siempre.

fact.text: From Latin semper, as in Semper Fidelis ('always faithful'), the motto of the US Marine Corps.

senses.note: Can also mean 'still': è sempre lì = it's still there. Per sempre = forever.

etymology: From Latin senātus.

fact.text: From Latin senātus, derived from senex (old man)—the Roman Senate was literally a council of elders.

etymology: From Latin senātōrem.

fact.text: Simply se + no, 'if not', fused into one word. The n doubles because of how Italian pronounces words after se.

senses.note: Common in speech: Sbrigati, sennò perdiamo il treno. Also written se no.

etymology: From Latin sēnsātiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin sensatio, related to sensus (sense, feeling). English 'sensation' is a direct cognate, both preserving the Latin root meaning perception through the senses.

etymology: From Latin sēnsus.

senses.note: non ha senso = it makes no sense. senso unico = one-way (street).

etymology: Borrowed from Old French sentier, from Early Medieval Latin sēmitārius, derived from Latin sēmita.
From Latin sentimentum.

senses.note: Means an emotional feeling. A physical feeling is a sensazione.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sentīre.

fact.text: One verb covers hearing, feeling and even smelling (sentire un profumo). It comes from Latin sentire, 'to perceive', the root of English 'sense' and 'sentiment'.

senses.note: Senti! = Listen! / Hey! Unlike ascoltare (to listen), sentire is just perceiving the sound.
Reflexive for how you are: mi sento bene = I feel well.
Ci sentiamo! = Talk soon! Also 'to feel': mi sento bene = I feel fine.

etymology: From Latin sine (“without”) conflated with absentia (“without, in the absence of”). Compare French sans.

fact.text: From Latin sine. English "senile" (without vigor) shares a distant root, though sine's origins are debated—possibly from Proto-Indo-European 'self' or 'this'.

senses.note: Preposition/conjunction. Often pairs with -re infinitives: senza dire (without saying).

etymology: From Latin sine (“without”) conflated with absentia (“without, in the absence of”). Compare French sans.

fact.text: From Latin sine. English "senile" (without vigor) shares a distant root, though sine's origins are debated—possibly from Proto-Indo-European 'self' or 'this'.

senses.note: Before personal pronouns use senza di: senza di te.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin sēparāre. Doublet of the inherited severare, older form of sceverare; compare also disceverare.

senses.note: Separarsi = to split up, for example a couple. Separati = separated.
Irregular past participle of seppellire (to bury).

etymology: From Latin sepultūra.

fact.text: From Latin sepultura, from sepelire 'to bury'. Italian sepolcro and English 'sepulchre' come from the same verb.

senses.note: Sepoltura celeste = sky burial. Related verb: seppellire (to bury).

etymology:
From Late Latin sēra, from ellipsis of Latin sēra diēs, from sērus (“late”).
Cognate with Venetan séra, Friulian sere, Sicilian sira, Romanian seară, Romansh saira and French soir m. See also Latin sērōtinus (“late; (relational) evening”).
Compare typologically Spanish tarde, Mongolian орой (oroj), Chinese 晚 (wǎn) (the terms meaning both “evening” and “late”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin sera dies, 'the late part of the day', from serus, 'late'. Related to French soir. In Spanish, tarde likewise means both 'late' and 'afternoon/evening'.

senses.note: Buona sera = good evening. Di sera = in the evening; stasera = this evening.

etymology: From sera (“evening”) + -ata.

fact.text: The suffix -ata turns a point in time into a span you live through: sera/serata, giorno/giornata, mattina/mattinata, anno/annata.

senses.note: serata = the evening as a span or event (una bella serata). sera = evening as a time of day.

etymology: From Latin serēnus (“calm”).

fact.text: The idiom un fulmine a ciel sereno, 'a lightning bolt from a clear sky', is Italian for a bolt from the blue: something completely unexpected.

senses.note: Of a person or mood: stai sereno = don't worry.
Of the sky or weather: cielo sereno = clear sky.

fact.text: From Old French 'sergeant' (one who serves), derived from Latin 'servientem' (servant). The word travelled through Romance languages and into English, maintaining its military sense.

etymology: From serio + -mente.

senses.note: Used like English 'seriously' to mean 'honestly, really': Seriamente, è bravo.

etymology: Derived from Latin seriēs.

fact.text: From Latin seriēs. English series is the direct borrowing from the same Latin word. Both languages use the identical form.

senses.note: Invariable in both singular and plural forms.

etymology: From Latin sērius (“grave, earnest, serious”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy”).

senses.note: Sul serio means 'seriously' or 'for real': Dici sul serio? = Are you serious?

etymology: From serrare.

fact.text: From serrare (to close/lock). A serra is a closed structure—the name reflects its defining characteristic of being sealed to trap heat.

etymology: From serrare + -tura.

senses.note: The mechanism in a door; the padlock is il lucchetto. Keyhole: il buco della serratura.

etymology: From Latin servīre.

senses.note: Mi serve aiuto = I need help (literally 'help is needed to me'). Uses essere.

etymology:
Borrowed from Latin servitium, from servus (“slave”).
Compare Portuguese serviço, French service, Norman sèrvice, Sicilian sirbizzu, Spanish servicio.

senses.note: On a restaurant bill it means a service charge. 'I servizi' = toilets or facilities.

etymology: From Latin sexāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱsḱomt, from earlier *swéḱs-dḱomt (“six-ten”).
From sessanta (“sixty”) + cinque (“five”).
From sessanta (“sixty”) + due (“two”).
From sessanta (“sixty”) + nove (“nine”).
From sessanta (“sixty”) + quattro (“four”).
From sessanta (“sixty”) + sei (“six”).
From sessanta (“sixty”) + sette (“seven”).
From sessanta (“sixty”) + tre (“three”).
From sessanta (“sixty”) + otto (“eight”).
From sessanta (“sixty”) + uno (“one”).
From Latin sexus.

fact.text: From Latin sexus. One theory links it to secare, 'to cut', as in humankind being divided into two halves. This is uncertain.

senses.note: Covers both senses: being male or female, and the act. 'Fare sesso' means to have sex.

etymology: From Latin sēta, from saeta, from Proto-Italic *saitā, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂ito-, *sh₂éyto-, from *sh₂ey-, *seh₂i- (“to bind”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese seda.

fact.text: Latin saeta first meant a bristle or stiff hair. Silk was called 'seta serica', the hair of the Seres (the Chinese), which was later shortened to just seta.

senses.note: Plural 'sete' looks just like 'sete' (thirst). Also means bristle.

etymology: From Latin sitim, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰgʷʰítis (“decay; destruction”), derived from the root *dʰgʷʰey- (“to decline; to perish”).

fact.text: Latin 'sitis' traces back to an Indo-European root meaning 'to waste away'. Its Greek cousin 'phthisis' (wasting) became an old English medical name for tuberculosis.

senses.note: 'Avere sete' = to be thirsty (literally 'to have thirst').

etymology: From Latin septuāgintā, from *septmāginta, from Proto-Indo-European *septm̥̄ḱomt, from earlier *septḿ̥-dḱomt (“seven-ten”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + cinque (“five”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + due (“two”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + nove (“nine”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + quattro (“four”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + sei (“six”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + sette (“seven”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + tre (“three”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + otto (“eight”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + uno (“one”).
From Latin septem, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.

fact.text: It comes from Latin septem, which also gave us September. That was the seventh month in the early Roman calendar, which started the year in March.

etymology: From Latin septem, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.

fact.text: It comes from Latin septem, which also gave us September. That was the seventh month in the early Roman calendar, which started the year in March.

etymology: From sette (“seven”) + cento (“hundred”).
From Latin September, Septembrem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin septem, 'seven'. It was the seventh month of the early Roman calendar, which began in March. Ottobre, novembre and dicembre likewise mean 'eight', 'nine', 'ten'.

senses.note: Months are not capitalised in Italian: a settembre = in September.

etymology: From Late Latin septimāna (“week”), from the Latin septimānus (“related to the seventh element of a series”, adjective), derived from septimus (“seventh”). Compare Romanian săptămână.

fact.text: From Late Latin septimana, which comes from septimus, 'seventh': a week was a unit of seven days. The same root is in English 'September'.

senses.note: Feminine: la settimana. Il fine settimana = the weekend.
Also an adjective meaning 'weekly'. Compare quotidiano (daily) and mensile (monthly).

etymology: From Latin sectōrem.
Borrowed from Latin sectiōnem.

senses.note: Also means department, class stream, or electoral district.

etymology: From s- + fiore, compare French effleurer.

fact.text: Formed from s- plus fiore, 'flower'. French effleurer is built the same way. The image is of touching only the top or flower of something.

senses.note: Also 'to come close to': sfiorare la vittoria = to nearly win.

etymology: From s- + fortuna.

senses.note: Che sfortuna! = What bad luck! The prefix s- negates fortuna (luck).

etymology: From s- + fortunato.

fact.text: Built with the prefix s- (un-) + fortunato (fortunate). It's a transparent negation, like saying 'un-fortunate' in English.

etymology: Deverbal from sforzare (“to force”) + -o or sforzarsi (“to strain oneself, to push oneself”) + -o. Compare French effort, Spanish esfuerzo, Catalan esforç, Portuguese esforço.

fact.text: A cousin of English 'effort' (from French), and both go back to Latin fortis 'strong'. The opening s- is a worn-down form of the Latin prefix ex- 'out'.

senses.note: fare uno sforzo = to make an effort.

etymology: From s- + frutto + -are.

fact.text: Composed of the prefix s- plus frutto (fruit/profit) plus the verb suffix -are. The root frutto relates to English 'fruit', reflecting the sense of extracting value or benefit.

senses.note: transitive; often implies unjust or excessive use of resources or labor

etymology: Deverbal from sguardare + -o, variant of guardare (“to watch”).

fact.text: From guardare (to watch) with the prefix s-, which intensifies the meaning. Sguardo literally captures the moment of looking itself, making it more vivid than the simple guardare.

senses.note: A brief or casual look

etymology: Borrowed from English shampoo, from Hindi चाँपो (cā̃po, “knead!”), from the Sanskrit root चपयति (capayati, “to pound, to knead”).

fact.text: Italian borrowed it from English, which took it from Hindi chāmpo, meaning 'press!' or 'knead!'. It first referred to a head massage, not to soap.

senses.note: Takes 'lo' because of the sh- sound. The plural doesn't change: gli shampoo.
Also written Sst! or Ssh! A worded alternative: Zitto! / Zitta! (Be quiet!).

etymology: From Latin se (“him-, her-, it-, themselves”, reflexive third-person pronoun). Cognate with Spanish se and Portuguese se and si.

fact.text: One accent changes everything: without it, si is the pronoun 'oneself'; with it, sì means 'yes'. Si sì? reads as 'oneself yes?' if you mix them up.

senses.note: Also impersonal 'one/you': non si può = you can't. Don't confuse with sì (yes).

fact.text: Same form as the present subjunctive of essere, 'be it'. So sia A sia B is literally 'be it A, be it B'.

senses.note: Used as sia… sia… or sia… che…. With che it can mean whether… or…. Either… or… is usually o… o….

etymology: Univerbation of sì (“as”) + come.

senses.note: Usually opens the sentence: Siccome piove, resto a casa. Never 'since' in the sense of time.

etymology: From Sicilia + -ano.

fact.text: From Sicilia (Sicily) + the suffix -ano, used to form adjectives relating to regions and peoples.

etymology: From sicuro + -mente.

senses.note: Can also mean 'safely', since sicuro means both 'sure' and 'safe'.

etymology: From sicuro + -ezza. Compare Romanian siguranță.

fact.text: From sicuro (secure) + -ezza. The suffix -ezza creates abstract nouns from adjectives, similar to how English -ness works: sicuro becomes sicurezza, just as English secure becomes security.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sēcūrus. Compare Spanish seguro.

fact.text: From Latin securus, from se- 'without' + cura 'care', so originally 'carefree'. English got both 'secure' and 'sure' from this same Latin word.

senses.note: Also means safe/secure: un posto sicuro = a safe place. Sicuro! = Of course!

fact.text: Borrowed from Spanish cigarro, whose origin is uncertain. It may come from cigarra (cicada), perhaps for its shape, or from a Mayan word for smoking, like Yucatec Maya siyar.

senses.note: Masculine: il sigaro, i sigari. A cigarette is la sigaretta.

etymology: From Latin significāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin significare, from signum (sign) + facere (to make), so literally 'to make a sign'. English 'signify' and 'significant' come from the same Latin root.

senses.note: Cosa significa? = What does it mean? Voler dire is a common everyday alternative.

etymology: From Medieval Latin seniōra, feminine form of senior (“lord”).

fact.text: Built on Latin senior, 'older', which came to mean 'lord'. English senior comes from the same word, and so, through Old French sire, does sir.

senses.note: Also Mrs before a surname: la signora Rossi. Drop the article when speaking to her directly.

etymology: From earlier segnore, from Latin seniōrem, comparative form of senex (“old”), from Proto-Indo-European *sénos. Doublet of sire.

fact.text: From Latin senior 'older', the source of English senior, and related to sir, sire and Spanish señor. Respect went to the elders.

senses.note: Also 'sir' when addressing a man. Il Signore = the Lord.
Drops the -e before a name: il signor Rossi.

etymology: From signora (“lady”) + -ina.

senses.note: Used for young or unmarried women. Many people now find it dated and use signora instead.

etymology: From Latin silentium.

senses.note: Masculine: il silenzio. 'Fare silenzio' = to be quiet.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin silentiōsus.

senses.note: Of people, places or machines: una strada silenziosa = a quiet street.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin syllaba, from Ancient Greek συλλαβή (sullabḗ).

fact.text: From Greek syllabe (from syn- together + lambanein to take). English syllable shares the same Greek ancestor.

etymology: From Latin similis.

fact.text: From Latin similis, 'like'. English borrowed the neuter form as 'simile', the figure of speech that compares two things using 'like' or 'as'.

senses.note: Stress on the first syllable: SÌ-mi-le. Simile a = similar to; una cosa simile = such a thing.

etymology: From simpatia (“sympathy”) + -ico (“-ic, -ical”), ultimately from Ancient Greek σῠμπᾰ́θειᾰ (sŭmpắtheiă, “sympathy”, literally “suffering together”).

fact.text: Despite the look-alike, this word doesn't mean 'sympathetic'. It means nice or likeable. Its opposite, antipatico, describes someone unpleasant.

senses.note: Used for pleasant, friendly people. 'Sympathetic' in English is comprensivo or solidale.
Simpatico describes a nice personality. Carino means cute or pretty, for people or things.

etymology: From Latin syndicus.

fact.text: It comes from Greek syndikos, 'advocate'. The related word sindacato means trade union, not a crime syndicate.

senses.note: Head of a comune (town council). Also used for a woman: la sindaca or il sindaco.

etymology: Borrowed from English single.

fact.text: Directly borrowed from English 'single'. Both derive from Latin singulus, a diminutive meaning 'one'.

etymology: Borrowed from English single.

fact.text: Directly borrowed from English 'single'. Both derive from Latin singulus, a diminutive meaning 'one'.

etymology: Probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin singulāris. By surface analysis, singolo + -are. Doublet of cinghiale.

fact.text: Same Latin source as cinghiale (wild boar). The boar was the singularis porcus, the 'solitary pig', because it lives alone.

senses.note: Grammar term, and also 'remarkable, odd': un tipo singolare = an odd character.

etymology: From Latin singulus.

senses.note: Means individual or separate. For 'unmarried' Italians say single, or celibe/nubile.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sinister.

fact.text: Latin sinister just meant 'left'. Because the left side was linked with bad omens, English 'sinister' came to mean threatening or evil.

senses.note: a sinistra = on/to the left. Also the political left. The adjective form is sinistro/a.

etymology: From Late Latin systēma, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma).

fact.text: Borrowed from Ancient Greek systema, meaning 'a whole made of parts'. The English word 'system' shares the same Greek root.

etymology: From sistema + -are.

senses.note: Transitive; can mean to arrange, organize, fix a problem, lodge someone, marry off, or find a job for.
senses.prompt: to arrange, lay out, or settle

etymology: From Latin situs (“position”), from a noun use of the perfect passive participle of sinō (“to put, lay”).

senses.note: Very often short for sito web/internet = website.

etymology: From situare + -zione.
From s- + mettere.

senses.note: Smettere di + infinitive: ho smesso di fumare = I quit smoking. Past participle: smesso.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *succursum, from Latin succursus. Compare French secours.

fact.text: In Italy, signs for 'Pronto Soccorso' (literally 'ready help') point you to a hospital's emergency department.

senses.note: Pronto soccorso = A&E / emergency room. 'Chiamare i soccorsi' = to call emergency services.

etymology: From Latin sociālis (“of or pertaining to companionship; social”), from socius (“associated, allied; partner, associate, companion”).

fact.text: Shares the Latin root socius (companion) with English 'associate' and 'society'. The root reflects the idea of people joined together.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin societātem ("community, society", accusative form), from socius (“partner, ally”). By surface analysis, socio + -età. The senses of "association" and "company" were borrowed later. Doublet of soccida, which was inherited from the Latin nominative societās.

fact.text: From Latin societās, from socius ('partner, ally'). The root shares the same PIE origin as English 'social'—meaning 'one who follows or accompanies'.

senses.note: Invariable noun; same form singular and plural.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin sociābilis, remodeled based on -evole. By surface analysis, socio (“affiliate, fellow”) + -evole.

senses.note: Poco socievole = unsociable, not very outgoing.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin socius (“partaking, associated; partner, associate”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷyo- (“companion”), derived from the root *sekʷ- (“to follow”). Compare also the inherited soccio.

fact.text: From Latin socius 'associate, companion', derived from Proto-Indo-European *sekw- meaning 'to follow'. A socio is literally someone who follows alongside you.

senses.note: Also slang term of address for a man: dude, pal.

etymology: From earlier satisfatto, from Latin satisfactus, past participle form of satisfaciō (“reparation, amends”).

fact.text: From Latin satisfactus (satisfied, from satisfacere: satis 'enough' + facere 'to do'). Literally 'having done enough'.

senses.note: Past participle form used as adjective. Agrees with gender/number.

etymology:
From Vulgar Latin *suffīctus, perfect passive participle of Latin suffīgō (“to fasten or fix onto”); compare Classical Latin suffīxus.
Cognate with Piedmontese sofit.

fact.text: English took 'soffit', the underside of an arch or roof overhang, from this word. Both go back to Latin suffigere 'to fasten underneath'.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *sufferīre, from Latin sufferre.

fact.text: From Latin sufferre (sub- 'under' + ferre 'carry, bear'), literally 'to carry under' or 'to bear/endure'; the same root gives English 'suffer'.

senses.note: Transitive or intransitive; can mean endure pain, hardship, or tolerate something.

etymology: From Latin subiectum.

senses.note: A school subject is 'materia', not soggetto. Colloquially, un bel soggetto = quite a character.

etymology: Deverbal from soggiornare (“to stay, sojourn”) + -o.

fact.text: A relative of English 'sojourn' (a short stay). Both come, via Old French, from Late Latin subdiurnare, meaning roughly 'to spend the day'.

senses.note: Also means a stay: un soggiorno a Roma = a stay in Rome. permesso di soggiorno = residence permit.

etymology: From Latin somniāre (“to dream; to daydream”). By surface analysis, sogn(o) (“dream”) + -are (first conjugation verbal suffix).

fact.text: Comes from Latin somniare, from somnium ('dream'). The same root is behind English insomnia and somnambulist.

senses.note: sognare di + infinitive: sogno di viaggiare. Can also be reflexive: me lo sono sognato.

etymology: From Latin somnium (“dream”), derived from somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Italic *swepnos, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *swépnos.

fact.text: From Latin somnium 'dream', from somnus 'sleep'. That Latin word is also behind English 'insomnia' and 'somnambulist' (sleepwalker).

senses.note: Sognare = to dream. Un sogno nel cassetto = a secret dream (literally 'a dream in the drawer').
