Past participle of the archaic verb soldare (“to pay a soldier or military member”), from soldo (“money, military pay”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese soldado, French soldat, Romansh schuldà.

fact.text: Literally 'paid one': the past participle of the old verb soldare 'to pay troops', from soldo 'pay', which goes back to the Roman gold coin solidus.

senses.note: Female: la soldata, or soldato used for both genders.

fact.text: Soldo comes from the Latin solidus, a Roman gold coin. English 'soldier' has the same source, because soldiers were men paid in coin.

senses.note: Always plural in this sense: i soldi. 'Denaro' is a more formal word for money.

etymology: Inherited from Latin soldus, syncopic form of (nummus) solidus (“solid (coin)”) (referring to the gold content), from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“whole”). Doublet of solido and sodo, and likely also saldo.

fact.text: Goes back to the solidus, a Roman gold coin. English soldier shares the root: through Old French, it first meant someone who fought for pay.

senses.note: The plural i soldi is the everyday word for money: non ho soldi = I have no money.

etymology: From Sole, from Latin sōlem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥. Cognates include Greek ήλιος (ílios), Icelandic sól, Hindi सूर्य (sūrya), and Russian со́лнце (sólnce).

fact.text: It comes from Latin sol, which goes back to the same Proto-Indo-European root as English sun. The Latin form also gave English solar and solstice.

senses.note: 'Prendere il sole' = to sunbathe.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin solidus. Doublet of sodo and soldo.

fact.text: Comes from Latin solidus, also the name of a Roman gold coin. That coin gave Italian soldo (money) and, through French, English 'soldier': someone paid in coins.

senses.note: Also figurative: un'amicizia solida = a solid, reliable friendship.

etymology: Inherited from Latin solitus, perfect active participle of Latin soleō (“to be accustomed to”), from which derives defective modal verb Italian solere.

fact.text: From Latin solere 'to be accustomed'. English 'insolent' shares the root: Latin insolens first meant 'unaccustomed', then 'unusual', then 'haughty' or 'rude'.

senses.note: come al solito = as usual; di solito = usually. Before a noun: il solito caffè.

etymology: From Latin sōlitūdinem.

fact.text: From Latin sōlitūdinem, from solus ('alone'). The same root as English 'solitude' and 'solitary'.

senses.note: The state or feeling of being alone; also a solitary place.

etymology: From Latin sollicitus.

fact.text: From Latin sollicitus, composed of sollus (whole, entire) and cieō (move, stir). Originally meant agitated or stirred up, evolving to mean attentive and prompt.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sublevāre. By surface analysis, so- + levare.

fact.text: From Latin sublevare, 'to lift from below'. It is built on levare, 'to raise', the same root as English lever, elevate and levitate.

senses.note: Also 'to raise' (sollevare una questione). Sollevarsi = to rise up or to feel relieved.

etymology: Derived from Latin sōlus.

fact.text: English borrowed solo from Italian music, where a piece for one performer was played 'alone'. The source is Latin solus, which also gave English sole and solitary.

senses.note: Da solo / da sola = by oneself. Sto solo = I'm alone.
Il solo amico = the only friend. Also an adverb: solo due euro = only two euros.

etymology: Derived from Latin sōlum.

fact.text: English borrowed solo from Italian music, where a piece for one performer was played 'alone'. The source is Latin solus, which also gave English sole and solitary.

senses.note: As an adjective, solo means 'alone': sono solo = I'm alone.

etymology: From solo (“only”) + tanto (used meaning "only" as Latin tantum).

senses.note: An adverb, like 'solo': 'Ho soltanto dieci euro.' For the adjective 'the only one', use 'unico'.

etymology: From Latin solūtiōnem.

senses.note: Verb: risolvere (to solve).

etymology: From Latin summa.

fact.text: From Latin summa, from summus (highest, topmost), the superlative of superus (upper). Literally the highest point, extended to mean total or aggregate.

senses.note: Also: amount, addition, gist, essence, summit, pinnacle

etymology: From Latin somnus, from Proto-Italic *swepnos, from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos, from the root *swep- (“to sleep”). Cognate with Dalmatian samno, French somme, Lithuanian sãpnas, Romanian somn, Spanish sueño.

fact.text: From Latin somnus, the source of English 'insomnia'. Its root, PIE *swep- 'to sleep', also gave Greek hypnos, which is where 'hypnosis' comes from.

senses.note: Avere sonno = to be sleepy. Don't confuse it with sogno (dream).
Form of essere. The same form also means 'they are'.

etymology: From Latin supportāre (“to carry, bring, convey, transport”), from sub- (“under”) + portāre (“to carry”). Doublet of supportare, a borrowing from French.

fact.text: From Latin supportāre (sub- 'under' + portāre 'to carry'). The English 'support' shares the same root, though Italian focuses on bearing/enduring.

senses.note: Common in phrases like 'non posso sopportare' (I can't bear).

etymology: Inherited from Latin suprā. Compare older sovra and Sicilian supra.

fact.text: Comes from Latin supra, 'above', which also gives English the prefix supra-, as in 'supranational'.

senses.note: Opposite: sotto (below). Also a preposition: sopra il tavolo = on/above the table.

etymology: Inherited from Latin suprā. Compare older sovra and Sicilian supra.

fact.text: Comes from Latin supra, 'above', which also gives English the prefix supra-, as in 'supranational'.

senses.note: Also an adverb: di sopra = upstairs. Before pronouns: sopra di me.

etymology:
From sopra- + tutto.
Akin to French surtout and Spanish sobre todo.

senses.note: Literally 'over everything', like French surtout and Spanish sobre todo.

etymology: From sopra- + vivere.

fact.text: Compound of sopra (over, beyond) + vivere (to live). Literally 'to live over or beyond', expressing survival through or past a challenge.

senses.note: Intransitive. Often takes 'a' (sopravvivere a una prova) or implies 'over/beyond' (sopra-vivere).

etymology: From Latin surdus (“silent”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“ringing, whistling”).

fact.text: From Latin surdus, 'deaf, silent'. English 'absurd' probably shares the root: Latin absurdus first meant 'out of tune', and 'surd' in maths is also linked to it.

senses.note: Also muffled or dull: un rumore sordo (a thud), un dolore sordo (a dull ache).

etymology: From Latin soror, from a diminutive form or based on the model of fratello. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *swezōr, from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr.

fact.text: Latin soror, its source, also gave English sorority. Further back, Latin soror and English sister both come from the same Indo-European word, *swésōr.

senses.note: Also used for a nun: suor(a). Sorellina = little sister.

etymology: From sorella + -astra.
First attested in the 13th century. From sor- + prendere, possibly on the calque of Old French sorprendre.

fact.text: From sor- (over) + prendere (to take). First attested in the 13th century. The compound mirrors meaning: to take/catch off guard or by surprise.

senses.note: Transitive; irregular verb with past participle sorpreso

etymology: From the feminine of sorpreso, past participle of the verb sorprendere.
From Vulgar Latin *subrīdĕre, from Latin subrīdēre.

fact.text: From Latin subridere, literally 'to laugh underneath': sub (under) + ridere (to laugh). A smile is a quiet, held-back laugh.

senses.note: Past participle sorriso is also the noun 'smile'. Sorridere a qualcuno = to smile at someone.

etymology: From Latin subrīsus.

fact.text: From Latin subridere, literally 'to laugh underneath', so a smile is a held-back laugh. Ridere ('to laugh') is also the root of English 'ridiculous'.

senses.note: Fare un sorriso = to smile. Verb: sorridere.

etymology: From a Vulgar Latin *sorta, itself from Latin sortem, possibly through French sorte.
From Latin sortem, from Proto-Italic *sortis, from the Proto-Indo-European root *ser- (“to sort, lineup”).

fact.text: Latin sors meant a lot drawn to decide something. Through French sorte the same word gave English 'sort', and it also appears in 'consort'.

senses.note: tirare a sorte = to draw lots; ironia della sorte = irony of fate.

etymology: From Latin suspendere.

fact.text: From Latin suspendere (sus- 'up' + pendere 'to hang'). English 'suspend' shares identical Latin origins, preserving the literal sense of hanging something up.

senses.note: Means to hang, interrupt, or suspend in any sense. Note: irregular past participle 'sospeso'.

etymology: From Latin suspectāre.

fact.text: From Latin suspectāre. The English 'suspect' comes from the same Latin root, so pronunciation and meaning are remarkably similar across both languages.

senses.note: transitive: you suspect someone or something

etymology: Borrowed from Latin suspectus (“mistrusted, suspected”, adjective), perfect passive participle of suspiciō (“to mistrust, suspect”).

fact.text: From Latin suspectus, past participle of suspicere ('to look up at, mistrust'), from sub- 'up' + specere 'to look'.

senses.note: Can also mean suspicion or doubt.

etymology: From Latin (nōmen) substantīvum.

senses.note: In grammar, 'nome' is also used for 'noun'.

etymology: From Latin subterraneus, possibly an adaptation to Italian or semi-learned term.

senses.note: As a noun, il sotterraneo means a basement or vault.

etymology: From Latin subtīlem (“thin, slender”).

fact.text: From Latin subtilis, probably sub + tela, 'web', so first 'finely woven'. English 'subtle' comes from the same word, and Italian keeps both meanings: thin and subtle.

senses.note: For objects: un foglio sottile. For a thin person, magro is more common. Also 'subtle'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin subtus, which is derived from Latin sub. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *supo, from Proto-Indo-European *upo. Cognate to French sous.

senses.note: Preposition: sotto il tavolo. Adverb: è qui sotto (it's down here). Opposite: sopra.

etymology: Inherited from Latin subtus, which is derived from Latin sub. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *supo, from Proto-Indo-European *upo. Cognate to French sous.

senses.note: sotto controllo = under control; sotto zero = below zero.

etymology: From sotto- + lineare.
From sotto- + titolo.

fact.text: Literally 'under-title,' from sotto (under) + titolo (title). The prefix sotto- appears in many Italian words meaning something positioned beneath or secondary.

senses.note: Can mean a heading below a title or text on screen in films

etymology: From earlier sottraggere, from Latin subtrahere (“to remove, withdraw”). By surface analysis, sott + trarre.

fact.text: From earlier sottraggere, from Latin subtrahere (to remove, withdraw). The sott- comes from Latin sub- (under), and trarre from trahere (to draw).

senses.note: Irregular verb. Also means 'to take away from' or 'to remove'.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French souvenir.

fact.text: Direct borrowing from French souvenir (remembrance). Both English 'souvenir' and Italian 'souvenir' come unchanged from the French word meaning 'memory'.

senses.note: Invariable; does not change in plural.

etymology: From earlier spata, from Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē), from Proto-Indo-European *sph₂dʰh₁éh₂, derived from *(s)peh₂- (“to draw”) + *dʰeh₁- (“to do; to put”) + *-eh₂ (feminine noun ending). Doublet of spata.

fact.text: From Ancient Greek spáthē meaning 'broad blade', via Latin spatha. The word traveled through multiple languages and influenced the English 'spade' (digging tool), which shares the same Greek root.

etymology: Plural of spaghetto, diminutive of spago (“cord, string”), from Latin spacus (“string”).

fact.text: Derives from spago (cord, string) through diminutive spaghetto. Ultimately from Latin spacus, reflecting the long, string-like shape of the pasta.

senses.note: Plural of spaghetto; the word is singular in Italian despite meaning pasta strands.

etymology: From spago + -etto (“meliorative suffix”).

fact.text: Comes from spago, 'string' or 'twine', plus a suffix meaning 'little'. So spaghetti are literally 'little strings'.

senses.note: Almost always used in the plural: gli spaghetti. The singular means one strand.

fact.text: The name comes from the Phoenician phrase for 'land of rabbits' (sphan/i-span), from a time when the Iberian peninsula was overrun with them. English 'Spain' shares the same origin.

senses.note: Proper noun, feminine (la Spagna). Named for the rabbits that once infested the peninsula.

etymology: From Spagna (“Spain”) + -olo (“derivative suffix”), possibly also from Old Occitan espaignol, from a Vulgar Latin *Hispāniolus, from Latin Hispānus. Compare French espagnol, Portuguese espanhol, Spanish español. Doublet of épagneul.

fact.text: From Latin Hispānus via Spanish España. Related English word 'Spaniard' and French 'épagneul' (spaniel dog breed, originally from Spain) share the same root.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *spatla, from Late Latin spatula, from Classical Latin spatha (“straight sword”). Compare spatola, a borrowed doublet.

fact.text: It comes through Late Latin spatula from spatha, a broad straight sword, probably because the shoulder blade is flat. English spatula comes from the same root.

senses.note: Alzare le spalle = to shrug. Can also mean a sidekick or straight man.

etymology: The modern sense of shooting derives jocularly from the older culinary sense, which is from Vulgar Latin *exparāre, formed as ex- (intensive prefix) + parō (“to prepare”).

fact.text: Its older meaning was culinary: to slit open game or fish to clean it. The shooting sense grew out of that meaning as a joke.

senses.note: Spararle grosse = to tell tall tales. To shoot a film is girare.

etymology: From s- + (ap)parire (“to appear”). Compare Sicilian spariri.

fact.text: From s- (intensive prefix) + apparire (to appear). The s- negates 'appear', creating its opposite. Compare how 'disrespect' flips 'respect'.

senses.note: intransitive; uses essere auxiliary

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *expaventāre, derived from the present participle of Classical Latin expaveō. Compare Spanish, Portuguese, Occitan, and Catalan espantar (also Catalan and Occitan espaventar); French épouvanter; Sicilian scantari; also Romanian înspăimânta.

fact.text: Built on Latin pavere 'to be terrified', via Vulgar Latin *expaventare. The same root gives paura 'fear' and Spanish espantar.

senses.note: Reflexive spaventarsi = to get scared.

etymology: From spavento + -oso.

senses.note: Colloquially also 'tremendous': un traffico spaventoso = terrible traffic.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin spatium, whence also Old Italian spazzo (“floor”), an inherited doublet.

senses.note: Takes lo: lo spazio. Also 'room': C'è spazio = there's room.

etymology: From spazzare + -tura.

fact.text: From spazzare (to sweep) plus the suffix -tura. Spazzatura literally refers to what gets swept up—rubbish or trash.

etymology: From spazzare + -ola, probably influenced by spatola.
From spazzola + -ino.

senses.note: In full: lo spazzolino da denti. Diminutive of la spazzola (brush).

etymology: From Vulgar Latin speclum, syncopated form of Latin speculum, from the verb speciō. Compare specolo, a borrowed doublet.

fact.text: From Latin speculum, from specere 'to look'. English 'speculate' and 'spectacle' come from the same root.

etymology: From Latin speciālis (“specific”, “particular”).

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural speciali.
Invariable singular form; plural rarely used.
Reflexive verb; use -si with reflexive pronouns.

etymology: From specializzare + -zione.
From special(e) (“special”, “particular”) + -mente (“-ly”, adverbial derivational suffix).

senses.note: Same meaning as soprattutto or in particolare.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin speciēs. Doublet of spezie.

fact.text: From Latin speciēs (appearance, form, kind), related to specere (to look). English 'species' shares the same Latin root but via a different path—the Italian specie is its doublet.

senses.note: Also: kind, type, sort. Invariable singular.

etymology: From Latin expedīre.

fact.text: From Latin expedire, literally 'to free the feet' (ex + pes, foot), the same root as English expedite and expedition.

senses.note: Used for mail, parcels and goods. An -isc- verb: spedisco, spedisci.

etymology: Inherited from Latin expingere, from ex- (“out”) + pingo (“paint”), with a semantic change from “remove colour” to “fade, dim”, probably influenced by extingere.

fact.text: Probably from Latin expingere, literally 'to paint out', so 'removing colour' came to mean fading and then putting out a light.

senses.note: Irregular: spengo, spengono; past participle spento. Also 'to put out' a fire or candle.

etymology: From Latin expendere, from ex- + pendō.

fact.text: It comes from Latin expendere, 'to weigh out, pay'. English 'spend' and 'expend' both go back to the same Latin verb.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle speso. For spending time, Italians usually say passare.

etymology: From sperare + -anza, or from Vulgar Latin spērantia, from Latin spērāns. Compare French espérance, Spanish esperanza, Portuguese esperança

fact.text: From Latin sperare + -anza. Cognate with Spanish esperanza and Portuguese esperança through the same suffix. The suffix -anza/-ence/-ence became productive across Romance languages for abstract nouns.

etymology: Inherited from Latin spērāre.

fact.text: From Latin sperare (to hope). English despair comes from the Latin de- plus sperare, so it literally means 'to stop hoping'.

senses.note: Spero di sì = I hope so. Sperare che usually takes the subjunctive.

etymology: From Late Latin expēnsa, from Latin expēnsus, from expendere. Compare Sicilian spisa, Venetan spexa, Romansh spaisa, spesa, Friulian spese, Ladin speisa, spëisa, Piedmontese spèisa, Old French espoise.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin expensa, the same source as English 'expense'. Over time Italian dropped the ex- and the n: expensa became spesa.

senses.note: Often plural: le spese = expenses, costs.
Fare la spesa = to do the grocery shopping. Fare shopping = to shop for clothes and similar.

etymology: Inherited from Latin spissus. Compare Spanish espeso, Portuguese espesso, French épais.

fact.text: Latin spissus meant 'thick, dense'. In Italian the idea of 'dense' stretched to time: things packed closely together happen often. French épais kept only 'thick'.

senses.note: Adjective, agrees with the noun: caviglie spesse = thick ankles.
Adverb, does not change: vengo spesso = I come often.

etymology: Inherited from Latin spissus. Compare Spanish espeso, Portuguese espesso, French épais.

fact.text: Latin spissus meant 'thick, dense'. In Italian the idea of 'dense' stretched to time: things packed closely together happen often. French épais kept only 'thick'.

senses.note: Adverb, invariable: spesso andavano in montagna.
Adjective that agrees with its noun: spesso/spessa/spessi/spesse (un muro spesso).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin spectābĭlis.

fact.text: From Latin spectabilis, 'worth looking at', from spectare 'to watch'. That is the same root as English spectacle and spectator, so a company addressed this way is literally 'remarkable'.

senses.note: Used in business letters, often shortened to Spett.le: Spett.le Ditta = Dear Sirs / Messrs.

etymology: From Latin spectāculum.

fact.text: From Latin spectaculum, from spectare 'to watch', the same source as English spectacle and spectator.

senses.note: Also 'sight, spectacle': che spettacolo! = what a sight!

etymology: From Latin spectāre.
From s- + pezzo + -are. Compare Sicilian spizzari.

Borrowed from a Germanic language, perhaps Gothic *𐍃𐍀𐌰𐌹𐌷𐌰 (*spaiha) or from a Frankish cognate, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (“to see, look”). Cognates include obsolete French épie (“spy”), Spanish espía (“spy”), English spy and German spähen (“to peek, to spy”).

fact.text: Cognate with English spy. Both derive from Gothic/Frankish sources related to Proto-Germanic spehōną (to see). French and Spanish cognates also exist.

senses.note: Also means informer; light/gauge (usually); symptom (figuratively).
Alternative form of dispiacere; often impersonal with dative

etymology: From s- + piaggia. The initial s- is an intensifying prefix. Cognate with French plage, Portuguese praia, Sicilian praja and Spanish playa.

fact.text: Formed from s- + piaggia, an old word for a shore or slope. Close relatives are French plage and Spanish playa.

senses.note: Andare in spiaggia = to go to the beach. Plural drops the i: spiagge.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *spiclu(m), contracted form of Latin spīculum, diminutive of spīcum, alternative form of spīca (“ear of grain”). Doublet of spigolo.

fact.text: Goes back to Latin spica, 'ear of grain', via the diminutive spiculum. It is a doublet of Italian spigolo, 'corner, edge'.

senses.note: uno spicchio d'aglio = a clove of garlic; uno spicchio d'arancia = an orange segment

etymology: Inherited from Latin explicāre. Doublet of esplicare, which was borrowed. Compare Albanian shpjegoj.

fact.text: Comes from Latin explicare, 'to unfold', the root of English 'explicit' and 'explicate'. The literal meaning is still alive: spiegare le vele means 'to unfurl the sails'.

senses.note: Spiegare qualcosa a qualcuno. Spiegarsi = to make oneself clear. Mi spiego? = Do you see what I mean?

etymology:
From spiegare + -zione.
Doublet of esplicazione.

senses.note: Plural-only noun (spinaci). Use as uncountable.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *expingere, from Latin ex- + pangere.

senses.note: Irregular past participle: spinto. Can also mean to drive or prompt someone to do something.

etymology: From Latin spiritus, from spiro.

fact.text: From Latin spiritus (breath, spirit), related to spīrō (to breathe). English spirit shares this ancient root.

senses.note: Reflexive, takes essere: mi sono spogliato. Spogliare (no si) = to undress someone, or to strip/rob.

etymology: From Latin spurcāre. Compare Romanian spurca.

senses.note: Reflexive sporcarsi = to get dirty. Add h before e/i: sporchi, sporcherò.

etymology: From Latin spurcus, with vowel shift reinforced by contamination of porco, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sperH-.

fact.text: Comes from Latin spurcus, 'filthy'. Its vowel shifted to o, probably influenced by porco, 'pig'.

senses.note: Also figurative: soldi sporchi (dirty money), una barzelletta sporca (a dirty joke).

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English sport. Doublet of diporto.

fact.text: A round trip: English 'sport' is a shortening of 'disport', from Old French 'desport' (fun, pastime). Italian borrowed it back from English, alongside its own native cousin 'diporto'.

senses.note: Invariable: lo sport, gli sport. 'Fare sport' = to play sports / exercise.
Also 'sports' (centro sportivo) and 'casual' (abbigliamento sportivo). As a noun: sportsman/sports fan.

etymology: From Latin spōnsāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin sponsare, 'to betroth'. It is related to English spouse and sponsor, which both go back to Latin spondere, 'to promise solemnly'.

senses.note: Ha sposato Luca = she married Luca. Sposarsi = to get married.

fact.text: From Latin sponsare, from sponsus, 'betrothed', which comes from spondere, 'to promise solemnly'. English 'spouse' and 'sponsor' share the same root.

senses.note: Sposarsi con qualcuno = to get married to someone; sposare qualcuno = to marry someone. Takes essere.

etymology: From sposare.

fact.text: Sposare comes from Latin sponsare ('to betroth'), from sponsus ('promised, betrothed'). That is also the source of English spouse.

senses.note: 'Married to' is sposato con: è sposata con Marco.

etymology: Inherited from Latin spōnsus.

fact.text: It comes from Latin sponsus, 'promised, betrothed'. English 'spouse' has the same origin, and 'sponsor' comes from the related verb spondere, 'to pledge'.

senses.note: The bride is la sposa. Gli sposi = the bride and groom, or newlyweds.

etymology: From s- (“out of”) + posto (“spot”) + -are.

fact.text: Literally 'to put out of its spot': s- (out of) + posto (place) + -are. Spostare un appuntamento means to reschedule an appointment.

senses.note: Means moving something to another place, or moving a date. Moving house is traslocare; moving yourself is spostarsi.

etymology: Uncertain. Possibly from Vulgar Latin *disperdicāre, from Latin disperdere, or from Vulgar Latin *dispergicāre, iterative of Latin dispergere, or alternatively from Vulgar Latin *exprecāre ("drive into ruin"), from Latin ex- + precāri.

senses.note: Noun: lo spreco (waste). Che spreco! = What a waste!

etymology: Unknown

senses.note: Fare uno spuntino = to have a snack.

etymology: Deverbal from squadrare + -a. May correspond to a Vulgar Latin *exquadra, from *exquadro, exquadrāre, from Latin ex- + quadrō, from quadrus. Compare French équerre.

fact.text: Related to Latin quadrus (square), like English 'square'. English 'squad' comes from it too, via French escouade, from soldiers drawn up in a square.

senses.note: Also squad or crew; in technical drawing, a set square.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin stabilis.

senses.note: Un lavoro stabile = a steady job. As a noun, uno stabile is a building.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin stabilīre.
From Latin stadium, from Ancient Greek στάδιον (stádion).

fact.text: Greek stadion was a unit of length, roughly 180 metres. It was also the name of the sprint race at Olympia that was run over that distance. The name later moved from the race to the venue.

senses.note: Takes 'lo' (st- start). Plural stadi. Also means stage or phase.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French stage.

fact.text: Not a theatre stage! Italians say palco or palcoscenico for that. This word comes from French and is said like 'stahzh', so it rhymes with 'garage', not with English 'stage'.

senses.note: Pronounced the French way (/staʒ/). Plural doesn't change: gli stage. The intern is lo/la stagista.

etymology: From earlier *stacione, from Latin statiōnem. Doublet of stazzo, stazzone, stazio, and stazione, the first two of which were also inherited from Latin, while the latter two were borrowed.

fact.text: Comes from Latin statio (a standing, a station), from stare (to stand), and is a twin of stazione. A season was a 'station' of the year.

senses.note: Used for the time of year, TV seasons and tourist seasons: alta/bassa stagione (high/low season).

etymology: Univerbation of 'sta (contraction of questa (“this”)) + mattina (“morning”).

fact.text: Here 'sta, short for questa (this), merged with mattina. The same trick gives stasera (this evening), stanotte (tonight) and stavolta (this time).

senses.note: Also written stamani or questa mattina. Compare stasera, stanotte.

etymology: Deverbal from stampare (“to press, stamp”).

senses.note: Can mean the device, printed media, the print itself, or the act of printing.

etymology: From Frankish *stampōn, from Proto-Germanic *stampōną.

fact.text: It comes from Frankish *stampōn, from the same Germanic root as English 'stamp'. The idea of pressing down to leave a mark moved from stamping to printing.

senses.note: Regular -are verb with avere. Related noun: la stampa, meaning printing or the press.

etymology: From the short past participle of stancare (“to tire out”) in Tuscan; compare the Standard Italian participle stancato.

senses.note: Stanco morto = dead tired. The verb is stancarsi (to get tired).

etymology: Univerbation of 'sta (“this”, apheretic form of questa f sg) + notte (“night”).

senses.note: Can also mean 'last night', depending on context. Compare stamattina and stasera.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *stantia (“standing, stopping-place”), from Latin stantem, from stāre.

fact.text: English took 'stanza' straight from Italian: a verse of a poem is one of its 'rooms'. Both go back to Latin stare, 'to stand, stay', so the first idea was a place to stop.

senses.note: Any room in a house. Camera is used for a bedroom or hotel room.

etymology: Inherited from Latin stāre. Cognate with Spanish estar and English state.

fact.text: Latin stare meant 'to stand'. English state, station and statue come from the same root, and Spanish estar is its twin.

senses.note: Stare a casa = to stay at home.
Come stai? = How are you? Sta lavorando = He/she is working.

etymology: Literally, “to stay afoot”.

senses.note: This means to be standing. To stand up is "alzarsi".

etymology: From 'sta (“this”, apheretic form of esta f sg) + sera (“evening”). Compare Romanian astă-seară.

fact.text: 'Sta' is a clipped 'questa' (this) glued to sera (evening). The same trick gives stamattina (this morning) and stanotte (tonight).

senses.note: Also 'this evening'. Compare stamattina (this morning), stanotte (tonight/last night).
Relational adjective; as in scuola statale (state school).

etymology: Inherited from Latin statūs (noun).

senses.note: Broad usage: physical state of matter, political state, condition, status.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin statiōnem. Doublet of stagione, stazzo, stazzone, and stazio, of which the first three were inherited from Latin, while the last was borrowed.

fact.text: Comes from Latin statio, 'a standing still', from stare, 'to stand'. Stagione (season) comes from the same Latin word, which Italian inherited directly instead of borrowing it.

senses.note: La stazione (feminine). Stazione ferroviaria = train station.

etymology: Inherited from Latin stēlla, from Proto-Italic *stērlā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr. Doublet of étoile.

fact.text: It comes from Latin stella, the source of English 'stellar' and 'constellation'. Further back, it shares an Indo-European root with English 'star'.

senses.note: Also a celebrity: una stella del cinema = a film star.

etymology: From Latin extendere, whence also Italian estendere (a borrowed doublet).

senses.note: Also to spread: stendere la tovaglia = to spread the tablecloth. Irregular: steso, stesi.
Stendere il bucato = to hang out the laundry.

etymology: Italianized form of English sterling.

fact.text: From English 'sterling', possibly from Old English steorling meaning 'small star', in reference to stars on certain English pennies.

senses.note: British currency
After a pronoun it means '-self': io stesso = I myself. 'Fa lo stesso' = it makes no difference.

etymology: Borrowed from French style, itself borrowed from Latin stilus. Doublet of stelo and stilo, which Italian inherited and borrowed from Latin respectively.

fact.text: From Latin stilus (writing stylus): same root as English 'style'. The word's journey shows how 'manner of writing' became 'manner' in general.

senses.note: Also: class, manner, fashion. From Latin stilus (writing implement, then manner of writing).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin stīpendium (“military pay, stipend”).

fact.text: Same root as English 'stipend'. Latin stipendium meant a soldier's pay. It is thought to come from stips, a small coin, plus pendere, to weigh out or pay.

senses.note: Regular pay, usually monthly. Hourly or daily wages are more often il salario or la paga.

etymology: From s- + tirare.

senses.note: Also 'to stretch'; stirarsi = to stretch yourself. Il ferro da stiro = the iron.
Mostly seen in compounds: ferro da stiro (iron), asse da stiro (ironing board).

etymology: Borrowed from Old French estival, of which the etymology is disputed: either from Medieval Latin aestivālis (“summerly”), in place of Classical Latin aestīvus (whence also Italian estivo), from aestās (“summer”), or from tībiālis (“tibial, of the tibia”), from tībia. Cognate with Sicilian stivala.

fact.text: Italians often call their country lo Stivale, 'the Boot', because of the peninsula's shape on the map.

senses.note: Usually plural: gli stivali (a pair of boots).

etymology: From Latin stomachus.

fact.text: Comes via Latin from Greek stómakhos, built on stóma, 'mouth'. It first meant the throat or the opening of an organ, and only later the stomach itself.

senses.note: Plural stomaci (stomachi also found). Mal di stomaco = stomach ache.

etymology: Borrowed from English stop.

senses.note: An English loanword, invariable: lo stop, gli stop.

etymology: From Old Italian istoria, borrowed from Latin historia, from Ancient Greek ἱστορία (historía, “learning through research”).

fact.text: English 'history' and 'story' both come from the same Latin word historia, from Greek historía, 'learning through research'. Italian simply kept one word for both.

senses.note: la storia d'Italia = the history of Italy.
È un'altra storia = that's another story. Also colloquially a relationship or fling.

etymology: From Latin historicus.

senses.note: Centro storico = old town/historic centre. As a noun, lo storico = historian.

etymology: From earlier *strata, from Late Latin strāta (“paved road”), from Latin [via] strāta, feminine of strātus, perfect passive participle of sternō.

fact.text: From Latin via strata, 'paved road'. The Romans' strata was also borrowed into early Germanic, which is where English 'street' comes from, so the two words are cousins.

senses.note: General word for road or street; via is used mainly in addresses (Via Roma).

etymology: From Latin extrāneus, possibly through an intermediate adjective *extranearius, or more likely based on the model of Old French estrangier.

fact.text: Looks like English 'stranger', and both come from Latin extraneus, 'from outside'. But in Italian it means 'foreign' or 'foreigner'. 'Strange' is strano, and a stranger is uno sconosciuto.

senses.note: Also a noun: uno straniero, a foreigner. Lingue straniere = foreign languages.

etymology:
A variant of the older stranio, from Latin extrāneus (“external, foreign; strange”), whence also estraneo (a borrowed doublet).
Cognate with English extraneous and Spanish extraño.

fact.text: Comes from Latin extraneus, 'external, foreign'. That word also gave English 'extraneous'. Something strange was originally something from outside.

senses.note: Forms: strano, strana, strani, strane. Che strano! = How odd!

etymology: From Gothic *𐍃𐍄𐍂𐌰𐍀𐍀𐍉𐌽 (*strappōn), from Latin struppus (“strap”), from Ancient Greek στρόφον (stróphon, “rope”).

fact.text: The word is traced back to Latin struppus (strap, thong), from a Greek word for rope. English 'strap' and 'strop' come from the same Latin word.

senses.note: Also means to snatch: strappare qualcosa di mano a qualcuno (to snatch it from someone's hand).

etymology: From Latin strīga, from strix, from Ancient Greek στρίξ (stríx). Compare Portuguese estria and Romanian strigă.

fact.text: From Latin strix, the name of a screech-owl in Roman mythology—an omen of death. The word travelled through Romance languages and into English 'stryx', maintaining the supernatural association.

etymology: Borrowed from English stress.

fact.text: Borrowed from English, but English stress comes via Old French from Latin distringere 'to pull apart', so a Latin root has come home to Italy.

senses.note: Invariable: lo stress. Essere stressato = to be stressed.
Never 'to emphasize' (that's sottolineare). Mi stai stressando = you're stressing me out.

etymology: From Latin strictus, perfect passive participle of stringō.

fact.text: From Latin strictus, 'drawn tight'. The same root gave English 'strict' and 'strait' (as in the Strait of Messina), since the word originally meant something squeezed or compressed.

senses.note: Also 'tight' (scarpe strette). As a noun, uno stretto = a strait.

etymology: From Latin strictus, perfect passive participle of stringō.

fact.text: From Latin strictus, 'drawn tight'. The same root gave English 'strict' and 'strait' (as in the Strait of Messina), since the word originally meant something squeezed or compressed.

senses.note: A narrow passage of water connecting two larger bodies of water.

etymology: From stronzo + -ata.

senses.note: Derogatory; derived from stronzo (feces/asshole) + -ata.

etymology: Germanic origin, borrowed from the Lombardic *strunz (“dung”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *strunt. Cognate with Sicilian strunzu.

fact.text: A Germanic loan from Lombardic *strunz 'dung', so the insult literally means 'turd'. Dutch stront 'shit' comes from the same Germanic root.

senses.note: Literally 'turd'. A very common, strong insult; also used as an adjective.

etymology: From earlier istrumento, instrumento, from Latin īnstrūmentum.

senses.note: Uses 'lo' (s + consonant): lo strumento musicale.
Also figurative: a means to an end.

etymology: From Latin strūctūra.
From Latin studentem.

senses.note: Female student = studentessa. Plural: studenti.

etymology: From Latin studeō, or through studio, from Latin studium. By surface analysis, studio + -are. Compare Spanish estudiar.

fact.text: From Latin studium, which first meant 'zeal, eagerness' rather than learning. A 'studious' person is, at root, an eager one.

senses.note: Also 'to devise or examine carefully': studiare un piano = to work out a plan.

etymology: From Latin studium (“study”).

fact.text: English borrowed 'studio' from Italian in the 1800s for an artist's workroom. In Italian it still also means a study or a professional office.

senses.note: Takes lo (lo studio). Also means a study room or a professional office: studio legale = law firm.

etymology:
From Latin stupĕndum, from stupēre.
Cognate with Piedmontese stupend.

fact.text: From Latin stupere 'to be stunned', the same root as English stupendous, and also stupid, which first meant dazed or stunned.

senses.note: Strong praise: È stupendo! = It's wonderful!

etymology: From Latin stupidus.

fact.text: Latin stupidus came from stupere, 'to be stunned or amazed'. It first meant dazed or struck senseless, and the same root gives English stupor and stupendous.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sūsum.

fact.text: From Latin susum, a form of sursum, 'upward' (sub + vorsum, 'turned from below'). It's the same sursum heard in the Latin Mass: 'Sursum corda', lift up your hearts.

senses.note: Adverb: vieni su! = come up! Also used as an exclamation: Su! = Come on!
Preposition, combines with articles: sul tavolo, sulla sedia. Also means 'about': un libro su Roma.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sūsum.

fact.text: From Latin susum, a form of sursum, 'upward' (sub + vorsum, 'turned from below'). It's the same sursum heard in the Latin Mass: 'Sursum corda', lift up your hearts.

senses.note: Used to urge someone on: Su, andiamo! = Come on, let's go! Also su con la vita! = Cheer up!

etymology: Inherited from Latin sūsum.

fact.text: From Latin susum, a form of sursum, 'upward' (sub + vorsum, 'turned from below'). It's the same sursum heard in the Latin Mass: 'Sursum corda', lift up your hearts.

senses.note: Combines with articles: sul, sulla, sui. Also 'about': un libro su Roma.
Adverb: vieni su = come up; su e giù = up and down; Su! = Come on!

etymology: Borrowed from Latin subitō.

fact.text: Musicians already know this one: in sheet music it means 'suddenly', as in subito piano (suddenly soft). It comes from Latin subito 'suddenly'.

senses.note: Very common: Arrivo subito! 'I'll be right there!'

etymology: Borrowed from Latin succēdere, from sub + cēdō.

fact.text: Doesn't mean 'to succeed' in the sense of achieving something. For that, use riuscire or avere successo. Successo does mean success, but it is also the past participle: 'happened'.

senses.note: Takes essere: Cosa è successo? = What happened? Also means to succeed someone, e.g. to a throne.

etymology: From Latin successivus.

fact.text: Not quite English 'successive': in everyday Italian it most often just means 'next, following', as in la settimana successiva, the following week.

senses.note: Il giorno successivo = the following day.

etymology: From Latin successus.

fact.text: Watch out: 'Cosa è successo?' doesn't mean 'what was success?' but 'What happened?', because successo is also the past participle of succedere, 'to happen'.

senses.note: Can also mean a hit song or bestseller. Not to be confused with 'è successo' = it happened.

etymology: From Late Latin succus, variant of Latin sūcus. Doublet of sugo. Cognate with Sicilian sucu.

fact.text: Comes from the same Latin word as sugo, the pasta sauce. Both trace back to sucus, 'juice, sap'.

senses.note: succo di frutta = fruit juice; freshly squeezed juice = spremuta. Figurative: the gist.

etymology: Borrowed from French sud, from Old English sūþ, from Proto-Germanic *sunþrą.

fact.text: A surprising English connection: French borrowed its compass points from Old English, and Italian took sud from French. So it goes back to Old English sūþ, the ancestor of 'south'.

senses.note: Capitalised, il Sud often means southern Italy.

etymology: From Latin sūdōrem.

fact.text: Latin sudor comes from the same Indo-European root as English sweat and Greek hidros. Sudor and sweat are distant cousins that began as the same word.

senses.note: The verb 'to sweat' is sudare. Col sudore della fronte = by the sweat of one's brow.

etymology: From Latin suggerō.

fact.text: From Latin suggerō, meaning to carry, bring up, or prompt. Also the root of English suggest.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sūcus, from Proto-Indo-European *sug-, *suk-. Cognate to English succulent via Latin. Doublet of succo. Cognate with Sicilian sucu.

fact.text: From Latin sucus (juice). Related to English 'succulent' and its own doublet 'succo'. The root refers to liquid extracted from food.

etymology: Borrowed from New Latin suīcīdium, from suī (“oneself”) and -cīdium (“-cide”). Up until the 19th century, the plural form was spelled suicidî, to distinguish it from the plural of suicida (“a suicidal person”).

fact.text: From New Latin suīcīdium, combining suī (oneself) and -cīdium (-cide). Until the 19th century, the plural was spelled suicidî to distinguish it from suicida (a suicidal person).

senses.note: su + il. Other forms: sullo, sulla, sull', sui, sugli, sulle.

fact.text: Unlike English his/her, the form follows the thing owned, not the owner. So la sua casa can be his house or her house, and suo fratello can be her brother.

senses.note: Agrees with the thing owned: suo, sua, suoi, sue. Usually takes an article. Capitalised Suo = your (formal).

etymology: From Latin suus, from Proto-Italic *sowos, from Proto-Indo-European *sewos, from *swé.

fact.text: Unlike English his/her, the form follows the thing owned, not the owner. So la sua casa can be his house or her house, and suo fratello can be her brother.

senses.note: Agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: suo zio = his or her uncle; sua madre = his or her mother.
Polite form, used with Lei: il Suo nome, signora?

etymology: From Latin socerus, variant of socer, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱuros.

fact.text: From Latin socer, from an ancient Indo-European word for father-in-law. The same word gave German Schwäher and Sanskrit śváśura.

senses.note: Mother-in-law = la suocera. The plural i suoceri means the in-laws (parents-in-law).

etymology: Inherited from Latin solum.

senses.note: More formal or technical. In speech, 'on the ground' is usually per terra.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sonāre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swenh₂- (“to sound, resound”). By surface analysis, suono (“sound”) + -are.

fact.text: English uses 'play' for both music and games, but Italian splits them: suonare la chitarra (play the guitar) but giocare a calcio (play football).

senses.note: For music: suonare il piano. For games and sports use giocare. Also: to ring (a bell).

etymology: Inherited from Latin sonus.

fact.text: From Latin sonus, which comes from a root meaning 'to sound'. The same root may be behind English swan, perhaps 'the sounding bird'. English sound itself comes from sonus via French.

senses.note: The related verb is suonare: to play an instrument or to ring.

etymology: Inherited from Latin soror (nominative) via loss of /-r/ and then adjustment of /-o/ to the more typical (for feminine nouns) /-a/.

fact.text: From Latin soror (sister), via Proto-Italic *swezōr and Proto-Indo-European *swésōr. The word shifted from general sister to nun as an institutional role.

etymology: From super- + -are, or borrowed from Latin superāre. Compare the inherited and obsolete doublet soprare.

senses.note: Also to pass (an exam), to exceed (a limit), to overtake (a car).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin superior.

senses.note: scuola superiore or le superiori = secondary school / high school

etymology: From super- + mercato.
From Latin suppōnere.

fact.text: From Latin supponere, from sub- 'under' + ponere 'to place'. Literally 'to place under', but evolved to mean 'to assume or posit' in both Latin and Italian.

etymology: Borrowed from French support, from the verb supporter, ultimately from Latin supportāre.
From s- + vantaggio; cognate with Piedmontese svantagi.

fact.text: From s- (negation) + vantaggio (advantage); literally the opposite of advantage.

etymology: Deverbal from svegliare (“to wake up”) + -a.

fact.text: From svegliare (to wake up), itself from Latin ex- (out) + vigilare (to watch)—what wakes you out of sleep.

etymology: Probably from Old Occitan esvelhar, from Vulgar Latin *exvigilāre [whence also Old French esveillier], from Latin ēvigilāre.

fact.text: Goes back to Latin vigilare 'to stay awake, keep watch'. That is the same root as English 'vigil' and 'vigilant'.

senses.note: To wake up yourself, use svegliarsi: mi sono svegliato = I woke up.
Reflexive, so it takes essere: mi sono svegliato. svegliare (no -si) = to wake someone up.

etymology: From s- + viluppo (“tangle”) + -are. Compare Piedmontese svilupé.
Deverbal from sviluppare + -o. Cognate with Piedmontese svilup.

senses.note: Can also mean growth, expansion, or strengthening.

etymology: From s- + volgere; cognate with Piedmontese svòlge.

fact.text: Built on volgere, from Latin volvere 'to roll', the root of English revolve and evolve. It literally means 'to unroll', and English evolve also first meant unrolling a scroll.

senses.note: Irregular: svolsi, svolto. Svolgere un compito/un lavoro. Svolgersi = to take place (L'azione si svolge a Roma).

etymology: From Latin sē. Compare with French soi, Portuguese si, and Spanish sí.

fact.text: From Latin sē. Cognate with French soi, Spanish sí, Portuguese si—all Romance languages preserve this ancient reflexive pronoun.

senses.note: Emphatic/disjunctive form used after prepositions or in emphasis. Also: herself, oneself.

etymology: From Latin sīc. In the “yes” sense, from sīc (est).

fact.text: Dante used the word for 'yes' to classify Romance languages: oc (Occitan), oïl (French), and sì (Italian), calling Italy the land 'where sì sounds'.

senses.note: The accent matters: si without it is a pronoun (oneself / one).

etymology: From Latin sīc. In the “yes” sense, from sīc (est).

fact.text: Dante used the word for 'yes' to classify Romance languages: oc (Occitan), oïl (French), and sì (Italian), calling Italy the land 'where sì sounds'.

senses.note: Invariable noun.

etymology: From tabacco + -aio.

fact.text: Italian tobacconists are marked by a big 'T' sign. Besides cigarettes, they sell bus tickets, stamps, lottery tickets and phone top-ups.

senses.note: Can mean the person or the shop. The shop is also called la tabaccheria.
A table of data or a chart, never furniture (that's il tavolo).

etymology: Borrowed from English tablet.

senses.note: Tablet computer. Borrowed from English.

etymology: Inherited from Latin tacēre, from Proto-Italic *takēō, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *tak- or *tHk-.
Deverbal from tagliare (“to cut”) + -a. Compare French taille.

fact.text: From tagliare (to cut): taglia originally meant the cutting/sizing of cloth. The same root gives French taille, explaining why European languages share this sense.

senses.note: Also: size/dimensions of animals (broadly); archaic: tribute, bounty, militia fee

etymology: From Late Latin tāliāre, a verb based on Latin tālea (“cutting taken from a plant”).

fact.text: From Late Latin taliare, 'to cut', from talea, 'a cutting from a plant'. Through Old French tailler, the same verb gave English 'tailor', 'detail' and 'retail'.

senses.note: Tagliare corto = to cut it short. Taglia = clothing size; also a bounty.

etymology: From tagliare (“to cut”) + -iere. Compare Portuguese talher.

senses.note: Cutting board; also breadboard

etymology: Deverbal from tagliare + -o.

senses.note: Versatile: a wound, reduction, section, hairstyle, fabric length, or edge.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Old French talent (“desire, wish”), from Classical Latin talentum (“a Grecian weight; a talent of money; (post-Classical) gift from God; (Medieval) skill, ability”), from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (tálanton, “balance; a particular weight, especially of gold; sum of money; a talent”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *tl̥h₂ent-, from the root *telh₂-.

fact.text: From Ancient Greek talanton, originally a balance or unit of weight (gold), then coined money. The figurative sense 'natural ability' arose through medieval interpretations of the Parable of the Talents in the Bible.

senses.note: Often marked obsolete; now chiefly used for natural ability or gift. Originally a unit of weight and currency from Ancient Greece.
Plural doesn't change: i talk show. Often written without the hyphen.

etymology: From Latin tālus.

fact.text: From Latin tālus, meaning ankle bone or die. The same root as English 'talus' (the bone in the foot).

senses.note: Medical: relating to ankle bone (talus). Entry appears problematic.

etymology: Univerbation of tale + volta.

fact.text: A univerbation of tale (such) and volta (time/turn), literally meaning such a time. Still transparent in the construction.

senses.note: Agrees with the noun: tanto, tanta, tanti, tante. Così tante uova = so many eggs.

etymology: Derived from Latin tantus.

senses.note: As an adverb it never changes. As an adjective it agrees: tanti amici, tante cose.

etymology: Derived from Latin tantus.

senses.note: As an adjective it agrees: tanto, tanta, tanti, tante. As an adverb it never changes: Ti amo tanto.

etymology: From Latin tapēte, from Ancient Greek τάπης (tápēs).

fact.text: It comes from Greek tapes (carpet), the same root as French tapis and English 'tapestry'.

senses.note: Also carpet. Andare al tappeto = to be knocked down (boxing).

etymology: From Latin tardē.

senses.note: 'È tardi' = it's late. But 'I'm late' = 'sono in ritardo', not 'sono tardi'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin tardus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin tardus, 'slow', the same source as English 'tardy' and 'retard' (originally just 'to slow down', as in a musical ritardando).

senses.note: As in tardo pomeriggio (late afternoon). 'Later' (adverb) is più tardi. Can also mean slow-witted.

etymology: From Arabic تَعْرِفَة (taʕrifa, “tariff, rate”).

fact.text: From Arabic taʕrifa (tariff, rate). Italian borrowed this term from Arabic commerce terminology, showing medieval trade influence. English 'tariff' comes from the same Arabic source.

senses.note: Rate, tariff, or charge for travel/services; used for transport prices.

etymology: From Frankish *taskā, from Proto-Germanic *taskǭ. Perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *das-, *des- (“to fray”).

fact.text: One of the Germanic words in Italian: it came in through Frankish taska. German Tasche (bag, pocket) is a close cousin.

senses.note: avere le mani in tasca = to have your hands in your pockets

etymology: From Latin taxa.

fact.text: From Latin taxa, the past participle of taxare. English tax shares the same Latin root.

etymology: From Latin tabula. Doublet of tabula and tavolo.

fact.text: From Latin tabula. English table comes from the same Latin root through French. Tavola preserves the original Italian pronunciation.

etymology:
From Latin tabula, with a change in gender and inflection.
Doublet of tavola and tabula.

fact.text: Latin tabula, meaning plank or board, is the source of English table and tablet, as well as Italian tavola.

senses.note: Use tavolo for the piece of furniture; tavola is the table laid for a meal, as in A tavola! = Dinner's ready!
Plural stays the same: i taxi. Prendere un taxi = to take a taxi.

etymology: From Arabic طَاس (ṭās).

fact.text: From Arabic tas 'bowl', the same source as French tasse. English borrowed 'tazza' from Italian for a shallow ornamental cup on a stem.

senses.note: 'Una tazza di caffè/tè'. Colloquially it can also mean the toilet bowl.

etymology: Inherited from Latin tē, from tū.

senses.note: Stressed form used after prepositions (di te, con te) and for emphasis. Not tè (tea).

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English team.

From Latin theātrum, from Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron, “a place for viewing”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek theatron, 'a place for viewing', from theaomai, 'to watch'. Theatre was originally named after what the audience did, not what the actors did.

senses.note: Also means drama as an art form. Plural: i teatri.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin technicus.

senses.note: In football it also means the coach or manager. As an adjective it means technical.

etymology: From tecno- + -logia.

From Early Medieval Latin theodiscus, from a Germanic language, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz (“of the people, popular, vernacular”), from *þeudō (“people”) + *-iskaz (“-ish, -ic, -al”). The Old English form is þēodisċ, the Old High German one diutisc (attested ca. 1090 in the Annolied). Compare also Friulian todesc, archaic or regional French thiois, Sicilian tudiscu.

fact.text: From Germanic theodiscus (of the people), the same root gave English 'Dutch'. Medieval scholars used theodiscus for the common Germanic language as opposed to Latin.

senses.note: Adjective agreeing with the noun it modifies (e.g. la lingua tedesca, i libri tedeschi)

etymology: From English television camera. By surface analysis, tele- + camera.
From tele- + film.

senses.note: Invariable: i telefilm. Often used for (especially American) TV series; serie TV is also common.

etymology: From telefono + -are.

senses.note: Takes 'a': telefonare a qualcuno (to call someone). Auxiliary avere.

etymology: From telefonare (“to phone”) + -ata (verbal noun suffix).

senses.note: Fare una telefonata = to make a phone call. Also: chiamata.

etymology: From tele- + -fono, influenced by English telephone and French téléphone.

fact.text: Italians often credit Antonio Meucci, who built voice-transmitting devices in the 1850s, before Bell. In 2002 the US House of Representatives passed a resolution honoring his work.

senses.note: A mobile phone is il cellulare or il telefonino. Essere al telefono = to be on the phone.

etymology: From tele- + giornale.

senses.note: Usually shortened to il TG, pronounced 'tiggì'.

etymology: From tele- + -gramma.

fact.text: From tele- (far) + -gramma (written message), combining Greek tele and -gram. The compound mirrors English 'telegram', reflecting 19th-century communication technology.

senses.note: Archaic in modern usage; superseded by email and instant messaging.

etymology: From tele- + visione.

senses.note: Often shortened to la tv (ti-vù) or la tele. Guardare la televisione = to watch TV.

etymology: Inherited from Latin timēre. Compare Portuguese and Spanish temer.

fact.text: Inherited from Latin timēre. Cognate with Spanish and Portuguese 'temer'—all Romance languages preserved this ancient verb intact.

etymology: From Latin temperātūra.

senses.note: Also 'fever' in avere la temperatura (to have a temperature).

etymology: Inherited from Latin tempestās via the nominative form. Doublet of tempestà.
Borrowed from Latin templum. First attested 14th century.

fact.text: From Latin templum, of uncertain origin, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *temp- (to stretch, pull), suggesting 'to measure'—referring to augury practices.

senses.note: Masculine. Plural: templi (or archaic tempî). Also used figuratively for 'seat, capital' or 'heaven' in poetic language.

etymology: From Latin tempus (“time”), from Proto-Indo-European *tempos (“stretch”), from the root *temp- (“to stretch, string”).

fact.text: From Latin tempus 'time', which also gave English temporary and contemporary. English borrowed the Italian word itself as the musical term tempo.

senses.note: Non ho tempo = I don't have time. For clock time, use ora: Che ore sono?
Che tempo fa? = What's the weather like?

etymology: From Latin temporālis.

fact.text: It comes from Latin temporalis, from tempus, which meant both 'time' and 'weather'. Italian tempo still means both, so a thunderstorm is literally a 'weather thing'.

senses.note: As an adjective, temporale also means 'temporal' (worldly, or relating to the temples).

etymology: From Early Medieval Latin or Late Latin tenda, from Vulgar Latin *tendita, substantivized feminine of *tenditus, as a variant form of tentus, perfect passive participle of Latin tendō. Compare Portuguese tenda, Spanish tienda, French tente, Friulian tinde, Romanian tindă, English tent.

fact.text: Both the tent and the curtain are 'stretched' cloth. The word comes from Latin tendere (to stretch), just like English tent.

senses.note: piantare la tenda = to pitch a tent.
Usually plural: le tende = the curtains.

etymology: Clipping of luogotenente.

fact.text: From luogotenente, literally 'place-holder' — someone holding the place of a superior officer. The English word traces the same origin via French lieu-tenant.

etymology: Inherited from Latin tenēre, from Proto-Italic *tenēō, stative from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, draw”).

fact.text: From Latin tenere, 'to hold', from a root meaning 'to stretch'. English gets 'tenant', 'tenacious', 'tenet' and 'retain' from the same family.

senses.note: Irregular: tengo, tieni, tiene, teniamo, tenete, tengono. Also 'to keep': tienili in ordine.

etymology: Inherited from Latin tenerum, from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, draw”).

senses.note: Used for meat, feelings and people. Also 'soft' (pane tenero) and 'cute' (che tenero!).

etymology: Borrowed from English tennis.

fact.text: Italian borrowed this from English, and English took it from Old French tenez, 'hold!' or 'here you go!', which players probably called out as they served.

senses.note: Invariable. To play tennis: giocare a tennis.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin tēnsiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin tēnsiō, derived from tendō meaning 'to stretch.' The same root gives English 'tender,' 'tent,' and 'extend.'

etymology: From Latin temptāre.
From Latin tentativus.
Borrowed from New Latin therapīa, from Ancient Greek θεραπεία (therapeía, “service, medical treatment”).

fact.text: From Greek therapeia (service, medical treatment), the same root as English therapy and therapeutic.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin termināre.

senses.note: Takes avere with an object (ho terminato il lavoro) and essere without one (il film è terminato).

etymology: Inherited from Latin terminus or the variant termen, termine, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ter- (“through”).

fact.text: From Latin terminus (boundary), cognate with English term. The root ter- means through in Proto-Indo-European.

senses.note: Also means limit, deadline, or term (word/condition).

etymology: From termo- + -metro.
From termo- + sifone.

fact.text: Literally 'thermo-siphon'. It's named after thermosiphon circulation, in which hot water rises and cool water sinks, so water moves through the pipes without a pump.

senses.note: A home heating radiator. A car radiator is 'il radiatore'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin terra, from Proto-Italic *terzā, from Proto-Indo-European *ters-eh₂, from *ters- (“dry”).

fact.text: From a root meaning 'dry': land was the dry part, as opposed to the sea. English thirst likely shares that root, and terrain, territory and Mediterranean come from Latin terra.

senses.note: a terra = on the ground / ashore; per terra = on the floor.
Usually capitalised for the planet: la Terra.

etymology: Borrowed from French terrasse, from Old Occitan terrassa. Related to terrazzo.

fact.text: Comes from French terrasse, based on terra, 'earth'. The related Italian word terrazzo gave English 'terrazzo', the speckled chip-stone flooring.

senses.note: A large open-air terrace. A small balcony is 'il balcone'.

etymology: From Latin terrēnum.

fact.text: From Latin terrenus 'of the earth', from terra. English terrain comes from the same Latin word, by way of French.

senses.note: Also soil, or a plot of land. Piano terreno = ground floor.

etymology: Derived from Latin terribĭlis.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural terribili.

etymology: From terrore + -ismo.
From terrore + -izzare.
From Latin tertius.

fact.text: It comes from Latin tertius, which also gave English 'tertiary'. Further back, it shares an Indo-European ancestor with English 'third' and 'three'.

senses.note: Also a noun: un terzo = a third (fraction).

etymology: Inherited from Latin thēsaurus (“treasure”), from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “storehouse”, “treasure”). Doublet of Tesauro (“a male given name”).

fact.text: From Greek thesauros, 'storehouse, treasure'. English borrowed the same word as thesaurus, a treasure-house of words.

senses.note: Literally 'treasure'. Used affectionately with partners and children: Ciao, tesoro!

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English test.

fact.text: A direct English borrowing, now naturalized in Italian and very common in academic and professional contexts. The word maintains the same form in both singular and plural (invariable).

senses.note: Invariable noun; same form in plural

etymology: From Latin testa. The semantic development is earthen pot → skull → head.

fact.text: Latin testa meant an earthen pot or shell. It became slang for the skull and then replaced the Latin word for head, caput. French tête has the same origin.

senses.note: Testa dura = stubborn person. Testa o croce? = heads or tails?

etymology: Back-formation from testimonî, plural of testimonio (“testimony; witness”), perceived as testimoni.

fact.text: Back-formation from the plural testimon/ē, reanalyzed as singular testimone. The word derives from Latin testimonium, giving us parallel English 'testimony'. A rare example of plural reanalysis creating new singular.

senses.note: Both masculine and feminine forms use the same noun; gender follows the person.

etymology: From testimonio + -are.
Learned borrowing from New Latin textus (“text”), from Latin textus (“woven”), perfect passive participle of texō (“weave”).

fact.text: From Latin textus (woven); literally refers to the weaving together of words and ideas into a cohesive whole.

senses.note: From Latin textus (woven), past participle of texere.

etymology:
From Late Latin titta, titia, from Frankish *titta, from Proto-Germanic *titt- (“teat; nipple; breast”), from Proto-Indo-European *tata- (“father; parent; nipple”).
Compare also French tette, Spanish and Portuguese teta, Romanian țâță, English teat. The word is found in many European languages and may simply be ultimately an expressive formation based on infantile language.

fact.text: From Late Latin titta, likely from Proto-Germanic *titt- ('teat'), cognate with English 'teat'. The word appears across many European languages (French tette, Spanish teta, Romanian țâță) and may be an infantile or expressive formation.

senses.note: Slang/vulgar term; informal and colloquial.

etymology: Inherited from Latin tēctum (“roof”). Compare French toit, Portuguese teto, Spanish techo.

fact.text: Comes from Latin tectum, 'something covered', from tegere, 'to cover'. The same verb gives English protect ('cover in front') and detect ('uncover').

senses.note: Also means a cap or limit: 'tetto di spesa' is a spending cap.
Misspelling (the → tè); listed as alternative form

etymology: From Latin tepidus.

senses.note: Also figurative: un'accoglienza tiepida = a lukewarm, half-hearted welcome.

etymology: From tifo + -oso.

fact.text: It comes from tifo, which is also the name of the disease typhus. Passionate supporters were compared to people in a feverish delirium, which is why Italian fans are tifosi.

senses.note: Feminine: la tifosa. Fare il tifo per means 'to root for'. An electric fan is un ventilatore.

etymology: From Latin tigris.

fact.text: It comes via Latin from Greek tigris, probably from an Iranian word related to 'sharp' or 'arrow'. That word is commonly linked to the name of the river Tigris, known for its swift current.

senses.note: Always feminine (la tigre), even for a male; say 'la tigre maschio' if needed. Plural: le tigri.

etymology: From Latin timidus.

senses.note: Usually means shy rather than fearful.

etymology: From Latin typicus.

fact.text: From Latin typicus, derived from Greek typos (impression, type): same root as English 'typical', 'type', and 'typography'.

senses.note: Also: characteristic, peculiar, local, classic.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin typus (“symbol”), from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “mark”, “figure”), derived from τύπτω (túptō, “to beat, strike”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp-.

fact.text: From Greek typos, 'mark left by a blow', from typtein, 'to strike'. English type has the same origin: a type was first the impression made by striking.

senses.note: un tipo strano = a strange guy. Feminine: una tipa.
che tipo di...? = what kind of...? Colloquially, tipo also means 'like': tipo cosa? = like what?

etymology: Univerbation of tira + mi + su, literally “pick me up”, from tira su (“pick up”, second person singular imperative of tirare su) + mi (“me”, unstressed first person singular object pronoun). Cognate to Venetan tiramesù.

fact.text: From tira + mi + su, literally 'pick me up'—from the imperative form of tirare su. The name playfully suggests the dessert's caffeine-boost effect.

senses.note: Italian dessert; invariable noun.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tīrāre.

fact.text: Look out for it on doors in Italy: TIRARE (or TIRA) means PULL, and SPINGERE (or SPINGI) means PUSH.

senses.note: Also 'to throw'. Tirare su = to pull up or cheer up; tira vento = it's windy.

etymology: From tirare (“to pull”).

senses.note: Tiro in porta = shot on goal. From tirare. Also: un brutto tiro = a dirty trick.

etymology: Derived from Latin titulus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin titulus, which also gave English 'tittle', the little dot over an i or j. Latin titulus itself may come from Etruscan, but its origin is uncertain.

senses.note: Also: titolo di studio = educational qualification; titoli = securities or shares in finance.

etymology: From Latin Titius: the name Tizio is usually the first placeholder name, which caused it to become a generic word for "a person".

fact.text: Tizio was the standard Roman placeholder name (like our 'John Doe'), so it evolved into everyday Italian meaning 'some guy' or 'someone-or-other'.

senses.note: Placeholder name from Latin Titius; means 'some fellow' or 'what's-his-name'

etymology: Pseudo-anglicism, from English toast.

fact.text: A pseudo-anglicism: Italian borrowed the word from English toast, but in Italian it means the prepared food, not just browned bread.

senses.note: Invariable singular noun in Italian.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tuccāre, of Germanic or onomatopoeic origin.

fact.text: It comes from Vulgar Latin tuccare, which probably imitated the sound of a knock. Old French toucher, from the same word, gave English touch, and the fencing cry touché.

senses.note: Tocca a te = it's your turn. Mi tocca lavorare = I have to work.

etymology: From earlier tollere, from Latin tollō (“to lift, remove”), from Proto-Italic *tolnō, from the Proto-Indo-European *telh₂- (“to bear, endure”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin tollere 'to lift, remove'. With ex- added, that gave extollere 'to raise up', the source of English 'extol'.

senses.note: Irregular: tolgo, togli, tolgono; past participle tolto.

etymology: From Late Latin tumba, from Ancient Greek τύμβος (túmbos).
Deverbal from tombolare.

fact.text: Named after the numbers tumbling (tombolare) out of the bag. It's a Christmas tradition in Naples, where each number has a meaning from 'la smorfia': 90 stands for fear.

senses.note: A traditional family game at Christmas. Fare tombola = to get a full card and win.
Italian metric tonne (1000 kg); also called tonnellata metrica.

etymology:
From Latin talpa (“mole”) with a change in gender. The original [ɫ] appears to have vocalized to [u̯] in pre-literary Tuscan, with the resulting [au̯] regularly yielding [ɔ], as in Latin aurum (“gold”) > Italian òro. Doublet of talpa.
The computing sense is a semantic loan from English mouse.

fact.text: Surprisingly, this comes from Latin talpa, meaning 'mole', with the gender changed. Modern Italian still uses talpa for the mole, so the two words are doublets.

senses.note: Also used loosely for rats. The computer mouse is usually just 'il mouse'. Mickey Mouse = Topolino.
tormentare + lo (him/it). Object pronouns attach to the infinitive: non tormentarlo!

Inherited from Latin tornāre (“to turn”).

fact.text: From Latin tornare, 'to turn on a lathe', from Greek tornos, 'lathe'. The same root gave English turn, and through French also tour and tournament.

senses.note: Takes essere in compound tenses: sono tornato/a. tornare a + infinitive = to do something again.
Alternative form of tornio; now archaic.

etymology: From Latin turrem, from Ancient Greek τύρρις (túrrhis), τύρσις (túrsis), likely ultimately a Mediterranean substrate loan.

fact.text: Comes from Latin turris and Greek túrsis, probably from an older Mediterranean word. It is related to English 'turret', and some link it to the Greek name for the Etruscans, Tyrrhenoi.

senses.note: Also the rook in chess. Plural: le torri.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin torrentem, accusative form of torrēns (“rushing”, “torrential”) (originally “scorching", then "powerful", "strengthful", "forceful"), present active participle of torreō (“to scorch, burn, parch”), from Proto-Italic *torzeō, causative of the Proto-Indo-European root *ters- (“dry”).

fact.text: From Latin torrere 'to scorch', the same verb behind torrid and toast. A 'scorching' stream came to mean a forceful, rushing one.

senses.note: Usually a fast, often seasonal stream, smaller than a fiume (river). Not always a raging torrent.

etymology: From Latin turta. Thought to derive from Latin tŏrta f (“twisted”), which yielded tòrta in Italian.

fact.text: The Latin word turta is first recorded on the Vindolanda tablets, written at a Roman fort near Hadrian's Wall in Britain. Where it came from is still unclear.

senses.note: Also pie or tart; torta salata = savoury pie or quiche.

etymology: From tortello + -ino, hypocorism of torta (“cake”).

fact.text: According to a popular legend from Emilia, an innkeeper got a peek at Venus (or Lucrezia Borgia) through a keyhole and shaped the pasta to look like her navel.

senses.note: Usually plural: tortellini in brodo (in broth) is a classic dish from Bologna and Modena.

etymology: From Latin tortum (“a wrong or injustice”), substantive use of tortus, perfect passive participle of torqueō. Compare French tort.

fact.text: From Latin tortum, the noun form of tortus (twisted, wrong). The verb torquere (to twist) is the root—a wrong is something twisted or distorted.

etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *(s)tew-
Proto-Indo-European *-d-
