Italian tosse
From Latin tussem, from Proto-Indo-European *tud-ti-s- (“cough”), from *(s)tewd-, from *(s)tew- (“to push, hit”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin tussis, 'cough', the same word behind the English medical term pertussis, the formal name for whooping cough.

senses.note: Avere la tosse = to have a cough.

etymology: Verb-object compound, composed of tosta (“to toast”) + pane (“bread”).

fact.text: A verb + noun compound, literally 'toasts-bread'. Italian builds many gadget names this way: apriscatole (can opener), cavatappi (corkscrew), lavastoviglie.

senses.note: Invariable: i tostapane.

etymology: From Late Latin tostare.

fact.text: From Late Latin tostare, related to the past participle tosus. The root connects to heat and drying, and appears in English 'toast' and 'roast' as well.

senses.note: Transitive verb; also means to roast (coffee/seeds) or, in slang, to thrash.

etymology: From Medieval Latin tōtālis.

senses.note: In totale = in total. Also an adjective: totale (complete).
Masculine and invariable: il tour, i tour. Pronounced as in French/English.

etymology: Probably from Old Occitan toalha, from Frankish *þwahilu. Cognate with Portuguese toalha (“towel”).

fact.text: Comes from the Germanic (Frankish) word for a washing cloth. Through Old French toaille, the same root gave English towel.

etymology: From tovaglia.

fact.text: A little tovaglia 'tablecloth'. That word came from a Germanic word for a cloth used for washing, which is also where English towel comes from.

senses.note: Table napkin. A tablecloth is la tovaglia.

etymology: From Latin intrā, with influence from Latin inter.

senses.note: Same as fra. With time it means 'in': tra un'ora = in an hour.
Fra cinque minuti means the same. Use tra/fra for time from now, not in.
'Fra poco' means the same. Ci vediamo tra poco = see you soon.

etymology: Deverbal from tracciare (“to mark out; to sketch”) + -a.

senses.note: Multiple senses: footprint/mark, vestige, clue, or in specialized contexts (math, astronomy, music).

etymology: From Latin trādere.
From tradizione + -ale; cognate with Piedmontese tradissional/tradissiunal.
From Latin trādūcō. Cognate with Piedmontese tradùe/tradüve.

fact.text: From Latin traducere, 'to lead across'. The same Latin verb gave English 'traduce' (to slander), from the idea of leading someone across in public to be shamed.

senses.note: Irregular like condurre: traduco, tradussi, tradotto. Tradurre in inglese = into English.

etymology: From Latin trāductiō, trāductiōnis (“transferring, translation”, literally “leading across”), from trādūcō (“to lead across”), from trāns (“across”) + dūcō (“to lead”).

fact.text: From Latin traducere: trans (across) + ducere (to lead). Literally 'leading across' words or meaning from one language to another.

etymology:
Potentially from Vulgar Latin *trānsfrīcō (“to rub across”), from trans- + frico; Klein instead suggests the Italian has ultimate origin in Arabic تَفْرِيق (tafrīq, “distribution, dispersion”), reshaped to match the native prefix tra- (“trans-”).
Cognate with Piedmontese tràfich/tràfic and Sicilian tràficu.

senses.note: Also illegal trade: traffico di droga = drug trafficking.

etymology: From Latin tragoedia, from Ancient Greek τρᾰγῳδῐ́ᾱ (trăgōidĭ́ā), from τρᾰ́γος (trắgos, “male goat”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).

fact.text: From Ancient Greek tragoidia, literally 'goat song' (tragos 'goat' + oide 'song'). Nobody knows for sure why goats were involved.

etymology: From traghettare.
Unadapted borrowing from English tram.

senses.note: Unadapted English loanword; invariable plural.

etymology: From tramontare (“to set, go down; to fade”, literally “to set beyond the mountains”). Compare Sicilian tracoḍḍu.

fact.text: Comes from tramontare, literally 'to go beyond the mountains', which describes the sun sinking behind the peaks.

senses.note: Figuratively, a decline: 'il tramonto di un impero' means the decline of an empire.

etymology:
Borrowed from Latin tranquillitātem (“calmness, stillness”).
From tranquille + -ità.

fact.text: From Latin tranquillitas. English tranquility and Italian tranquillità are direct cognates, both preserving the Latin form with minimal change.

senses.note: invariable noun (no plural form)

etymology: Borrowed from Latin tranquillus (“quiet, calm, still, tranquil”), from Proto-Italic *trānskʷīlos.

senses.note: Stai tranquillo! / Tranquillo! = Relax! Don't worry!

etymology: From Frankish *trappa (whence French trappe (“trap”)) + -ola.

fact.text: From Frankish trappa (source of French trappe). Same root as English trap, which entered English from Old French.

etymology: From tras- + correre; cognate with Piedmontese trascore.

fact.text: Made from tras- ('across, through') + correre ('to run'), so you literally 'run through' your time. Takes avere when you spend time, essere when time passes by.

senses.note: Only for time (trascorrere le vacanze). For money, use spendere.

etymology: From tras- + corso.

senses.note: Past participle of trascorrere: ho trascorso un anno = I spent a year. As an adjective: past, bygone.

etymology: From Latin trānsferō.

senses.note: Takes essere: mi sono trasferito a Roma. Non-reflexive trasferire = to transfer something.

etymology: From Latin trānsfōrmāre.

senses.note: Use trasformarsi for 'to turn into' (intransitive).

etymology: From tras- + locare.

fact.text: Built from tras- (across) and locare (to place, from Latin locus 'place'), the same parts as English 'translocate'. Locus also gives English 'location' and 'local'.

senses.note: Uses avere: abbiamo traslocato. The move itself is il trasloco. To move an object, use spostare.
Fare un trasloco = to move house. Verb: traslocare.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin trānsmissiōnem.

senses.note: Often means a TV or radio programme: una trasmissione televisiva.

etymology: From Medieval Latin trānspārentem (“transparent”), present participle of trānspareō, from Latin trāns + pareō.

senses.note: Also figurative: clear, sincere.

etymology: From Latin trānsportāre.

senses.note: Regular -are verb. Lasciarsi trasportare = to get carried away.

etymology: Deverbal from trasportàre + -o.

senses.note: Plural i trasporti often means the transport system: trasporti pubblici = public transport.

etymology: Inherited from Latin tractāre (“to drag; to handle; to practise”), from tractus (“dragged”), perfect passive participle of trahō (“to drag; to extract”).

fact.text: From Latin tractare 'to handle, drag about', which came from trahere 'to drag'. English got treat from the same word through French, and tractor and traction come from trahere.

senses.note: trattarsi di = to be about: Di cosa si tratta? = What is it about?

etymology: From Latin tractus.

fact.text: From Latin tractus, the past participle of trahere (to drag). The modern sense developed from the idea of a line or stroke drawn—hence 'feature' as a distinctive mark or characteristic line.

senses.note: Often used in plural: i tratti somatici (facial features).

etymology: Inherited from Latin trēs, from Proto-Italic *trēs, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes. Compare Sicilian tri.

senses.note: No accent on its own, but compounds take one: ventitré, trentatré.

etymology: Inherited from Latin trēs, from Proto-Italic *trēs, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes. Compare Sicilian tri.
From Vulgar Latin trecentum, from Latin trecenti.
From Latin trēdecim.
Borrowed from French train.

fact.text: Comes via French train from Old French trahiner 'to drag'. A train was first something dragged behind, like the train of a gown, long before railways.

senses.note: Prendere il treno = to take the train; in treno = by train.

etymology: Inherited from Latin trīgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *tri(d)ḱomt (“thirty”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + cinque (“five”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + due (“two”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + nove (“nine”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + quattro (“four”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + sei (“six”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + sette (“seven”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + tre (“three”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + otto (“eight”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + uno (“one”).
From Latin tribūnal.

fact.text: From Latin tribunal, the raised platform where Roman magistrates sat to judge cases. English tribunal comes from the same word.

senses.note: The court of law, not a sports court (campo). Masculine despite the -e ending.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin triplus.

fact.text: From Latin triplus (threefold), which also gave English 'triple', 'treble', and 'triplet'. The prefix tri- (three) is ancient Indo-European.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin trīstis. Compare tristo, inherited from Vulgar Latin trīstus, from the same source.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural tristi.

etymology:
From Late Latin troia, troja, of uncertain origin, but possibly:
* from Latin (porcum de) Troia (“(hog of) Troy”), after the Trojan horse,
* or alternatively of Celtic origin, from a Gaulish root *trogja, from a root meaning “to pull” and thence also “fertile," Proto-Celtic *trāglo-, for which see Latin traho.
* or possibly simply of imitative origin, from the sound of a pig's grunt. Compare French truie, Catalan truja.

fact.text: Possibly derived from Latin 'Troia' (Troy), perhaps referencing the Trojan horse, or from Celtic roots meaning 'to pull' and 'fertile'. The exact origin remains uncertain.

senses.note: Female pig; also used pejoratively in Italian slang.

etymology: From a Germanic source (Frankish *trumba, Old High German trumpa, Old Norse trumba), all imitative.

fact.text: From Germanic roots (Frankish *trumba) and is imitative—the word itself echoes the brassy, blaring sound the instrument makes.
Probably from Late Latin troppus 'flock', from a Frankish word for a cluster or village, related to Old English 'thorp' and to 'troop'. A crowd or heap became 'too much'.

senses.note: Agrees with its noun: troppi soldi (too much money), troppe persone (too many people).

etymology: From Early Medieval Latin troppus, borrowed from Frankish *þorp (“a cluster, agglomeration", also "collection of houses, village”), from Proto-Germanic *þurpą (“village”), from Proto-Indo-European *trab-, *treb- (“dwelling, room”). Cognate with French trop (“too much”), Piedmontese tròp/trop. More at trop, thorp and troop.

fact.text: Probably from Late Latin troppus 'flock', from a Frankish word for a cluster or village, related to Old English 'thorp' and to 'troop'. A crowd or heap became 'too much'.

senses.note: As an adverb it doesn't change: è troppo caro. As an adjective it agrees: troppi soldi.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *tropāre, a verb probably based on Classical Latin tropus. Compare French trouver.

fact.text: Probably from Latin tropus, a figure of speech or melody, so the first sense may have been 'to compose'. Its Occitan cousin trobar gave trobador, which became English troubadour.

senses.note: Trovarsi = to be located / to find oneself; andare a trovare qualcuno = to visit someone.

etymology:
Deverbal from truccare + -o, from French truquer.
Compare Piedmontese truch, French truc.

fact.text: Watch out: this word also means makeup. Truccarsi is to put on makeup, and a truccatore is a makeup artist. The word comes from French truc 'trick'.

senses.note: Also very commonly 'makeup'. Plural: trucchi.

etymology: Inherited from Latin tū, from Proto-Italic *tū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂.

fact.text: Shares an ancestor with English 'thou': both come from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂. English dropped the informal 'thou', but Italian still uses it every day.

senses.note: Subject pronoun, used with friends and family. Formal 'you' is Lei.

etymology: From English tunnel.

fact.text: Borrowed directly from English 'tunnel'. Invariable in Italian: 'i tunnel' keeps the same form.

senses.note: Invariable noun; borrowed from English.
Usually takes the article: il tuo libro. Formal = Suo; for several people = vostro.

etymology:
From Latin tuus, from Proto-Italic *towos.
In the singular, Latin tuum underwent *ʊu > *ou > *ɔu dissimilation, cf. Sardinian tou, and also Latin ōvum > Italian òvo, Spanish huevo, ultimately producing [ˈtwɔu], and a plural [ˈtwɔi]. Italian then underwent its regular *wɔV > *uV sound change, cf. *bwɔe > bue, *mjɛu > mio, producing ultimately [ˈtu.o]. This latter sound change is blocked by a following [i], which explains the plural form tuoi, cf. *mjɛi > miei.

senses.note: Usually with the article: il tuo libro. Forms: tuo, tua, tuoi, tue.

etymology:
From Latin tuus, from Proto-Italic *towos.
In the singular, Latin tuum underwent *ʊu > *ou > *ɔu dissimilation, cf. Sardinian tou, and also Latin ōvum > Italian òvo, Spanish huevo, ultimately producing [ˈtwɔu], and a plural [ˈtwɔi]. Italian then underwent its regular *wɔV > *uV sound change, cf. *bwɔe > bue, *mjɛu > mio, producing ultimately [ˈtu.o]. This latter sound change is blocked by a following [i], which explains the plural form tuoi, cf. *mjɛi > miei.

senses.note: Usually with an article: il tuo, la tua, i tuoi, le tue. It agrees with the thing owned.

etymology: From Latin tonus (“thunderclap; sound, tone”), from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos). Doublet of tono.

fact.text: Thunder and 'tone' share an origin: both go back to Latin tonus, from Greek tonos, and Italian tono is its doublet. The deeper root means 'to stretch', as in a taut string.

etymology: Borrowed from French tourisme, from English tourism.

fact.text: Italian turismo comes from French tourisme, which in turn borrowed from English 'tourism'. The word travelled from English to Italian via French.

etymology: Borrowed from French touriste, from English tourist.

senses.note: Same form for men and women: il/la turista. Plurals: turisti (m), turiste (f).

etymology: Borrowed from French tourner.

senses.note: È il tuo turno = it's your turn. Also a work shift: turno di notte.

etymology:
From Latin tota via (“always”).
Compare Spanish todavía, Portuguese todavia and French toutefois.

fact.text: From Latin tota via, 'the whole way', which first meant 'always'. Spanish todavia took a different path and now means 'still' or 'yet'.

senses.note: More formal than 'però'. Often used at the start of a sentence.

fact.text: Comes from Latin totus 'whole', the root of English 'total'. The double t comes from the Vulgar Latin variant tottus.

senses.note: Takes the article and agrees with the noun: tutta l'estate = all summer, tutti i giorni = every day.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin tōttus, alteration of Latin tōtus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin totus 'whole', the root of English 'total'. The double t comes from the Vulgar Latin variant tottus.

senses.note: Adjective: tutto il giorno (all day), tutti i libri (all the books). Pronoun: tutto = everything.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin tōttus, alteration of Latin tōtus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin totus 'whole', the root of English 'total'. The double t comes from the Vulgar Latin variant tottus.

senses.note: With a noun it takes the article: tutto il giorno (all day). On its own it means everything: tutto è pronto.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin tōttus, alteration of Latin tōtus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin totus 'whole', the root of English 'total'. The double t comes from the Vulgar Latin variant tottus.

senses.note: Also an adjective: tutto il giorno (all day); tutti i miei antenati (all my ancestors). Tutti = everyone.

etymology: From tutto (“everything”) + fare (“to do”), calque of French (bonne à) tout faire.

fact.text: Literally 'do-everything', copied from French bonne à tout faire. English has a Latin twin with the same meaning: factotum, from fac totum, 'do all'.

senses.note: Invariable: il/la tuttofare, i/le tuttofare. Also used as an adjective: domestica tuttofare.

etymology: Borrowed from French thé, from Dutch thee, from Hokkien 茶 (tê).

fact.text: Came from Hokkien tê, carried by sea by Dutch traders, just like English tea. Its doublet chai went overland from Chinese chá, so tea and chai are really the same word.

senses.note: Written with a grave accent: tè. Invariable: un tè, due tè.
Reflexive and takes essere: si è ubriacato. The adjective ubriaco means drunk.

etymology: From Late Latin ēbriācus, derived from Latin ēbrius, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁egʷʰ- (“to drink”). Cognate with Sicilian mmriacu.

fact.text: Goes back to Latin ebrius 'drunk', the same root as English inebriated and sobriety's opposite, ebriety.

senses.note: Also used as a noun (un ubriaco = a drunk). ubriaco fradicio = blind drunk.

etymology: From Late Latin aucellus m (“little bird”), a diminutive ultimately based on Latin avis f (“bird”), from Proto-Italic *awis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwis. Doublet of augello, which was borrowed from Occitan. Compare Neapolitan auciello, Ligurian öxéllo, Sicilian auceḍḍu.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin aucellus, 'little bird', a diminutive built on Latin avis, 'bird'. Avis is also the root of English aviation and aviary.

senses.note: Also a common vulgar slang word for penis, so watch the context.

etymology: From Old Italian occidere, from Latin occīdō (“to kill, slay”). Compare Romanian ucide.

fact.text: Latin occidere is built on caedere, 'to cut, to kill'. That root is also behind English words ending in -cide, like homicide and pesticide.

senses.note: Irregular past forms: ucciso, uccisi.

etymology: Imitative or onomatopoeia.

senses.note: Shows impatience or boredom. Children often whine it: 'Uffa, che noia!'

etymology: From earlier officio, borrowed from Latin officium (“duty, office”), derived from ops (“wealth, resources”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *h₃ep- (“to work”). Doublet of opificio and officina.

fact.text: Latin officium was a squeezed form of opificium, roughly 'work-doing'. English office comes from the same word, and Italian officina (workshop) is its twin.

senses.note: Ufficio postale = post office. Also used for 'duty, role' in formal language.
Masculine: l'ufficio informazioni. Plural: gli uffici informazioni (informazioni does not change).

etymology: From earlier equale, from Latin aequālis, derived from aequus (“equal, even”).

fact.text: 'Per me è uguale' is an everyday way of saying 'It's all the same to me' or 'I don't mind'.

senses.note: Followed by 'a': uguale a. Also means 'the same' (sono uguali).
An interjection for surprise, disappointment or annoyance.

etymology: Inherited from Latin ulteriōrem.

fact.text: Not English 'ulterior' in the hidden-motive sense: it just means additional or further. An ulterior motive is 'un secondo fine'.

senses.note: Usually goes before the noun: ulteriori informazioni = further information.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ultimus.

fact.text: A learned borrowing from Latin ultimus 'farthest, last', the same word behind English ultimate and ultimatum.

senses.note: Before a noun means last in a series: l'ultimo giorno. For 'last week' use la settimana scorsa.

etymology: Inherited from Latin hūmidus or ūmidus.

senses.note: In cooking, in umido = stewed. As a noun, l'umido is food waste in recycling.

etymology: From Latin hūmōrem. Doublet of humour.

fact.text: Same word as English humour, both from the medieval idea that body fluids (humours) control your temper. In Italian it mainly means mood. Funny humour is umorismo.

senses.note: Essere di buon/cattivo umore means to be in a good/bad mood. 'Sense of humour' is umorismo.

etymology: From uno, from Latin ūnus (“one”).

senses.note: Use uno before s+consonant, z, gn, ps; feminine una, or un' before a vowel.

fact.text: English 'million' was borrowed from Italian milione (via French). The Italian word is mille 'thousand' + the augmentative -one, so it is literally 'a big thousand'.

senses.note: Colloquial. Literally 'a sack of', e.g. 'un sacco di soldi' (loads of money).
Un sacco di is colloquial. Molti/molte agrees with the noun: molti amici, molte idee.
Masc.: un, but uno before s+consonant, z, gn, ps. Fem.: una, but un' before a vowel.

etymology: From Latin ūndecim.
Derived from Latin unguentum (“ointment, unguent”).

fact.text: From Latin unguere, 'to smear, to anoint', which also gave English unguent and unction, as in the 'extreme unction' given to the dying.

senses.note: Also figurative: a remedy or balm.

etymology: From Latin ūnicus, from ūnus; see also -ico.

senses.note: Un'occasione unica = a unique opportunity.
Figlio unico = only child; senso unico = one-way street.

etymology: From Latin ūnitātem.

fact.text: Cognate with English 'unity'. Both derive from Latin unitas, sharing the same root *unus- 'one'. Used in Italian just as in English: unità di misura 'unit of measurement'.

senses.note: Invariable noun; same form in singular and plural.

etymology: Borrowed from Classical Latin ūniversitātem (“the whole” → (Late Latin) “(whole) group; company; corporation” → (Medieval Latin) “university”).

fact.text: Latin universitas meant 'the whole', then any corporation or guild. Medieval universities such as Bologna, the oldest, were guilds of students and teachers.

senses.note: Stress on the final -à; invariable plural: le università.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ūniversus.

fact.text: From Latin universus (uni- 'one' + versus 'turned'), literally 'turned into one', referring to the cosmos as a unified whole.

etymology: Inherited from Latin ūnus, from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos.
Inherited from Latin homō (nominative). The plural reflects Latin hominēs.

fact.text: From Latin homo, 'human being'. The odd plural uomini goes back to Latin homines. The same root gives English homicide and hominid.

senses.note: Irregular plural: l'uomo → gli uomini. L'uomo can also mean mankind.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin (*)ŏvum, from Latin ōvum n.

fact.text: From Latin ovum, 'egg', the root of English 'oval' (egg-shaped), 'ovum' and 'ovulation'.

senses.note: Irregular: masculine in the singular (l'uovo) but feminine in the plural (le uova).

etymology: From Late Latin urgentia. Cognate with Piedmontese urgensa/ürgensa.

senses.note: Con urgenza = urgently. D'urgenza = emergency (e.g. intervento d'urgenza, emergency operation).

etymology: Dissimilation of inherited Latin ululāre (“to howl”), ultimately from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root.

fact.text: From Latin ululāre (to howl), a dissimilation of an original form. Ultimately from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin ūsāre. Cognate with French user.

senses.note: Usare + infinitive can mean 'to be in the habit of' (literary or formal).

etymology:
From older escire, from Latin exīre, from ex + eō (“to go”). The word may have been phonetically influenced by the etymologically unrelated uscio (“door”).
Compare Sicilian nèsciri, Catalan eixir, Romanian ieși, Old Spanish exir and Old French issir.

fact.text: It comes from Latin exire (ex + ire, to go out), which also gave English exit. Its u- may come from the unrelated word uscio, meaning door.

senses.note: Irregular: esco, esci, esce, usciamo, uscite, escono. Uses essere in compound tenses: sono uscito.

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of uscire (“to go out, to exit”). Cognate with Sicilian nisciuta.

senses.note: uscita di sicurezza = emergency exit. From uscire (to go out).

etymology: Inherited from Latin ūsus (“use, employment”), from Proto-Italic *oissos.

senses.note: fare uso di = to make use of; also 'custom': secondo l'uso = according to custom.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin ūtilis.

senses.note: As a noun, l'utile means 'profit' or 'benefit'.

etymology: From utile + -izzare.

senses.note: A bit more formal than the everyday usare.

etymology: Inherited from Latin ūva.

senses.note: Usually treated as singular or mass noun in Italian.

fact.text: Literally 'it goes well', from andare (to go). It's the same va as in 'Come va?' (How's it going?), so one reply to that question is simply 'Va bene!'

senses.note: Used to agree or accept. In a resigned tone it can mean 'whatever' or 'never mind'.

etymology: Borrowed from French vacance, derived from Latin vacantia (“emptiness, leisure”).

fact.text: From Latin vacantia 'emptiness', from vacare 'to be empty': a holiday is time with nothing scheduled. English vacant and vacuum come from the same root.

senses.note: Often plural: le vacanze. Andare in vacanza = to go on holiday. A public holiday is un giorno festivo.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin vagārī (“to ramble, wander, stroll about”).

fact.text: From Latin vagari, from vagus 'wandering', the root of English vague, vagabond and vagrant. A vague idea is one whose meaning wanders.

senses.note: Spelling change before e/i: vaghi, vaghiamo. Everyday Italian prefers girovagare or girare.

fact.text: It's a verb form turned into a noun: 'vaglia' is the subjunctive of valere, 'to be worth', so roughly 'let it be worth (this sum)'.

senses.note: Masculine and invariable: il vaglia, i vaglia. Often 'vaglia postale'.

etymology: Borrowed from French wagon, from English wagon, itself from Dutch wagen.

fact.text: Borrowed from English wagon (possibly via French), which itself came from Dutch wagen. So an Italian train word started in Dutch and passed through English.

senses.note: Vagone letto = sleeping car; vagone ristorante = dining car. Also used for freight wagons.

etymology: Inherited from Latin valēre.

fact.text: From Latin valere 'to be strong, to be worth', the root of English value, valid, valiant and available. Romans even said 'vale' to mean goodbye.

senses.note: Irregular: valgo, valgono, varrò. Ne vale la pena = it's worth it.

etymology:
Borrowed from a language of Northern Italy (cf. Venetan valís, Lombard valiza), from Medieval Latin valesia, valixia, from Late Latin valisia, possibly from Gaulish *valisia (“leather bag”), from Proto-Celtic *wal- (“to enclose, surround”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH-. Or, possibly from Arabic وَلِيهَة (walīha, “large bag”).
Related to French valise and Spanish valija, though it is unclear if either term was borrowed from the other.

fact.text: Related to French valise, which English borrowed as 'valise' for a small travelling bag. It may go back to a Gaulish word for a leather bag, but the origin is uncertain.

senses.note: fare la valigia = to pack (your suitcase). Plural: valigie.

etymology: From Latin vallem, of uncertain origin. Cognate with Sicilian vaḍḍuni.

senses.note: a valle = downhill or downstream (opposite: a monte).

etymology: From Late Latin valōrem, from Latin valeō.

fact.text: From Late Latin valōrem, from valēre (to be worth, to be strong). The root meaning 'to be strong' shifted to 'to have worth', showing how value connects to strength and capability.

etymology: Borrowed from French vampire, from Serbo-Croatian vàmpīr, from Proto-Slavic *ǫpyrь.
Borrowed from Spanish vainilla, a diminutive form of vaina.

fact.text: Spanish vainilla (little pod) entered Italian from the Nahuatl word tlilxochitl, making vanilla's name a journey from Aztec through Spanish to European languages.

etymology: Borrowed from French avantage, with rebracketing.

fact.text: English advantage comes from the same Old French avantage (avant 'before' + -age). Italian dropped the first a- by rebracketing, much as English 'a napron' became 'an apron'.

senses.note: Essere in vantaggio = to be ahead; trarre vantaggio da = to benefit from.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin variābilis.

senses.note: Same form for m/f. Common in forecasts: tempo variabile = changeable weather.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin varius (“diverse, various”), whence also Italian vaio, an inherited doublet.
Probably from a Latin clipping of vāsculum (“small vessel”). Compare with Friulian vascje.

senses.note: In full: vasca da bagno. Also a basin or tank; 'fare le vasche' = to swim lengths.

etymology: From Latin vāsum.

fact.text: Latin vas meant any vessel or container, including blood vessels. Its diminutive vasculum gave English 'vascular'.

senses.note: Also jar or flowerpot; vaso sanguigno = blood vessel.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin veclus, from Latin vetulus.

fact.text: From Latin vetulus, a diminutive of vetus, 'old'. Vetus is also the root of English veteran.

senses.note: Before a noun it can mean long-standing or former: un vecchio amico = an old friend.

etymology: Inherited from Latin vidēre, from Proto-Italic *widēō, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *weyd-.

fact.text: From Latin videre, which gave English video (literally 'I see'), vision and evident. The same Indo-European root *weyd- also produced English wit and wise.

senses.note: Vedersi = to see each other / meet up: ci vediamo! = see you!
Takes essere: 'ci siamo visti'. 'Ci vediamo!' = See you! Also 'to see oneself'.

etymology: From Latin viduus, through a Vulgar Latin *viduvus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin viduus, 'bereft', which shares a very old Indo-European root with English widow. The spider called a black widow is la vedova nera in Italian.

senses.note: As a noun: il vedovo, 'widower'; la vedova, 'widow'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin venēnum. The first /n/ was dissimilated to /l/; a more straightforward descendant would have been *veneno.

fact.text: From Latin venenum, the source of English venom. Italian changed the first n into an l, which is why it isn't 'veneno'.

senses.note: Also figurative: malice, spite (sputare veleno = to spit venom).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin vēlōcem.

fact.text: From Latin velox 'swift', the source of English velocity and the dinosaur name velociraptor, 'swift thief'.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural veloci. Adverb: velocemente.

etymology: From veloce + -mente.

senses.note: Built from veloce + -mente. In everyday speech, people often just say veloce or in fretta.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin vēlōcitātem.

senses.note: Invariable noun; also means velocity, rate, pace, or rapidity.

etymology: Inherited from Latin vēndere (“to sell”).

senses.note: Vendere qualcosa a qualcuno = to sell something to someone; in vendita = for sale.

etymology: Inherited from Latin vindicta (“vengeance”), from vindico (“to claim, to vindicate”), from vindex (“defender”).

fact.text: From Latin vindicta (vengeance), from vindico (to claim, vindicate). Also root of English vindicate; vendetta entered English as a loanword.

etymology: From Latin Veneris diēs, variant of diēs Veneris (“day of Venus”).

fact.text: Means 'day of Venus', from Latin Veneris dies. English Friday is named after Frigg, a Germanic goddess who was treated as the equivalent of Venus.

senses.note: Invariable. Not capitalised. Il venerdì = on Fridays; venerdì = this Friday.

etymology: Inherited from Latin venīre.

fact.text: From Latin venire 'to come', the root of English venue (where people come), advent, convene and event.

senses.note: Irregular (vengo, vieni, viene); takes essere: sono venuto.

etymology: From Late Latin vĭnti, from Latin vīgintī, from Proto-Italic *wīgentī, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wih₁ḱm̥ti, *dwi(h₁)dḱm̥ti.
From venti (“twenty”) + cinque (“five”).
From venti (“twenty”) + due (“two”).
From venti (“twenty”) + due (“two”).
From ventilare + -tore. Cf. English ventilator, Latin ventilator, Piedmontese ventilatur.

senses.note: An electric fan. A handheld fan is il ventaglio; a sports fan is un tifoso.

etymology: From venti (“twenty”) + nove (“nine”).
From venti (“twenty”) + quattro (“four”).
From venti (“twenty”) + sei (“six”).
From venti (“twenty”) + sette (“seven”).
From venti (“twenty”) + tre (“three”).
Inherited from Latin ventus (“wind”), from Proto-Italic *wentos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁n̥ts, from *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).

fact.text: From Latin ventus, from a root meaning 'to blow'. English 'wind' is a Germanic cousin from the same ancient root, and 'vent' and 'ventilate' come straight from the Latin.

senses.note: C'è vento = it's windy. Plural venti, as in i quattro venti.

etymology: From venti (“twenty”) + otto (“eight”).

fact.text: Tens drop their final vowel before uno and otto: venti + uno gives ventuno, and venti + otto gives ventotto. The same happens with trentuno, quarantotto and so on.

senses.note: Before a noun it often shortens: ventun anni (21 years).

fact.text: Tens drop their final vowel before uno and otto: venti + uno gives ventuno, and venti + otto gives ventotto. The same happens with trentuno, quarantotto and so on.

etymology: From vera (“true”, feminine singular) + -mente (“-ly”). Compare among others French vraiment.

senses.note: At the start of a sentence it can soften a reply: 'Veramente, preferirei...' = Actually, I'd rather...

etymology: From Latin verbum (“word, verb”), from Proto-Italic *werðom (“word”), from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰo- (“word”), from root *werh₁- (“to speak, to say”) + extension *-dʰ-.

fact.text: From Latin verbum, which first meant just 'word'. It shares a common ancestor with English word. The grammar meaning 'verb' was copied from Greek rhema.

senses.note: Il Verbo is also 'the Word' in a religious sense (John 1:1).

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin virdis, syncopated from Classical Latin viridis, from vireō. Cognate with English verdure, French vert, and various Romance homonyms.

fact.text: Essere al verde, literally 'to be at the green', is a common idiom meaning to be broke, with no money left.

senses.note: Also means unripe. Same form for masculine and feminine: verde/verdi.

etymology: From verde (“green”) + -ura (“noun-forming suffix”), or from Vulgar Latin *virdūra.

fact.text: It is built on verde, 'green', so it is much like saying 'greens' in English.

senses.note: Often a collective singular: mangia la verdura! = eat your vegetables! Plural le verdure for different kinds.

etymology: From Latin virginem.

fact.text: From Latin virginem, the same root as English 'virgin' and 'virginity'. Both languages directly inherited this Latin word.

senses.note: Can mean untouched, blank (of film, recording)

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *verecunnia, from Latin verēcundia, possibly influenced by cunnus (“vagina”). Doublet of verecondia, which was borrowed. Compare Galician vergoña ~ vergonza, but Portuguese and Occitan vergonha, Sicilian virigogna ~ vrigogna, Spanish vergüenza.

fact.text: From Latin verēcundia, influenced by cunnus ('vagina'). The third sense (private parts) reflects this etymological link and survives mainly in plural.

senses.note: Plural 'vergogne' also used metaphorically.
reflexive verb

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin vēritātem, in this form probably a semi-learned term which was altered based on the Latin etymology. The older, now obsolete forms vertà, vertade, and vertate were inherited.

fact.text: From Latin vēritātem. Italian kept the Latin form rather than inherited the regular vernacular evolution seen in older obsolete forms vertà, vertade.

senses.note: Invariable plural

etymology: From Medieval Latin vernix, from Latin veronix, from Byzantine Greek βερενίκη, βερονίκη (bereníkē, beroníkē, “resin amber”), from Ancient Greek βερενίκιον, βερονίκιον (bereníkion, beroníkion, “soda”), from Βερενίκη (Bereníkē). Cognate with Piedmontese vernis/vërnis.

fact.text: Shares its origin with English 'varnish'. Both go back through Medieval Latin vernix to Greek Berenike, a name usually linked to Berenice, an ancient city in Libya.

senses.note: Also varnish, and patent leather ('scarpe di vernice'). 'Vernice fresca' = wet paint.

etymology: Inherited from Latin vērus (“true”), from Proto-Italic *wēros, from a Proto-Indo-European *weh₁-ros, from *weh₁- (“true”).

fact.text: From Latin verus, 'true', the root of English verify and verdict. Even English 'very' comes from it, through Old French verai, 'true'.

senses.note: Also 'real, genuine'. As a tag question, ..., vero? = ..., right? / isn't it?

etymology: From Latin versāre (“to turn, to twist”).

fact.text: From Latin versare, 'to turn', because you turn a jug over to pour from it. Related English words include 'reverse', 'versatile' and 'conversation'.

senses.note: Also to spill or shed (versare lacrime), and to pay money into an account.

etymology: From Medieval Latin versiōnem.

fact.text: Comes from Medieval Latin versiōnem, ultimately from the Latin verb vertere (to turn), reflecting the idea of a version as a different turning or direction of the original.

etymology: From Latin versus (past participle of vertere). Cognate to French vers (“towards”).

fact.text: Shares a root with English 'verse': Latin vertere, 'to turn'. A line of verse ended where the writer turned, like a plough at a furrow's end. 'Towards' means turned to face something.

senses.note: Also means 'around' a time: 'verso le otto'. With pronouns, use 'di': 'verso di me'.

etymology: From Late Latin verticālis.
From Latin vestīre.

senses.note: Reflexive, takes essere: mi sono vestito/a. 'Vestirsi da' = to dress up as.

etymology: From Latin vestītus.

fact.text: It comes from Latin vestitus, 'clothed', from vestire, 'to dress'. English vest, vestment and invest (originally 'to clothe in an office') share the same root.

senses.note: Can also mean a man's suit. 'Vestito da sera' = evening dress.
With this meaning it's used in the plural: i vestiti.

etymology: From vetro + -ina.

senses.note: Guardare le vetrine = to go window-shopping. Also means a display cabinet.

etymology: From Latin vitrum, from Proto-Italic *wedrom, from Proto-Indo-European *wedro- (“water-like”), derived from the root *wed- (“water”). Cognate with French verre, Portuguese vidro, Spanish vidrio.

fact.text: It comes from Latin vitrum, the source of English 'vitreous'. It may come from a root meaning 'water-like', but that origin is uncertain.

senses.note: Means the material or a pane. A drinking glass is il bicchiere.

etymology: See voi.

senses.note: Vi vedo = I see you (all); vi lavate = you wash yourselves. Comes before the verb.

etymology: From Latin via.

fact.text: Comes from Latin via, 'road', which also gave English via and trivial. Trivial comes from trivium, the place where three roads meet, traditionally where idle chatter happened.

senses.note: Follows verbs: andare via (go away), mandare via (send away). As a noun, via means 'street'.

etymology: From Latin via.

fact.text: Comes from Latin via, 'road', which also gave English via and trivial. Trivial comes from trivium, the place where three roads meet, traditionally where idle chatter happened.

senses.note: Also an adverb, 'away': andare via = to go away; è via = he's away.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French voyagier. By surface analysis, viaggio + -are.

fact.text: Borrowed from Old French voyagier, so it is a cousin of English voyage. Both go back to Latin viaticum, meaning provisions for a journey.

senses.note: Takes avere: ho viaggiato molto. viaggiare in treno = to travel by train.

etymology:
Borrowed from Old Occitan viatge and Old French viage, veiage, from Latin viāticum, from the adjective viāticus, from via (“road, path”) + -āticus (“pertaining to”). By surface analysis, via + -aggio.
Doublet of viatico and cognate to Catalan viatge, French and English voyage, Spanish viaje, Portuguese viagem, Norman viage, Sicilian viaggiu, Maltese vjaġġ, Romanian voiaj.

fact.text: Comes from Latin viaticum, meaning provisions for a journey, from via (road). English got voyage from the same word through Old French.

senses.note: Also travel in general. Fare un viaggio = to take a trip. Buon viaggio! = Have a good trip!

etymology: From via + -ale.

senses.note: A wide, tree-lined street or boulevard.

etymology: From Latin vicem.
Ultimately from Latin vicis (“change, turn”).

fact.text: From Latin vicis, 'change or turn'. Cognate with English 'week'—both derive from Proto-Indo-European *weyk- (to bend, turn), reflecting how weeks and events cycle and recur.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin vēcīnus, from Latin vīcīnus.

fact.text: It comes from Latin vicinus, from vicus, 'village', so a neighbour was first someone from your own village. English 'vicinity' comes from the same root.

senses.note: vicino a = near to. As a noun, il vicino means 'neighbour'.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin vēcīnus, from Latin vīcīnus.

fact.text: It comes from Latin vicinus, from vicus, 'village', so a neighbour was first someone from your own village. English 'vicinity' comes from the same root.

senses.note: Before a noun use 'vicino a': vicino alla stazione. Also an adjective (near) and a noun (neighbour).

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin vēcīnus, from Latin vīcīnus.

fact.text: It comes from Latin vicinus, from vicus, 'village', so a neighbour was first someone from your own village. English 'vicinity' comes from the same root.

senses.note: Feminine: la vicina. As an adjective or adverb, vicino means 'near' or 'close': vicino a casa.

etymology: From Latin vīculus.

senses.note: Masculine. Plural: vicoli. A narrow street or passageway, especially in old towns.

etymology: Borrowed from English video.

fact.text: Borrowed directly from English 'video'. The Italian word was formed in analogy to 'audio', both deriving from Latin roots meaning 'to see' and 'to hear' respectively.

senses.note: Invariable noun; same form in plural.

etymology: From Latin vetāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin vetare, 'to forbid'. English 'veto' is the Latin form veto, 'I forbid', once used by Roman tribunes to block a decision. So when you veto something, you are speaking Latin.

senses.note: vietare qualcosa a qualcuno; vietare di + infinitive. Common on signs: 'vietato fumare' (no smoking).

etymology: Inherited from Latin vigilem.

fact.text: From Latin vigil, 'awake, watchful', so a vigile is literally 'the watchful one'. English vigil and vigilant come from the same Latin root.

senses.note: Short for vigile urbano (local police). Feminine: la vigile. Vigile del fuoco means firefighter.

etymology: From Latin vīlla (“country house”).

fact.text: Latin vīlla, a country estate, also gave English village and villain. A villain was first just a farmhand on a villa, and only later a scoundrel.

senses.note: Can also mean a large public park on an old estate, e.g. Villa Borghese in Rome.

etymology: From Old French village. Cognate with Piedmontese vilagi.

senses.note: villaggio turistico = holiday resort.

etymology: Inherited from Latin vincere, from Proto-Italic *winkō, from Proto-Indo-European *wi-n-k-, from *weyk- (“to overcome”) with a nasal infix.

fact.text: It comes from Latin vincere, the same root behind English victory, vanquish, convince and invincible.

senses.note: Irregular past participle: vinto (ho vinto = I won). Also 'to defeat, to overcome'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin vīnum, from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wéyh₁nom, derived from *wéyh₁ō (“vine, wine”). Cognates include Albanian verë, Armenian գինի (gini) and Greek οίνος (oínos).

fact.text: It comes from Latin vinum, which early Germanic peoples borrowed to give English wine. Greek oinos, the source of oenology (the study of wine), goes back to the same ancient root.

senses.note: Vino rosso / bianco = red / white wine. Il vino della casa = house wine.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin viola.

fact.text: Purple is considered unlucky in Italian theatre. A traditional explanation is that it is the colour of Lent, when shows were once banned and actors went unpaid.

senses.note: Invariable: una gonna viola, due gonne viola.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin violentia.

senses.note: It can also mean a violinist: il primo violino is the first violin, or concertmaster.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin virgula. Doublet of vergola, which was inherited.

fact.text: From Latin virgula, 'little twig', from virga, 'branch'. The punctuation mark got this name because it looks like a tiny twig.

senses.note: Italian also uses it as the decimal point: 3,5 is read 'tre virgola cinque'.

fact.text: From Latin virgula, meaning 'small rod' or 'twig'. The term refers to the comma-like marks used to set off quoted text—originally suggesting small strokes or lines in the margin.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin vīrus.
From Latin vīsiōnem.
Deverbal from visitare (“to visit”) + -a.
From Latin vīsitāre (“to see, to visit”), frequentative of visō.

senses.note: For friends, andare a trovare is more common. A doctor visita a patient, meaning examines them.

etymology: Inherited from Latin vīsus.

fact.text: From Latin vīsus (appearance, sight), the past participle of vidēre (to see) — the same root gives English 'vision' and 'visit'.

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of vedere (“to see”).

fact.text: Formed from the feminine past participle of vedere, 'to see', so it is literally 'something seen'. English borrowed it directly as 'vista', a sweeping view.

senses.note: Also eyesight: avere la vista buona. A prima vista = at first sight.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vīsitus, from Latin vīsus, or from a form *vīditus.

fact.text: Literally means 'seen'. A visa is a document that officials have seen and approved. English 'visa' has the same idea, from Latin charta visa, 'paper that has been seen'.

senses.note: Also the past participle of vedere ('seen'). Visto per l'Italia = visa for Italy.

etymology: From visualizzare + -zione.

senses.note: Internet/social media term for a single viewing of video content

etymology: From Latin vīta, from Proto-Italic *gʷītā, possibly a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wo-teh₂, from the root *gʷeyh₃- (“to live”).

fact.text: From Latin vita 'life', which also gave English vital, and vitamin, coined in 1912 from vita + amine. In clothing, though, vita means waist.

senses.note: Also means waist (giro vita = waist size). Plural vite.

etymology: From Latin vitellus. Compare Romanian vițel, French veau, Catalan vedella .

fact.text: From Latin vitellus (a bull calf). Related to English vitals and vital. French veau, Spanish ternera, and Portuguese vitela share the same Latin origin.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin victima.

fact.text: This noun is always grammatically feminine, whoever it refers to. A man who is a victim is still 'la vittima', and adjectives agree in the feminine: la vittima è stata ferita.

senses.note: Always feminine, even for a man: lui è la vittima.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin victōria, from vincere.
From Latin vīvere, from Proto-Italic *gʷīwō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷíh₃weti (“to live, be alive”).

fact.text: Its Indo-European root also gave English 'quick', which originally meant 'alive', as in 'the quick and the dead'. Latin vivere also gave English 'vivid' and 'survive'.

senses.note: Irregular past participle: vissuto. Takes essere or avere.

etymology: From Latin vīvus (“alive”, “living”), from Proto-Italic *gʷīwos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós (“alive”).

senses.note: dal vivo = live (a performance or broadcast).

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin vōcālis (“vowel”).

fact.text: Gender changes the meaning: la vocale is a vowel, while il vocale is everyday slang for a voice message (short for messaggio vocale), as in 'ti mando un vocale'.

senses.note: In the 'vowel' sense the noun is feminine: la vocale, le vocali.

etymology: Inherited from Latin vōx, vōcem.

fact.text: English borrowed sotto voce, 'under the voice', from Italian for speaking quietly. The Latin root vox also gives English voice, vocal and vocabulary.

senses.note: Ad alta voce = aloud. Also means a dictionary entry or a rumour (corre voce).

etymology: Borrowed from Russian во́дка (vódka), diminutive of вода́ (vodá, “water”).

fact.text: Vodka comes from Russian vódka, a diminutive of vodá meaning water, revealing the drink's humble linguistic origins.

etymology: From Latin volō through a Vulgar Latin root *volia, or from voglio. Cf. also Romanian voie from root *volia

fact.text: The same word also means birthmark. An old folk belief held that a pregnant mother's unsatisfied craving left a mark on her baby, often shaped like the food she wanted.

senses.note: avere voglia di = to feel like; non ne ho voglia = I don't feel like it.

etymology:
From Latin vōs, from Old Latin vōs, from Proto-Italic *wōs, ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *yúHs.
Cognates with the same usage are the French vous and the Russian вы (vy).

fact.text: In 1938 the Fascist regime campaigned to replace the polite Lei with voi, calling Lei foreign and servile. The rule disappeared after the war.

senses.note: Plural 'you'. In older or southern usage it can be a polite form for one person.

fact.text: A French borrowing: literally vois là, 'see there!' Italian's own equivalent is ecco.

senses.note: Borrowed from French, used as in English. Often written without the accent.

etymology: Inherited from Latin volāre, from Proto-Italic *gʷelāō.

fact.text: Domenico Modugno's 1958 hit 'Nel blu dipinto di blu', known everywhere as 'Volare', won Sanremo and then Record and Song of the Year at the very first Grammy Awards.

senses.note: Usually takes avere (ho volato). Use essere for things flying off: è volato via.

etymology: From Old French volentiers, from Latin voluntāriē, from the adjective voluntārius.

senses.note: 'Volentieri!' on its own means 'I'd love to!' when you accept an invitation.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin volēre, regularized from Latin velle.

fact.text: Shares its Latin root (volo, 'I want') with English volition, voluntary and benevolent, which literally means 'wishing well'.

senses.note: Irregular: voglio, vuoi, vuole, vogliamo, volete, vogliono. Vorrei (I would like) is the polite form.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin volēre, regularized from Latin velle.

fact.text: Shares its Latin root (volo, 'I want') with English volition, voluntary and benevolent, which literally means 'wishing well'.

senses.note: Irregular. Vorrei (I would like) is the polite way to ask for things.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin vulgārem.

fact.text: Il volgare was the everyday spoken language, as opposed to Latin. Dante wrote the Divine Comedy in Florentine volgare and defended it in De vulgari eloquentia.

senses.note: Crude or coarse. It can also mean common or vernacular: il volgare = the vernacular language.

etymology: From volare (“to fly”).

fact.text: From Latin volare, meaning 'to fly'. The same root appears in English 'volatile' and 'volley'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin voluntātem.

fact.text: From Latin voluntatem, derived from the present participle stem *welont- plus the nominalization suffix -(t)ās. Related to volens (willing).

senses.note: Invariable feminine noun. Also used for 'testament': testamento della volontà.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *volta, from *volŭta (perhaps via *volvita (“a turn”)), from Latin volūta, feminine of volūtus, perfect passive participle of volvō. Also possibly from the past participle of volgere (volto), or from the verb voltare. Compare Spanish vuelta; cf. also Spanish bóveda, French voûte. Cognate with Sicilian vota.

fact.text: Comes from Latin volvere, 'to turn'. English 'volte-face' (a complete U-turn in opinion) traces back to Italian voltafaccia, 'turn face'.

senses.note: Una volta = once; due volte = twice; questa volta = this time. For time as duration, use 'tempo'.

etymology: From Latin vultus (“expression, face”). Compare Portuguese vulto (“aspect”).

fact.text: From Latin vultus (face, expression). Cognate with Welsh gweld (to see). The sense of 'face' originally meant 'expression' or 'appearance'.

senses.note: literary/poetic for face or expression

etymology: From Latin vomitāre.

senses.note: Belongs to voi. Usually with an article: il vostro, la vostra, i vostri, le vostre.

etymology: Inherited from Latin vostrum, which is the accusative of voster, which derives from the older form vester, from Proto-Italic *westeros.

senses.note: Agrees with the noun: vostro, vostra, vostri, vostre. Usually takes the article: il vostro libro.

etymology: Derived from Latin vōtum, from voveō. Compare Spanish and Portuguese votar, French vouer.

fact.text: From Latin votum 'vow', from vovere 'to vow'. English vote, vow and devote share this root, and the Italian verb can still mean 'to vow' or 'to dedicate'.

senses.note: Votare per / a favore di = to vote for; votare contro = to vote against. Auxiliary: avere.

etymology: From Latin vōtum.

fact.text: From Latin vōtum ('vow, wish'). The sense evolved from 'vow' to 'wish' to 'formal expression of will' (voting), showing how meaning shifted with democratic practice.

senses.note: Also means 'mark, grade' in academic context.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vocitum.

fact.text: English 'void' has the same source: Vulgar Latin *vocitus, which became Old French vuide and then English void.

senses.note: As a noun, il vuoto = emptiness, void, vacuum. Sottovuoto = vacuum-packed.

etymology: Borrowed from French water, and this a pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of French water-closet.

fact.text: False friend: it means the toilet, not water. It's short for 'water-closet', came into Italian through French, and is usually pronounced 'VAH-ter'.

senses.note: Means the toilet bowl, never water (that's acqua). Usually said 'vater'. Same form in the plural.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English weekend.

senses.note: Invariable masculine noun; unadapted English borrowing.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English west.

senses.note: An English loanword used just as in English. Native options: Caspita! Accidenti!

etymology: Internationalism, ultimately from Sanskrit योग (yoga, “yoking, union”). Near-doublet of giogo (“yoke”).

fact.text: From Sanskrit yoga (yoking, union). 'Yoga' is a near-doublet of giogo (yoke) in Italian—both mean joining or yoking together.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Ottoman Turkish یوغورت (yoğurt).

fact.text: From Ottoman Turkish yoğurt. Italian borrowed it unchanged, like most European languages. The word traveled westward with the food itself from the Eastern Mediterranean.

senses.note: Invariable masculine noun; also spelled yogurt.

etymology: From Lombardic zeina (“basket”). Doublet of zana (“basket”).

fact.text: Comes from the language of the Lombards, Germanic invaders of Italy, where zeina meant 'basket'. Its doublet zana still means basket or cradle.

senses.note: Takes lo (lo zaino, gli zaini) because it starts with z.

etymology: Borrowed from Arabic سِكَّة (sikka, “die for coining, coin”).

fact.text: It comes from Arabic sikka, a die for striking coins. Nuovo di zecca means 'brand new', literally fresh from the mint, much like English 'in mint condition'.

senses.note: Nuovo di zecca = brand new. A separate word zecca also means tick (the parasite).

etymology: Derived from New Latin zerum, from Medieval Latin zephirum, from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “nothing”, “cipher”). Doublet of cifra.

fact.text: It comes from Arabic ṣifr, 'nothing', by way of Medieval Latin. The same Arabic word also gave Italian cifra and English 'cipher', so zero and cipher are twins.

senses.note: Also 'nil' in scores: due a zero = two-nil.

etymology: Derived from New Latin zerum, from Medieval Latin zephirum, from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “nothing”, “cipher”). Doublet of cifra.

fact.text: It comes from Arabic ṣifr, 'nothing', by way of Medieval Latin. The same Arabic word also gave Italian cifra and English 'cipher', so zero and cipher are twins.

etymology: From Late Latin thia, from Ancient Greek θεία (theía).

fact.text: Unusually for a family word, it comes from Greek: theia (aunt), via Late Latin thia. Spanish tía and Portuguese tia come from the same source.

senses.note: Uncle is zio. Possessives with a singular family member take no article: mia zia.

fact.text: Unlike most Italian family words, it comes from Greek: Late Latin thius, from Greek theios 'uncle'. Spanish tío shares the same origin.

senses.note: Plural of zio. Also means aunt and uncle together: i miei zii.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin thius, from Ancient Greek θεῖος (theîos). Compare Spanish tío, Portuguese tio, Sicilian ziu, Sardinian tiu or tziu, Venetan sio.

fact.text: Comes from Greek theîos 'uncle' through Late Latin thius, not from a native Latin word. Spanish tío and Portuguese tio come from the same Greek source.

senses.note: Takes lo: lo zio, gli zii. Aunt = zia. In slang, zio can also mean 'dude' or 'mate'.

etymology: From Latin zōna.

fact.text: From Latin zōna, which originally meant a belt or girdle. The sense of a geographical area developed from the idea of a bounded region.

etymology: From Late Latin cucutia (via metathesis and apheresis), from Latin cucurbita (“gourd”). Doublet of cocuzza and cucurbita.

fact.text: From Late Latin cucutia (via metathesis), which comes from Latin cucurbita. The word underwent sound changes over centuries before arriving at modern zucca.

senses.note: Also: squash, marrow.

etymology: From Late Latin suppa, borrowed from Proto-Germanic *supô, *suppa (“slice of soaked bread; soup”) (whence English soup).

fact.text: Comes from a Germanic word for bread soaked in broth, which also gave English soup and sop. Zuppa inglese, 'English soup', is a trifle-like dessert.

senses.note: Usually a thick soup, often with bread. Thinner soups are minestra or brodo.
